Around 1050 Boniface III of Tuscany occupied the duchy and ceded it to his daughter Matilda, who donated it to the Papal States. After the year 1000, however, it had become an independent commune. The troops of Manfred of Sicily destroyed it in 1256 and killed much of its population. Gentile Da Varano, one of the refugees who returned in 1262, founded a fiefdom for his family that lasted three centuries.

In 1382 Giovanni da Varano built a wall 12 kilometres long to defend the city, and Giulio Cesare Da Varano built a Ducal Palace, now one of the most important Renaissance buildings in central Italy. Giulio Cesare's daughter Camilla Battista da Varano was canonised in 2010. Cesare Borgia nearly extinguished the family in 1502. The university was founded in 1336, was recognised by the Kingdom of Italy in 1861 and became the public University of Camerino in 1958.

Camerino is a town in the province of Macerata in Marche. Its Ducal Palace is the seat of the university's Faculty of Jurisprudence. Its cathedral was rebuilt in the early 19th century, and the Porta Malatestiana dates from 1511.
cameroon: Cameroon covers 475,442 square kilometres in Central and West Africa, on the Bight of Bonny, part of the Gulf of Guinea. It is often called Africa in miniature because it has the coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna of the continent. The country divides into five major geographic zones, among them a hot and humid coastal plain and the South Cameroon Plateau, covered by equatorial rainforest.

A chain of mountains, hills and plateaus, the Cameroon range, runs from Mount Cameroon on the coast, the highest point at 4,095 metres, almost to Lake Chad in the north. Volcanism there has created crater lakes. On 21 August 1986 one of them, Lake Nyos, released carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.

Excavations at Shum Laka in the Northwest Region show human occupation dating back 30,000 years. The Baka are counted among the longest continuous inhabitants, and Bantu migrations into eastern, southern and central Africa are believed to have begun from this area about 2,000 years ago. The Sao culture arose around Lake Chad about 500 CE and gave way to Kanem and its successor, the Bornu Empire, while kingdoms, fondoms and chiefdoms arose in the west. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1472 and named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, the Shrimp River, after the ghost shrimp they found there. In 1896 Sultan Ibrahim Njoya created the Bamum script for the Bamum language.

Germany built a warehouse on the Wouri estuary in 1868, and in 1884 the German Empire claimed the territory as the colony of Kamerun after Gustav Nachtigal made a treaty with a local king. The people resisted in the Bafut Wars and Adamawa Wars. Commercial companies ran local administration and used forced labour on banana, rubber, palm oil and cocoa plantations, a policy criticised by other colonial powers. After World War I the territory was divided between France and the United Kingdom as League of Nations mandates. The French-administered part became independent as the Republic of Cameroun in 1960 under Ahmadou Ahidjo, and the southern part of British Cameroons federated with it in 1961.

Yaoundé is the capital and Douala, the economic capital and main seaport, is among the largest cities. Cameroon is a unitary presidential republic. Its official languages are French and English, and its people speak some 250 native languages. Christianity is the majority religion, with significant minorities practising Islam and traditional faiths. Cameroon is a member of the African Union, the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
camille-pissarro: Jacob Abraham Camille Pissarro was born on 10 July 1830 at Charlotte Amalie to Frederick Abraham Gabriel Pissarro, a merchant of Portuguese Jewish descent who held French nationality, and Rachel Manzano-Pomié. His father's marriage to his late uncle's widow caused a stir in the small Jewish community, and the four children were sent to an all-black primary school. In 1855, at 25, Camille moved to Paris and worked as an assistant to the painter Anton Melbye. He found the teaching at the École des Beaux-Arts and the Académie Suisse stifling and asked Corot for instruction instead.

His first painting was accepted by the Paris Salon in 1859. Corot inspired him to paint outdoors, and at the Académie Suisse he met Claude Monet, Armand Guillaumin and Paul Cézanne, who shared his dissatisfaction with the Salon. During the Franco-Prussian War he moved his family to Norwood near London, since he had only Danish nationality. Of the 1,500 paintings he left in France, only 40 remained, since soldiers had used many as floor mats. In 1871 he married Julie Vellay, with whom he had seven children, six of them painters. The family settled at Éragny-sur-Epte in April 1884.

The first Impressionist exhibition, in 1874, shocked critics, who found the subjects vulgar and the brushwork sketchy. Pissarro showed five landscapes, and Émile Zola praised them. In 1885 he met Georges Seurat and Paul Signac and for about three years used their method of small dabs of pure colour, showing such works in 1886 at the eighth exhibition. By the end of the 1880s he found the method too restrictive, but kept a stronger attention to colour. He was also drawn to anarchist circles, and in 1889 made an album of thirty drawings, Turpitudes sociales.

In 1892 Monet helped Pissarro and Julie buy the Éragny house, and in 1893 Pissarro converted the barn into a studio. In old age a recurring eye infection kept him from working outdoors except in warm weather, so he painted from hotel windows in Rouen, Paris, Le Havre, Dieppe and London. He died in Paris on 13 November 1903, aged 73, of sepsis, and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery. The art historian Diane Kelder wrote that no member of the Impressionist group did more to mediate the disputes that threatened to break it apart. Cézanne said that Pissarro had been a father for him.
camille-saint-saens: Saint-Saëns was born in Paris, the only child of Jacques-Joseph-Victor Saint-Saëns, an official in the French Ministry of the Interior, and Françoise-Clémence, née Collin. Less than two months after the christening his father died of consumption. The boy was taken to the country for his health and lived for two years with a nurse at Corbeil, 29 kilometres south of Paris. He always considered himself a true Parisian.

On leaving the Conservatoire in 1853, Saint-Saëns became organist at Saint-Merri, where weddings and funerals gave him a comfortable income and spare time to compose. In 1861 he took his only teaching post, at the École Niedermeyer, in charge of piano studies. He scandalised some austere colleagues by introducing his students to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, and Gabriel Fauré remembered the lessons with lasting gratitude.

In 1870, with Romain Bussine, he discussed a society to promote new French music. He served in the National Guard in the Franco-Prussian War. The Société Nationale de Musique, with the motto Ars Gallica, was founded in February 1871, with Bussine as president and Saint-Saëns as vice-president. He was elected to the Institut de France in 1881, and in 1906 and 1909 he made successful tours of the United States as pianist and conductor.

Saint-Saëns was the first major French composer to write piano concertos. The Second, in G minor (1868), became one of his most popular works, and the pianist Zygmunt Stojowski said it begins like Bach and ends like Offenbach. The Fifth, the Egyptian concerto of 1896, was written while he was wintering in Luxor. His Third Symphony has prominent parts for piano and organ and is dedicated to the memory of Liszt.

He wrote twelve operas. Henry VIII became a repertory piece in his lifetime, but since his death only Samson et Dalila has been regularly staged. He composed more than 140 mélodies and set Victor Hugo most often. Committed to the structures of earlier French composers, he came into conflict in later years with the impressionist and expressionist schools.
camillo-benso-count-of-cavour: Camillo Benso was born in Turin on 10 August 1810, during Napoleonic rule, into a family that had acquired estates during the French occupation. His godparents were Napoleon's sister Pauline and her husband, Prince Camillo Borghese. He joined the Engineer Corps of the Royal Sardinian Army in 1827. Reading Jeremy Bentham and Benjamin Constant made him a liberal and a suspect to the police, and he resigned his commission in November 1831. He managed the family estate at Grinzane and served as its mayor until 1848, held that economic progress had to come before political change, and backed railways and canals.

The Revolutions of 1848 let him enter politics, and he founded the newspaper Il Risorgimento. After the Piedmontese defeat at Novara and the abdication of Charles Albert in favour of Victor Emmanuel II, he became minister of agriculture, commerce and the navy in 1850 and of finance in 1851. His railway programme gave Piedmont 800 kilometres of track by 1860. With Urbano Rattazzi he formed a coalition that brought down Massimo d'Azeglio's cabinet in November 1852, and he became prime minister. His methods included heavy use of emergency powers and rigging elections, and the national debt rose sixfold. Piedmont joined the Crimean War on 10 January 1855, which earned it a place at the Congress of Paris.

At Plombières in July 1858 Cavour agreed with Napoleon III that France would help Piedmont fight Austria in return for Savoy and Nice. After Magenta and Solferino Napoleon signed the Armistice of Villafranca on 11 July 1859, and Cavour resigned in fury. Recalled on 20 January 1860, he ceded Savoy and Nice to France to annex Tuscany and Emilia. Garibaldi's thousand volunteers landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860 and conquered Sicily and then Naples. Cavour invaded Umbria and Marche to stop them marching on Rome, and Garibaldi handed the south to the king.

In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II declared the Kingdom of Italy and Cavour became its first prime minister. He held that Rome should be the seat of a free church in a free state. Exhausted, he fell ill, presumably with malaria, and was bled several times. He died on 6 June 1861 and was buried at Santena. Venice joined Italy in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Cavour had at first aimed to expand Piedmont rather than to unite Italy, but by his death the state was five times its earlier size and ranked among Europe's great powers.
camino-de-santiago: The Camino de Santiago is a network of pilgrim routes leading to the shrine of the apostle James in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, where tradition holds that his remains are buried. The main route follows an earlier Roman trade road that continues to Cape Finisterre on the Atlantic coast, which the Romans called Finisterrae, the end of the world. Pilgrims can take one of dozens of routes, and traditionally the way begins at one's own home. The Camino Francés, the French Way, is the most popular, and the Via Regia forms its last portion.

The Way was established in the early 9th century after the discovery of the relics of Saint James the Great, and the earliest records of visits to the shrine come from the time of the Kingdom of Asturias and Galicia. The earliest recorded pilgrims from beyond the Pyrenees came in the mid-11th century, and by the early 12th century the pilgrimage was highly organised.

Pope Callixtus II promoted it and began the Compostelan Holy Years. The Codex Calixtinus, published around 1140, served as the guide: four routes from France met at Puente la Reina, and from there a defined road crossed northern Spain through Burgos, León and Astorga.

Hospitals along the route met the pilgrims' needs, and contributed to the modern idea of the hospital. Romanesque churches with massive arches were built for the crowds, and pilgrims took home a Galician scallop shell as proof of completion, which became the badge of the pilgrim. The Church also imposed the pilgrimage as penance for grave sins. The Black Death, the Reformation and political unrest in the 16th century brought a decline, though in 1779 John Adams followed part of the route in reverse on his way to Paris. Few modern pilgrimages predate the 1957 publication of Walter Starkie's The Road to Santiago.

Whenever St James's Day, 25 July, falls on a Sunday, the cathedral declares a Holy Year. In 1987 the Camino was named the first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe, and the French Way and the Northern routes in Spain were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, followed by the routes in France in 1998. Pilgrims come mostly on foot, some by bicycle or horse, and many walk the final 100 kilometres to earn the Compostela certificate.
campania: Campania lies in the south-west of the Italian Peninsula, with a coastline of about 500 km on the Tyrrhenian Sea. It also includes the Phlegraean Islands of Ischia, Procida, Vivara and Nisida, and the island of Capri. The mountainous interior is broken into several massifs, while close to the coast stand the volcanic massifs of Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei. The Romans knew the region as Campania felix, the fertile or happy countryside.

From the beginning of the 1st millennium BCE the interior was inhabited by Oscan-speaking Italic tribes, among them the Osci, Samnites, Sidicini, Hirpini and the Campanians, after whom the region is named, and by Etruscans. Between the 8th and 7th centuries BCE its coastal areas were colonised by the Greeks of Magna Graecia. Capua was then the leading city, while Naples was predominantly Greek-speaking.

By the end of the 4th century BCE Campania was a full part of the Roman Republic, valued for its pastures and rich countryside. Naples made it a centre of Hellenistic culture for the Romans. In 275 BCE the Romans under the consul Curius Dentatus won the Battle of Beneventum in the Samnite city of Maleventum, which they renamed Beneventum. During the Second Punic War, in 216 BCE, Capua allied with Carthage and was cut off from the rest of Campania, which stayed loyal to Rome; Naples resisted Hannibal behind its walls.

In the Middle Ages the area held many duchies and principalities, in the hands of the Byzantine Empire and the Lombards. The Normans brought the smaller states together within the Kingdom of Sicily. The kingdom then passed to the Hohenstaufen, and Frederick II founded the University of Naples, making the city the intellectual centre of the kingdom. In 1266 Pope Innocent IV crowned the Angevin duke Charles I as king, and Charles moved the capital from Palermo to Naples. In September 1943 Salerno was the scene of Operation Avalanche, and from February to July 1944 it was the temporary capital of the Kingdom of Italy.

Campania is an administrative region of Italy with Naples as its capital and more than five million people. It has ten of Italy's UNESCO sites, including Pompeii, Herculaneum, the Royal Palace of Caserta, the Amalfi Coast, the Longobardian Church of Santa Sofia in Benevento and the historic centre of Naples. Other ancient sites include Oplontis, Paestum, Stabiae and Velia. Its agriculture is known for tomatoes, nuts and the buffalo milk used for mozzarella di bufala.
campeche: Campeche lies in southeast Mexico, bordered by Tabasco, Yucatán and Quintana Roo, by the Petén department of Guatemala to the south and the Orange Walk District of Belize, with 523 kilometres of shoreline on the Gulf of Mexico. The name derives from Can Pech, the Maya name of a chiefdom of the southwestern Yucatán Peninsula at the time the Spanish arrived; its capital, Ah-Kin-Pech, stood where the city of Campeche is now. The native name means place of snakes and ticks.

The Maya were the first people to dominate the area, and their main cities were Edzná, Xtampak and later Calakmul and Becán. The civilization reached its height between 600 and 900 CE, and from about 1000 the cities were abandoned for unknown reasons. In 1517 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba and Antón de Alaminos landed at Can-Pech and renamed it San Lázaro. At Champotón Hernández de Córdoba was attacked and died of his wounds, so the Spanish called the bay the Bay of the Bad Fight. The conquest of the peninsula began in earnest in 1540 under Francisco de Montejo, father and son, and the capital was founded that year.

The city was a rich port during the colonial period and suffered more than 21 major pirate attacks. After the sack of 1685 by English and French buccaneers, who plundered the surroundings for two months, fortifications were begun that took 24 years to complete: a wall with four main gates, three to the land and one to the sea, and forts including San Carlos, Santa Rosa, San Juan and San Francisco. Only one pirate, Barbillas, found a way in, in 1708. After Mexican independence the city declined, and Campeche split from the province of Yucatán in the mid-19th century, mostly because of political friction with Mérida.

Campeche is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the 32 federal entities of Mexico, and has thirteen municipalities. Much of its territory is filled with archaeological sites, almost all Maya, among them Calakmul, Edzná, Becán, Chicanná and Río Bec. The Calakmul Biosphere Reserve was created in 1989. The historic buildings of the capital, formally San Francisco de Campeche, are protected by decree.
campi-flegrei: The Phlegraean Fields are a large volcanic caldera west of Naples, part of the Campanian volcanic arc, which also includes Mount Vesuvius. The caldera area consists of 24 craters and volcanic edifices, most of them under the Gulf of Naples. Part of the city of Naples is built over it, and the area also takes in Pozzuoli, Bacoli, Ischia and Procida. The Solfatara crater has steaming fumaroles and many pools of boiling mud, and was believed in ancient Rome to be the home of Vulcan, the god of fire. Lake Avernus fills one of the tuff craters.

Geologists distinguish three phases. In the first, about 39,280 years ago, the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption, rated VEI 7, spread ash across a large part of eastern Europe; one theory holds that it contributed to the extinction of the Neanderthals. The second period, 35,000 to 10,500 years ago, produced the Neapolitan yellow tuff, with Pozzuoli at its centre; the last major eruption came about 12,000 years ago. The third, from 8,000 to 500 years ago, formed Lake Avernus and Monte Nuovo, which an eight-day eruption built as a new hill in 1538.

The ground rises and falls slowly, a process called bradyseism, most evident at the Macellum of Pozzuoli, where bands of holes bored by marine molluscs in marble columns show that the level of the site against the sea has varied. Between 1982 and 1986 an uplift raised the ground by 1.8 metres.

The ancient Greeks had a colony at Cumae, seat of the Cumaean Sibyl. Lake Avernus was believed to be an entrance to the underworld and is portrayed so in Virgil's Aeneid. Baiae was a fashionable coastal resort with summer villas of Julius Caesar, Nero and Hadrian, who died there.

Pozzuoli has the Flavian Amphitheatre, the third largest in Italy, and Baiae, now partly submerged, had the largest ancient dome before the Pantheon. Quarries of piperno stone supplied much of the building stone of Naples from Roman times to the early 20th century. The tombs of Agrippina the Elder and Scipio Africanus lie in the area. In 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences listed the site among 100 geological heritage sites, for its part in the development of volcanology in the 18th and 19th centuries.
canaan: Canaan was an ancient Semitic-speaking civilization and region of the southern Levant in the late 2nd millennium BCE. Egyptian texts of that millennium use the name for an Egyptian-ruled colony whose boundaries broadly match those of the Hebrew Bible: the Mediterranean Sea to the west, the vicinity of Hamath in Syria to the north, the Jordan Valley to the east and a line from the Dead Sea to around Gaza to the south. The Egyptians also called the Levantine coast Retjenu, and the region between Ascalon and the Lebanon, inland to the Sea of Galilee, Djahy.

The name appears as Kinâḫna in the Amarna letters of the 14th century BCE. Its origin is uncertain; one early explanation derives it from a Semitic root meaning to be low or subjugated. The Akkadian word kinahhu referred to purple-dyed wool, a key export, and the Greeks may have taken the name Phoenikes for the Canaanites from their word for crimson or purple.

Scholars use several periodizations. Metalworking Ghassulian settlers entered Canaan around 4500 BCE, at the start of the Chalcolithic. In the Early Bronze Age Ebla was incorporated by about 2300 BCE into the Akkadian Empire of Sargon the Great and Naram-Sin. In the Middle Bronze Age, from 2000 to 1550 BCE, urbanism returned and the region was divided among small city-states, of which Hazor seems to have been the most important, within a wide international trading network.

In the early Late Bronze Age, Canaanite confederacies centred on Megiddo and Kadesh were fully brought into the Egyptian and Hittite empires. By the Early Iron Age the southern Levant was dominated by the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the Philistine city-states, and Moab, Ammon, Aram-Damascus and Edom. The Neo-Assyrian Empire conquered the whole region in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE and held it for three hundred years.

The name Canaanites is attested many centuries later as the endonym of the people the Greeks called Phoenicians from about 500 BCE, and the Punics of North Africa used a form of it of themselves. In the Hebrew Bible Canaan and the Canaanites appear some 160 times, and Canaan is the land of the Promised Land. The biblical scholar Mark Smith, citing archaeology, holds that Israelite culture largely overlapped with and derived from Canaanite culture.
canada: Canada is the second-largest country by total area, encompassing 9,984,670 square kilometres, and has the world's longest coastline, of 243,042 kilometres. It shares the world's largest land border with the United States, spanning 8,891 kilometres. The country has seven physiographic regions, among them the Canadian Shield, the Interior Plains and the Western Cordillera. It has over 2,000,000 lakes, and boreal forests prevail throughout. Canadian Forces Station Alert, on the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost settlement.

Indigenous peoples have continuously inhabited what is now Canada for thousands of years, and they include the First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Their population at the time of the first European settlements is estimated at between 200,000 and 2 million, and it declined by 40 to 80 percent as a consequence of colonization, through European diseases, conflicts over the fur trade, conflicts with colonial authorities and settlers, and the loss of land.

British and French expeditions explored and later settled along the Atlantic coast from the 16th century, and France ceded nearly all of its colonies in North America in 1763. Early interactions were relatively peaceful, but friendship and peace treaties gave way to the dispossession of Indigenous lands.

Canada was formed in 1867 through Confederation as a federal dominion of four provinces. Settler colonialism peaked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the government funded Indian residential schools administered by Christian churches. These are considered part of a genocide of Indigenous peoples because of their forced assimilation and the large-scale removal of children from their families. A reconciliation commission was formed in 2008. Autonomy from the United Kingdom grew through the Statute of Westminster, 1931, and the Canada Act 1982 severed the remaining legal dependence.

Canada has ten provinces and three territories, with Ottawa as the capital and Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver as the three largest metropolitan areas. It is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, and it is officially bilingual in English and French in the federal jurisdiction. The 2021 census enumerated 36,991,981 people, and the population is estimated to have passed 40,000,000 in 2023. About 80 percent live within 150 kilometres of the border with the contiguous United States. Multiculturalism is official state policy.
canal-du-midi: A canal between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean was an old idea. Leaders including Augustus, Nero, Charlemagne, François I, Charles IX and Henry IV are said to have dreamed of it. In 1516 François I brought Leonardo da Vinci to France and commissioned a survey of a route from the Garonne at Toulouse to the Aude at Carcassonne. Such a waterway would spare ships and goods a voyage around the Iberian Peninsula that could take a month and carried the danger of piracy.

Royal authority for the work came in October 1666, when Jean-Baptiste Colbert authorised it by edict after a committee of experts had studied the route for several months. Colbert believed that trade favoured the Dutch rather than the kingdom, and grain prices and wine production had fallen. The edict gave the work to its designer, Pierre-Paul Riquet, and his descendants, with rights of expropriation, a tax-exempt fief and the right to levy tolls.

The canal is about 240 km long. It was first called the Canal Royal en Languedoc and was renamed the Canal du Midi in 1789. It climbs from Toulouse over 52 km to the Seuil de Naurouze, its summit level at 189.43 m, and then descends 188 km to Les Onglous on the Étang de Thau. The central difficulty was bringing water from the Montagne Noire to the summit. Riquet sent François Andreossy and Pierre Roux there to work on the supply, which uses the reservoirs of Lampy, Cammazes and Saint-Ferréol and channels called rigoles.

The first locks, rectangular and built on wooden stilts, collapsed, and Riquet redesigned them with thicker, rounded walls, a form later called Baroque. Construction lasted from 1666 to 1681. Riquet died in October 1680, shortly before completion, and the first inspection began on 2 May 1681. In 1686 Vauban found the canal in poor repair and ordered new work, including the Cammazes tunnel and a strengthening of the Saint-Ferréol reservoir.

At first the canal was used mainly by small sailing barges with lowered masts, hauled by gangs of men. By the middle of the 18th century horses had largely taken over, and steam tugs appeared in 1834. By 1838 273 vessels worked the canal regularly, and mail boats carried passengers. The record year for trade was 1856, with nearly 100,000 passengers.

Railways then took the traffic. In 1858 Napoleon III entrusted the canal for 40 years to the railway company Chemins de fer du Midi, which favoured its own line, and boat traffic declined. Commercial shipping ended around the late 1980s, and the canal is now used mainly by boaters and tourists. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
canary-islands: The Canary Islands are an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, about 100 kilometres off the northwest coast of Africa. The seven main islands, from largest to smallest by area, are Tenerife, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro. All are volcanic in origin, and with the Azores, Cape Verde, Madeira and the Savage Isles they form the Macaronesia ecoregion. Historically the chain was called the Fortunate Isles.

The western islands, El Hierro, La Palma and La Gomera, are influenced by the moist Canary Current and carry extensive subtropical laurisilva forest, while Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, nearest to Africa, are effectively desert or semi-desert. Mount Teide on Tenerife is the highest peak in Spain.

Linguistic, genetic and archaeological analyses indicate that indigenous peoples were living on the islands at least 2,000 years ago, possibly 3,000, and shared a common origin with the Amazighs of the nearby North African coast. They may have reached the islands in several small boats, landing first on Lanzarote and Fuerteventura. They came to be known collectively as the Guanches, although that name had belonged only to the indigenous inhabitants of Tenerife.

According to a 2024 study by the University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, archaeological evidence shows that the Romans were the first to establish contact, between the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE. During the Age of Sail the islands were the main stopover for Spanish galleons on the way to the Americas, which sailed that far south to catch the prevailing northeasterly trade winds.

The archipelago is the southernmost autonomous community of Spain, established in 1982. It has two provinces, Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas, created by splitting the Province of Canary Islands in 1927, and the cities of Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria are joint capitals.

The name Islas Canarias probably derives from the Latin Canariae Insulae, meaning Islands of the Dogs, from Pliny the Elder's account of vast multitudes of very large dogs on Canaria. The canary bird takes its name from the islands. San Cristóbal de La Laguna on Tenerife is a World Heritage Site, as is Mount Teide.
canberra: Canberra lies near the Brindabella Ranges, part of the Australian Alps, about 150 km inland from Australia's east coast. Its urban area has an elevation of about 580 m, and the highest point near it is Mount Majura at 888 m. The Molonglo River was dammed to form Lake Burley Griffin, and it then flows into the Murrumbidgee. The area was a flood plain before the lake was filled.

The name derives from the Ngunnawal language of a local clan that the first British colonists called the Canberry, Kanberri or Nganbra tribe. Joshua John Moore, the first European landowner in the region, named his grant Canberry in 1823. The form Canberra began to appear around 1857. Suggested meanings include meeting place.

The first peoples of the area include the Ngunnawal and Ngambri. Archaeological evidence suggests human activity there 21,000 years ago. The Canberry or Nganbra clan lived mostly around Sullivan's Creek and had ceremonial grounds at the base of Galambary (Black Mountain), while the Pialligo clan had land around what is now Canberra Airport. The people managed the land with fire, farmed yams and hunted. Galambary was a meeting and business site, mainly for men, and an initiation site.

European settlement began in the first half of the 19th century. The federation of the Australian colonies was achieved on 1 January 1901, and the new capital was founded and formally named Canberra in 1913, as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne. It is an entirely planned city, based on a design by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, influenced by the garden city movement and aligned with landmarks such as Black Mountain, Mount Ainslie and Capital Hill.

Canberra is the capital of Australia and the largest population centre in the Australian Capital Territory, with an estimated 484,630 people. It is the country's largest inland city. It is the seat of the federal government, with Parliament House, Government House and the High Court, and it hosts all foreign embassies in Australia.

Among its national institutions are the Australian War Memorial, the Australian National University, established in 1946, the National Gallery, the National Museum and the National Library. The Royal Military College Duntroon is also there, and Floriade is the largest flower festival in the Southern Hemisphere.
candide: Voltaire was already a well-established author when he wrote Candide, which became a model for the contes philosophiques of the 18th and early 19th centuries, a genre that included his earlier Zadig and Micromegas. Several events lie behind it: the publication of Leibniz's Monadology, the Seven Years' War and the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, which posed a problem for the optimism founded on the theodicy of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, which insisted on God's benevolence in spite of such disasters.

It is not known exactly when Voltaire wrote it. Scholars estimate that it was mainly composed in late 1758 and begun as early as 1757, in part at Les Délices near Geneva. A popular legend that he wrote it in three days probably rests on a misreading of an 1885 book. He did not openly admit his authorship until 1768, and signed it until then as Doctor Ralph.

The story has thirty short chapters. Candide, the illegitimate nephew of a baron in Westphalia, lives in the baron's castle, where the tutor Pangloss teaches that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds. Expelled for his love of the baron's daughter Cunégonde, he is swept through war, earthquake and cruelty, first in Europe, then in the Americas, where he reaches El Dorado, and finally back to Europe and the Ottoman Empire. Many of the events are based on real happenings.

Its method is to set great tragedy against comedy, told in a matter-of-fact tone. At Portsmouth Candide sees an admiral, thought to stand for John Byng, shot for failing to engage a French fleet, merely pour encourager les autres, a phrase Voltaire is credited with originating. The book ends with Candide dismissing optimism but offering no system in its place, only the practical precept that we must cultivate our garden, and critics still dispute what that means.

Immediately after publication the work and its author were denounced by secular and religious authorities because it openly derides government and church, and it was widely banned on grounds of blasphemy and sedition. A sequel by other hands appeared in 1760. Candide is the most widely read of Voltaire's works and is listed in Harold Bloom's The Western Canon. Its parody and picaresque methods influenced later black humorists such as Joseph Heller, Thomas Pynchon and Kurt Vonnegut.
cangas-de-onis: Cangas de Onís is a municipality in the eastern part of the province and autonomous community of Asturias, in the north-west of Spain. Its Asturian name, Cangues d'Onís, is explained as the valleys of Onís. More than seventy square kilometres of the municipality form part of the Parque nacional de los Picos de Europa. Because of its range of heights it has many kinds of plants, among them mountain shrubs, heather, oak and ash, surrounded by grassland. The municipality is divided into eleven parishes, and the capital is the parish of Cangas de Onís, with 4,326 inhabitants according to the figures of 2005.

Within the national park lies the village of Covadonga, where the battle of Covadonga, about 722, was the first major victory of a Christian military force in Iberia after the Islamic conquest and is taken to mark the starting point of the Reconquista. Cangas de Onís is known as the first capital of the Kingdom of Asturias and is the site of the first church built in Iberia after the conquest, Santa Cruz de Cangas de Onís of 737, which was built on an ancient dolmen.

A parish named Cangas de Onís is attested for the 14th century, and the stone bridge over the Sella River was built in the 14th or 15th century. The town was represented in the Junta General of the principality of Asturias in 1504. Covadonga began to develop as a pilgrimage site in the 16th century, which attracted commerce, and the settlement of Cangas de Onís grew rapidly in the middle of the 19th century. It was bombarded several times in the Spanish Civil War, and it was the seat of the Regional Council in the pre-autonomous regime of 1978 to 1981, before the Statute of Autonomy of the Principality of Asturias came into force on 31 January 1982.

The main economic activities of the region are agriculture, cattle rearing and rural tourism, and the nearby Covadonga Sanctuary and its surrounding lakes are among the main tourist destinations in Asturias, within the national park.
canillo: Canillo is the name of one of the seven parishes of Andorra and of its main town. It borders France to the north and east and is the largest parish of Andorra, at 121 square kilometres. Its localities include Soldeu, El Tarter, Incles, Prats and Meritxell, and the Estany de Juclà in the Incles valley is the largest lake in Andorra. Much of the parish is still characterised by active farms.

The name of the parish is pre-Roman in origin. It is first documented in the 9th century, in the deed of consecration of the cathedral of La Seu d'Urgell, as Kanillave, and appears as Canilau in 1176. At Prats stands the sanctuary of Roc de les Bruixes, a set of rock engravings dating from the Bronze Age to the early Middle Ages. Remains of the late 7th and 8th centuries show early Christianity in Andorra. The church of Sant Joan de Caselles, Romanesque and from the end of the 11th century, holds a 12th-century Romanesque Majesty on a mural painting.

Canillo is also the site of the sanctuary of Our Lady of Meritxell. According to legend a shepherd found an image of the Virgin under flowering roses, and when he took it home it returned three times to the same place, so a chapel was built there. In 1873 she was declared patron saint of the country, and 8 September 1921 was declared the national holiday. The Romanesque sanctuary burned down in 1972, and the architect Ricardo Bofill Levi designed the new one, inaugurated in 1976.

The parish had 4,826 inhabitants in 2011 and is a tourist destination, notably for the ski resort of Soldeu-El Tarter, though farming continues. The sanctuary of Meritxell was declared a minor basilica in 2014.
cankiri: Çankırı lies about 140 kilometres north-east of Ankara, some 800 metres above sea level. Its ancient name Gangra seems to mean a goat in Paphlagonian. The earlier town stood on the hill behind the modern city, where the ruins of a late fortress remain, while the Roman city occupied the site of the present one.

Gangra seems once to have been the capital of Paphlagonia, since Strabo says that Deiotarus Philadelphus, the last king of Paphlagonia, lived there, though he also calls it only a small town and a garrison. It was absorbed into the Roman province of Galatia on the king's death in 6 or 5 BCE. It was later named Germanicopolis, after Germanicus or possibly the emperor Claudius. In Christian times it was the metropolitan see of Paphlagonia, and its bishop Hypatios, venerated as a saint in the Orthodox tradition, was killed by Arians on his return from the Council of Nicaea in 325.

In the 4th century Gangra was the scene of an important synod, whose date is disputed. Twenty-one bishops met to act against Eustathius of Sebaste and his followers, who disowned marriage and denounced riches. The synod issued twenty canons, declared ecumenical by the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and said it condemned not virginity but the dishonouring of marriage, and not poverty but disparagement of honest wealth. In 1400 and 1401 the patriarch Matthew I appointed George Kontophe metropolitan of Gangra, at the request of its people, who were threatened by the Turkomans.

Çankırı is the seat of Çankırı Province and of Çankırı District, with about 90 thousand inhabitants. Wheat, maize, beans and apples are grown in the surrounding fields, and Çankırı Karatekin University was founded there in 2007.
cannes: Cannes is a resort city on the French Riviera, in the Alpes-Maritimes department of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur. Le Suquet, the old town on its hill, overlooks the Promenade de la Croisette, the waterfront avenue with palm trees, beaches and luxury hotels. Off the coast lie the Lérins Islands, and the history of Cannes is closely tied to theirs. Cistercian monks are the only inhabitants of the smaller Île Saint-Honorat, where monks have lived since 410 CE. On the Île Sainte-Marguerite the Man in the Iron Mask was held; his identity has never been proven.

By the 2nd century BCE the Ligurian Oxybii had established a settlement known as Aegitna. In 154 BCE it was the scene of a short conflict between the Oxybii and the troops of Quintus Opimius. By the 10th century the town was known as Canua, a name that may derive from the word for a reed. An attack in 891 by the Saracens, who stayed until the end of the 10th century, devastated the country, and the insecurity of the islands forced the monks to settle on the mainland at the Suquet. A castle was built in 1035, and around 1530 Cannes became independent of the monks who had controlled it for hundreds of years.

Henry Brougham, 1st Baron Brougham and Vaux, bought land at the Croix des Gardes around 1838, when the place was little more than a fishing village, and built the Villa Eleonore-Louise. His improvements attracted English aristocrats, who built winter residences. In the late 1860s casinos, villas, hotels, roads and a railway followed, cutting the journey from Paris to 23 hours. After the First World War winter tourism gave way to summer tourism, and the city council proposed an international film festival shortly after the Second World War.

The Cannes Film Festival, founded in 1946, is held annually, usually in May, at the Palais des Festivals et des Congrès. The city also hosts the Cannes Lions festival of creativity, Midem and the trade markets MIPIM and MIPCOM. In 2021 it was designated a City of Film by the UNESCO Creative Cities Network. Its economy rests on tourism, trade fairs and aviation, and the technopolis of Sophia Antipolis lies in the hills beyond it.
canning: The Dutch are noted as the first to tin food: their navy is reported to have carried cleaned and brine-cooked salmon in tin-plated iron boxes as early as 1772. Shortly before the Napoleonic Wars the French government offered a cash award of 12,000 francs for a cheap and effective way of preserving military rations for the Grande Armée.

In 1809 Nicolas Appert, a confectioner and brewer, observed that food cooked inside a jar did not spoil unless the seals leaked, and developed a method of sealing food in glass jars. Count Montelivert, the minister of the interior, awarded him the prize in 1810. The reason the food kept was unknown, since it would be about 50 years before Louis Pasteur demonstrated the role of microbes in spoilage. The Grande Armée tried issuing canned food, but the process was too slow for the wars to benefit.

The tin can process was allegedly developed by the Frenchman Philippe de Girard, who used the London merchant Peter Durand as his agent to patent the idea in 1810. Durand sold the patent in 1811 to Bryan Donkin and John Hall, and Donkin developed the packaging of food in sealed airtight cans of tinned wrought iron. Each large can was made by hand and could take up to six hours to cook, so the food was too dear for ordinary people. By 1817 Donkin had sold £3000 of canned meat in six months, chiefly to the British Army and Royal Navy.

Arctic expeditions carried canned food, among them William Edward Parry's in 1824. Robert Ayars set up the first American canning factory in New York City in 1812. The Crimean War, the American Civil War and the Franco-Prussian War introduced working-class men to canned food, and companies such as Underwood, Nestlé and Heinz later sold it to urban households. By the 1860s smaller machine-made steel cans were possible and cooking times had fallen from about six hours to thirty minutes.

In the mid-19th century canned food was a status symbol among middle-class European households. Early cans were sealed with poisonous lead solder. Max Ams invented the double seam in 1888, which made an airtight seal without solder and sped up manufacture. Can openers did not appear for another thirty years, and soldiers at first opened cans with bayonets or rocks.

In the First World War armies needed vast quantities of cheap food, and British soldiers lived largely on canned pork and beans, bully beef and Maconochie's stew. After complaints about quality, the French Army issued canned dishes such as coq au vin from 1917. Peter Durand's cans largely replaced fragile glass jars in commercial canneries, though glass remains common in home canning.
cannon: The word cannon derives from the Old Italian cannone, meaning large tube, from the Latin canna and the Greek kanna, reed. It has referred to a gun since 1326 in Italy and 1418 in England. The earliest known depiction of cannons may appear in Song dynasty China as early as the 12th century, but solid evidence does not appear until the 13th century. The cannon was probably a parallel development or evolution of the fire lance, a short-range weapon combining a gunpowder-filled tube and a polearm, whose paper and bamboo barrels were eventually replaced by metal.

Elsewhere the dates are less settled. There is no clear consensus on when the cannon first appeared in the Islamic world, with dates ranging from 1260 to the mid-14th century. Documentary evidence of cannons in Russia does not appear until 1382, and Ivan III established the first Russian cannon foundry in Moscow in 1475. Cannons reached the Javanese Majapahit Empire when a Mongol-Chinese army under Ike Mese invaded Java in 1293.

A cannon has the form of a truncated cone with an internal cylindrical bore that holds the charge and the projectile. The thickest and strongest part lies near the charge, which is ignited through a thin tube called the vent. The main body is divided into the chase, the reinforce and the cascabel, and a cannon's calibre is determined by the diameter of its bore. By the 16th century cannons were made in great variety, and the general rule was that the longer the barrel, the longer the range.

Cannons were used primarily as anti-infantry weapons until around 1374, when large cannons were recorded breaching walls for the first time in Europe. In 1464 the Ottoman Empire cast the Great Turkish Bombard, which weighed 16,000 kilograms. Larger guns forced engineers to build stronger castle walls, and in India the fort of Raicher had gun ports built into its walls for defensive cannons. Field artillery became more important after the introduction of the limber, which greatly improved mobility.

In the 1770s a cannon was manned by two gunners, six soldiers and four officers of artillery. The bore was cleaned with a wet sponge, powder was added, then wadding and the ball, which was rammed down; at 45 degrees the ball had its utmost range. Decoys also had a use: the Quaker gun, a painted log, was used by Colonel William Washington's Continental Army in 1780, when about 100 Loyalists surrendered rather than face bombardment.
cantabria: Cantabria is bordered on the east by the Basque Country, on the south by Castile and León, on the west by Asturias and on the north by the Cantabrian Sea, part of the Bay of Biscay. It belongs to Green Spain, the strip of land between the Bay of Biscay and the Cantabrian Mountains, named for its lush vegetation, which results from a wet, temperate oceanic climate. The region has a coastal strip of low, wide valleys, meeting the ocean in a line of cliffs, and mountains to the south. Its rivers are short and rapid and flow at right angles to the coast, except for the Ebro.

Cantabria has archaeological sites from the Upper Paleolithic, and the first signs of human occupation date from the Lower Paleolithic. The cave of Altamira, with paintings from about 37,000 BCE, was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO along with nine other Cantabrian caves. The region corresponds to the territory of the Cantabri in the second half of the 1st millennium BCE. The first written reference to the name appears around 195 BCE, when Cato the Elder wrote in his Origines that the Ebro rises in the land of the Cantabri. The origin of the name is uncertain.

After the Roman Empire collapsed, Cantabria regained its independence from the Visigoths. In 574 King Liuvigild captured the south of the country, including the city of Amaya, and established there a Visigothic province, the Duchy of Cantabria, as a frontier zone against the Cantabri and the Vascones. In 714 a mixed Arab and Berber army invaded the upper valleys of the Ebro and captured Amaya, forcing the Cantabrians back to their traditional frontiers, where they joined forces with the Kingdom of Asturias.

The modern province was constituted on 28 July 1778 at Puente San Miguel, Reocín. During the War of Independence of 1808 to 1814 Bishop Rafael Tomás Menéndez de Luarca promoted himself as Regent of Cantabria and set up the Cantabrian Armaments in Santander to detain French troops at the mountain passes. In 1936 the Republican Federal Party drafted an autonomy statute for a Cantabrian-Castilian Federal State, which the Civil War prevented from passing.

Cantabria is an autonomous community and province of northern Spain with Santander as its capital. Its Statute of Autonomy, approved on 30 December 1981, gave it its own institutions of self-government, and it is called a historic community in the statute. Spanish is the official language, and remnants of the Cantabrian language, a dialect of the Astur-Leonese continuum, survive in the west and in the Pas and Soba valleys. The traditional sport is bolos, or skittles.
cantar-de-mio-cid: The poem is anonymous and survives in a 14th-century codex in the Spanish National Library in Madrid, which lacks its first page and two others in the middle. A colophon names Per Abbad, in English Abbot Peter, and puts the date 1207 after his name. Current thinking is that this claim was simply copied with the text of an earlier manuscript now lost. Ramón Menéndez Pidal counted the work among the poems passed down and varied by minstrels, while others believe a single learned author wrote it. Date and authorship remain open to debate.

The original title is unknown, and the present one was proposed by Menéndez Pidal. Cid comes from the Arabic sidi or sayyid, a title like Sir. The poem has been translated into English many times since 1879, among others by John Ormsby, W. S. Merwin and Burton Raffel.

Since 1913 the poem, of more than 3,700 verses, has been divided into three parts. In the first, enemies accuse Rodrigo Díaz of keeping tribute owed to King Alfonso VI, who exiles him from Castile and León. He leaves his wife, Doña Ximena, and his daughters, Doña Elvira and Doña Sol, at the monastery of Cardeña and grows rich from raids on Moorish territory. In the second he takes Valencia and defeats the Almoravid king Chufa ibn Tashfin, and the king pardons him and allows his daughters to marry the infantes of Carrión.

In the third part the infantes show cowardice, fleeing a lion in the court and a campaign against the Moors. In revenge they beat their wives and leave them tied to trees at Corpes. The Cid asks the court of Toledo for justice, his men defeat the infantes in a duel, and his daughters marry the heirs of Navarre and Aragon. The tone is realist, with no magic: the archangel Gabriel appears only in a dream.

The poem is the oldest preserved Castilian epic and is considered a national epic of Spain. It departs from history: it does not mention the Cid's son, and his daughters were not called Elvira and Sol. It echoes the plot devices of the Song of Roland.
canterbury: Canterbury lies on the River Stour, not far from its mouth on the Strait of Dover, in east Kent. The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. The Roman name Durovernum Cantiacorum means Durovernum of the Cantiaci, and replaced an earlier British name reconstructed as Durouernon, meaning stronghold by the alder grove. In Sub-Roman Britain it was Cair Ceint, the stronghold of Kent, and the Jutes who occupied it called it Cantwareburh in Old English.

Canterbury was first recorded as the main settlement of the Cantiaci. In the 1st century CE the Romans captured it and rebuilt it with a grid of streets, a theatre, a temple, a forum and public baths. They kept no major garrison, but its position on Watling Street, in relation to the ports of Richborough, Dover and Lymne, gave it strategic importance. In the late 3rd century they built an earth bank and a wall with seven gates round it. It later served as capital of the Jute kingdom of Kent.

A large Viking army besieged Canterbury in 1011, and the city was pillaged. Remembering the destruction caused by the Danes, its inhabitants did not resist William the Conqueror in 1066, and William ordered a wooden castle built beside the Roman wall, rebuilt in stone in the early 12th century. In the mid-16th century Canterbury hosted the first congregation of Huguenot refugees in England, founded around 1548 and scattered in 1553–4 under Mary I. In 1647, during the English Civil War, the Plum Pudding Riots broke out, and the trial of the rioters led to a Kentish revolt.

Canterbury is a World Heritage Site and its cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury. Its surviving past includes a city wall founded in Roman times and rebuilt in the 14th century, the Westgate Towers, the ruins of St Augustine's Abbey and the Norman castle. The Canterbury and Whitstable Railway, which ran from 1830 to 1953, was the first regular passenger steam railway in the world. The city's economy rests on tourism, higher education and retail.
canusium: Canusium, the modern Canosa, lies on the right bank of the Ofanto river, the ancient Aufidus, nearly 20 kilometres from the Adriatic Sea. The town stands on the edge of the Murgia plateau at between 105 and 140 metres above sea level. Its soil is sand or clay over a layer of soft limestone tuff, which is easily excavated. This allowed the digging of underground grottoes and a hypogeum, and the stone taken out of them went into buildings above ground.

The ancient Greeks and Romans ascribed the foundation of the town to the Homeric hero Diomedes. Archaeologists place human presence in the area as far back as the 7th millennium BCE. The surrounding fields were one of the main centres of the Dauni, a northern branch of the Iapyges, and buildings and tombs at Toppicelli point to a wealthy aristocracy. The town became an important commercial centre for craftsmen, above all of ceramics and pottery, and is thought to have become a Greek polis in the age of Magna Grecia.

After Hannibal defeated the consuls Paullus and Varro at Cannae in 216 BCE, Canusium sheltered the fleeing remnants of the Roman army within its walls. In the second year of the Social War it joined the rebels and resisted a Roman siege. It suffered heavily in that conflict or in the civil wars that followed, but became a self-governing municipium in 88 BCE. Some of its bishops are known from the 4th century, and it came to be called the city of bishops. Bishop Stercorius attended the Council of Sardica in 343, and the diocese reached its height under Saint Sabinus (514 to 566), later the town's patron saint.

Earthquakes damaged the town repeatedly, notably in 1361, 1456, 1627, 1659, 1694 and 1851. It was sacked by the Tarantini in 1451 and by Napoleon in 1803. As a fief it passed through several families, and Tiberio Capece was named prince of Canosa in 1712.

Canosa di Puglia is a town and comune in the province of Barletta-Andria-Trani in Apulia, between Bari and Foggia, and is counted among the oldest continually inhabited cities in Italy. Its Cathedral of San Sabino was founded in the 8th century by Duke Arechis II of Benevento and was named after Sabinus in 1101. Bohemond I of Antioch, a commander of the First Crusade, is buried in its mausoleum. The so-called castle is the acropolis of the ancient town, and the remains of a Roman amphitheatre lie at its southern foot. The archaeological museum, founded in 1934, holds about 2,000 finds from the tombs and the town.
cao-cao: Cao Cao, courtesy name Mengde, came from Qiao County in Pei State, in present-day Bozhou, Anhui. His father, Cao Song, bought his way into the office of Grand Commandant under Emperor Ling and served less than half a year; Cao Song was the foster son of the eunuch Cao Teng. Nominated as a xiaolian around the age of 19, Cao Cao became Commandant of the North District of Luoyang and later Chancellor of Jinan State, where he proposed dismissing about 80 percent of its officials for corruption.

In 189 Cao Cao spent his family fortune on an army to oppose Dong Zhuo, and between 191 and 192 Yuan Shao made him Administrator of Dong Commandery, which marks the start of his career as a warlord. His attacks on Tao Qian in Xu Province followed the murder of his father there, and he massacred thousands of civilians. In 196, on the advice of Xun Yu and Cheng Yu, he received Emperor Xian, who had escaped his captors, and set up the capital at Xuchang. The emperor and government came under his control, though he kept up nominal allegiance.

After defeating Yuan Shao at the Battle of Guandu in 200, he spent seven years defeating Yuan Shao's sons and allies and brought much of northern China under his rule. In 208 he marched south but was defeated at the Battle of Red Cliffs by Sun Quan and Liu Bei, when disease had also broken out in his army. Emperor Xian made him Duke of Wei in 213 and King of Wei in June 216, with privileges once reserved for emperors.

Cao Cao died in Luoyang on 15 March 220. In November 220 his son Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian and founded the state of Cao Wei, an event commonly seen as a usurpation, and gave his father the title Emperor Wu. Opinion of Cao Cao has been divided since the Jin dynasty: some praise his poetry and career, others condemn his cruelty and alleged treachery. Traditional Chinese culture stereotypically shows him as a sly tyrant opposed to Liu Bei, a portrait shaped by the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
cao-pi: Cao Pi was the second son of the warlord Cao Cao, but the eldest of the sons of Cao Cao's concubine, later wife, Lady Bian; the eldest of all, Cao Ang, died early. In 211 he became General of the Household for All Purposes and Vice Imperial Chancellor, second only to his father.

For years it was unclear whom Cao Cao intended as heir. He favoured his third son Cao Zhi, known for his literary talent, and in 216 Cao Zhi's party falsely accused two officials who supported Cao Pi, Cui Yan and Mao Jie; Cui Yan was executed. In November or December 217 Cao Cao, by then King of Wei, named Cao Pi heir apparent.

When Cao Cao died in spring 220, Cao Pi declared himself King of Wei before Emperor Xian had confirmed it, and sent his brothers, Cao Zhang and Cao Zhi among them, back to their fiefs. In the winter of 220 he pressed Emperor Xian to yield the throne. He declined three times, a pattern later usurpers in Chinese history followed, and then accepted, founding the state of Cao Wei. This ended the Han dynasty and began the Three Kingdoms period.

Sun Quan briefly submitted to Wei, and Cao Pi rejected the strategist Liu Ye's advice to attack him, granting him the title King of Wu instead; most historians believe this choice confined Wei to northern and central China. After the Battle of Xiaoting in 222 Sun Quan broke with Wei and founded Eastern Wu, and Cao Pi's attacks over the next years made no significant advances. In 225 he remarked that Heaven created the Yangtze River to divide the north and the south.

Historians view him as a competent but unspectacular administrator. He formally established Chen Qun's nine-rank system as the basis of civil service nomination, but he reduced the princes' power and restricted their use of military force. He named Cao Rui crown prince only in summer 226, when seriously ill, and entrusted him to Cao Zhen, Chen Qun and Sima Yi.

Cao Pi was a poet and scholar like his father and his brother Cao Zhi. His Yan Ge Xing is the first Chinese poem with seven syllables to the line. He also wrote over a hundred articles, and the collection of strange tales Lieyi Zhuan is attributed to him. After his death Cao Rui gave him the posthumous name Emperor Wen and the temple name Gaozu.
cao-wei: Late in the Eastern Han dynasty northern China came under Cao Cao, chancellor to the last Han ruler, Emperor Xian. In 213 the emperor made him Duke of Wei, and in 216 King of Wei. Cao Cao died on 15 March 220, and his son Cao Pi inherited the title. On 11 December that year Cao Pi forced Emperor Xian to abdicate and established the state of Wei. Liu Bei contested the claim and declared himself Emperor of Han a year later. Sun Quan, nominally a vassal king under Wei, declared independence in 222 and proclaimed himself Emperor of Wu in 229. The capital was first Xuchang and later Luoyang.

Cao Pi ruled until his death on 29 June 226 and was succeeded by his son Cao Rui, who ruled until 22 January 239. Between 228 and 234 the Shu chancellor Zhuge Liang led five campaigns against Wei's western borders, aiming at Chang'an, but Wei armies repelled them. Fighting with Wu through the 220s and 230s mostly ended in stalemate. In 238 Sima Yi invaded Liaodong and, after a three-month siege, captured the Gongsun capital of Xiangping. In the Goguryeo–Wei Wars from 242, Wei defeated Goguryeo and destroyed its capital Hwando in 244.

Imperial authority collapsed in 249 when the regent Sima Yi seized power from his co-regent Cao Shuang, reducing the emperor Cao Fang to a puppet. His son Sima Shi deposed Cao Fang in 254. In 263 Wei armies conquered Shu. On 4 February 266 Sima Yan forced Cao Huan to abdicate and replaced Wei with the Jin dynasty.

Wei's government inherited much from the Eastern Han. Cao Pi set up bodies to reduce the authority of the Imperial Secretariat, and cut provincial governors to inspectors, with military affairs handled by regional officers. The minister Chen Qun developed the nine-rank system for civil service nomination, adopted by later dynasties until the Sui. It also set rigid lines in law between commoner and noble households and enabled hereditary officeholding by aristocratic families, whose bonded clients and retainers paid no state taxes or labour service. The kaishu style of calligraphy and the Jian'an poetry style developed in this period, as did the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove.
caodaism: Caodaism began in 1925 in Saigon as a Spiritualist club called AĂÂ, founded by Cao Quỳnh Cư, Cao Hoài Sang, Lê Văn Trung and Phạm Công Tắc, clerks in the colonial government who practised mediumship and ouija sessions. After a séance in 1926 the group believed it had received a revelation predicting a universal religion, and Ngô Văn Chiêu signed the Declaration of the Founding of the Cao Đài Religion on 7 October 1926.
Ngô Văn Chiêu declined the office of Pope and founded the separate Chiếu Minh branch; Lê Văn Trung became acting Pope, and after his death in 1934 Phạm Công Tắc took the role.

The full name is Đại Đạo Tam Kỳ Phổ Độ, the Great Faith for the Third Universal Redemption. This monotheistic faith combines ethical precepts from Confucianism, practices from Taoism, karma and rebirth from Buddhism and a hierarchical organisation from Catholicism. Its God, Cao Đài, is accompanied by the Holy Mother, Diêu Trì Kim Mẫu, and they stand for yang and yin. Followers hold that history has three periods of revelation: in the first two, figures such as Gautama Buddha, Laozi, Confucius and Jesus founded religions that later became corrupted, and the third comes through Cao Đài. Victor Hugo, Sun Yat-sen and Trạng Trình are named as its main prophets.

Adherents practise prayer, ancestor veneration, nonviolence and vegetarianism, aiming at union with God and release from saṃsāra. The church is headed by a Pope over an Executive Body, with a Legislative Body under the Hộ Pháp. Lê Văn Trung was the only Pope ordained at Tây Ninh, and the office has stayed vacant.

By 1940 Caodaism had over a million members, between a fifth and a quarter of the population of Cochinchina. From 1941 to 1946 Phạm Công Tắc and other leaders were jailed in French penal colonies in Madagascar. During the First and Second Indochina Wars, Caodaists took part in political and military struggles against the French and against Ngô Đình Diệm.

After the fall of Saigon in April 1975 the communist government banned the practice; legal recognition came in 1997. Between 1934 and 1975 the religion split into as many as thirty sects, of which eleven have been recognised by the authorities. Estimates of followers in Vietnam differ widely, up to about six million, and the Holy See at Tây Ninh is a major pilgrimage site.
cap-haitien: Spanish explorers took the Taíno name Guárico for the area. Puerto Real, one of the first Spanish towns of Hispaniola, was founded near Cap-Haïtien in 1503 and abandoned in 1578. Cap-Français was founded in 1670 by a dozen colonist-adventurers under Bertrand d'Ogeron, and its formal foundation dates from 1711. The French built large sugar plantations on the northern plains and imported tens of thousands of African slaves. Cap-Français became the colony's main commercial centre and its capital until 1770, when the capital moved to Port-au-Prince, and its wealth earned it the nickname Paris of the Antilles. Two thirds of its 15,000 inhabitants in 1790 were enslaved.

The Haitian Revolution began nearby. At Bois Caïman, on 14 August 1791, the maroon leader Dutty Boukman and a mambo named Cécile Fatiman led a Vodou ceremony at which those present swore to die rather than endure slavery, and the insurrection began on 22–23 August. At Vertières, on 18 November 1803, Jean-Jacques Dessalines's army defeated a French army under the Comte de Rochambeau, and Haiti declared independence in 1804. Henri Christophe renamed the city, and it was the first capital of his Kingdom of Haiti until 1820.

Cap-Haïtien is the capital of the department of Nord, with about 300,000 people. Near Milot stand the Citadelle Laferrière, a mountaintop fortress built by Henri Christophe, and the ruins of his Sans-Souci Palace, damaged in the earthquake of 7 May 1842, which destroyed most of the city. UNESCO listed both as a World Heritage Site in 1982. After the United States occupation of Haiti from 1915 to 1934, the streets of the central city were renamed with letters running north to south and numbers running east to west. Its well-preserved 19th-century architecture, with gingerbread houses, resembles that of New Orleans.
cape-coast: Cape Coast lies on the Gulf of Guinea, about 130 km from Accra. Its traditional name is Oguaa, from the Guan Awutu word gua, meaning market. Early Portuguese navigators called it Cabo Corso, short cape, which the British later corrupted to Cape Coast. It became the principal town of the Fetu Kingdom, an old Guan kingdom whose paramount seat lay about 16 km to the north. A market called Ogua grew into an active commercial centre, and the King of Fetu appointed a chief to represent it.

The English navigator William Towerson, the first documented English visitor to reach the Guinea coast, landed in 1555. Around 1650 Hendrik Carloff bought a plot from the King of Fetu for Dutch privateers working against the Dutch West India Company. The fort built on the site of Carolusborg changed hands several times before 1664, when a joint English and Dutch force captured it from the Dutch. The Danes built Fort Frederiksborg on a hill plot, which the English later bought.

The Asante invaded the coast in 1806. Cape Coast escaped the attack, but the townspeople's confidence in British protection fell. The town had been largely burnt down in 1817. It was the most important anchorage on the coast until Sekondi Harbour was built in the 1890s. Cape Coast was capital of the Gold Coast from 1821 until 1877, when the seat moved to Accra, which badly damaged its economy.

Cape Coast is the capital of the Central Region of Ghana. Its 2010 census population was 108,374, mostly Fante. Cape Coast Castle is a World Heritage Site. The University of Cape Coast, established in 1962, helped make it an educational centre. The main festival is Fetu Afahye, held on the first Saturday of September.
cape-cod: Cape Cod extends into the Atlantic Ocean from the south-eastern corner of Massachusetts and is coextensive with Barnstable County, running from Provincetown in the north-east to Woods Hole in the south-west. It is divided into fifteen towns. Most of the land consists of glacial landforms, terminal moraine and outwash plains, which mark the southernmost extent of glacial coverage in south-eastern New England. Geologically it is young, laid down some 16,000 to 20,000 years ago. Since 1914 the Cape Cod Canal has separated most of the peninsula from the mainland.

The Wampanoag have lived on Cape Cod for centuries. They lived from the sea, farmed, and lit controlled fires to keep the underbrush in check. They helped the Pilgrims, who arrived in the fall of 1620, to survive at Plymouth Colony, and later gradually lost their lands through cessions and violent conflict with settlers. The Wampanoag tribe was federally recognized in May 2007.

Bartholomew Gosnold coined the name Cape Cod in 1602, and it is the ninth-oldest English place-name in the United States. It applied at first only to the tip of the peninsula. The Cape was among the first places settled by Puritan colonists, with Sandwich founded in 1637 and Barnstable and Yarmouth in 1639. The canal was developed from 1870 to 1914. Lighthouses were built from 1797, and from the end of the 19th century improved rail transport made the Cape a summer haven for city dwellers from Boston.

Cape Cod has a year-round population of about 220,000 and a tourist season in the warmer months. Henry David Thoreau wrote about his 1849 travels there in Cape Cod, published in 1865, and Henry Beston's The Outermost House of 1928 describes a year spent in a cottage in Eastham.
cape-colony: An expedition of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) led by Jan van Riebeeck established a trading post and naval victualling station at the Cape of Good Hope in 1652. Its aim was a harbour of refuge for company ships on the long voyages between Europe and Asia. Within about three decades the Cape held a large community of vrijburgers, or free citizens, former company employees who undertook to farm the land for at least twenty years in exchange for tax exemption and loans of tools and seeds. In 1688 the company also sponsored the immigration of nearly two hundred French Huguenot refugees.

Colonists on the frontier, known as Boers, moved far beyond the colony's first borders, and some, the trekboers, became permanently nomadic. The period of company rule saw bitter, genocidal conflicts between the colonists and the Khoe-speaking peoples, and later the Xhosa, who were seen as competitors for farmland. The company also imported thousands of slaves from the Dutch East Indies and other parts of Africa. By the end of the eighteenth century the population included about 26,000 people of European descent and 30,000 slaves.

In 1795 Britain occupied the Cape after France occupied the Dutch Republic, defeating the company's militia at the Battle of Muizenberg. The Treaty of Amiens returned it to the Batavian Republic in 1803, but Britain took it again after the Battle of Blaauwberg and set up a colony on 8 January 1806. The Dutch formally ceded sovereignty in 1814. British settlers arrived at Port Elizabeth in 1820, and slavery was abolished in 1834. Resentment among the Boers of this change and of English language and culture led many to trek inland in the Great Trek and form the Boer Republics.

The colony became a Crown colony with representative government in 1853 and elected its first parliament in 1854, with a franchise based on a property qualification regardless of race. It achieved responsible government in 1872 under its first Prime Minister, John Molteno.

The colony stretched from the Atlantic coast inland and eastward along the southern coast, about half of modern South Africa, with its eastern boundary at the Fish River after several wars against the Xhosa. In 1910 it joined three other colonies to form the Union of South Africa and became the Province of the Cape of Good Hope. In 1994 the Cape Province was divided into the Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Western Cape, with smaller parts in North West province.
cape-horn: Cape Horn lies on Hornos Island in the Hermite Islands group, at the southern end of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago in southern Chile, at about 56 degrees south. It is not the most southerly point of South America, which is Águila Islet, but it marks the northern boundary of the Drake Passage, the strait between South America and Antarctica, and the place where the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans meet. The cape lies in Chilean territorial waters, within Cabo de Hornos National Park, and the Chilean Navy maintains a station on the island with a residence, chapel and lighthouse.

The Dutchmen Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire first rounded the cape in 1616 and named it Kaap Hoorn after the city of Hoorn in the Netherlands. The Strait of Magellan, between the mainland and Tierra del Fuego, had been used for trade well before the Horn was discovered, but is narrow, and for decades Cape Horn was a major milestone on the clipper route by which sailing ships carried trade around the world. The need to round it was greatly reduced by the opening of the Panama Canal in August 1914.

The passage is regarded as perhaps the most dangerous ship route in the world, and many ships have been wrecked and many sailors have died attempting it. Winds in these latitudes blow from west to east almost uninterrupted by land, and the Andes and the Antarctic Peninsula funnel them into the narrow Drake Passage. The waves become shorter and steeper over the shallow water south of the Horn, and rogue waves of up to 30 metres are reported west of it. Icebergs are a further hazard. Passage from east to west, against the winds and currents, was a particular problem for traditional sailing ships.

There are no regular commercial routes around the Horn, although cruise ships and vessels bound for the Antarctic Peninsula pass it. Rounding the Horn remains one of the major challenges in yachting. A memorial near the station, a sculpture by José Balcells of the silhouette of an albatross, was erected in 1992 in remembrance of the sailors who died attempting to round the Horn. The cape belongs to the commune of Cabo de Hornos, whose capital is Puerto Williams.
cape-of-good-hope: The Cape of Good Hope is a rocky headland on the Atlantic coast of the Cape Peninsula in South Africa, about 2.3 kilometres west and a little north of Cape Point. It is a common misconception that it is the southern tip of Africa; the southernmost point is Cape Agulhas, about 150 kilometres to the east-southeast. Following the western African coastline from the equator, however, the Cape of Good Hope marks the point where a ship begins to travel more eastward than southward. Cape Town lies about 50 kilometres to the north, in Table Bay.

Herodotus records that around 600 BCE Necho II reputedly commissioned Phoenicians to sail from the Red Sea around Africa to the mouth of the Nile, which would be the first completion of the Cape Route. The account came to him by oral tradition. Eudoxus of Cyzicus, a Greek navigator for Ptolemy VIII, found in about 116 BCE the wreck of a ship that appeared to have come from Gades, and concluded that it had sailed round Africa; his own later attempt failed and his fate is unknown. The Fra Mauro map of 1450 depicts the Indian Ocean as connected to the Atlantic and records a voyage by an Indian junk around 1420.

The first European to reach the cape was the Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias, who named it the Cape of Storms, Cabo das Tormentas. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope because of the optimism the opening of a sea route to India and the East engendered. The Khoikhoi lived in the area when the Dutch first settled in 1652. On 6 April of that year Jan van Riebeeck established a resupply camp for the Dutch East India Company in Table Bay, which developed into Cape Town and became known as the Tavern of the Seas. On 31 December 1687 a community of Huguenots arrived from the Netherlands, since the Company needed skilled farmers.

British troops occupied the Cape Colony in 1795, after the Dutch Republic was occupied by France, and again on 19 January 1806 following the Battle of Blaauwberg. The colony existed from 1795 to 1802 and again from 1806 to 1910. Today the cape is a section of Table Mountain National Park, with fynbos vegetation that belongs to the Cape Floristic Kingdom, and at least 250 bird species, including a mainland colony of African penguins. In legend it is the home of the Flying Dutchman, and the poet Luís de Camões invented the giant Adamastor in Os Lusíadas, first printed in 1572, as a symbol of the dangers of rounding the Cape of Storms.
cape-town: Cape Town stands on the shore of Table Bay, at a latitude of about 33.55 degrees south. Table Mountain, with near vertical cliffs and a flat summit more than 1,000 metres high, forms a mountainous backdrop with Devil's Peak and Lion's Head on either side and creates the City Bowl, which holds the central business district. To the south the Cape Peninsula runs 40 kilometres into the Atlantic Ocean and ends at Cape Point, and many suburbs lie on the Cape Flats, a plain that joins the peninsula to the mainland. Robben Island in Table Bay is part of the city, and Table Mountain National Park lies within its boundaries.

The earliest known remains of human occupation in the region were found at Peers Cave in Fish Hoek in the late 1920s; earlier estimates of an upper Pleistocene origin have since been revised to the mid-Holocene. Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to reach the area, arrived in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, because the opening of a sea route to India raised such optimism, and Vasco da Gama recorded sighting it in 1497. In 1510, at the Battle of Salt River, the Portuguese admiral Francisco de Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed by the Khoikhoi Goringhaiqua, who used cattle trained to respond to whistles and shouts.

Ships of several nations, mainly Portuguese, regularly stopped in Table Bay in the late sixteenth century on the way to the Indies. They traded tobacco, copper and iron with the Khoikhoi clans of the region for fresh meat and other provisions. In 1652 Jan van Riebeeck and other employees of the United East India Company were sent to establish a way-station for ships travelling to the Dutch East Indies, and they built the Fort de Goede Hoop, later replaced by the Castle of Good Hope.

The settlement grew slowly because adequate labour was hard to find. The shortage led the local authorities to import enslaved people from Indonesia and Madagascar, many of whom are ancestors of the present Cape Coloured and Cape Malay communities.

Cape Town is the legislative capital of South Africa, the seat of its Parliament, and the capital of the Western Cape. It is the country's oldest city. It has the highest density of Cape Dutch buildings in the world, a style that combines the architectural traditions of the Netherlands, Germany, France and Indonesia. Mostert's Mill in Mowbray, built in 1796, is the only complete windmill in South Africa. The Cape Floristic Region, including Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
cape-verde: Cape Verde is a horseshoe-shaped cluster of ten volcanic islands, nine of them inhabited, and eight islets, with a land area of about 4,033 square kilometres. They lie between 600 and 850 km west of Cap-Vert on the Senegalese coast, from which the country takes its name. Cap-Vert comes from the Portuguese Cabo Verde, meaning green cape, a name Portuguese explorers gave to the headland in 1444.
