It became an independent margraviate with its own Slavic margrave at Kranj, subject first to the governor of Bavaria and after 976 to the Dukes of Carinthia. Frederick II of Austria obtained the title of duke in 1245, and in 1268 Ulrich III willed his lands to Ottokar II of Bohemia. When Duke Henry of Carinthia died in 1335, Albrecht, Duke of Austria, received Carniola, and Rudolf IV proclaimed it a duchy in 1364. It then stayed Habsburg almost continuously until 1918, though Ottoman raids from the 15th century and local rebellions troubled it.

The capital moved from Kranj to Kamnik and finally to Ljubljana. French troops occupied the region in 1797 and in 1805-1806, and by the Treaty of Vienna it joined the French Illyrian Provinces in 1809-1814, with Ljubljana as capital. It was returned to Austria and from 1816 to 1849 belonged to the Kingdom of Illyria. In 1849 it became a crown land in its own right and in 1867 part of Cisleithania. It then covered 9,904 square kilometres.

In 1918 the duchy ceased to exist, and its territory joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs and then the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Its western part, including Postojna and Idrija, was annexed to Italy in 1920 and included in Yugoslavia in 1947. Since 1991 the region has been part of independent Slovenia.
carnuntum: Carnuntum stood on the Danube in what is now Lower Austria, halfway between Vienna and Bratislava, near the villages of Petronell-Carnuntum and Bad Deutsch-Altenburg. It was a Roman legionary fortress and the headquarters of the Pannonian fleet from about 50 CE, and it grew into a city of roughly 50,000 inhabitants. It was a major trading centre for amber, because the main arm of the Amber Road crossed the Danube there.

Carnuntum first appears in history in 6 CE, when Tiberius made it his base in the campaigns against Maroboduus. It became the garrison of the Legio XV Apollinaris before 14 CE, and in about 50 CE the emperor Claudius ordered a legion to be stationed on the Danube to protect the defeated party in a dispute between the Quadi and the Marcomanni. Legio XIV Gemina made it its permanent quarters in 117–118 and stayed for three centuries. Hadrian made it a municipium, and it became the capital of Pannonia Superior.

Marcus Aurelius lived there for three years, 172 to 175, during the war against the Marcomanni, and wrote part of his Meditations there. Septimius Severus, then governor of Pannonia, was proclaimed emperor by his soldiers there in 193. Under the Severan dynasty the city boomed, and Caracalla raised it to colony status. In 308 Diocletian chaired the Conference of Carnuntum with Maximian and Galerius to settle tensions within the Tetrarchy. An earthquake damaged it around 350, and in 374 Germanic invaders, the Quadi and Iazyges, destroyed it. Valentinian I partly restored it, but it never regained its importance, and Vindobona became the chief military centre.

The site was eventually abandoned, used as a cemetery and a source of building stone, and its remains became buried and forgotten. The Carnuntum Archaeological Park now covers 10 square kilometres. It includes a rebuilt Roman house, palace ruins, an amphitheatre for about 15,000 spectators, and the Heidentor, the ruin of a triumphal arch put up between 354 and 361, probably under Constantius II. A gladiator school was found in 2011 by aerial photography and ground-penetrating radar.
carol-i-of-romania: Carol was born Karl Eitel Friedrich Zephyrinus Ludwig on 20 April 1839 at Sigmaringen in southern Germany, the second son of Prince Karl Anton of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen and Princess Josephine of Baden. His family belonged to the Catholic Swabian branch of the House of Hohenzollern, was related to the Prussian royal family and, through both grandmothers, to the Bonaparte family. He trained at the cadet school in Münster and the artillery school in Berlin and served as a Prussian officer until 1866, taking part in the Second Schleswig War.

In 1866 a coup removed Alexandru Ioan Cuza, the prince of the united Moldavia and Wallachia, and the country risked disintegration. Philip of Flanders refused the throne. Napoleon III then suggested Karl, and the politician Ion Constantin Brătianu went to negotiate with his family. Karl travelled incognito through Switzerland under a Swiss passport, was elected Domnitor on 20 April 1866 and entered Bucharest in May, swearing his oath in French because he did not yet speak Romanian.

On 29 June 1866 parliament adopted a constitution modelled closely on that of Belgium, which guaranteed freedom of speech and the press and separated powers. It also barred non-Christians from citizenship, which heavily affected the Jewish population. In 1869 Carol married Princess Elisabeth of Wied. Their only child, Maria, born in 1870, died in 1874, and the throne later passed to his nephew Ferdinand.

In the Russo-Turkish War Romania declared independence on 10 May 1877. After the Russian advance stalled at Pleven, Carol took command of the combined Russian and Romanian forces there, and Osman Nuri Pasha surrendered the town on 28 November 1877. The Treaty of Berlin recognised Romanian independence on 13 July 1878 and gave Romania Northern Dobruja. The constitution was amended in March 1881 and Carol was crowned king on 10 May, wearing a crown made from steel of a captured Ottoman cannon.

He built Peleș Castle in the Carpathian mountains and ordered the engineer Anghel Saligny to build a bridge over the Danube between Fetești and Cernavodă. In 1883 he arranged a secret alliance with the Central Powers, unknown to parliament and the public until the First World War. A peasant revolt in 1907 was bloodily suppressed. Romania gained Southern Dobruja in 1913. Carol died on 10 October 1914 (27 September, Old Style), and Romania, neutral at first, joined the Allies in 1916.
carol-ii-of-romania: Carol was born in Peleș Castle as the son of Crown Prince Ferdinand and Crown Princess Marie, the first male member of the royal family to be born in Romania. He spent much of his childhood under his domineering great-uncle, King Carol I, who kept his parents out of his upbringing. His marriage to Zizi Lambrino, who was not of royal lineage, was dissolved, and in March 1921 he married Princess Helen of Greece and Denmark, with whom he had a son, Michael.

His affair with Elena Lupescu ended the marriage. The National Liberal Party used it to argue that he was unfit to be king. In 1925 he renounced his rights to the throne in favour of Michael and went into exile in France with Lupescu. Michael inherited the throne at the age of five on the death of Ferdinand in 1927, and Helen divorced Carol in 1928.

Carol returned to Romania on 7 June 1930 in a coup engineered by the National Peasant prime minister Iuliu Maniu, deposed Michael, who was still under a regency, and was recognised as king by Parliament the next day. After the December 1937 elections no coalition could be formed. On 10 February 1938 he suspended the constitution, proclaimed martial law and set up a royal dictatorship, abolishing all parties and forming the National Renaissance Front.

When the Second World War began he proclaimed neutrality. After the fall of France in 1940 Carol moved towards Nazi Germany in the hope of avoiding invasion. In June the Soviet Union demanded Bessarabia and northern Bukovina by ultimatum, and Carol gave way without fighting. The Treaty of Craiova ceded Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria, and the Second Vienna Award of 30 August 1940 gave northern Transylvania to Hungary. Demonstrations demanded his abdication, and General Ion Antonescu forced him to abdicate on 6 September 1940 in favour of Michael.

Carol left Romania by train with thirty truckloads of his fortune; the Iron Guard shot at the train at Timișoara in a failed attempt to kill him. He went to Portugal and then to Cuernavaca in Mexico, where from 1941 he tried to organise a Free Romania movement, which gained no recognition. He married Lupescu in Rio de Janeiro on 3 June 1947 and died at Estoril in 1953. The historian Stanley G. Payne called him the most cynical, corrupt and power-hungry monarch of twentieth-century Europe. His remains were returned to the Curtea de Argeș monastery in 2003.
caroline-islands: The Caroline Islands form a widely scattered archipelago of about 500 small islands in the western Pacific Ocean, north of New Guinea and east of the Philippines. They stretch for approximately 3,540 kilometres, from Tobi in Palau in the west to Kosrae in the east. Most are low, flat coral atolls, though some rise high above sea level. Yap lies 1,900 kilometres from Manila, and the group was once called Nuevas Filipinas, or New Philippines, because it formed part of the Spanish East Indies and was governed from Manila.

Different islands tell different stories of their origins. On Pohnpei, the people divide their pre-colonial history into three eras: building or peopling before 1100, the reigns of the Saudeleur from 1100 to around 1628, and the era of the tribal chiefs, the nahnmwarki, from around 1628 to 1885. According to Pohnpeian legend, the Saudeleur came from beyond the islands and imposed an increasingly oppressive centralised rule. A foreigner named Isokelekel invaded, overthrew them and set up the more decentralised nahnmwarki system.

The Portuguese navigators Diogo da Rocha and Gomes de Sequeira, carried east by a storm in 1525, were the first Europeans to reach the islands. In 1528 Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón claimed the Ulithi Islands for the king of Spain. Francisco de Lezcano, arriving at Yap in 1686, named the group Las Carolinas in honour of Charles II of Spain. A missionary, Juan Antonio Cantova, was killed in 1731, and Spain broke off relations until 1787. Whaling ships from Britain, the United States and Australia called there through the 19th century, the first known being the London whaler Britannia at Ngatik in December 1793.

In 1885 a Spanish representative signed an agreement with the chiefs of Koror and Artingal establishing Spanish sovereignty. When Germany and the United Kingdom disputed Spain's right to collect customs duties, Pope Leo XIII arbitrated and decided in Spain's favour west of the 164th meridian east. After the Spanish-American War, Spain sold the Carolines and the Northern Marianas to Germany in 1899 for 25 million pesetas. Japan occupied the islands in 1914, received a League of Nations mandate over them in 1920, and kept a large base at Truk Lagoon in World War II. The islands then became a United States trust territory.

The group is divided between the Federated States of Micronesia in its central and eastern parts, which became independent in 1986, and Palau at its western end, independent from 1994. Pohnpeian, Chuukese, Carolinian, Kosraean, Palauan and Yapese are among the languages spoken. Yap is known for its huge stone discs quarried in Palau, which serve as tokens of wealth.
carolingian-empire: The Carolingian dynasty had ruled as kings of the Franks since 751 and as kings of the Lombards in Italy from 774. Its rise rested on Charles Martel, who took neither the title of king nor of emperor but was the absolute ruler of virtually all of continental Western Europe north of the Pyrenees. He earned his surname, Martel, meaning the Hammer, through his defence of Christian Europe against a Muslim army at the Battle of Tours in 732. In 800 Pope Leo III crowned his grandson Charlemagne as Roman emperor in return for political protection, disregarding the universalist claims of the weakened Byzantine Empire.

Under Charlemagne the empire covered most of Western Europe, as the Roman Empire once had. His son Louis the Pious, originally crowned king of Aquitaine at the age of three, became emperor unexpectedly after the deaths of his older siblings. His reign was overshadowed by a dynastic struggle that ended in a civil war from 840 to 843. In 843 his three sons settled the partition in the Treaty of Verdun. Lothar received the imperial title, the kingship of Italy and the lands between the Rhine and the Rhone. Louis took the lands east of the Rhine, and Charles those west of the Rhone.

After the death of Charles the Bald in 877 the empire was attacked by the Vikings in the north and west and faced internal struggles from Italy to the Baltic. In 884 Charles the Fat reunited all the Carolingian kingdoms for the last time, but the Frankish nobility deposed him in 887, and the empire dissolved when he died in 888. The legitimate line was restored in the western kingdom in 898 and ruled until 987, with an interruption from 922 to 936.

The empire had no permanent capital, since the court moved from place to place, as in other Western European kingdoms. Charlemagne began building the Palace of Aachen in the 780s, and its chapel, completed in 796, later became Aachen Cathedral. Aachen was meant as a meeting place for aristocrats and churchmen, where patronage was distributed, assemblies were held and laws written. The language of official acts was Latin. Carolingian Empire is a modern term, not used by contemporaries.

Frankish forces campaigned almost every year. Charlemagne gathered an assembly around Easter and launched a campaign through the summer,. The population is estimated at between 10 and 20 million, and the empire held Franks, Alemanni, Bavarians, Frisians, Lombards, Romans, Celts, Basques and Slavs, whose ethnic identities helped decide which law codes applied to them.
carolingian-renaissance: The expression does not imply that Western Europe was barbaric before the Carolingians. Pierre Riché points out that the ancient schools did not vanish abruptly after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, and that Martianus Capella, Cassiodorus and Boethius kept the liberal arts alive. Irish monastic scriptoria spread over Europe, and Charlemagne's union of most of Western Europe brought peace and an economic revival.

Charlemagne found that many parish priests could not read the Vulgate Bible, which alarmed him because the clergy were to instruct his subjects. His Admonitio generalis of 789 and his letter De litteris colendis served as manifestos, and a capitulary of 787 ordered schools to be created. He drew leading scholars to court, among them Peter of Pisa, Paul the Deacon, the Spanish Goth Theodulf of Orléans and Alcuin of York, a Northumbrian monk who headed the Palace School from 782 to 796.

Alcuin wrote textbooks and word lists and established the trivium and quadrivium as the basis of education. Theodulf produced a scholarly edition of the Vulgate from manuscripts of Spain, Italy and Gaul, and the original Hebrew. At Corbie and Tours scribes developed Carolingian minuscule, a book-hand with lower-case letters, consistent letter heights, punctuation and spaces between words. Renaissance humanists later took it for Roman script. Carolingian workshops produced an estimated 100,000 manuscripts in the 9th century, of which some 6,000 to 7,000 survive, and the earliest surviving copies of Cicero, Horace, Lucretius and Julius Caesar are Carolingian.

Conrad Leyser notes that fewer than 2,000 Latin manuscripts survive from before 800, against over 7,000 from the century after. The Carolingians preserved texts through their own values, and Christian works were favoured, though secular texts were also kept. Some historians contest the word renaissance, since the project was a top-down initiative driven by royal patronage, unlike the later Italian movement, and recent writing tends to see it as a religious reform. Its effects were mostly limited to a small group of court scholars. John Contreni describes its effect on education and culture as spectacular, on art as debatable and on the moral regeneration of society as unmeasurable.
carpathian-mountains: The Carpathians form an arc across Central and Southeast Europe, about 1,500 kilometres long and covering 190,000 square kilometres. After the Alps they are the most extensive mountain system in Europe. They do not form an uninterrupted chain but consist of several geologically distinct groups, which run from the Western Carpathians through the Eastern Carpathians to the Southern Carpathians. Their width varies from 12 to 500 kilometres. The highest peak, Gerlachovský štít in the Tatra Mountains of Slovakia, rises 2,655 metres. About half the range lies in Romania, 21 per cent in Slovakia and 10 per cent each in Poland and Ukraine.

The mountains are separated from the Alps by the Danube and are surrounded on all sides by plains, among them the Pannonian plain to the south-west. They form the watershed between the northern seas and the Black Sea. They arose in the Alpine orogeny, in the Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras, and iron, gold and silver were found in great quantities in the Western Carpathians.

The name Carpates is first recorded in the Geographia of Ptolemy in the second century CE, though in most languages the modern form of the name is a neologism. It is strongly associated with the Dacian tribes called Carpes or Carpi, who lived east of the mountains. Late Roman documents called the Eastern Carpathians the Montes Sarmatici, the Sarmatian Mountains. Hungarian documents of the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries called them Thorchal or Tarczal, or less often Montes Nivium, the Snowy Mountains, and the Rus' chronicles called them the Hungarian Mountains.

The origin of the name is not firmly established. Some connect it with a root meaning rock or rugged, others with one meaning to turn, referring to the bend of the range. After the Roman emperor Trajan conquered Dacia, he brought back to Rome over 165 tons of gold and 330 tons of silver.

The mountains stretch through Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Poland, Ukraine, Romania and Serbia. They are habitat for the largest European populations of brown bears, wolves, chamois and lynxes, and they hold over a third of all European plant species. Romania has one third of Europe's thermal and mineral waters, many of them in the Carpathians. The area is the most seismically active in Central Europe, and the last volcanic activity occurred at Ciomadul about 30,000 years ago.
carpathian-ruthenia: The region rests on the southern slopes of the eastern Carpathian Mountains, bordered to the east and south by the Tisza River and to the west by the Hornád and Poprad rivers. It borders Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania. The landscape is mostly mountainous and the region is predominantly rural and infrastructurally underdeveloped. Its two major cities, Uzhhorod and Mukachevo, each have about 100,000 people. Most inhabitants regard themselves as Ukrainians or Rusyns, and there are also Hungarians, Romanians, Slovaks and Poles. Jews made up over 13 per cent of the population in 1930.

In the 8th and 9th centuries the Slavic tribe of White Croats densely settled the valleys on both slopes, and Kievan Rus' conquered those who stayed in the late 10th century. The Hungarians crossed the Carpathians in 896. In 1526 the region was divided between the Habsburg Kingdom of Hungary and the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, which became the Principality of Transylvania from 1570. The Union of Brest of 1595 and the Union of Uzhhorod of 1646 brought the region's Orthodox churches under the jurisdiction of Rome as Eastern Catholic churches. After 1867 it lay in the Hungarian part of Austria-Hungary.

After the First World War the region was briefly claimed by the West Ukrainian Republic, but for most of 1918 and 1919 it was held by the Hungarian Democratic Republic. The Treaty of St. Germain of 10 September 1919 granted the Carpathian Ruthenians autonomy, which Prague upheld only in part. In 1928 Czechoslovakia was divided into four provinces, one of them Subcarpathian Rus, with Užhorod as its capital until 1938. Under the First Vienna Award of November 1938 Czechoslovakia ceded the south of the region to Hungary, and in December the rest was renamed Carpathian Ukraine.

In March 1939 Carpathian Ukraine declared independence under Avhustyn Voloshyn, and Hungary occupied and annexed it, setting up the Governorate of Subcarpathia. The Red Army secured most of the region by 28 October 1944, and on 29 June 1945 Czechoslovakia signed a treaty with the Soviet Union ceding it. It became part of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic and remained part of Ukraine when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
carpentras: Carpentras is a commune in the Vaucluse department of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur in south-eastern France. It stands on the banks of the river Auzon, a tributary of the Sorgue, 23 kilometres south-west of Mont Ventoux and 23 kilometres north-east of Avignon. Its climate is borderline between humid subtropical and hot-summer Mediterranean, with cool winters and hot summers. Its Provençal Occitan name is Carpentràs, and its Latin name was Carpentoracte.

Greek merchants used the site as a commercial centre in ancient times. The Romans knew it at first as Carpentoracte Meminorum, a name mentioned by Pliny, and then renamed it Forum Neronis, the Forum of Nero. A Roman triumphal arch survives, enclosed by the bishops' palace, which was rebuilt in 1640 and is now a law court, along with a machicolated city gate, the Porte d'Orange.

At the beginning of the Avignon Papacy, Pope Clement V took up residence in Carpentras with the Roman Curia in 1313. His successor, Pope John XXII, settled definitively at Avignon. As capital of the Comtat Venaissin, the town was frequently the residence of the Avignon popes, and the Papal States kept the Venaissin until the French Revolution. Until 1791 Carpentras belonged to the Papal States, not to the Kingdom of France. After the coup of 18 Fructidor on 4 September 1797, counter-revolutionaries attacked its Hôtel de Ville on 22 October.

In the 18th century the Hôtel-Dieu was built between 1750 and 1760 at the commission of Joseph-Dominique d'Inguimbert. It now houses the Bibliothèque Inguimbertine. Carpentras has long been an important centre of French Judaism, and its synagogue, opened in 1367, is the oldest in France. In May 1990 the Jewish cemetery was desecrated, which caused a public uproar and a demonstration in Paris attended by 200,000 people, including President François Mitterrand.

Carpentras is a commercial centre for the Comtat Venaissin and is known for its black truffle market, held every Friday morning in the winter months. Its traditional confectionery is the berlingot, a small hard candy with thin white stripes, originally made from the syrup left over from preserving fruit. The Renaissance composer known as Carpentras, Elzéar Genet (c. 1470 to 1548), and the politician Édouard Daladier, prime minister of France at the start of the Second World War, were born there.
carrack: The carrack evolved from the single-masted cog and was first used for European trade between the Mediterranean and the Baltic. As the Portuguese and Spaniards pushed their trade south along Africa's Atlantic coast in the 15th century, they needed larger, more durable ships. They developed their own oceanic carracks by combining features of the ships they knew, with a more advanced rig that sailed well in the heavy winds and waves of the Atlantic and a hull that carried larger cargoes.

In its most developed form the carrack was carvel-built, stable in heavy seas and large enough to carry a big cargo and the provisions for very long voyages. Later carracks were square-rigged on the foremast and mainmast and lateen-rigged on the mizzenmast, with a high rounded stern, aftcastle, forecastle and bowsprit. The São Gabriel, a typical three-masted carrack, had six sails.

From 1498 Portugal began direct and regular exchanges with India through the Cape Route, a voyage of about six months that required substantial vessels. On average four carracks connected Lisbon to Goa, carrying gold to buy spices, mainly pepper, and from Goa one went on to Ming China to buy silk. From 1541 the Portuguese traded with Japan, exchanging Chinese silk for Japanese silver, and from 1550 the Crown leased the annual captaincy to Japan, giving exclusive rights to a single carrack each year. In 1557 they acquired Macau for this trade, which lasted until 1638, when Japan's rulers banned it for smuggling in Catholic priests. The Japanese called the ships Black Ships, kurofune, after their hulls.

Among the carracks named in the sources are the Grace Dieu, commissioned by Henry V of England and one of the largest ships in the world when launched in 1418, the Santa María of Columbus's voyage of 1492, the São Gabriel, flagship of Vasco da Gama in 1497, and the Flor de la Mar, built in 1502, which sank in 1512 with Afonso de Albuquerque and a large booty. The first galleons were developed from the carrack in the middle of the 16th century and came to replace it, although carracks were still in use in the middle of the 17th century because of their larger cargo capacity.
carrara: Carrara is a town in Tuscany on the Carrione River, some 100 kilometres west-northwest of Florence, notable for the white or blue-grey marble quarried there. Its name likely comes from a pre-Roman element, kar, meaning stone, through the Latin carrariae, quarries. Its motto, Fortitudo mea in rota, or My strength is in the wheel, refers to the wheel of the cart that carried marble blocks from the quarry. The Pantheon and Trajan's Column in Rome are built of Carrara marble, and many sculptures of the Renaissance were carved from it.

The Apuan Ligures lived in the region as early as the ninth century BCE. The present town grew from a borough built for workers in the marble quarries that the Romans opened after conquering Liguria in the early second century BCE. In the early Middle Ages it was a Byzantine and then a Lombard possession, and then it fell to the bishops of Luni, to whom Emperor Otto I gave it. It became a city-state in the early 13th century. The bishops regained it in 1230, and their rule ended in 1313, after which it passed to the republics of Pisa, Lucca and Florence, and later to Gian Galeazzo Visconti of Milan.

After the death of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1447 the Malaspina family fought for Carrara, and moved the seat of their lordship there in the second half of the 15th century. Carrara and Massa formed the Duchy of Massa and Carrara, which passed to the Duchy of Modena through the last Malaspina, Maria Teresa, who married Ercole III d'Este. At the end of the 19th century Carrara became the cradle of Italian anarchism, above all among the quarry workers and stone carvers, who led the Lunigiana revolt of January 1894. The Congress of Carrara in 1968 founded the International of Anarchist Federations.

The town lies in the province of Massa and Carrara. Its sights include the 12th-century cathedral and the Ducal Palace, also called the Palazzo Cybo Malaspina, which now houses the Fine Arts Academy and combines a 13th-century castle with a Renaissance palace begun in the late 16th century.
cartagena-colombia: Cartagena faces the Caribbean Sea in the north of Colombia, on a bay with two entrances, Bocachica in the south and Bocagrande in the north. Its position between the Magdalena and Sinú rivers gave easy access to the interior of New Granada and made it a main port for trade between Spain and its overseas empire, with its importance established by the early 1540s. Settlement by indigenous peoples around the bay dates from about 4000 BCE, and the Puerto Hormiga culture of the nearby coast produced the oldest ceramic objects found in the Americas.

Rodrigo de Bastidas travelled to the Pearl Coast and the Gulf of Urabá in 1500-01. On 14 January 1533 Pedro de Heredia entered the Bay of Cartagena under contract to Queen Joanna of Castile with three ships, 150 men and 22 horses. He found the village of Calamari abandoned, fought an all-day battle at Turbaco, and returned to Calamari in April with gold, including a solid gold porcupine weighing 132 pounds. In later expeditions he raided the gold tombs and temples of the Sinú. The city was founded on 1 June 1533 and named after Cartagena in Spain, and by extension after Carthage; Heredia governed it for 22 years and died on his return to Spain in 1544.

Cartagena was a centre of political, church and economic life in the Spanish Empire, a key port for exporting silver to Spain and for importing enslaved Africans under the asiento system, and it could be defended against pirate attacks. In the 18th century, after the Bourbon dynasty ended the Carrera de Indias convoys, it became the gateway to the Indies of Peru under the Viceroyalty of New Granada. It had 13,700 inhabitants by 1777. The Battle of Cartagena de Indias was fought here in 1741 during the War of Jenkins' Ear between Spain and Britain.

Cartagena was under Spanish rule for more than 275 years. On 4 June 1810, after the Peninsular War began, the Royal Commissioner Antonio Villavicencio and the city council banished the Spanish governor Francisco de Montes. A Supreme Junta was formed, and on 11 November a declaration of independence proclaimed a free and sovereign state, helped by the artisan leader Pedro Romero. The city is now the capital of the Bolívar Department, with 876,885 people at the 2018 census. Its colonial walled city and fortress were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.
cartago-costa-rica: Cartago was founded in 1563 by Juan Vásquez de Coronado and was the first successful establishment in Costa Rica. King Philip II of Spain granted it a coat of arms in 1565, and the Cortes gave it the title Muy Noble y Muy Leal in 1814. It served as the first capital of Costa Rica.

In 1823 the republican leader Gregorio José Ramírez moved the capital to the larger city of San José. Cartago had wanted to unite the newly independent province of Costa Rica with Iturbide's Mexican Empire, while San José and Alajuela supported a republican system. Major earthquakes severely damaged the city in 1822, 1841 and 1910. The eruption of the Irazú Volcano in 1963 badly damaged farmland around Cartago, but not the city itself.

Cartago stands at 1,435 metres above sea level at the base of the Irazú Volcano, and is the head city of Cartago canton in Cartago Province. Its Basílica de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles is the country's principal church, to which many pilgrims come on the feast day of the Virgin of the Angels, 2 August. It holds a statue of a Black Madonna known as La Negrita, believed to have healing powers.

According to folklore, an indigenous girl found the statue in 1635, though the only inhabitants of the area were then enslaved black and mulatto people living in a village named La Puebla. The rock where it was found is kept as a relic in the basilica. In the Plaza Mayor stand the Santiago Apóstol Parish Ruins, which are not true ruins but an unfinished building damaged by the 1910 earthquake. The Costa Rica Institute of Technology and the city museum are also in Cartago.
cartersville-georgia: Cartersville lies in south-central Bartow County, 42 miles north-west of downtown Atlanta and 76 miles south-east of Chattanooga, Tennessee. The Etowah River flows through a broad valley south of the downtown and on to Rome, where it forms the Coosa River. The city limits extend upriver as far as Allatoona Dam, which forms Lake Allatoona. Its highest point is the summit of Pine Mountain at 1,562 feet. The Etowah Indian Mounds, an archaeological Native American site, lie south of the city.

The town was founded by English-Americans in 1832 and was first called Birmingham. It was incorporated as Cartersville in 1854, taking the name of Col. Farish Carter of Milledgeville, the owner of a large plantation. It became the seat of Bartow County in 1867, after Sherman's March to the Sea during the American Civil War destroyed Cassville, and it was incorporated as a city in 1872. Amos Akerman, who lived there for a long time, was United States attorney general under President Ulysses S. Grant and led the federal prosecution of members of the Ku Klux Klan, which made him one of the most important public servants of the Reconstruction era.

On 26 February 1916 a mob of fifty men and boys took Jesse McCorkle, a Black man arrested the night before on an accusation of assaulting a woman, from the jail and lynched him in front of city hall. The evangelist Samuel Porter Jones also lived in Cartersville, and his house, Rose Lawn, is now a museum.

Cartersville is a city in north-western Georgia and the seat of Bartow County, at the north-west edge of the Atlanta metropolitan area, with 23,187 inhabitants in the 2020 census. Manufacturing, tourism and services are part of its economy. Its museums include the Booth Western Art Museum, the Tellus Science Museum and the Bartow History Museum in the old courthouse of about 1870. A Coca-Cola sign painted in 1894 on a downtown pharmacy wall is described as the world's first outdoor Coca-Cola sign.
carthage: Carthage was founded on the eastern side of the Lake of Tunis. Tradition credits Queen Elissa, or Dido, originally from Tyre, though her historicity has been questioned. In the myth she asked a local tribe for land and was told she could have as much as an oxhide could cover, so she cut the hide into strips and laid out the perimeter of the city. The name derives from the Punic qrt-ḥdšt, new city, implying a new Tyre. The Carthaginians were Phoenician settlers who spoke Canaanite, a Semitic language, and followed a local variety of Canaanite religion. Unlike other colonisers who required only respect from their colonies, Carthage is said to have sent its own magistrates to govern overseas settlements.

The city stood on a promontory between Sicily and the Tunisian coast, so that every ship crossing the sea passed it. It had two artificial harbours, one for a navy of 220 warships and one for trade, and walls described as 37 kilometres long, with the 4.0 to 4.8 kilometres across the isthmus truly massive and never penetrated. The Byrsa citadel stood roughly in the middle. The surrounding farmland, the Chora, was worked by Punic owners, and a retired general named Mago wrote a 28-volume work on agriculture in Punic, later translated into Latin and Greek and now lost except for passages in other Latin works.

Carthage contested the western Mediterranean with Greek cities in the Sicilian Wars and the Pyrrhic War, and with Rome in the Punic Wars. The Roman Republic destroyed the city in 146 BCE after a siege of nearly three years, the Byrsa being the last place to fall.

Gaius Gracchus founded a short-lived colony there by 122 BCE, and Julius Caesar built a new city between 49 and 44 BCE. By the first century it was the second-largest city in the western half of the Roman Empire, with a peak population of 500,000, and the centre of the province of Africa. In 698 Hasan ibn al-Nu'man defeated Emperor Tiberios III in the Battle of Carthage, and the Umayyad forces destroyed Roman Carthage, tearing down its walls and cutting its aqueducts to prevent a Byzantine return. In the 13th century the Crusaders took it from the Hafsids, massacring its inhabitants in the Eighth Crusade, and the Hafsids then destroyed its defences.

Christian Tuxen Falbe surveyed the site in 1830, and Charles Ernest Beulé, Alfred Louis Delattre and French archaeologists after 1921 excavated it. Scholars disagree on whether child sacrifice was practised in ancient Carthage. Carthage became a municipality in 1919 as a suburb of Tunis, and the ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
cartography: What counts as the earliest known map is debated, partly because the term map is not well defined and some artifacts that might be maps may be something else. A wall painting that might depict the ancient Anatolian city of Çatalhöyük has been dated to the late 7th millennium BCE, and prehistoric alpine rock carvings at Mount Bego in France and Valcamonica in Italy, dated to the 4th millennium BCE, are widely interpreted as showing cultivated plots.

Other maps of the ancient world include the Minoan House of the Admiral wall painting of about 1600 BCE, showing a seaside community in oblique perspective, and an engraved map of the Babylonian city of Nippur from the Kassite period. The oldest surviving world maps are from Babylonia of the 9th century BCE; one shows Babylon on the Euphrates, surrounded by Assyria, Urartu and several cities, all encircled by a bitter river.

Cartography is the study and practice of making and using maps, combining science, aesthetics and technique. Its traditional objectives are to select the traits to be mapped, to represent terrain on flat media through map projections, to remove irrelevant characteristics through generalization, and to arrange the elements of the map to convey its message.

Maps are divided into general maps, made for a general audience, and thematic maps, which concern specific geographic themes, such as a map of corn production. A topographic map describes a place, with contour lines showing elevation, while a topological map disregards scale and detail to communicate route information; Beck's London Underground map is the usual example.

About 1,100 medieval European mappae mundi survive, of which some 900 illustrate manuscripts. In 1154 the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi produced his atlas Tabula Rogeriana, and his world map, mostly Ptolemaic in conception, remained the most accurate for the next three centuries. In 1492 Martin Behaim, advisor to King John II of Portugal, made the oldest extant globe, and Hartmann Schedel was among the first to use the printing press for maps.

The Selden map, made by a Chinese cartographer around 1620, though historians debate the date, shows trading routes, a compass rose and a scale bar. Enlightenment maps used copper plate intaglio rather than woodcut, and mapmakers often plagiarized: Herman Moll's Beaver Map of 1715 closely reproduces Nicolas de Fer's work of 1698. Some scholars argue that maps are inherently biased, and that cartography served imperial power in the conquest of Africa.
casablanca: Casablanca stands on the Atlantic coast of the Chaouia plain in the central-western part of Morocco. It has about 3.22 million inhabitants in the urban area, making it the most populous city in the Maghreb, and its port is one of the largest artificial ports in Africa. Before the 15th century the settlement was called Anfa. The sociologist André Adam favoured a Tamazight origin for the name, such as anfa meaning hill or promontory on the sea, though he found the information insufficient to say which.

Berbers settled the area by the seventh century BCE, and the Phoenicians and then the Romans used it as a port. Under the Merinids in the 14th century Anfa rose in importance as a port, and after the last Merinids were ousted in 1465 it became independent again, a safe harbour for pirates and privateers. The Portuguese bombarded it into ruins in 1468, and the town that grew up around it was called Casa Branca, white house.

Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah built the port and rebuilt the town between 1756 and 1790, after the earthquake of 1755. It was named ad-Dār al-Bayḍāʼ, the Arabic translation of Casa Branca. In the 19th century it grew as a supplier of wool to the British textile industry. The Treaty of Algeciras of 1906 formalised French preeminence in Morocco, and the Treaty of Fez of March 1912 established the French protectorate. The population rose from about 12,000 to 110,000 by 1921, largely through shanty towns.

Casablanca hosted the Anfa, or Casablanca, Conference in January 1943, where Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt discussed the progress of the war, with Charles de Gaulle and Henri Giraud attending in minor roles. In the 1940s and 1950s it was a major centre of anti-French rioting.
casale-monferrato: Casale Monferrato lies in the province of Alessandria in Piedmont, about 60 kilometres east of Turin, on the right bank of the Po, where the river runs at the foot of the Montferrat hills. An ancient Roman municipium, it has been the most important trade and manufacturing centre of the area for centuries. Its origins are fairly obscure. A Gaulish settlement called Vardacate stood on the Po here, and by the beginning of the 8th century a small town under Lombard rule, probably called Sedula or Sedulia, occupied the site.

The cult of Saint Evasius, said by late and unreliable accounts to have been beheaded here with 146 followers, flourished, and by 988 the town was known as Casale di Sant'Evasio. In the time of Charlemagne it came under the bishops of Vercelli, and Frederick Barbarossa freed it from their power. Troops from Vercelli, Alessandria and Milan sacked it in 1215, and it was rebuilt and fortified in 1220. It fell under the Marquess of Montferrat in 1292 and later became the capital of the marquessate. The Visconti of Milan held it from 1370 to 1404. The condottiere Facino Cane was born there.

In the 15th and early 16th centuries Casale was the capital of the House of Palaiologos, and in 1471 William VIII, Marquess of Montferrat, made it the permanent seat of his court. In 1536 it passed to the Gonzagas of Mantua, who fortified it strongly. It was besieged during the War of the Mantuan Succession. In 1745, after the Piedmontese defeat at the Battle of Bassignano, French and Spanish troops occupied it and damaged many buildings; the Baroque rebuilding that followed shaped the town's appearance. During the Wars of Italian Independence it resisted the Austrians in 1849 and was strengthened in 1852. Its Jewish ghetto lasted until the emancipation of the Jews in Piedmont after Charles Albert granted a constitution in 1848.

Limestone deposits in the nearby hills led to the opening of several cement factories in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and Casale became known as the cement capital of Italy. An Eternit asbestos-cement factory operated there from 1907 to 1986, and some 1,800 deaths from mesothelioma and other asbestos-related diseases in the area have been linked to it.

The historic centre is built around Piazza Mazzini, the site of the Roman forum. Nearby are the Lombard Romanesque cathedral of Sant'Evasio, founded in 742 and consecrated in 1107, and the 11th-century Torre Civica. The castle of the Paleologi is a 15th-century hexagonal fortress with four round towers and a moat. The synagogue, built in 1595, is recognised as one of the most beautiful in Europe and its women's galleries hold a Jewish museum. Casale is also known for krumiri biscuits.
casbah-of-algiers: The Casbah lies at the centre of Algiers and forms its historic core, on a slope with a height difference of 118 metres facing the Mediterranean. It has a triangular shape with its base on the Bay of Algiers, so that from the sea it appears as a pyramid or triangular amphitheatre. Its narrow, winding streets, some ending in dead ends or vaulted passages called sabat, are closed to cars, and donkeys have been used for rubbish collection since the Regency. The name comes from the citadel above, the Arabic al-qaṣabah, and originally meant the highest point of the old city before it came to mean the whole medina.

A Phoenician port called Ikosim was probably founded at Algiers after the late 6th century BCE, and it later became a Roman city, Icosium. The medina itself was built in the 10th century by Bologhin Ibn Ziri of the Zirid dynasty on the ruins of the Roman city, in the territory of the Berber Beni Mezghenna. The name Al-Djaza'ir, the Islets, probably refers to the islands that once faced the port.

In 1529 the Barbarossa brothers expelled the Spanish from the Peñón islet, and Aruj Barbarossa joined it to the mainland to make a port, turning Algiers into the main base for corsairs in the western Mediterranean and capital of its regency. Charles V's expedition failed in 1541, and the city was then enclosed with a wall and gates such as Bab Azoun and Bab El Oued. The citadel was begun in 1597 and became the seat of the dey's power in 1817.

The French entered Algiers on 5 July 1830. They demolished much of the lower Casbah, built what is now Place des Martyrs and pulled down the walls. In 1956 leaders of the FLN, among them Abane Ramdane, Larbi Ben M'hidi and Krim Belkacem, settled in the Casbah, which offered hideouts, couriers and clandestinity for urban guerrilla warfare. After independence many native families moved to European-style apartments elsewhere.

The Casbah has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992. Its houses, typically 30 to 60 square metres and presenting a single façade, are grouped close together, a pattern thought to date from the Zirid era. Its palaces include Dar Aziza and Dar Hassan Pacha, and its mosques include Jamaa Ketchaoua, Jamaa el Kebir and Jamaa el Jdid. The Thaâlibiyya Madrasa of 1904 is in the neo-Moorish style. Many films were shot there, among them Pépé le Moko (1937) and Gillo Pontecorvo's The Battle of Algiers (1969).
casimir-iii-the-great: Casimir was born on 30 April 1310 in Kowal in Kuyavia, the third son of Władysław I Łokietek and Jadwiga of Kalisz. His father was crowned king in Kraków on 20 January 1320, and in 1325 Casimir married Aldona of Lithuania, daughter of Grand Duke Gediminas, an alliance sought against the Teutonic Order. The war against Bohemia, Brandenburg and the Teutonic Order went badly for Poland, and when his father died on 2 March 1333 Casimir inherited a small, weakened realm of two ravaged provinces, Lesser Poland and Greater Poland.

Casimir was crowned at Wawel Cathedral on 25 April 1333. John of Bohemia was still widely regarded as the rightful king of Poland, and Casimir's main strength was his alliance with Hungary. An arbitration at Visegrád in November 1335 returned Dobrzyń Land and Kuyavia to Poland, while Casimir renounced Pomerania and the Chełmno Land to the Teutonic Order. He accepted the loss of Silesia to Bohemia and turned east, conquering Galicia-Volhynia, known as Red Ruthenia, which roughly doubled the kingdom and opened access to Black Sea trade.

At the Sejm in Wiślica on 11 March 1347 he sanctioned civil and criminal codes for Greater and Lesser Poland, which earned him the title the Polish Justinian. About thirty towns received walls and some fifty castles were built, and towns grew under Magdeburg rights. In 1364, with the permission of Pope Urban V, he founded the University of Kraków. On 9 October 1334 he confirmed the privileges granted to Jews in 1264 and allowed them to settle in large numbers.

Casimir left no legitimate son. In 1355, at Buda, he named his nephew Louis I of Hungary as heir should he have no male child. After Casimir died in 1370, Louis travelled quickly to Kraków, had a will that adopted another heir set aside by bribing the nobles with future privileges, and was proclaimed king. Casimir was the last Piast king of Poland.
casimir-iv-jagiellon: Casimir was the third and youngest son of King Władysław II Jagiełło and his fourth wife, Sophia of Halshany, who was 40 to 50 years younger than her husband. This prompted rumours of adultery, and after Casimir's birth Sophia swore an oath of innocence and the charges were dismissed. Many of the children closely resembled their elderly father. Casimir was baptised on 21 December 1427.

In 1440, after the assassination of Sigismund Kęstutaitis, Lithuanian magnates led by Jonas Goštautas invited the thirteen-year-old Casimir to Vilnius, and the Council of Lords proclaimed him Grand Duke of Lithuania on 29 June 1440, contrary to the wishes of Polish nobles. In his reign the rights of the Lithuanian nobility were put on an equal footing with those of the Polish szlachta.

Władysław III died at Varna in 1444, and after a three-year interregnum Casimir was elected King of Poland and crowned on 25 June 1447. In 1454 the Prussian Confederation asked his help against the Teutonic Order, and the Thirteen Years' War began. The Polish army crushed the Teutonic force at Świecino in September 1462, and the Order's fleet was sunk at the Vistula Lagoon a year later. In the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 the Order recognised Polish sovereignty over Royal Prussia and overlordship over the rest of its state.

In 1454 Casimir married Elizabeth of Austria, which tied the house of Jagiellon to Hungary and Bohemia. His son Vladislaus II was crowned King of Hungary in 1490, having been King of Bohemia. Casimir's Code of 1468, the Grand Duchy's first unified code of criminal and procedural law, was written in Ruthenian.

Casimir died on 7 June 1492 and was buried in the Holy Cross Chapel of Wawel Cathedral, in a red marble tomb by Veit Stoss. John I Albert succeeded him as King of Poland and Alexander became Grand Duke of Lithuania. His children included Vladislaus II, three kings of Poland and Saint Casimir, who chose religious life. Under Casimir the Jagiellonian dynasty became one of the leading royal houses of Europe.
caspar-david-friedrich: Friedrich was the sixth of ten children, raised in the strict Lutheran creed of his father Adolf Gottlieb Friedrich, a candle-maker and soap boiler. Records of the family's finances are contradictory; some sources say the children were privately tutored, others that they lived in relative poverty. He knew death early: his mother Sophie died in 1781, a sister a year later, and another sister in 1791. In 1787 he witnessed his younger brother Johann Christoffer, aged thirteen, fall through the ice of a frozen lake and drown.

He studied in Copenhagen from 1794 to 1798, then settled permanently in Dresden. There he made etchings and designs for woodcuts, but he worked mainly in ink, watercolour and sepia, and did not work extensively in oils until his reputation was more established.

His landscapes, mostly of northern Germany, were inspired by trips from 1801 to the Baltic coast, Bohemia, the Krkonoše and the Harz Mountains. He made pencil studies of places such as the cliffs on Rügen and the Elbe, but rendered the atmospheric effects of mist, sun and moon from memory. His key innovation was to treat landscape not as a backdrop subordinated to human drama but as a self-contained emotive subject. He often used the Rückenfigur, a person seen from behind, to draw the viewer into sharing the contemplation of nature.

Resentment of the French occupation of Pomerania in 1813 led him to put motifs from German folklore in his work. In Old Heroes' Graves (1812) and Fir Forest with the French Dragoon and the Raven (c. 1813) he conveyed political symbols by means of the landscape alone, a first in the history of art. He suffered depressive episodes, and after 1826 vultures, owls, graveyards and ruins became permanent motifs, while his colours grew darker.

Friedrich married Caroline Bommer on 21 January 1818, and found patrons in Russia: Grand Duke Nikolai Pavlovich visited his studio in 1820, and the poet Vasily Zhukovsky helped him for decades. His reputation nevertheless fell over his last fifteen years, and he lived as a recluse in relative poverty. A first stroke in June 1835 greatly reduced his ability to paint. He died in Dresden on 7 May 1840, little noticed by the artistic community.

A Berlin exhibition of thirty-two of his works in 1906 began a renewed appreciation. He influenced Expressionist artists and the Surrealists, among them Max Ernst. The Nazis used his work to promote their ideology in the 1930s, and the association damaged his reputation for decades. Scholars later placed him in a purely art-historical context, and since the 1970s he has been regarded as one of the most important artists of German Romanticism.
caspe: Caspe lies 104 kilometres south-east of Zaragoza on the banks of the Guadalope river, a few kilometres from the Ebro, in one of the most arid areas of Aragon. A popular belief derives the name from ancient inhabitants from the Caspian Sea, but this lacks philological support. The name appears in Andalusi sources as Qsp, Qasp or Qasb, and may be related to an Arabic word or to an Indo-European root meaning oak.

The area was among the last of Lower Aragon to be settled, although a biface of 150,000 to 100,000 years ago shows the passage of Neanderthal hunter-gatherers. Towns and tumular necropolises of the Celtic Hallstatt culture appeared around the 8th century BCE. From 713 to the Christian reconquest in the first half of the 12th century the lands of the Ebro formed the northernmost mark of Al-Andalus. King Alfonso II of Aragon took Caspe between June and September 1169, in a campaign led by Arnau Mir de Tost, Count of Pallars. Until 1610 Christian and Muslim communities lived in the town, each with its own municipal area.

Because of its position Caspe suffered in many of Spain's conflicts from the 17th century. In the War of the Spanish Succession it supported the Bourbon cause while its neighbours chose the Austrian claimant. French troops occupied it from June 1809 to 1813, and the local lawyer Agustín de Quinto, who collaborated with them, was named commissar of the left bank of the Ebro, which made Caspe capital of the lower half of Aragon. In June 1813 Colonel Ramón Gayán retook it after a siege of fifteen days, using tunnels to blow up part of the castle where the French were barricaded.

The Statute of Autonomy of Aragon of 1936, also called the Statute of Caspe, was drafted in the town. During the Spanish Civil War it was the seat of the anarchist Regional Defense Council of Aragon, which a military intervention dissolved in August 1937, when the 11th Division under Enrique Líster arrested its president, Joaquín Ascaso.

Caspe is the seat of the comarca of Bajo Aragón-Caspe, and its municipality of 503 square kilometres is the fourth largest in Aragon. Its heritage includes the Plano del Pulido cave paintings, declared a World Heritage Site in 1998, the Roman Miralpeix Mausoleum and the remains of the Castle of the Commitment, built by the knights of the Hospital Order.
caspian-sea: The Caspian Sea is an endorheic basin lying east of the Caucasus, west of the steppe of Central Asia, south of the plains of Southern Russia and north of the Iranian Plateau. It covers 371,000 square kilometres, stretches 1,200 kilometres from north to south with an average width of 320 kilometres, and lies about 27 metres below sea level. Its salinity is about a third of that of average seawater. The Volga, Europe's longest river, is its main freshwater inflow, entering at the shallow north end.

Like the Black Sea, it is a remnant of the ancient Paratethys Sea, and it became landlocked in the Late Miocene, about 5.5 million years ago, through tectonic uplift and a fall in sea level. The Caspian seal is the only aquatic mammal endemic to it, and the sea is known for its caviar and oil industries.

The earliest hominid remains found around the Caspian are from Dmanisi, about 1.8 million years old, and finds in the Hotu and Kamarband caves in Iran suggest human habitation south of the sea as early as 11,000 years ago. The sea's name derives from the ancient Caspi people, who lived to its southwest. Strabo wrote that the territory called Caspiane was named after the Caspian tribe, as was the sea, but that the tribe had disappeared. Greeks and Persians in antiquity called it the Hyrcanian Sea.

Other names reflect later powers. Arabic writers called it the sea of the Khazars, and Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen still call it the Khazar sea after the Khazar Khaganate, a large empire based north of the sea between the 7th and 10th centuries. Since the medieval period traders reached it by portages linking the Volga with the Don and with rivers flowing into the Baltic, and canals followed from the early 18th century. Its shores were bordered in turn by Safavid, Afsharid, Zand, Qajar and Pahlavi Iran, and by the Tsardom of Russia, the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union.

Five states border the sea along about 4,800 kilometres of coastline: Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan. A treaty of 1931 between Iran and the Soviet Union stated that the sea belonged to both. Whether it is in law a sea or a lake was long debated among the five, because the answer decides access to oil and natural gas, fishing and international waters.
cassander: Cassander was a son of Antipater and a contemporary of Alexander the Great. He was taught by the philosopher Aristotle at the Lyceum in Macedonia and educated beside Alexander with Hephaestion, Ptolemy and Lysimachus. His family were distant collateral relatives of the Argead dynasty. At 25 he still sat upright at dinner, evidently not having killed a boar unaided, which has been taken to suggest ill health or disability.

He is first recorded at Alexander's court in Babylon in 323 BCE, sent by Antipater, most likely to uphold his father's regency, though a later hostile writer claimed he went to poison the king. He returned to Macedonia and helped his father govern, and from 321 to 320 BCE served as chiliarch to Antigonus, probably to watch him.

When Antipater neared death in 319 BCE he gave the regency to Polyperchon, not Cassander. Cassander rejected this, sought the support of Antigonus, Ptolemy and Lysimachus, destroyed Polyperchon's fleet, put Athens under Demetrius of Phaleron and declared himself regent in 317 BCE. He besieged Olympias in Pydna, and when the city fell in spring 316 BCE she was killed; Alexander IV and Roxana were confined at Amphipolis. Cassander married Alexander's half-sister Thessalonike and founded Thessalonica and Cassandreia, and rebuilt Thebes.

Alexander IV and Roxana were secretly poisoned in 310 or 309 BCE, and Cassander bribed Polyperchon to kill Heracles. He proclaimed himself king in 305 BCE. From 307 to 304 BCE he fought Athens, and Demetrius Poliorcetes drove him from central Greece. He then rebuilt the coalition with Lysimachus, Ptolemy and Seleucus against Antigonus, who was killed at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE.

After Ipsus Cassander held Macedon undisputed, but he died of dropsy in 297 BCE. His dynasty did not last: his son Philip died of natural causes, and his sons Alexander and Antipater fought each other. Demetrius I ended it by killing Alexander V and founding the Antigonid dynasty.

Cassander stood out among the Diadochi in his hostility to Alexander's memory; Arrian reported that he could not pass a statue of Alexander without feeling faint. He is seen as ambitious and unscrupulous and was responsible for the deaths of more Argeads than other Diadochi, but John D. Grainger argues this owes much to stories spread by his rivals. His refounding of Therma as Thessalonica, named for his wife, was of lasting significance.
cassava: Cassava, Manihot esculenta, is a woody shrub of the spurge family, native to South America and grown for its starchy tuberous root. Its wild ancestor, a subspecies called flabellifolia, is centred in west-central Brazil, where cassava was likely first domesticated no more than 10,000 years ago. Cassava pollen appears in the Gulf of Mexico lowlands by 4600 BCE. The oldest direct evidence of cultivation comes from the 1,400-year-old Maya site of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador. By the time of European contact in 1492 it was a staple of peoples of northern South America, southern Mesoamerica and the Taino of the Caribbean, who grew it by a high-yielding form of shifting agriculture.

Cassava is grown in sweet and bitter varieties. Both contain cyanogenic glycosides, but the bitter ones hold far more, up to about 1,000 milligrams of cyanide per kilogram of fresh root against as little as 20 in sweet ones. Improper preparation can therefore cause poisoning. The Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean removed the poison by peeling, grinding and mashing the root, pressing the mash through a basket tube called a sebucan or tipiti, and drying and sieving it into flour. Cassava starch is called tapioca, and the Brazilian farofa and West African garri are coarse flours made by grating, pressing and roasting the root.

Cassava is the third-largest source of carbohydrates in the tropics, after rice and maize, and more than 500 million people depend on it. It tolerates drought and poor soil, and it yields more food energy per hectare each day than rice, wheat or maize. It has several uses besides food, including cassava beers such as the Brazilian cauim, animal feed and laundry starch. Haitian bambouri and Jamaican bammy combine Indigenous Caribbean cassava cooking with African practice. The Tupí myth of Maní tells that manioc sprang from the grave of an Indigenous girl of that name. Viruses such as the African cassava mosaic virus, which caused a major famine in Africa in the 1920s, remain a serious threat.
cassiodorus: Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator was born at Scylletium, near present-day Catanzaro in Calabria, into a family of Syrian origin. Senator was part of his surname, not his rank. His family had served the state for generations: his great-grandfather held a command defending the coasts of southern Italy against Vandal sea-raiders, his grandfather appears in a Roman embassy to Attila the Hun, and his father of the same name served Odovacer and then Theoderic the Great, finally as Praetorian Prefect. Cassiodorus began his career about his twentieth year as his father's consiliarius, a legal adviser in complex cases.

He was quaestor sacri palatii from about 507 to 511, consul in 514 and later magister officiorum under Theoderic and under the regency for Theoderic's young successor Athalaric. At Ravenna his rhetorical skill led to his drafting important public documents. He rose to praetorian prefect for Italy, effectively the head of the Ostrogothic civil government. James O'Donnell considers it almost indisputable that in 523 he accepted advancement as the immediate successor of Boethius, who was imprisoned and later executed, and notes that Cassiodorus's letters never mention it.

Athalaric died in early 534, and the rest of Cassiodorus's public career was dominated by the Byzantine reconquest and Ostrogothic dynastic intrigue. His last letters were drafted in the name of Vitiges. Around 537–38 he left Italy for Constantinople, where he stayed for almost two decades, concentrating on religious questions. He had earlier worked with Pope Agapetus I on a plan for a library of Greek and Latin texts to support a Christian school in Rome. In retirement he founded the monastery of Vivarium on his family estates on the shore of the Ionian Sea.

His writings include the Chronica, ending at 519, a Gothic History of 526 to 533 known only through the abridgment by Jordanes, the Variae epistolae, Theoderic's state papers, and an Exposition of the Psalms. The Institutiones divinarum et saecularium litterarum, written between 543 and 555, guided the monks' studies in place of the school he had planned in Rome. Its first book treats Christian texts and its second the liberal arts, which he valued mainly as aids to the study of divinity. His last known work, De orthographia of about 580, was completed when he was 93.

Vivarium had a communal monastery and a retreat for hermits, apparently without a strict rule. Cassiodorus had a complete Bible in a single volume, the Codex Grandior, made for his monks. Ceolfrith bought it in 679–80 and took it to Wearmouth Jarrow, where it served as the model for the Codex Amiatinus. The library was later dispersed, but his promotion of regular manuscript copying in monasteries helped preserve classical and Christian literature.
cassius-dio: Lucius Cassius Dio was the son of Cassius Apronianus, a Roman senator of the Cassia gens who was born and raised at Nicaea in Bithynia. Byzantine tradition holds that his mother was the daughter or sister of the Greek orator and philosopher Dio Chrysostom, though this has been disputed. Although Dio was a Roman citizen he wrote in Greek. He kept a love for Nicaea, which he called my home, while he described his villa at Capua as the place where he spent his time whenever he was in Italy.

For most of his life Dio served the state. He was a senator under Commodus and became a suffect consul in about 205. After the death of Septimius Severus he was governor of Smyrna, and he was also proconsul in Africa and in Pannonia. Severus Alexander held him in the highest esteem and made him consul a second time in 229. In his later years Dio went back to Bithynia, where he died. He was either the grandfather or the great-grandfather of another Cassius Dio, consul in 291.

Dio's Roman History, written in Greek in 80 books, began with the arrival of Aeneas in Italy and the founding of Rome by his descendant Romulus, and ran through the Republic and Empire to 229 CE. By his own account he spent ten years collecting the achievements of the Romans down to the death of Severus in 211, and twelve more composing the work. Until the first century BCE he gives only a summary of events; after that his accounts become more detailed. It is one of only three written Roman sources for the revolt of Boudica in 60 to 61 CE.

The work survives unevenly. The first 21 books are partly reconstructed from fragments and from the 12th-century epitome of Joannes Zonaras, and books 22 to 35 were already lost by his time. Books 36 to 54, covering 65 to 12 BCE, are nearly complete, as are books 56 to 60, from 9 to 54 CE. For the last twenty books only fragments and the abridgement by the 11th-century monk John Xiphilinus remain. Dio has often been dismissed as unreliable, but some recent scholars have stressed the sophistication of his political and historical interpretation.
caste: A caste is a fixed social group into which an individual is born within a system of social stratification. Members are expected to marry only within the same caste, to follow lifestyles often linked to a particular occupation, and to hold a ritual status within a hierarchy. Interaction between castes follows cultural notions of exclusion, with some castes considered more pure and others more polluted. The standard ethnographic example is the division of India's Hindu society into rigid groups, whose roots lie in South Asia's ancient history. Scholars have used it as a model for studying caste-like divisions elsewhere.

The English word comes from the Spanish and Portuguese casta, which a Spanish dictionary of 1569 defined as race, lineage, tribe or breed, and which derives from a Gothic word for a group of animals. The Portuguese, the first Europeans to reach India by sea in 1498, were the first to use casta in its modern sense, applying it to the thousands of endogamous, hereditary Indian groups they met. The spelling caste with this meaning is first attested in English in 1613.

In India the system rests on an old four-fold theoretical classification called varna, Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra, laid over the social groups called jāti. One 2016 genetic study concluded that endogamous jatis originated during the Gupta Empire. From 1901 British census authorities sorted all jatis into the four varna categories. Today there are around 3,000 castes and 25,000 sub-castes in India.

Writers have reported caste systems in many regions. In Nigeria the osu caste among the Igbo is determined by birth and brings ostracism. In Rwanda and Burundi the Maquet study of 1961 described the Tutsi, Hutu and Twa as ranked by birth. The Songhai economy was based on a caste system, with metalworkers, fishermen and carpenters among the most common groups. In Bali, ethnographers described three or four castes modelled on the Indian pattern. For centuries the Cagots of the Pyrenees and the Basque provinces were treated as an inferior caste and obliged to use separate church doors.

In colonial Spanish America, mixed-race groups were called castas, but the social order was otherwise fluid, and scholars dispute how far the Latin American and South Asian systems can be compared. The term is also used in biology for groups of ants and bees, which early observers named after the Indian system. Some scholars, such as Heidi Fjeld for pre-1950s Tibet, argue that other societies were functionally caste systems, while others reject the label.
castel-santangelo: The tomb of the Roman emperor Hadrian was erected on the right bank of the Tiber between 134 and 139. Originally it was a decorated cylinder with a garden on top and a golden quadriga. Hadrian's ashes were placed there a year after his death at Baiae in 138, together with those of his wife Sabina and of his first adopted son, Lucius Aelius, who died in 138. The remains of later emperors were also deposited there, the last recorded being Caracalla in 217. Hadrian also built the Pons Aelius, which faces the mausoleum and still gives an approach from the centre of Rome.

The building became a military fortress in 401 and was included in the Aurelian Walls under Flavius Honorius Augustus. Visigoth looters scattered the urns and ashes during Alaric's sack of Rome in 410. When the Goths besieged Rome in 537, the defenders threw the original bronze and stone statuary down upon them, as Procopius recounts. Stone from the tomb was later reused: Giorgio Vasari writes that columns were taken from it for Saint Peter's. The capstone of a funerary urn, probably Hadrian's, ended up in Saint Peter's Basilica, covered the tomb of Otto II and was later built into a Renaissance baptistery.

The popes turned the structure into a castle, beginning in the 14th century, and linked it to Saint Peter's Basilica by a covered fortified corridor, the Passetto di Borgo. Pope Clement VII took refuge there from the Landsknechte of Charles V during the Sack of Rome in 1527. Leo X built a chapel, and Paul III added a rich apartment so that a pope would have a fitting place to stay in any later siege. The Papal State also used it as a prison, and Giordano Bruno, held there for six years, and Benvenuto Cellini were among its prisoners.

According to legend, the Archangel Michael appeared on top of the mausoleum and sheathed his sword to mark the end of the plague of 590, which gave the castle its present name. In 1536 Raffaello da Montelupo made a marble statue of Saint Michael to stand on the roof. Peter Anton von Verschaffelt's bronze statue of the same subject replaced it in 1753, and Montelupo's can be seen in a courtyard inside. The castle is the setting for the third act of Giacomo Puccini's opera Tosca of 1900. It was decommissioned in 1901 and is now the Museo Nazionale di Castel Sant'Angelo.
castor-and-pollux: Castor and Pollux, or Polydeuces, are twin half-brothers whose mother was Leda. The sources disagree about their parentage. In the Homeric Odyssey they are sons of Tyndareus alone, the king of Sparta, and in the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women sons of Zeus. Pindar's Nemean Odes gives the conventional account, in which only Pollux was fathered by Zeus, which explains why Pollux was granted immortality and Castor was mortal. In the Iliad, Helen says that her brothers are dead and buried at home in Lacedaemon, which suggests that in some early traditions both were mortal. Scholars connect them with the Indo-European horse twins, such as the Vedic Ashvins.

Both brothers were excellent horsemen and hunters. They took part in the hunt of the Calydonian Boar and joined the crew of the Argo, on which Pollux defeated King Amycus of the Bebryces in a boxing contest. When Theseus abducted their sister Helen, they invaded Attica to rescue her and took Theseus's mother Aethra to Sparta as her slave.

They then carried off the Leucippides, Phoebe and Hilaeira, who were betrothed to their cousins Idas and Lynceus. A cattle raid ended in a quarrel, and Idas fatally wounded Castor with a spear. Pollux killed Lynceus, and Zeus struck Idas dead with a thunderbolt. Zeus then offered Pollux a choice between all of Olympus and sharing his immortality with his dying brother. Pollux chose to share it, so the twins alternate between Olympus and Hades. They became the two brightest stars of the constellation Gemini, and were said to appear to sailors as St. Elmo's fire. They were regarded as patrons of travellers, sailors, horsemen and athletes, intervening at moments of crisis.

The twins were important at Sparta. A symbol of them was two upright posts joined by crossbars, called dokana, and it was carried before the army in the field. Their grave-shrine was at Therapne, across the Eurotas from Sparta. The Etruscans venerated them as Kastur and Pultuce.

The Romans revered them from the 5th century BCE, probably through the Greek colonies of Magna Graecia. According to legend the twins fought at the head of the Roman army at the Battle of Lake Regillus and brought the news of victory to Rome, and the temple of Castor and Pollux was built in the Roman Forum to fulfil a vow made after that battle. On 15 July, their feast day, 1,800 equestrians paraded through Rome. After the rise of Christianity, Pope Gelasius I in the 5th century still attested a cult of the Castores that people did not want to abandon, and the church adopted Saints Peter and Paul in place of the twins as patrons of travellers.
castries: Castries stands on a flood plain and is built on reclaimed land, laid out in a grid. Its sheltered, deep-water harbour gave the settlement its first name, Carénage, a French word meaning safe anchorage. The harbour receives cargo vessels, ferries and cruise ships. Morne Fortune, a hill of 258 metres, rises above the city and carries Fort Charlotte.

In 1650 a group of 40 Frenchmen led by de Rousselan founded a fort near the Petit Cul-de-Sac and the Carénage river, when the island of Saint Lucia had been purchased from the French West India Company by du Parquet and Houel. Governor Baron de Micoud moved the capital to the south side of the harbour in 1769. The village of Carénage was renamed Castries after Charles Eugène Gabriel de La Croix, marquis de Castries, the French Minister of the Navy and Colonies; his title comes from a commune in southern France.

Castries has been rebuilt many times after major fires, on 15 October 1805, on 6 April 1813 and, most severely, on 19 June 1948. Under British rule a wharf was built to serve the coal trade, and the first steamship, the RMS Solway, arrived in 1841. On 9 March 1942 the German submarine U-161 entered the harbour at night and sank two Allied ships, among them the Canadian ocean liner RMS Lady Nelson, which was refloated and taken to Canada to be converted into a hospital ship.

Castries is the capital and largest city of Saint Lucia and the seat of government, with an urban population of about 20,000 and a district of just under 70,000. Landmarks include the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, the Government House and Derek Walcott Square, renamed from Columbus Square for the island's Nobel Prize-winning poet, who was born in the city, as was the economist Arthur Lewis. The city also hosts the secretariat of the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States and the headquarters of the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court.
castro-urdiales: Castro Urdiales was originally called Portus Amanum and was the chief city of the Autrigones. In 74 a Roman colony was established there under the name Flaviobriga, in the reign of Vespasian, most likely to mine the abundant iron of the area. A Roman milestone opposite the Church of Santa María dates to 61, and the water channel of El Chorrillo is a Roman work of hydraulic engineering.

The town received its municipal charter in 1163. It lay at the western tip of the coastline of Navarre until 1200, when Alfonso VIII of Castile invaded the kingdom. It profited from its place at a crossroads of trade between northern Europe and Castile. It remained in Biscay until at least 1476, and until the 18th century it tried to rejoin Biscay, attempts that Bilbao refused because they could tip the balance against its own trade. The French destroyed the town in 1813, but it was rebuilt and fortified. Its growth dates from iron mining and railways after 1879.

Castro Urdiales is a port on the Bay of Biscay in Cantabria. Its chief industries are tourism, fishing and the oil-packing of fish, especially sardines and anchovies. The old quarter, the Puebla Vieja, was declared a Conjunto histórico in 1978. The Gothic church of Santa María de la Asunción was built in the 13th century under Alfonso VIII, finished in the 15th and declared a National Monument in 1931. The Castle of Santa Ana stands near the port. The Cave of El Cuco holds Paleolithic rock carvings and paintings of deer, goats and horses.
catamarca-province: Catamarca lies in the northwest of Argentina and covers 102,602 square kilometres. It borders Salta, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero, Córdoba and La Rioja, and to the west the country of Chile. Eighty percent of the territory is covered by mountains, which fall into four systems: the Pampean sierras in the east and centre, the Narváez-Cerro Negro-Famatina system in the west, a cordilleran transition area at the western extreme, and the Puna, an elevated portion in the northwest.

The province is semi-arid, and the scarce water determines where people live: agriculture is concentrated in pockets and valleys between the mountains, and in the east the population gathers around watercourses from which canals and ditches carry the water. The Puna in the extreme west has a desert climate with very low precipitation, and snow cover is permanent at the highest peaks of the Sierra del Aconquija.

Before the Spanish conquest most of what is now Catamarca was inhabited by the Diaguita people, among them the fierce Calchaquí. In 1558 Juan Pérez de Zurita founded Londres de la Nueva Inglaterra, but it was constantly attacked by indigenous people, its population stayed small, and it was re-founded several times at new sites with new names. The sixth foundation, by Fernando de Mendoza Mate de Luna on 5 July 1683, bore the name San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca. The name of the province is believed to come either from Quechua cata, slope, and marca, fortress, or from Aymara catán, small, and marca, town.

When the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata was created in 1776, Catamarca became a subintendencia under the Salta intendency. In 1821 the province claimed its autonomy and elected Nicolás Avellaneda y Tula as its first governor. The mountains kept it isolated from the rest of Argentina until 1888, when the railways first reached it. Its valleys and dry climate attracted immigrants from Lebanon and Iran, who found it reminiscent of the orchard-lined mountain valleys they had left.

Catamarca is a province of Argentina with its capital at San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca, usually shortened to Catamarca. Its population was 429,556 at the 2022 census, and other important cities are Andalgalá, Tinogasta and Belén. The province is divided into sixteen departments.

Mining is important in its economy, notably the Bajo de la Alumbrera copper and gold mine. Among its sights are Antofagasta de la Sierra, the San Francisco Pass, the archaeological park Las Huellas del Inca and prehistoric petroglyphs.
catania: Catania faces the Ionian Sea at the base of the active volcano Mount Etna. The Sicels, the ancient indigenous people of Sicily, named their villages after features of their location, and the Siculian word katane means grater or skinning place, or a crude tool apt to pare. The geographer Strabo observed that the site was both a curse and a blessing: eruptions have destroyed large parts of the city, while volcanic ash makes fertile soil, especially suited to vines. The city has been buried by lava seventeen times, and the Roman city and the earlier Greek settlement lie beneath the present one.

Around 729 BCE Chalcidian Greek settlers from nearby Naxos occupied the village of Katane under a leader named Euarchos, and the native population was rapidly Hellenised.
