The walls of the Tschudi compound rise up to twelve metres and are wider at the base, which suits an earthquake zone. Ordinary housing took the form of small irregular rooms that doubled as workshops. UNESCO designated Chan Chan a World Heritage Site on 28 November 1986. Excavations by Michael Moseley and Carol J. Mackey began in 1969, and rain and floods from El Niño threaten the adobe walls.
chanakya: No documented historical information about Chanakya survives. Narratives about him come from tales preserved in traditions dating from the 4th to the 11th century CE. Thomas Trautmann distinguishes four accounts of the legend of Chanakya and Chandragupta: a Buddhist version in the Mahavamsa and its commentary, a Jain version in the Parishishtaparvan of Hemachandra, a Kashmiri version in the Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva and the Brihat-Katha-Manjari of Ksemendra, and the Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta, which he regards as largely fictional.

The versions differ on his origins. In the Buddhist account Chanakya was a Brahmin from Takshashila, learned in the three Vedas and in politics, with an ugly appearance. In the Jain account he was born to lay Jain parents in the village of Chanaka, and Hemachandra calls him a Dramila, implying a native of South India. Both say he was born with a full set of teeth, taken as a sign that he would become a king, and that a parent broke them to prevent his arrogance.

In all four versions Chanakya is insulted by the Nanda king and vows to destroy him. In the Buddhist account the emperor Dhana Nanda has him thrown out of an alms-giving ceremony for Brahmins at Pataliputra. Chanakya breaks his sacred thread in anger, curses the emperor and escapes in the disguise of an Ajivika. In the Jain account he sits on the emperor's throne and is kicked off it by a servant. In the Kashmiri version he unties his topknot and vows not to retie it until the emperor is destroyed, and in the play he makes the same vow, which fits the removal from the first seat of the empire.

After dethroning the Nanda, Chanakya installs Chandragupta as king. According to these narratives he served as chief adviser and prime minister to both Chandragupta Maurya and his son Bindusara. In the play, Chanakya engineers an alliance between Chandragupta and the king Parvata, whose army of Bahlika, Kirata, Parasika, Kamboja, Shaka and Yavana soldiers invades Pataliputra and defeats the Nandas. The Nanda minister Rakshasa continues to resist, and Chanakya foils each of his plots by cunning and the use of spies.

Chanakya has conventionally been identified with Kautilya, also called Vishnugupta, to whom the ancient Indian treatise on politics and economics, the Arthashastra, is attributed. Its composition and the date of its attribution to Chanakya remain matters of scholarly debate. In India he is regarded as a great thinker and diplomat, and many Indian nationalists regard him as one of the earliest people to envision a united India spanning the entire subcontinent.
chand-dynasty: The traditional genealogical lists of the Chand kings, the vamshavalis, were compiled in the mid-19th century and are not completely reliable. They place Som Chand in the 7th century, and a British report of 1849 accordingly dated the start of Chand rule to 685 CE. Historians dispute this, because the Katyuri kingdom is known to have ruled Kumaon until the third quarter of the 10th century.

Tradition makes Som Chand an immigrant from Jhusi and a relative of the king of Kannauj. The historian Krishna Pal Singh suggests that he came to Kumaon during the upheaval of the Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj in 1018–1019, and dates the beginning of Chand rule to 1019–1021. By the early 13th century the Chands appear to have ruled as feudatories: the Baleshwar Temple inscription of 1223, set up by Krachalla Deva, a conqueror from present-day Nepal, lists men whose names suggest that they belonged to the family.

Rudra Chand (1565–1597) seized Sira in 1581 and made the first of several attacks on the Garhwal Kingdom, all of which were repulsed. In 1587 he visited the Mughal emperor Akbar at Lahore as a mark of obeisance, and the Ain-e-Akbari lists a Sarkar of Kumaon. Baz Bahadur Chand (1638–78), one of the most powerful of the line, joined Shahjahan in an attack on Garhwal in 1655 that captured the Terai region including Dehradun, and extended his territory east to the Karnali river. In 1672 he began a poll tax whose revenue was sent to Delhi as tribute.

In 1744 the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan sent a force that took Almora against weak resistance. The Rohillas stayed seven months and left after a payment of three lakh rupees; a second attack was defeated at Barakheri. Hill troops under Dip Chand later fought beside the Rohillas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Internal strife over the following thirty years cost the kings most of the land they had held in the plains.

The Gurkhas invaded early in 1790, crossing the Kali River, and the Chands were driven to the Bhabhar and finally expelled. Nepalese rule lasted twenty-four years. During the Anglo-Nepalese War Harak Deo Joshi, minister of the last Chand raja, sided with the British, who captured Almora on 26 April 1815; with the Treaty of Sugauli, ratified on 4 March 1816, Kumaon passed to British rule. Champawat, the first capital, keeps a medieval fort and the Baleshwar and Nagnath temples, and Chand kings also built temples at Bageshwar, Bhimtal and Almora.
chandannagar: Chandannagar came into being in colonial times, since no medieval Bengali text such as the Chandimangal mentions it. Historians think the French created the town by joining several localities, notably the villages of Gondalpara, Boro and Khalisani. The first Frenchman to hold land there was Du Plessis, who bought 13 arpents at Boro Kishanganj for 401 taka in 1673-74. In 1688 the director of the French East India Company, Boureau-Deslandes, paid 40,000 coins to the Mughal subahdar to gain control of the area and build a factory. The name Chandernagor first appears in a letter of 1696.

Joseph François Dupleix became governor in 1730, and more than two thousand brick houses were built during his administration. From his time until 1756 Chandannagar was the main centre of European commerce in Bengal, trading in opium, indigo, silk, rice, rope and sugar, and its fine cloths were exported to Europe. The prosperous merchant Indranarayan Chaudhari, who built the Nandadulal Temple in 1740, made a great fortune there.

War between France and Great Britain began in 1756, and on 23 March 1757 Colonel Robert Clive and Admiral Charles Watson bombarded and captured Chandannagar. Its fortifications and many houses were demolished, and its commercial importance passed to Calcutta downriver. It was restored to France in 1763, retaken by the British in 1794 during the Napoleonic Wars and returned in 1816 with a 3 square mile enclave. It was governed as part of French India from Pondicherry until 1950. By 1900 it was a quiet suburb of Calcutta with 25,000 people.

A municipality was created on 1 August 1880 with Charles Dumaine as first mayor. Citizens could elect a representative to each French parliamentary house. The guillotine was last used in the town on 22 July 1895.

After Indian independence, France recognised the right of self-determination of its Indian settlements in 1948. A referendum on 19 June 1949 found that 98.5 per cent of Chandannagar's residents wished to join India. On 2 May 1950 the French allowed the Indian government to assume de facto control, and on 2 October 1954 the city was integrated into West Bengal. The inhabitants could keep French nationality.

The city on the Hooghly retains Indo-French buildings, among them the Strand promenade with Fort d'Orleans, the Sacred Heart Church inaugurated in 1884, a gate of 1937 marking Bastille Day, and a museum founded in 1961. Jagaddhatri Puja, held ten days after Diwali, is held across the city with a large procession.
chandragupta-i: Chandragupta was the son of the Gupta king Ghatotkacha and grandson of the dynasty's founder, Gupta. The Allahabad Pillar inscription calls both of these earlier rulers Maharaja, 'great king'. Chandragupta took the higher title Maharajadhiraja, 'great king of kings', and issued gold coins, which suggests that he was the first imperial ruler of the dynasty.

He certainly reigned in the first quarter of the 4th century, but the exact period is uncertain. V. A. Smith and P. L. Gupta date his accession to 319-320, the supposed start of the Gupta era, though this is an assumption. D. C. Sircar and R. C. Majumdar think the era marks the coronation of his son Samudragupta. He probably reigned long, since he appears to have named his son successor in old age.

Little is known of Chandragupta beyond his ancestry, his marriage and the expansion of Gupta power implied by his title. He married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi. The Lichchhavis were an ancient clan whose seat had been Vaishali in present-day Bihar, though which Lichchhavi kingdom she came from is uncertain. Samudragupta is called Lichchhavi-dauhitra, 'Lichchhavi daughter's son', in Gupta inscriptions, which suggests the family thought the marriage important.

Most historians accept that the marriage helped Chandragupta extend his power. Because Samudragupta's inscription lists the kings he defeated, scholars infer that his father's kingdom did not reach far beyond Prayaga in the west and excluded southern Bengal. R. C. Majumdar thought it may have covered the whole of present-day Bihar and parts of Uttar Pradesh and Bengal. Ashvini Agarwal holds that it included central and eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar but not Bengal.

Gold coins found at Mathura, Ayodhya, Varanasi, Bayana and Hajipur show portraits of Chandragupta and Kumaradevi with the legend Lichchhavayah, 'the Lichchhavis', and a goddess seated on a lion on the reverse. Scholars disagree whether Chandragupta, Samudragupta or the Lichchhavis issued them. The goddess is variously identified as Durga or Lakshmi.

The Allahabad Pillar inscription and the Eran inscription of Samudragupta state that Chandragupta chose his son as the next king, and the former suggests he gave up the throne in old age. Some coins of a Gupta ruler named Kacha raise a debate: Kacha may be another name for Samudragupta or an elder brother who succeeded first. Samudragupta further expanded the empire.
chandragupta-ii: Chandragupta II was a son of Samudragupta and queen Dattadevi, as his own inscriptions attest. The official Gupta genealogy has him succeed his father directly. The Sanskrit play Devichandraguptam, read with other evidence, suggests that an elder brother named Ramagupta reigned first. In the play Ramagupta agrees to surrender his queen Dhruvadevi to a Shaka enemy when besieged, but Chandragupta goes to the enemy camp disguised as the queen and kills him, and later dethrones Ramagupta. Historians debate whether this narrative rests on real events or is fiction.

The Udayagiri inscription of his foreign minister Virasena shows that Chandragupta had a distinguished military career, and places his empire from the mouth of the Indus and northern Pakistan in the west to Bengal in the east, and from the Himalayan foothills to the Narmada River in the south. Inscriptions of c. 401 to 413 found in central India, together with the Western Kshatrapa coinage that ends abruptly in the last decade of the 4th century, point to his conquest of the Western Kshatrapas. Modern scholars generally identify him with King Chandra of the Delhi iron pillar inscription, though not with complete certainty.

He also built power through marriage. He married Kuvera-naga, apparently a princess of the Naga dynasty, and their daughter Prabhavatigupta married the Vakataka king Rudrasena II. After her husband's death in c. 390 she acted as regent for her minor sons for about twenty years, and some historians regard the Vakataka kingdom as practically part of the Gupta empire in that time. His queen Dhruvadevi was the mother of his successor Kumaragupta I.

Chandragupta's coins and inscriptions call him a devotee of Vishnu, yet his officers built a temple to Shiva at Udayagiri and made donations to a Buddhist monastery at Sanchi. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian spent about six years in the Gupta kingdom during his reign. He recorded no name for the king, but his description of a peaceful and prosperous land is generally taken to be true, though idealised.

A later tradition places nine scholars, the Navaratnas, at the court of Vikramaditya. The text that names them is considered a later forgery, and there is no evidence that they were contemporaries. Several scholars nevertheless think the poet Kalidasa may have been a court poet of Chandragupta.
chandragupta-maurya: There are no historical facts about Chandragupta's origins and early life, only legends, and the narrative of his reign is deduced mainly from a few fragments in Greek and Roman sources and a few Indian religious texts, all written centuries after his death. Plutarch says that in his youth he saw Alexander the Great during the invasion of India, which led one scholar to propose a birth after 350 BCE. The Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa calls him Vrishala, a word that one later commentator read as meaning a shudra, while the historian Radha Kumud Mukherjee argued that it means the best of kings.

He rose in the unrest after Alexander's death in 323 BCE, in Magadha, a region then ruled by the unpopular Nanda dynasty. The exact chronology remains debated. His conquest of Magadha is generally dated to about 322 to 319 BCE and his expansion into the Punjab to about 317 to 312 BCE, though some scholars think he first consolidated in the Punjab, and an alternative chronology places these events in about 311 to 305 BCE. According to Mudrarakshasa, his mentor Chanakya assisted him and later became his minister. The Roman writer Justin says Chandragupta led the people in killing Alexander's Greek governors, and then oppressed those he had freed.

Seleucus I Nicator, who had established the Seleucid Empire at Babylon, confronted him between about 305 and 303 BCE, intending to retake the former Persian satrapies along the Indus. The two formed a dynastic marriage alliance, with Seleucus receiving five hundred elephants and Chandragupta gaining control of the regions bordering the Indus. The administration was decentralised, with provinces, local governments and a council of ministers.

Digambara Jain accounts say that Chandragupta abdicated in favour of his son Bindusara and became a monk under Bhadrabahu at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, where he fasted to death. These legends developed about 900 years later; contemporary Greek evidence says he drank wine, hunted and performed Vedic sacrifices, and no contemporary source supports his conversion to Jainism.

His reign is called the sheet anchor of Indian chronology, because in 1793 Sir William Jones identified him with the Sandracottus of Greek and Roman writers, allowing Indian and Greek history to be dated together. The empire he founded reached its peak under his grandson Ashoka. Western and Indian historians differ in their views of him, the latter often presenting him as the founder of the first Indian nation.
chandrapur: Chandrapur, earlier called Chanda, the official name until 1964, is a city and municipal corporation in Chandrapur district, Maharashtra, at the confluence of the Erai and Zarpat rivers. By tradition the place was once called Lokapura, then Indpur, and finally Chandrapur. According to the founding legend, the Gond king Khandkya Ballal Sah, afflicted with tumours, found a healing spring on the dry bed of the Zarpat River. The Achaleshwar Temple was raised there after the deity appeared to him in a dream, and he later founded the fortified city.

The area lies on terrain rich in coal and is called a geological museum for its variety of rocks, minerals and fossils. There are many Stone Age sites in the district, and signs of pottery suggest settlement in Neolithic times.

The area passed through many hands. Between 322 BCE and 187 BCE it belonged to the Maurya Empire, then to the Shunga Empire until 78 BCE and to the Satavahana Empire from the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE. The Vakataka dynasty ruled from the mid-3rd century CE to 550, followed by the Kalachuri dynasty in the 6th and 7th centuries, the Rashtrakuta dynasty between the 7th and 10th centuries and the Chalukya dynasty to the 12th century. The Seuna (Yadava) dynasty of Devagiri held a kingdom including the area from about 850 to 1334.

The Gond kings built the city's walled fort, with strong walls 15 to 20 feet high and four main gates, and the Mahakali temple, built around the 16th century by Dhundya Ram Sah. The Bhonsles of Nagpur took Chandrapur in 1751 during the Maratha period. When the last Bhonsle ruler, Raghuji Bhonsle III, died in 1853 without issue, it was annexed to British India under the Doctrine of Lapse. In 1956 the district was transferred to Bombay state, and in May 1960 it became part of Maharashtra.

Chandrapur had a population of about 518,000 at the 2011 census, and Marathi is spoken by most people, with Gondi spoken by most of the Gonds. It is a centre of coal mining. The old city, with the fort and the Anchaleshwar Temple, where the Gond kings' samadhi stands, lies at the river confluence.

The Tadoba Andhari Tiger Reserve lies about 30 kilometres north of the city. The Chandrapur Super Thermal Power Station, whose foundation stone was laid in 1977, supplies a large share of the state's electricity.
chandrayaan-3: Chandrayaan-3 is the third mission of the Chandrayaan programme, a series of lunar-exploration missions developed by ISRO. Its name comes from the Sanskrit chandra, Moon, and yana, craft. ISRO had earlier launched Chandrayaan-2, with an orbiter, a lander and a rover. Its lander lost contact with mission control, deviated from its intended trajectory while attempting to land near the lunar south pole, and crashed. Chandrayaan-3 consisted of a lander, Vikram, and a rover, Pragyan, as replacements for those of Chandrayaan-2, together with a propulsion module. The mission aimed to land safely and softly on the Moon, to show the rover driving there, and to carry out experiments on the lunar surface materials.

Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 aboard an LVM3 M4 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. It entered lunar orbit on 5 August, and on 17 August the Vikram lander separated from the propulsion module, which had carried it to a lunar orbit of 100 kilometres.

On 23 August 2023 the lander fired its four engines as a braking manoeuvre at 30 kilometres above the Moon. It then rotated from a horizontal to a vertical position using eight smaller thrusters. It slowed to roughly 150 metres, where it hovered for about 30 seconds to find a good landing spot, and touched down near the lunar south pole, at 69 degrees south, at 12:33 UTC.

The rover's laser-induced breakdown spectroscope reported sulfur near the south pole, and ISRO released temperature profiles from the top 10 centimetres of the lunar surface, in which a high range of 70 °C near the surface was not expected. The lander also made a short hop of about 40 centimetres. The lander and rover were built to operate for one lunar daylight period, or 14 Earth days, and not to endure the night temperatures of minus 120 °C. The rover was put into sleep mode on 3 September, and neither responded to wake-up calls later in September.

With the landing, ISRO became the fourth national space agency to land successfully on the Moon, after the Soviet space programme, NASA and CNSA, and the first to make a soft landing near the lunar south pole. The Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi, named the touchdown point Station Shiv Shakti and declared 23 August National Space Day. The live stream of the landing on ISRO's YouTube channel had eight million concurrent viewers, the highest on YouTube for a live video. ISRO chairman S. Somanath said that the agency had learnt a lot from its failure and corrected it.
changan: The site south of the Wei River in central Xi'an has been inhabited since Neolithic times. The Yangshao culture had a major centre at Banpo to its south from around 5000 to around 4300 BCE. Fenghao, the twin capitals of the Western Zhou, lay to its southwest, and the Qin had their capital at nearby Xianyang, north of the Wei. Chang'an itself was only a small village under the Qin. When Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty he first ruled from Luoyang, but he accepted the advice of the soldier Lou Jing and the general Zhang Liang that the Guanzhong Region, the Zhou and Qin heartland, could support a larger core population and offered much greater natural protection.

Liu Bang moved his court to the Changle Palace in 200 BCE. The neighbouring Weiyang Palace served as the imperial palace of many later dynasties and became the largest palace ever built, covering 4.8 km2, before its destruction under the early Tang. Chang'an was the Western Jin capital from 312 to 316, then capital of the Han-Zhao, the Former Qin and the Later Qin. Under the Later Qin ruler Yao Xing it became an important hub for Buddhism in China.

In 582 Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty built a new capital southeast of the ruined Han city and named it Daxing. It was renamed Chang'an in 618, when Li Yuan proclaimed himself Emperor Gaozu of Tang. Along with Constantinople and Baghdad, Tang Chang'an was one of the largest cities in the world. Most modern estimates put the population within its walls at around 800,000 to 1,000,000. In 904 the warlord Zhu Wen forcibly moved most of the remaining population to Luoyang. The city lost importance, became a regional centre again under the Northern Song, and was renamed Xi'an under the Ming, who built walls around the former Sui and Tang palace district, about an eighth of the medieval city's size.

Tang Chang'an was laid out as a rectangle of about 78 km2 inside walls 5.5 m high, divided by eight avenues into nine districts and 160 walled wards. It had a Palace City reserved for the emperor, an Imperial City for administrators and an Outer City with about 110 wards, two markets and religious institutions. Grain for the residents came from the surrounding region and from granaries supplied by canals. The site lies in the modern city of Xi'an, in Shaanxi Province.
changchun: Changchun lies in the middle portion of the Northeast China Plain at a moderate elevation of 250 to 350 metres, with a small area of low mountains in the east, the highest being Laodaodong Mountain at 711 metres. It has a humid continental climate, with long, cold, windy but dry winters from November to March and hot, humid summers. Its name means long spring in Chinese. The municipality is administered as a sub-provincial city of Jilin province.

Changchun began as a small trading post and frontier village, dealing mainly in furs and other natural products. In 1800 the Jiaqing Emperor selected a village on the east bank of the Yitong River and named it Changchun Ting. At the end of the eighteenth century peasants from overpopulated provinces such as Shandong and Hebei began to settle in the region, and in 1889 the village was promoted to a city known as Changchun Fu. In May 1898 it received its first railway station, at Kuancheng, on the southern branch of the Chinese Eastern Railway built by the Russian Empire between Harbin and Lüshun.

After Russia lost the southern section of this line in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, the Kuancheng station became the last Russian station on the branch. The next station to the south, the new Japanese Changchun station, became the first of the South Manchuria Railway. The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred the railway between Changchun and Port Arthur to Japan in 1906, and the Japanese government sent planners and engineers to choose the best site for a new station.

On 10 March 1932 the capital of Manchukuo, a Japan-controlled puppet state in Manchuria, was established in Changchun, and on 13 March it was renamed Hsinking, meaning new capital. The Emperor Puyi lived in the Imperial Palace, now a museum. The region experienced harsh suppression, forced conscription and labour and brutal warfare on the civilian population, and at the same time rapid industrialisation and militarisation. On 20 August 1945 the Soviet Red Army captured the city and renamed it Changchun; Soviet forces remained until 1946.

Changchun became the capital of Jilin in 1954. Construction of the First Automobile Works began in 1953, with Soviet technical support, and production of the Jiefang CA-10 truck, based on the Soviet ZIS-150, started in 1956. In 1958 it introduced the Hongqi limousines. The city is known as China's City of Automobiles and is home to Jilin University and Northeast Normal University. Among its sights are the Badabu, the group of buildings of the former eight Manchukuo ministries, the Museum of the Manchu State Imperial Palace and the Jilin Provincial Museum.
changsha: Changsha lies in northeastern Hunan, in the lower reaches of the Xiang River and the western part of the Changliu Basin. Most of the rivers in the area belong to the Xiang system, and fifteen tributaries flow into the Xiang. The city has a humid subtropical climate with distinct seasons, long and very hot summers, and a mean January temperature of 5.3 °C. It forms a metropolitan region with Zhuzhou and Xiangtan, known as the Changzhutan City Cluster. The name means long sandy place and is attested as early as the eleventh century BCE, when a vassal lord sent King Cheng of Zhou a gift described as a Changsha softshell turtle.

Settlement is said to have begun around 3000 BCE with the proliferation of the Longshan culture, although there is no firm evidence of such a link; people certainly lived in the area during the Bronze Age. The name appears in the Yi Zhou Shu, written before the Qin, and the Qin set up the Changsha Commandery. In the Western Han dynasty the Changsha Kingdom was established. The historian Ying Shao wrote in the second century that the Qin use of the name for the area continued its old name. In the Tang dynasty the Tongguan Kiln in Changsha produced the world's earliest underglaze porcelain, which was exported to Western Asia, Africa and Europe.

During the period of the Five Dynasties Changsha was the capital of Southern Chu. In the Northern Song dynasty the Yuelu Academy, later Hunan University, was one of the four major private academies of the last thousand years. Under the Qing, Changsha was the capital of Hunan and prospered as one of China's chief rice markets. During the Taiping Rebellion rebels besieged the city for three months, in 1852 or 1854, but it never fell. The rebels moved on to Wuhan, and Changsha became the principal base for the government's suppression of the rebellion.

Changsha is the capital of Hunan and among the first cities designated a National Historical and Cultural City in China. It has a history of more than 2,400 years of urban construction. Its main industries include construction machinery and new materials, and it is home to the Hunan Broadcasting System. Sights include the Yuelu Academy and the statue of the young Mao Zedong on Orange Isle. Changshanese, a kind of Xiang Chinese, is spoken in the downtown area, and Hunan cuisine, hot and spicy, remains the most popular.
channel-islands: The Channel Islands are an archipelago in the English Channel, to the west of the Cotentin Peninsula and off the Normandy coast. Channel Islands is a geographical term, not a political unit, first used around 1830, possibly by the Royal Navy. The two major islands, Jersey and Guernsey, make up 99 per cent of the population and 92 per cent of the area. The highest point is Les Platons in Jersey at 143 metres.

Humans lived on what is now Jersey at least 250,000 to 200,000 years ago, as La Cotte de St Brelade shows Neanderthal occupation when the island was connected to the mainland. Rising sea levels detached the islands in the Mesolithic period. Dolmens, the burial mound of La Hougue Bie in Jersey and the statue menhirs of Guernsey show a population large and organised enough for constructions of considerable size. In the sixth century Christian missionaries visited, and saints such as Samson of Dol and Helier are associated with the islands.

In 933 Raoul, King of Western Francia, granted the islands to William Longsword, and they were annexed to the Duchy of Normandy. When King John lost mainland Normandy to King Philip II of France, he kept control of the islands, and by the Treaty of Paris of 1259 Henry III surrendered his claim to the duchy while retaining them. Since around 1290 they have been split into two bailiwicks. In the Wars of the Three Kingdoms Jersey held out for the Royalist cause and gave refuge to Charles, Prince of Wales, while Presbyterian Guernsey favoured Parliament. Charles II rewarded George Carteret, bailiff and governor of Jersey, with a grant of land in America, which he named New Jersey.

The islands form two self-governing Crown Dependencies, the Bailiwick of Jersey and the Bailiwick of Guernsey, which includes Alderney, Sark and Herm. Neither is part of the United Kingdom, which is responsible for their defence and international relations. Each has its own laws, elections and representative bodies. The capitals are Saint Helier and Saint Peter Port. German forces occupied the islands in the Second World War: the British government demilitarised them in June 1940, and 6,600 of 50,000 people left Jersey and 17,000 of 42,000 left Guernsey, among them thousands of children evacuated with their schools.
chao-phraya-river: The Chao Phraya begins at the confluence of the Ping and Nan rivers at Nakhon Sawan and flows south for 372 kilometres to Bangkok and the Gulf of Thailand. At Chai Nat it splits off the Tha Chin River, which runs parallel and reaches the gulf at Samut Sakhon. Its watershed, 157,924 square kilometres, is the largest in Thailand.

The plain falls only about 80 metres over 500 kilometres from the hills to the sea, so the rivers run sluggishly and boats could be poled or paddled upstream for most of the year, which made water the most convenient transport before the modern era. The delta took its present form late: the coast reached the site of Bangkok between 3000 and 1000 BCE and settled near its present position by 500 CE.

The basin saw the rise of some of the earliest civilisations of Southeast Asia, notably Dvaravati from the 7th to the 11th century. The river was crucial to the Lavo kingdom and to its successors, and formed the basis of the Ayodhya Kingdom, incorporated into the Ayutthaya Kingdom in the 14th century. Rice growing intensified from the 13th century under Sukhothai and Ayutthaya with the introduction of floating rice from Bengal.
During the Ayutthaya period shortcut canals were dug across river loops, the first in 1538 on the order of King Chairachathirat, and the river's course has since followed many of them.

Rattanakosin, now Bangkok, was founded in 1782 on the east bank, a position that protected it from Burmese invasions from the west. Canalisation and cultivation of the southern swamps followed, and Thailand began to export rice in 1855. The name Chao Phraya is documented in writing only from the reign of King Mongkut in the 19th century; earlier maps usually called the river the Menam. It probably comes from Bang Chao Phraya, the settlement now called Samut Prakan, recorded from about 1660.

The provinces along the river, from Nakhon Sawan to Samut Prakan, include Ayutthaya, Nonthaburi and Bangkok, among the most historically significant and densely populated in Thailand. Its many canals, called khlong, irrigate the rice paddies of the plain, and in Bangkok the river is a major transport artery for ferries and long-tail boats. The original swamp forests of the lowlands have almost entirely been cleared for farming and cities.
charcoal: Charcoal is a lightweight black residue of carbon, made by strongly heating wood or other plant and animal material in minimal oxygen so that all water and volatile constituents are driven off. In the traditional process, called charcoal burning, part of the starting material is itself burnt to supply the heat, with a limited supply of air. The properties of the product depend on the material charred and on the temperature: charcoal made at about 300 degrees Celsius is brown, soft and friable, while charcoal made at higher temperatures is hard and brittle.

Wood charcoal has been made since ancient times wherever wood was abundant. Billets of wood were stacked on end in a conical pile, with openings at the bottom to admit air and a central shaft serving as a flue. The pile was covered with turf or moistened clay and lit at the bottom of the flue, and the fire spread slowly outward and upward. In the clamp used in Britain, logs leaned against a chimney of four stakes and were covered with soil and straw, and burned into charcoal over about five days.

The skill lay in controlling the combustion, so the work was left to professional charcoal burners, or colliers, who often lived alone in small huts to tend their piles. In the Harz Mountains of Germany they lived in conical huts called Köten, which still exist.

Charcoal has served for art, medicine, pigment and as a constituent of black powder, but its most important use has been as a metallurgical fuel. It burns at more than 1,100 degrees Celsius, and its heat can be moderated by controlling the flow of air, so it remains the traditional fuel of the blacksmith's forge. It has been used to make iron and steel, where it also supplies carbon, since at least 2000 BCE, with remains found in Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük.

The demand was great enough that charcoal making became a major cause of deforestation, especially in Central Europe, where at its height it employed hundreds of thousands of people. In the 16th century England passed laws to keep the country from being stripped of trees by iron production, and many woods were managed as coppices, cut and regrown in cycles. Growing scarcity of wood helped drive the move to coal, and in the 19th century coke largely replaced charcoal in steelmaking.
charente-maritime: Charente-Maritime lies on the west coast of France, named after the river Charente, with an area of 6,864 square kilometres. It was created by a decree of the Constituent Assembly of 22 December 1789, which took effect on 4 March 1790, as one of the 83 original departments of the French Revolution. It encompasses most of the former province of Saintonge, nearly all of Aunis and the Pays d'Aulnay from Poitou. Initially named Charente-Inférieure after the lower course of the river, it was renamed on 4 September 1941, reflecting its Atlantic coast identity. Saintes, the capital of Saintonge, was the prefecture from 1790 until Napoleon decreed its transfer to La Rochelle in 1810.

Human settlement dates to the Lower Paleolithic, and a Neanderthal skeleton found at Roche à Pierrot in Saint-Césaire in 1979, dated to about 36,300 years ago, confirmed an overlap with Cro-Magnons. The Santoni made the oppidum at Pons their political and trading hub in the La Tène period, and after the Gallic War Mediolanum Santonum, now Saintes, became the first capital of the Roman province of Aquitaine under Augustus. It was burned by the Alamanni in 276. In 418 the Visigoths settled in the region, and Clovis ousted them after defeating Alaric at Vouillé in 507.

La Rochelle grew in the twelfth century under the Dukes of Aquitaine and received a communal charter from Henry II in 1175. Eleanor of Aquitaine's marriage to Henry Plantagenet in 1152 tied the region to England, and the Hundred Years' War devastated it until the French recaptured Montguyon in 1451. La Rochelle became a Protestant stronghold in the Wars of Religion. In 1627 Cardinal Richelieu began a siege of the city, with a dike blocking its access to the sea, and famine and disease reduced the population from 28,000 to 5,000 before it surrendered on 28 October 1628. Explorers Pierre Dugua de Mons and Samuel de Champlain, from Saintonge, founded Québec in 1608.

The nineteenth century brought prosperity under the Second Empire, driven by cognac, until the phylloxera crisis. German forces occupied the department in the Second World War and built sea defences, including pillboxes on Oléron. Royan was nearly destroyed by an RAF raid on 5 January 1945, and La Rochelle was freed on 9 May 1945.

The prefecture is La Rochelle, and the department lies in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine. The islands of Ré and Oléron belong to it. The Paléosite centre at Saint-Césaire, opened in 2005, presents the Neanderthal find, and Saintes keeps Roman monuments such as a votive arch and an amphitheatre.
charibert-i: Charibert was the second-eldest son of King Chlothar I and his first wife Ingund; his elder brother Gunthar died before their father. In 556 Chlothar sent Charibert and his brother Guntram against their stepmother, called Chunna, and their half-brother Chramn, who were in revolt. Chramn was hiding on Black Mountain in the Limousin. During negotiations a thunderstorm prevented a battle, and Chramn sent forged letters falsely reporting the death of Chlothar. Charibert and Guntram returned at once to Burgundy to secure their positions.

After Chlothar died in 561 the Frankish kingdom was divided among his sons, each of whom ruled a realm named after the city he ruled from, which need not be geographically coherent. Charibert received the old kingdom of Childebert I: Neustria, the region between the Somme and the Loire, with Aquitaine and Novempopulana, and Paris as his capital. His other chief cities were Rouen, Tours, Poitiers, Limoges, Bordeaux, Toulouse, Cahors and Albi. Guntram received Burgundy, Sigebert Austrasia with its capital at Metz, and Chilperic a compact kingdom around Soissons.

Charibert married Ingoberga, and their daughter Bertha married Æthelberht, the pagan King of Kent. She took Bishop Liudhard with her as her private confessor, and her influence at the Kentish court was important to the success of the mission of St. Augustine of Canterbury in 597, which converted the first Anglo-Saxon ruler.

Gregory of Tours found Charibert eloquent and learned in the law but one of the most dissolute of the early Merovingians. He kept four wives at once, two of them sisters, and Germanus excommunicated him, the first excommunication of a Merovingian king. He was buried in disgrace at Blavia castellum, a stronghold in the Tractus Armoricanus.

After his death his brothers divided his realm, agreeing at first to hold Paris in common. His surviving queen, Theudechild, proposed a marriage with Guntram, though a council at Paris had outlawed such matches as incestuous. Guntram, unwillingly, had her housed in a nunnery at Arles. Charibert of Hesbaye, said to be his son, received nothing. The main source for his life is Gregory of Tours' History of the Franks, and from the English side Bede's Ecclesiastic History of the English People.
chariot: The critical invention that allowed light, horse-drawn chariots was the spoked wheel. Chariots emerged in the early 2nd millennium BCE. The oldest known come from burials of the Sintashta culture in present-day Russia, dated to about 1950 to 1880 BCE, although some scholars classify those finds as carts rather than true chariots. Cylinder seals from Kültepe in central Anatolia of about 1900 BCE also depict them. The first certain attestation of chariots in the Hittite empire dates to the late 17th century BCE, and they reached Egypt around 1650 BCE during the Hyksos invasion. The Hittites developed a lighter design with four-spoked wheels, wide enough for a driver, an archer and a shield-bearer.

A chariot was a fast, light, open, two-wheeled vehicle drawn by two or more horses harnessed side by side, little more than a floor with a waist-high guard at the front and sides. Greek chariots had no seat and no suspension. Egyptian chariots served as mobile archery platforms with two men, and the best preserved examples are the four found in the tomb of Tutankhamun. By the 7th century BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire used heavy chariots with a crew of four. In Roman usage a two-horse chariot was a biga, a three-horse chariot a triga and a four-horse chariot a quadriga.

Chariots played a major role in Late Bronze Age warfare, including the Battle of Kadesh, fought about 1274 BCE between the Hittites and the Egyptian Empire. The Mycenaean Greeks, who most probably adopted them from the Hittites, recorded large inventories of them on Linear B tablets. In China the earliest evidence is a burial at Hougang, Anyang, from about 1250 BCE, and their use there peaked from the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE. Massed chariot warfare became all but obsolete after the Warring States period, as crossbows, long halberds and cavalry took over.

Elsewhere cavalry likewise replaced them, though chariots remained in use for travel, processions, games and races. British chariots were described by Julius Caesar, and the last mention of chariots in battle seems to be at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 84 CE. In the Roman Empire they were used in racing at the Circus Maximus and in triumphal processions.
charites: The Charites, called the Graces in English and the Gratiae in Latin, personify beauty and grace. In Hesiod's Theogony they are the three daughters of Zeus and the Oceanid Eurynome: Aglaia, Euphrosyne and Thalia. Accounts differ, however, in names, number and parentage. Homer mentions Pasithea as one of the younger Graces, and Pausanias reports that the Athenians worshipped two Charites, Auxo and Hegemone, and the Spartans two, Cleta and Phaenna, while by Boeotian tradition Eteocles, king of Orchomenus, fixed the number at three.

They have little independent mythology and mostly attend the Olympian gods, above all Aphrodite, whom they bathed and anointed at Paphos. Pindar says they arranged feasts and dances for the Olympians and danced with Apollo and the Muses. One of them was the wife of the smith god Hephaestus: Hesiod calls her Aglaia, and in the Iliad she is called Charis.

Their cult is very old, and their name appears to be pre-Greek in origin. Its purpose seems to have resembled that of the nymphs, concerned with fertility and nature and with springs and rivers. An inscription of the sixth century BCE on Thera records a cult, and dance was strongly linked with it. At least four temples were dedicated to them alone, at Orchomenus, Hermione, Sparta and Elis. The most important was at Orchomenus in Boeotia, where the cult was thought to have begun. There the goddesses were worshipped at a very ancient site with a trio of stones and received a share of the produce of the rich plain, and Strabo says that Eteocles founded their temple.

In Greek art of the Archaic and Classical periods the Charites were dressed and shown in a line as dancers. The Roman and later pose, a nude interlaced group, developed later; Pausanias says he could not find who first showed them naked. The earliest known image is from a temple of Apollo at Thermon, of the seventh or sixth century BCE. A Classical relief of the Charites and Hermes at the entrance to the Acropolis was popularly ascribed to Socrates. In the Renaissance the nude group allowed pagan beauty to appear in art, and the Graces were painted by Botticelli in Primavera and sculpted by Antonio Canova and Bertel Thorvaldsen.
charlemagne: Charlemagne was the eldest son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon. His year of birth is uncertain, and the biographer Einhard reports him as 72 at his death. He was probably functionally bilingual in Germanic and Romance dialects from an early age, also spoke Latin and, according to Einhard, could understand and perhaps speak some Greek. After Pepin's death in 768 he and his brother Carloman I became kings of the Franks, and he became sole ruler three years later.

Charlemagne continued his father's policy of protecting the papacy and removed the Lombards from power in northern Italy in 774. His first war against the Saxons began what became over thirty years of nearly continuous warfare. After a defeat in 782 the annals record that he had 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded in the massacre of Verden, a figure historians think may be exaggerated although the event itself is not in doubt. The Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae, with the death penalty for pagan practices, has been described as a programme for forced conversion. His campaigns of the 790s were more destructive still, and his court settled at Aachen, where he built a palace and a chapel. His forces also brought down the kingdom of the Avars.

Pope Leo III was attacked by his enemies in April 799 and fled to Charlemagne. After an assembly in Rome at which Leo swore an oath of innocence, Leo crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans at St Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day 800. He was the first reigning emperor in the west since 476, and historians debate the significance of the coronation. From 801 he ruled more from Aachen and rarely led armies in person. He sought recognition of his title from Constantinople, which Emperor Michael I finally confirmed after a peace in 810.

In September 813 Charlemagne crowned his only surviving son, Louis, as co-emperor at Aachen. He died in 814 and was buried in the Palatine Chapel at Aachen. His reign inspired the cultural revival known as the Carolingian Renaissance, for which he promoted learning to create a more effective clergy. He held 23 synods and required the Rule of St Benedict in monasteries. After Louis's death the Treaty of Verdun divided the empire among his sons, and Carolingians ruled in East Francia until 911 and in West Francia until 987. Otto the Great was crowned emperor in 962, founding or re-establishing the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.
charles-albert-of-sardinia: Charles Albert was born on 2 October 1798 at the Palazzo Carignano in Turin, the son of Charles Emmanuel, Prince of Carignano, and Maria Cristina of Saxony. The Carignano line was a junior branch of the House of Savoy, so his chances of succeeding to the kingdom were slim at his birth. His father, sympathetic to liberalism, joined the French cause after the invasion of 1796, and the family was sent to Paris and kept under surveillance. Charles Albert grew up there and received a liberal education.

In March 1821 young liberal officers met him as they planned to force a constitution on Victor Emmanuel I. When the king abdicated, Charles Albert was made regent, but he left Turin secretly on the night of 21 March, and Charles Felix ordered him to Tuscany. To show his penitence he joined the French expedition against the Spanish liberals in 1823.

Charles Albert became king on 27 April 1831, when Charles Felix died without an heir and the direct line of Savoy came to an end. Alarmed by the July Revolution in France, he made an alliance with Austria, signed on 23 July 1831. His rule was conservative at first, yet he set up a Council of State, abolished torture and had new codes drawn up: a civil code in 1837, a criminal code in 1839, and commercial and procedural codes in 1842.

In 1848, as revolutions spread across Europe, he granted the Albertine Statute, which remained in force until 1947. On 23 March 1848 he issued a proclamation to the people of Lombardy and Veneto and sent his troops against the Austrians in the First Italian War of Independence. Pope Pius IX and Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies abandoned the cause, and he was defeated at Novara in 1849.

After the defeat Charles Albert abdicated in favour of his son Victor Emmanuel II. He left Novara just after midnight on 23 March 1849; stopped at an Austrian roadblock, he gave his name as the Count of Barge, a title he held, and was allowed to pass. He reached Porto in Portugal, where his health failed, and he died there on 28 July 1849.

He was nicknamed the Hesitant King, because he hesitated between constitutional monarchy and absolute rule, and the Italian Hamlet by Giosuè Carducci. His war was the first attempt by the House of Savoy to alter the settlement of the Congress of Vienna, and his son carried it to success in 1861.
charles-borromeo: Charles Borromeo was born in the castle of Arona on Lake Maggiore on 2 October 1538. His father, Gilbert, was Count of Arona, and his mother, Margaret, belonged to the Milanese branch of the House of Medici. The Borromeo family was one of the oldest and wealthiest in Lombardy. Charles received the tonsure at about twelve and, when given the income of a rich Benedictine abbey, told his father that whatever exceeded the cost of his preparation for the church belonged to the poor. He studied law at the University of Pavia and took his doctorate on 6 December 1559.

When his uncle was elected Pope Pius IV on 25 December 1559, he summoned Borromeo to Rome and made him a cardinal on 31 January 1560. He organised the third and last session of the Council of Trent in 1562 and 1563 and had a large share in the Tridentine Catechism. The death of his brother Federico in November 1562, and his contacts with the Jesuits and Theatines, led him to a stricter life and to put into practice a bishop's duties as the Council set them out. He was formally appointed archbishop of Milan in 1564 and entered the city in September 1565.

Milan was the largest archdiocese in Italy, with over 3,000 clergy and 800,000 people, and no archbishop had been present for about 80 years. Borromeo found indulgences and offices sold and monasteries in disorder. He made pastoral visits and, believing that abuses arose from ignorant clergy, founded seminaries and colleges, the Oblates of St Ambrose and the first Sunday school classes. Some members of the Humiliati, an order that opposed him, plotted against his life, and a shot fired at him in his chapel missed.

In 1576 famine struck Milan, followed by plague, and the governor and many nobles fled. Borromeo stayed, tried to feed 60,000 to 70,000 people daily and went into debt to do so. In 1583, as apostolic visitor to the Swiss cantons, he repressed Protestantism in the valleys. In the Valle Mesolcina 150 people were arrested for witchcraft, and the civil authorities condemned eleven women and the provost of Roveredo to be burned alive.

Borromeo's uncompromising stance brought him into conflict with secular leaders, priests and even the pope. He fell ill in 1584 and died in Milan on 3 November, aged 46. Paul V canonised him on 1 November 1610, and he is the patron saint of bishops, catechists and seminarians.
charles-bridge: The bridge replaced the Judith Bridge, built between 1158 and 1172 and severely damaged by a flood in 1342. Czech legend holds that Charles IV himself laid the first stone at 5:31 in the morning of 9 July 1357, chosen because the figures, 1357, 9/7, 5:31, form a palindrome, a numerical bridge in the eyes of an emperor who believed in numerology. The bridge was completed in 1402. It was originally called the Stone Bridge or the Prague Bridge and has been called Charles Bridge only since 1870. Until 1841 it was the only way across the Vltava, which made Prague important on the trade route between Eastern and Western Europe.

The bridge is 516 metres long and nearly 10 metres wide. Following the example of the Stone Bridge at Regensburg, it was built as a bow bridge with 16 arches shielded by ice guards. Three towers protect it, two on the Lesser Quarter side and the Old Town Bridge Tower on the other. An avenue of 30 statues stands along the balustrade, mostly Baroque and mostly erected between 1683 and 1714, among them John of Nepomuk. Since 1965 all have been replaced by replicas, and the originals are shown in the Lapidarium of the National Museum.

The bridge has survived floods and wars. A flood in 1432 damaged three pillars, and in 1496 the third arch broke down. After the Battle of White Mountain the heads of leaders of the anti-Habsburg revolt, executed on 21 June 1621, were displayed on the Old Town Bridge Tower. In 1648 the heaviest fighting for the Old Town took place on the bridge, as the Swedes advanced from the west bank. A flood on 2-5 September 1890 tore down three arches and two pillars, and the bridge reopened on 19 November 1892. A capital repair from 1965 to 1978 secured the pillars, and all vehicles have been excluded since then.
charles-cornwallis-1st-marquess-cornwall: Charles Cornwallis was born in Grosvenor Square, London, on 31 December 1738, the eldest son of the 5th Baron Cornwallis. His mother was a niece of Sir Robert Walpole, and his uncle Frederick was Archbishop of Canterbury. The family had been established at Brome Hall, near Eye in Suffolk, since the 14th century. He was educated at Eton College and Clare College, Cambridge, and received his first commission as an ensign in the 1st Foot Guards in December 1757. He then studied at the military academy of Turin and served as a staff officer in the Seven Years' War.

On the outbreak of war in North America he put his misgivings aside and sought active service. He fought under Sir Henry Clinton at the failed siege of Charleston in 1776, led the advance at the Battle of Long Island and chased George Washington across New Jersey. In 1780 he defeated the Continental Army at the Battle of Camden, and in March 1781 he won a costly victory at Guilford Court House. His campaign through the southern colonies was marked by quarrels with Clinton. He surrendered his army at Yorktown in October 1781. The surrender did not end the war, but it ended major fighting in North America.

He kept the confidence of George III and later governments. In 1786 he became Governor-General and commander-in-chief in India, having refused the post until it carried military command. He ended the East India Company's practice of letting its employees trade on their own account, raised their salaries, and introduced advancement by merit. He enacted the Cornwallis Code, which included the Permanent Settlement, and led the Third Anglo-Mysore War from 1789 to 1792 against Tipu Sultan.

After a spell as Master-General of the Ordnance he became Lord Lieutenant of Ireland in June 1798, in response to the Irish Rebellion. He oversaw the defeat of the rebels and of a French force under General Jean Humbert, and helped to bring about the Union of Great Britain and Ireland. On 25 March 1802 he signed the Treaty of Amiens for the United Kingdom.

Reappointed Governor-General of India in 1805 to curb the expansionist policy of Lord Wellesley, he arrived in July and died of a fever at Gauspur, near Ghazipur, on 5 October 1805. He was buried there above the Ganges, and his tomb is a protected monument. A memorial to him stands in St Paul's Cathedral. His son Charles became the 2nd Marquess, and the marquessate ended with him.
charles-darwin: Charles Robert Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 at The Mount, his family's home in Shrewsbury, Shropshire, the fifth of six children of the wealthy doctor and financier Robert Darwin and Susannah Darwin, née Wedgwood. His grandfathers Erasmus Darwin and Josiah Wedgwood were both prominent abolitionists, and Erasmus had praised general concepts of evolution and common descent in his Zoonomia (1794). His mother died in July 1817. In October 1825 he entered the University of Edinburgh Medical School, found lectures dull and surgery distressing, and neglected his studies. He assisted Robert Edmond Grant's research on marine invertebrates, then studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, from 1828 to 1831.

His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, established him as an eminent geologist, and his observations supported Charles Lyell's concept of gradual geological change. The Voyage of the Beagle (1839) made him a popular author. Puzzled by the distribution of the wildlife and fossils he had collected, he devised his theory of natural selection in 1838, but he needed time for extensive research and his geological work had priority.

In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay outlining the same idea, which led to a joint submission to the Linnean Society of London. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, and later The Descent of Man (1871), on human evolution and sexual selection. His final book was The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881). He and his wife and cousin Emma Wedgwood had ten children, two of whom died in infancy.

Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey. By the 1870s the scientific community and most of the educated public accepted evolution as a fact, though many favoured explanations that gave natural selection only a minor role. A broad consensus that natural selection is the basic mechanism came with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s to the 1950s. Later movements, among them eugenics and Social Darwinism, invoked his name, sometimes against his own comments; he insisted that social policy should not be guided simply by concepts of struggle and selection.
charles-de-foucauld: Charles Eugène, vicomte de Foucauld de Pontbriand, was born in Strasbourg on 15 September 1858 into an old noble family from Périgord. His parents died within months of each other in 1864, and he and his sister were brought up in Strasbourg by their maternal grandfather, Colonel Beaudet de Morlet. In 1870 the family fled the Franco-Prussian War and later settled in Nancy. At 15 he lost his faith and for twelve years believed, in his later words, nothing. He entered the Saint-Cyr Military Academy in 1876, graduating 333rd of 386, and led an extravagant life after inheriting his grandfather's fortune.

Posted to the 4th Regiment of Chasseurs d'Afrique in Algeria, he grew bored with garrison service and travelled in Morocco in 1883–84, the Sahara in 1885 and Palestine in 1888–89. His research on the geography and culture of Algeria and Morocco won the gold medal of the Société de Géographie de Paris in 1885, and he published an account of his Moroccan journey in 1888. On 14 January 1890 he entered the Trappist monastery of Notre-Dame des Neiges. He was later sent to Akbès on the Syrian-Turkish border, and left the order in 1897 after seven years, working as a servant near a convent of Poor Clares in Nazareth.

He was ordained a priest on 9 June 1901 and settled at Béni Abbès in the Algerian Sahara, building a hermitage for adoration and hospitality, though nobody joined him. He then moved to Tamanghasset among the Tuareg and spent ten years studying their language and traditions, using the Assekrem as a place of retreat. His Tuareg dictionary, published after his death in four volumes, is known to specialists for its rich and apt descriptions, and he also collected Tuareg poetry.

On 1 December 1916 a group of tribal bandits dragged de Foucauld from his bordj at Tamanrasset, intending to kidnap him. Interrupted by two soldiers of the French Camel Corps, a startled 15-year-old shot him dead, and the soldiers were also killed. The Tuareg buried him the next morning. His remains were moved in April 1929 to El Meniaa. René Bazin's biography made him widely known, and the Little Brothers of Jesus, the Little Sisters of Jesus and many other congregations and fraternities draw on his life and writings. He was beatified on 13 November 2005 and canonised on 15 May 2022.
charles-de-gaulle: Charles André Joseph Marie de Gaulle was born on 22 November 1890 in Lille, the third of five children. He was raised in a devoutly Roman Catholic, conservative and monarchist family. His father, Henri de Gaulle, was a professor of history and literature at a Jesuit college and later founded his own school.

In 1909 he won a place at the military academy of Saint-Cyr, finishing 119th out of 221. Before entering he served a year in the ranks in the 33rd Infantry Regiment at Arras. His company commander declined to make him a sergeant at first, remarking that the young man evidently thought nothing less than Constable of France good enough for him.

In the First World War he was wounded in the knee at the Battle of Dinant on 15 August 1914 and later taken prisoner by the German Empire. After the armistice he served on the French military mission to Poland and won the Polish Virtuti Militari. In the interwar years he advocated mobile armoured divisions.

When the German invasion came in May 1940 he led an armoured division in a counterattack and was appointed Undersecretary for War. Refusing his government's armistice with Germany, he went to Britain and urged the French to fight on in his Appeal of 18 June. He led the Free French Forces and in June 1944 became head of the Provisional Government of the French Republic. He resigned in 1946 and withdrew to Colombey-les-Deux-Églises to write his War Memoirs.

During the May 1958 crisis, as the Algerian War threatened the Fourth Republic, the National Assembly brought him back to power. He commissioned a new constitution and was elected President of France on 21 December 1958. He withdrew France from NATO's integrated military command and launched an independent nuclear force, and on 22 January 1963 he signed the Élysée Treaty with Chancellor Konrad Adenauer. He resigned in late April 1969 after losing a referendum on decentralisation.

De Gaulle died suddenly on 9 November 1970 from an abdominal aortic aneurysm while watching television. His successor Georges Pompidou announced his death by saying simply, "General de Gaulle is dead. France is a widow." French political parties and leaders claim a Gaullist legacy, and streets and monuments in France and elsewhere bear his name.
charles-dickens: Charles John Huffam Dickens was born on 7 February 1812 at Landport in Portsea Island (Portsmouth), the second of eight children of Elizabeth and John Dickens, a clerk in the Royal Navy Pay Office. He spent his formative years at Chatham in Kent, reading widely, including Tobias Smollett, Henry Fielding and The Arabian Nights. At 12 he left school to work in a boot-blacking factory when his father was imprisoned for debt, and after three years he returned to school.

Dickens began as a political journalist, reporting Parliamentary debates and election campaigns. His journalism in periodicals formed Sketches by Boz in 1836, Boz being a family nickname. His literary success began with the serial publication of The Pickwick Papers in 1836, and within a few years he was an international celebrity. In December 1845 he became editor of the Daily News but resigned after ten weeks.

On 9 June 1865, returning from Paris with Ellen Ternan, he was in the Staplehurst rail crash in Kent, in which ten passengers were killed. He tended the wounded until rescuers came and went back for the manuscript of Our Mutual Friend.

Dickens wrote 15 major novels, several novellas and many short stories. Most were published in weekly or monthly instalments, which became the dominant Victorian mode, and let him judge his audience's reaction and sometimes change his plot. Among his works are A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield (1849 to 1850) and Bleak House (1852 to 1853), a satire on the judicial system that helped support a reformist movement leading to the legal reform of the 1870s. His works have never gone out of print.
charles-edward-stuart: Charles Edward Louis John Sylvester Maria Casimir Stuart was born on 31 December 1720 at the Palazzo Muti in Rome, where his father had been given a residence by Pope Clement XI. His mother was Maria Clementina Sobieska, a Polish noblewoman and granddaughter of John III Sobieski. His grandfather James II and VII had been deposed in the Revolution of 1688, and the Jacobite cause aimed to restore the Stuarts to the thrones of England and Scotland.

In 1734, aged thirteen, he went with his cousin the Duke of Liria to the siege of Gaeta, his first experience of war. His mother died in January 1735. A tour of Italian cities from 1737 shocked him: most courts, wishing not to antagonise Britain, would receive him only as the Duke of Albany, and Venice was the exception.

Charles went to France in 1744 to join a planned invasion that storms partly wrecked. Encouraged by Irish and Scottish exiles, he borrowed some 180,000 livres from Paris bankers, using the Sobieski crown jewels as security, and fitted out two ships. He landed on the west coast of Scotland, won the support of Donald Cameron of Lochiel, and raised his father's standard at Glenfinnan on 19 August 1745. Lord George Murray joined him at Perth on 4 September.

The Jacobites won at Prestonpans in September 1745, and Charles held court at Holyrood Palace. A Prince's Council of senior leaders was formed, and he resented it as an imposition on his divinely appointed monarch. The council agreed to invade England by way of Carlisle. After a victory at Falkirk Muir in January 1746 the siege of Stirling Castle was abandoned and the army moved north to Inverness, pursued by the Duke of Cumberland. Defeat at Culloden in April 1746 effectively ended the Stuart cause, and Charles landed back in France on 10 October 1746.

The French received him warmly but gave no further help. He was arrested at the opera in December 1748 and expelled under the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. After his father's death in 1766 he lived mostly in Rome and Florence, and he married Princess Louise of Stolberg-Gedern in 1772. His health declined and he was said to be an alcoholic. He died in Rome of a stroke on 30 January 1788; his brother, Cardinal Henry, had the record read as 31 January, since 30 January was the anniversary of the execution of Charles I.

He was buried at Frascati and in 1807 his remains were moved to the crypt of St Peter's Basilica. His escape from Scotland made him a romantic figure of heroic failure, and songs such as The Skye Boat Song and Mo Ghile Mear commemorate his flight.
charles-emmanuel-iii-of-sardinia: Charles Emmanuel was born in Turin to Victor Amadeus II of Savoy and his first wife Anne Marie d'Orléans. As Duke of Aosta he was not at first the heir, but his older brother died in 1715. His father had been made king of Sicily in 1713 under the Treaty of Utrecht and was forced to exchange Sicily for the less important Kingdom of Sardinia in 1720.

On 3 September 1730 Victor Amadeus abdicated. His son, whom he had not favoured and whose education he had neglected except in military matters, became king. Victor Amadeus soon reclaimed the throne, accusing his son of incompetence, and settled at Moncalieri. Charles Emmanuel had him arrested by the Crown Council to prevent an attack on Milan that might have brought an invasion of Piedmont. The old king was confined at the Castle of Rivoli, where he died without further interference.

In the War of the Polish Succession Charles Emmanuel sided with the French-backed King Stanislaw I and, after an alliance signed at Turin on 28 October 1733, marched on Milan and occupied Lombardy. He refused to let Spain take Milan and Mantua, which would have restored Spanish domination in Italy, and voluntarily thwarted the expedition against Mantua. His army was victorious at Crocetta and Guastalla, but when Austria and France made peace he had to leave Lombardy and received instead Langhe, Tortona and Novara.

In the War of the Austrian Succession he sided with Maria Theresa, with financial and naval support from Great Britain and the Dutch Republic. A Franco-Spanish invasion took Savoy and the County of Nice, and in 1744 he defended Cuneo against besiegers. In 1745, with some 20,000 men against armies totalling some 60,000, he lost Alessandria, Asti and Casale; with Austrian reinforcements he recaptured Alessandria and Asti in 1746, and in 1747 he won a crushing victory over the French at the Battle of Assietta. At the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle he regained Nice and Savoy and obtained Vigevano and other lands in the Po plain.

Charles Emmanuel declined to take part in the Seven Years' War and concentrated on administrative reforms, a well-disciplined army and stronger fortresses. He restored the universities of Sassari and Cagliari to improve the condition of Sardinia. He added many paintings to the collection he inherited, which came to hold the largest collection in Italy of 16th and 17th-century Flemish and Dutch paintings in the Sabauda Gallery, and he founded a tapestry workshop in Turin in 1731. He married three times, and all three wives died young. He died in Turin in 1773 and was buried in the Basilica of Superga. He was the paternal grandfather of the last three mainline kings of Sardinia.
charles-fourier: François Marie Charles Fourier was born in Besançon on 7 April 1772, the son of a small businessman. He cared more for architecture than for his father's trade and as a boy was most interested in geography. When his father died in 1781 he received two-fifths of an estate valued at more than 200,000 francs, which allowed him to travel through Europe. From 1791 to 1816 he worked in Paris, Rouen, Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux as a travelling salesman and correspondence clerk, complaining of serving the knavery of merchants. He wrote most of his works between 1816 and 1821 and died in Paris on 10 October 1837.

His first book, the Theory of the Four Movements and the General Destinies, appeared anonymously in Lyon in 1808 and sold few copies. Fourier held that cooperation is the key to social success. People would live in communities called phalanxes, housed in phalanstères, four-storey apartment complexes where the richest had the upper floors. Jobs would be assigned by interest and desire, with higher pay for unattractive work. He counted 12 common passions and 810 types of character, so that an ideal phalanx would have 1,620 people. The phalanstères remained concepts, since he never obtained the money to build them.

Fourier argued that important jobs should be open to women by skill, and he never married. He saw poverty rather than inequality as the chief cause of disorder. He also wrote of Jews as the ruin of the body politic, called trade, which he associated with them, the source of all evil, and proposed that Jews be made to farm in the phalansteries. John K. Roth and Richard L. Rubenstein see his antisemitism as economic and religious, not the racial kind that emerged later.

Fourier's proposals inspired intentional communities in the United States, among them Utopia in Ohio, the North American Phalanx in New Jersey and Brook Farm in Massachusetts, and the Familistery of Guise in France. His follower Victor Considerant carried his ideas into the 1848 Revolution and the Paris Commune. Friedrich Engels named him one of three major utopian socialists, and Peter Kropotkin saw him as founder of the libertarian branch of socialism.
charles-george-gordon: Charles George Gordon was born at Woolwich on 28 January 1833, the son of Major General Henry William Gordon. The men of the family had been army officers for four generations, and all of his brothers also became officers. He grew up in England, Ireland, Scotland and the Ionian Islands as his father was posted from place to place, and was educated at Taunton School and the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich. In the Crimean War he arrived at Balaklava in January 1855, after writing several letters to the War Office asking to be sent there.

Gordon volunteered for service in China in 1860 and arrived at Hong Kong too late for the fighting of the Second Opium War. In March 1863 he took command of the Ever Victorious Army, a force of Chinese soldiers led by European officers, at Songjiang. He moved his men and supplies by the canals and rivers, treated prisoners well, and enlisted many former Taipings. After he took Suzhou in November 1863 he guaranteed humane treatment for any rebel who laid down arms, but Imperial forces executed the Taiping prisoners, which enraged him. He disbanded the army in June 1864, having won thirty-three battles in succession at a cost of about 1,000 of his 3,500 soldiers killed or wounded.

In 1871 he was British representative on the commission for navigation of the mouth of the Danube. He entered the service of the Khedive of Egypt in 1873, with the approval of the British government, and later became Governor-General of the Sudan, where he worked to end the slave trade and abolished torture and public floggings. Corrupt officials ignored many of his orders against the trade. He left the Sudan and returned to Europe in 1880.

A revolt had broken out in the Sudan under Muhammad Ahmad, who proclaimed himself the Mahdi. In early 1884 Gordon was sent to Khartoum to arrange the evacuation of loyal soldiers and civilians. He removed about 2,500 civilians but stayed, and the siege by Mahdist forces began on 18 March 1884. He held out for almost a year, which won him the admiration of the British public but not of the government, which had decided to abandon the Sudan. A relief force under General Wolseley reached Khartoum two days after the city fell, and Gordon was killed in January 1885.

How he died is uncertain. The popular account, in which he met the Ansar unarmed in his dress uniform, was promoted by the British press and by George William Joy's painting of 1893. Public grief in Britain was great, and the Gordon Boys Home, now Gordon's School at Woking, was founded as his memorial.
charles-i-of-anjou: Charles was the youngest child of King Louis VIII of France and Blanche of Castile, and the first Capetian to be named for Charlemagne. The late king willed that his youngest sons be prepared for a career in the Church, and Charles was destined for it until the early 1240s. He received a good education and had a documented passion for poetry, medicine and law. In December 1244 Louis IX took a vow to lead a crusade, and Charles took the cross too, despite his mother's opposition. The crusaders took Damietta in 1249, and the brothers were captured on 6 April 1250 and released for a ransom. Charles returned to France in October 1250.

Charles held Provence and Forcalquier through his wife's inheritance. After returning from Egypt he put down a rebellion in Provence: Arles surrendered in April 1251, Avignon in May, and Marseille, the last to resist, made peace in July 1252. In 1263 he accepted the Holy See's offer of the Kingdom of Sicily, called the Regno. He was crowned in Rome on 5 January 1266, annihilated Manfred's army and occupied the Regno almost without resistance. His victory over Conradin at Tagliacozzo in 1268 secured his rule. In 1272 he took the title King of Albania, in 1277 he purchased a claim to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and in 1278 he became Prince of Achaea.

His rule in the Regno rested on heavy taxation, notably the subventio generalis, which the popes called illegal. In 1281 Pope Martin IV authorised a crusade against the Byzantine Empire. The Sicilian Vespers rebellion of 30 March 1282 ended his rule on the island, and Peter III of Aragon was declared king of Sicily at Palermo on 4 September.

Charles prepared a campaign to regain Sicily, but fell seriously ill, made his will on 6 January 1285 and died on 7 January. His body was buried in Naples, and his heart was placed at the Couvent Saint-Jacques in Paris. Two realms, each ruled by a king styled of Sicily, then coexisted for more than a century. The chroniclers Bartholomaeus of Neocastro and Saba Malaspina strongly influenced modern views of Charles, though both were biased: the first called him a tyrant to justify the Vespers. He gave estates in the kingdom to about 700 noblemen from France or Provence.
charles-i-of-england: Charles was born at Dunfermline Palace on 19 November 1600, the second son of King James VI of Scotland and Anne of Denmark, and was created Duke of Albany. He was a weak and sickly infant and stayed in Scotland when his family went to England in 1603 after James inherited the English throne. He became heir apparent in 1612 on the death of his elder brother Henry Frederick. An unpopular attempt to marry him to the Spanish Infanta Maria Anna ended with a visit to Spain in 1623, and on 1 May 1625 he married the French princess Henrietta Maria by proxy.

Charles believed in the divine right of kings and was determined to govern according to his own conscience. He quarrelled with the English Parliament, and many subjects opposed his levying of taxes without its consent. In January 1629 MPs held the Speaker down in his chair so that resolutions against Catholicism, Arminianism and tonnage and poundage could be read. Charles dissolved Parliament and imprisoned nine leaders, among them Sir John Eliot. To raise money he revived the Distraint of Knighthood, a law unused for over a century, and fined men who had not attended his coronation in 1626.

His religious policies and his Catholic marriage made Puritans and Scottish Covenanters distrust him. His attempts to make the Church of Scotland adopt high Anglican practices led to the Bishops' Wars, the first beginning in 1639. The Long Parliament assembled on 3 November 1640 and began proceedings against his leading counsellors. In mid-1642 both sides armed, and Charles raised the royal standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642, setting up his court at Oxford.

After defeat in 1645 by the New Model Army he surrendered to a Scottish force and was handed over to the Long Parliament. He escaped from Hampton Court on 11 November 1647 but was confined at Carisbrooke Castle. In January 1649 the Rump Parliament's House of Commons indicted him for treason, though the House of Lords rejected the charge, and the Chief Justices of the three common law courts opposed the indictment as unlawful. He was executed on 30 January 1649. The monarchy was abolished and the Commonwealth of England established; the monarchy was restored in 1660 under his son Charles II.

A memoir purportedly by him, the Eikon Basilike, went on sale ten days after his death and proved effective royalist propaganda. King Charles the Martyr was added to the Church of England's calendar in 1660.
charles-i-of-hungary: Charles was born in 1288 as Caroberto, the only son of Charles Martel, Prince of Salerno, and Clemence of Austria. His grandmother Mary, daughter of Stephen V of Hungary, claimed Hungary after her brother Ladislaus IV died in 1290, though the lords and prelates chose Andrew III instead. She passed the claim to her son and, after his death in 1295, to the seven-year-old Charles. His grandfather Charles II of Naples preferred his third son, Robert, and in 1296 gave him the rights of a firstborn, which excluded Charles from Naples.

In August 1300 the twelve-year-old Charles landed at Split, invited by the Croatian lord Paul Šubić. After Andrew III died on 14 January 1301 he was crowned with a provisional crown at Esztergom, but most Hungarians held the coronation unlawful and elected Wenceslaus of Bohemia.

Charles was elected king in Pest on 27 November 1308 and crowned with the Holy Crown at Székesfehérvár on 27 August 1310, his third coronation, yet his rule stayed nominal over most of the kingdom, which had broken into about a dozen provinces under oligarchs. He won his first decisive victory at Rozgony on 15 June 1312 against the Aba family and Matthew Csák. By 1323 he had taken full possession of his kingdom and moved his capital to Visegrád. Croatia kept its autonomous status.

Charles introduced a system of office fiefs, under which officials enjoyed revenues only while they held a royal office, and founded the Order of Saint George, the first secular order of knights.
