On 6 December 1917 the Council of People's Commissars decided that a special commission was needed to apply the most energetically revolutionary measures. It was established on 20 December 1917 (7 December Old Style), with Felix Dzerzhinsky as its head. Its official name was the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission for Combating Counter-Revolution and Sabotage, shortened to VChK or Cheka, and its members were called Chekists.

In its first months the Cheka had only 40 officials, with a regiment of soldiers and a group of Red Guards, and worked mainly in Petrograd. It soon had sections for railways and branches in every guberniya and uyezd. By the end of the Civil War it had at least 200,000 personnel. Although it was created to protect the revolution from class enemies such as the bourgeoisie and the clergy, within a month it had extended its repression to all political opponents of the Bolshevik government, including anarchists. On 11 and 12 April 1918 it attacked 26 anarchist centres in Moscow, killing forty anarchists and arresting about 500.

At Vladimir Lenin's direction it carried out mass arrests, imprisonments and executions without trial in what came to be known as the Red Terror, which Dzerzhinsky implemented on 5 September 1918. Its special punitive troops fought desertion from the Red Army, which had more than three million deserters in 1919 and 1920, and took and shot hostages to force compliance. It also policed labour camps, requisitioned food and put down worker and peasant rebellions.

Estimates of its executions vary widely. Its own officer Martyn Latsis gave 12,733 for 1918 to 1920, a figure that historians generally regard as far too low. Estimates run from at least 50,000 to as many as 200,000, and many put the total at about 100,000. The Cheka was dissolved in February 1922 and succeeded by the State Political Directorate, the GPU. It was the first of a long succession of Soviet secret police bodies, and the name Chekists long remained a name for their members.
chelm: Chełm lies in the Lublin Voivodeship in eastern Poland, south-east of Lublin and about 25 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. Its name is most often derived from the Proto-Slavic word for a hill, in reference to the fortified settlement on Wysoka Górka. Its landmarks are Castle Hill with the Baroque Basilica of the Birth of the Virgin Mary and the Chełm Chalk Tunnels, which run for about 15 kilometres under the city.

Settlement in the area dates from at least the 9th century, and in the 10th a fortified town served first as a centre of pagan worship. In 981 the Kievan Rus' annexed it from Poland. In 1235 Daniel of Galicia granted the town a city charter, and after the Mongols destroyed Halych in 1240 and 1241 he moved the capital of his domain to Chełm, where it stayed until 1272. He built a new castle on the hill in 1237, one of the few Ruthenian castles to withstand Mongol attacks, and set up an Orthodox eparchy at the basilica. In 1366 Casimir III the Great of Poland took control of the region.

The city prospered in the 15th and 16th centuries, when Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Protestants and Jews lived there, and declined in the 17th through wars that ravaged Poland. After the Third Partition it passed to Austria, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna awarded it to Russia. Poles liberated the city from Austrian rule on 2 November 1918, nine days before Poland officially regained independence.

In September 1939 about 18,000 of the city's people, 60 per cent, were Jews. German forces occupied the city in October. On 1 December 1939 around 2,000 Jewish men were driven on a death march to Hrubieszów, and perhaps 400 survived. In 1942 the Jews of Chełm were deported to the Sobibór extermination camp or killed in the city, and only an estimated 60 survived the Holocaust.

Chełm is a city of mostly industrial character with 60,231 inhabitants. From 1975 to 1998 it was the capital of its own voivodeship. Its Jewish past lives on in folklore: Chełm became the setting of Yiddish stories of foolish wise men, retold by writers such as Isaac Bashevis Singer.
chelmno: Chełmno is a town near the Vistula in northern Poland. Its name comes from chelm, an old Polish word for hill. Because of its regional importance in the Middle Ages it gave its name to Chełmno Land, to the local Catholic diocese and to the Kulm law, used by over 180 cities and towns in Central Europe, among them Warsaw, Gdańsk, Toruń, Königsberg and Klaipėda. Its population was mixed, Poles and Germans, with Poles two thirds in the second half of the 19th century.

The first written mention is in a document allegedly issued in 1065. In 1226 Duke Konrad I of Masovia invited the Teutonic Knights to Chełmno Land, and in 1233 the town received the city rights known as Kulm law, renewed in 1251. In 1243 it became the nominal see of the Diocese of Chełmno, though the cathedral was at neighbouring Chełmża. A member of the Hanseatic League, it grew prosperous. In 1440 it was a founder of the Prussian Confederation against the Order's rule, and after the Thirteen Years' War the Order recognised it as part of Poland. In 1692 the local gymnasium became the Chełmno Academy.

Prussia annexed the town in 1772 and called it Kulm. The Prussians expelled the Kraków professors, abolished the Polish academy and closed Catholic monasteries. The surgeon Ludwik Rydygier opened a clinic in 1878 and performed pioneering operations. Polish troops entered the town on 22 January 1920. In 1939 the German authorities murdered 5,000 Polish civilians in the territory, and the rest of the Polish population was expelled to the General Government.

Chełmno keeps a well-preserved medieval centre with five Gothic churches, a Renaissance town hall in the market square, rebuilt in 1567–1572, and city walls surviving almost whole. The Old Town was designated one of Poland's official Historic Monuments on 20 April 2005.
chemical-weapons: A chemical weapon is a munition that uses chemicals formulated to inflict death or harm on humans. The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons defines it as a chemical compound intended as a weapon, or its precursor, that can cause death, injury, temporary incapacitation or sensory irritation through its chemical action. Lethal agents include nerve agents such as sarin and VX and blister agents, chiefly mustard gas; non-lethal ones include tear gases. Toxic agents used for another property, such as the herbicide Agent Orange or incendiary white phosphorus, are not chemical weapons under this definition. Lethal chemical weapons are counted among weapons of mass destruction with biological, radiological and nuclear weapons.

Simple chemical weapons were used sporadically in antiquity and into the industrial age. In the First World War most major powers used them on a large scale, including mustard gas, phosgene and chlorine, which caused lung scarring, blindness and death. Between the wars, European colonial forces used them to put down rebellions. In the Second World War the Allies never used them and the Axis only sparingly; Nazi Germany discovered nerve agents but did not use them. Japan used mustard gas and lewisite in China. Nazi Germany used Zyklon B in gas chambers to commit genocide against Jews and other peoples, the largest death toll from chemical weapons in history.

After the war, about 100,000 Iranian troops became casualties of Iraqi chemical weapons in the Iran–Iraq War, and Iraq used mustard gas and nerve agents against its own civilians in the Halabja attack of 1988. In the Cold War the Soviet and United States programmes became the largest in history.

The First Hague Conference of 1899 prohibited employing poison and poisoned arms. The Geneva Protocol, signed on 17 June 1925 and in force from 8 February 1928, prohibited the use of chemical and biological weapons in international armed conflicts, though not their production or storage. The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 outlaws the development, production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons and is administered by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, based in The Hague. After the Second World War the Allies dumped large quantities of captured German chemical weapons into the Baltic Sea, mostly in wooden crates.
chemnitz: Chemnitz lies in the Ore Mountain Basin, with the Ore Mountains to the south and the Central Saxon Hill Country to the north, on the Chemnitz River, which is formed by the confluence of the Zwönitz and the Würschnitz. The name of the city and of the river is of Slavic origin, derived from the root for stone (Upper Sorbian kamjeń), so that the river's name means stony brook.

The area was sparsely settled by Slavic tribes related to the modern Sorbs. The first recorded mention of Chemnitz comes in 1143, when King Conrad III of Germany confirmed the rights of a Benedictine monastery, including permission to hold a royal public market, and a town grew around the market. It passed to the Margraviate of Meissen in 1307 and to the Electorate of Saxony in 1356. After it received the bleaching privilege in 1357 it became a regional centre of weaving, linen manufacture and textile trade, employing more than a third of its people. The scholar Georgius Agricola, author of De re metallica, was city physician from 1533 and died there in 1555.

By the early 19th century the city was an industrial centre, called the Saxon Manchester. Its population was 320,000 in 1913, and Auto Union was founded there in 1932. Allied bombing in the Second World War destroyed 41 percent of its built-up area, and Soviet troops occupied the city on 8 May 1945. On 10 May 1953 the East German government renamed it Karl-Marx-Stadt. In a referendum on 23 April 1990, 76 percent voted for the old name, and Chemnitz was officially restored on 1 June 1990.

Chemnitz is the third-largest city in Saxony, after Leipzig and Dresden, and is home to Chemnitz University of Technology. Mechanical engineering, metal processing and vehicle manufacturing are its main industries. The red tower, built in the late 12th or early 13th century as part of the city wall, is its most conspicuous landmark, and the Karl Marx Monument by Lev Kerbel, nicknamed Nischel by locals, stands in the centre. The city was a European Capital of Culture in 2025.
chengdu: Chengdu lies in central Sichuan on a vast plain with an elevation of 450 to 720 metres, crossed by the Jin River. The Chengdu Plain is known as the Country of Heaven and the Land of Abundance, a phrase the Shu Han minister Zhuge Liang used of the region. The Qin Mountains far to the north shield the city from cold Siberian winds, so its winters are milder than those of the lower Yangtze.

Archaeological finds at Sanxingdui and the Jinsha Site show that the surrounding area was inhabited more than four thousand years ago. In the time of the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties it formed a separate bronze-working culture that, after partial sinification, became known to the Chinese as Shu. The city is said to have been founded by the Kingdom of Shu in the 4th century BCE. Qin conquered Shu in 316 BCE, and the settlement was re-founded by the Qin general Zhang Yi.

The name Chengdu is attested from the Warring States period, and the city has been called the only major Chinese city to keep both its location and its name through the imperial, republican and communist eras, although it was briefly known as Xijing in the 17th century.

Under the Han, Chengdu brocade became fashionable throughout China, and a Brocade Official was appointed to oversee its production and trade. After the fall of the Eastern Han, Liu Bei ruled Shu Han from Chengdu. Under the Tang it was considered the second most prosperous city in China after Yangzhou, and the poets Li Bai and Du Fu lived there; Du Fu's thatched cottage of 760 is commemorated by the Caotang, built in 1078.

In 1911 Chengdu's branch of the Railway Protection Movement helped trigger the Wuchang Uprising. During the Second World War refugees from eastern China fleeing the Japanese settled there, and after the war the city was briefly the capital of the Nationalist government before it withdrew to Taipei. A railway to Chongqing was built in 1952.

Chengdu is the capital of Sichuan province, with 20,937,757 inhabitants at the 2020 census. The nearby Dujiangyan irrigation system and Mount Qingcheng, an important Taoist site, are World Heritage Sites. Among its landmarks are the Wuhou Shrine, built to honour Zhuge Liang, the Jinsha Site museum and the Daci Temple, where the monk Xuanzang was initiated. UNESCO recognised it in 2011 as a city of gastronomy.
chennai: Chennai lies on the Eastern Coastal Plains, a flat stretch of clay soil on the Bay of Bengal, at an average elevation of 6.7 m. It receives most of its rain from the northeast monsoon, and cyclones are common in that season. The name derives from Chennappa Nayaka, a Nayak ruler who served as a general under Venkata Raya of the Vijayanagara Empire and from whom the East India Company took the town on lease in 1639. The first official use of the name was in August 1639, in a sale deed to Francis Day of the Company.

Stone Age implements have been found near Pallavaram. In the 2nd century CE the region was part of Tondaimandalam, ruled by the Early Cholas, and the Pallavas of Kanchi ruled it independently from the 3rd to the 9th century. The Later Cholas under Aditya I defeated the Pallavas in 879, Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan brought the region under Pandya rule in 1264, and the Vijayanagara Empire held influence over it in the 15th century.

In 1639 the East India Company obtained a grant of coastal land containing the fishing village of Madrasapattinam and built Fort St George, the first British fortress in India. The Corporation of Madras was established on 29 September 1688. In the 18th century the British and the French fought for control of the city, and by the late 18th century the British had conquered most of the region and made Madras the capital of the Madras Presidency. The idea of the Indian National Congress was conceived there after a Theosophical convention in December 1884. After 1947 Madras became capital of Madras State, the predecessor of Tamil Nadu.

Chennai is the capital and largest city of Tamil Nadu, officially renamed from Madras in 1996. The 2011 census counted 4,646,732 people within the city's 174 km2, and Tamil is the language of most residents. Its oldest surviving buildings date from the 6th to 8th centuries CE, among them the Kapaleeshwarar Temple in Mylapore and the Parthasarathy Temple in Triplicane. The Madras Music Season, begun by the Madras Music Academy in 1927, brings Carnatic music performances each December.
cheongju: Cheongju is the largest city of North Chungcheong Province as well as its capital. The Geum River runs through its centre, and the tributaries Musim and Miho join in the north of the city, with the mountains of Wuam and Bumo to the east and west. The climate is temperate, with four seasons. On 1 July 2014 Cheongju and Cheongwon County were unified, and the city is now divided into four districts: Heungdeok, Seowon, Sangdang and Cheongwon.

Cheongju has been an important provincial town since ancient times. Ruins from the Old Stone Age to the Bronze Age have been found in the Cheongju Mountains, and the Durubong Cave Site is associated with the Paleolithic. After Silla unified the Three Kingdoms in 676, Buddhism spread through the region. Under King Gwangjong of Goryeo several Buddhist monuments were made, among them the Cheoldanggan, an iron flagpole of twenty cylinders, 13.1 metres tall, raised in 962 near the remains of Yongdu Temple to hang the flag that honours the Buddha. It was designated a National Treasure in 1962. Under the Joseon dynasty the region took up Confucianism as its main faith, and temples in Cheongju played a part in the advance of Korean printing.

In 1593, during Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea, the Battle of Cheongju was fought between Japanese forces and Joseon, and more than 8,000 Korean warrior monks took part. The fortress of Sangdangsanseong linked the northern and southern provinces after the Japanese invasion of 1592.

The provincial government moved to Cheongju from Chungju in 1908. Under Japanese colonial rule Cheongju County and Munui County were merged in 1914, and the opening of the Chungbuk line in 1926 spurred regional development. Cheongju and Cheongwon County were separated in 1946, and Cheongju was made a city in 1949. Its population almost quadrupled, from 147,000 in 1970 to 582,158 in 2000.

Sangdangsanseong lies on the slopes of Mount Uam within the city. Its wall, 3 to 4 metres high and 4.2 kilometres around, dates in its present form to a restoration in 1716. Cheongju National Museum, near the mountain, holds artefacts of the region. The Early Printing Museum on the site of Heungdeoksa Temple is dedicated to the history of printing and to the Jikji. Chojeonghaenggung, a temporary palace where King Sejong stayed for treatment of an eye disease, is said to be where he completed the creation of Hangul. Cheongju is also a seat of several universities.
chernigov: Chernigov, in Ukrainian Chernihiv, stands on the upper right bank of the Desna River, about 150 kilometres north-north-east of Kyiv. Its name begins with the Slavic root for black; the medievalist Martin Dimnik connects it with the worship of a black god, Chernibog.

The city was a tribal centre of the Siverians and is first mentioned in the Rus'–Byzantine Treaty of 907, though the time of its founding is unknown. From the early 11th century it was the seat of the Principality of Chernigov, the largest in Kievan Rus, which reached Murom, Ryazan and Tmutarakan; its rulers at times vied with the Kievan grand princes and often took the seat at Kiev for themselves. The city's population peaked at about 25,000 before Batu Khan's hordes sacked it in 1239, and it then entered a long period of obscurity.

The area fell under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in 1353. The Crimean khan Meñli I Giray burned the city in 1482 and 1497, and in the 15th to 17th centuries it passed several times between Lithuania, Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which held it from 1618 to 1648. It received Magdeburg rights in 1623. After the Khmelnytsky Uprising it rose again as the base of a regiment of the Hetman State, and the Treaty of Andrusovo of 1667 ceded suzerainty over the area to the Tsardom of Russia.

After the Hetmanate was abolished, Chernigov became a provincial capital of the Russian Empire, as a governorate from 1808. In 1897 it had 27,006 inhabitants, 11,000 of them Jews. Under Soviet rule it industrialised, and it was severely damaged in the Second World War, during which the German army occupied it from 9 September 1941 to 21 September 1943.

Chernihiv is the administrative centre of Chernihiv Oblast, with 282,747 people. Its monuments record two flourishing periods, that of Kievan Rus in the 11th and 12th centuries and that of the Cossack Hetmanate in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. They include the Transfiguration Cathedral, commissioned in the early 1030s by Mstislav the Bold and one of the oldest churches in Ukraine. The historic centre has been on UNESCO's Tentative List since 1989.
chernobyl-disaster: Reactor 4 of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, near Pripyat in the Ukrainian SSR, was an RBMK reactor cooled by water circulated by electrically driven main pumps. More than 6% of the heat comes from radioactive decay, which goes on after fission stops, so cooling must continue to prevent the core from overheating.

The accident happened during a test meant to simulate the cooling of the reactor in a serious accident with a blackout. The operators carried out the test after an accidental drop in reactor power. Four of the eight main circulating pumps were to run on power from the coasting turbine. As the turbine slowed, the water flow fell and steam voids formed in the coolant.

The test began at 01:23:04 on 26 April 1986. The reactor was shut down in an unstable condition, and underlying design flaws led to a huge, uncontrollable power surge. The reactor components ruptured and lost coolant, and steam explosions and a meltdown destroyed the reactor building, followed by a core fire that spread radioactive contaminants across the Soviet Union and Europe. The explosion killed two engineers and severely burned two others.

Of 237 workers hospitalised, 134 showed symptoms of acute radiation syndrome, and 28 of them died within three months. Pripyat was not evacuated at once and its people were not warned during the night. An exclusion zone with a 10-kilometre radius was set up 36 hours after the accident and about 49,000 people were evacuated. It was later extended to 30 kilometres, and about 68,000 more people left. The Soviet government did not acknowledge the disaster until two days after the explosion.

The response involved more than 500,000 personnel. Workers removed an estimated 100 tonnes of debris from the roof, using about 60 remote-controlled robots designed mainly for lunar exploration or policing work, and the concrete sarcophagus was completed in December 1986. Pripyat was abandoned and replaced by the purpose-built city of Slavutych.

Estimates of the long-term toll vary: the United Nations puts deaths at up to 4,000 in Ukraine, Belarus and Russia, and other estimates reach 16,000 across Europe. By 2005 about 6,000 cases of childhood thyroid cancer had occurred in the affected populations, 15 of them fatal. The International Nuclear Safety Advisory Group blamed the operators' actions in its first report, in 1986, and the reactor's design in its revised report of 1992.
chernozem: Chernozem is a black soil containing a high percentage of humus, between 4% and 16%, and high percentages of phosphorus and ammonia compounds. Its name comes from the Russian words for black and for soil or earth. It is very fertile and, with its high capacity to store moisture, gives high agricultural yields, but prolonged farming depletes its nutrients as the humus decreases, so it still needs fertilisers.

Chernozem covers about 230 million hectares in two main belts. One is the Eurasian Steppe, which includes the Pontic-Caspian, Kazakh and Mongolian-Manchurian steppes. The other runs from the Canadian Prairies in Manitoba through the Great Plains of the United States as far south as Kansas. Its layer varies from a few centimetres to 1.5 metres thick.

Several explanations for its formation were proposed. Mikhail Lomonosov suggested in 1763 that it came from the decomposition of plants and animals; Sir Roderick Murchison argued in 1840 that it weathered from Jurassic marine shales, and Karl Eichwald in 1850 that it was lake sediment. In 1866 Franz Josef Ruprecht proposed decomposed steppe grasses, in 1929 Otto Schlüter proposed that it was man-made, and in 1999 Michael W. I. Schmidt proposed Neolithic burning of biomass.

No single reconstruction of past climate could explain the variations in chemistry found in the chernozems of central Europe. Charcoal is a prominent component of grassland soils in the Russian Steppe, the Great Plains and the Pampa, and burning of vegetation could account for chernozem's high magnetic susceptibility. The term therefore covers black soils of the same appearance but different histories of formation.

In 1883 the geologist Vasily Dokuchaev studied the steppe soils of the Poltava region in the Russian Empire. He found that the peasants named soils by colour, and he adopted such names. He was the first to describe the chernozem of the European part of the Russian Empire and to recognise its fertility, and he published Russian Chernozem, a complete study of the soil, in that year. It shares many chemical and physical properties with the terra preta of the Amazon rainforest, though it is classified separately.
cherokee: The Cherokee, who call themselves Aniyvwiya, meaning Principal People, are one of the Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands. Before the 18th century they lived in towns along river valleys in what is now southwestern North Carolina, southeastern Tennessee, southwestern Virginia, parts of western South Carolina, northern Georgia and northeastern Alabama, with hunting grounds reaching into Kentucky, together about 40,000 square miles. Their language belongs to the Iroquoian family.

Scholars hold two main views of their origins. One is that they migrated to Southern Appalachia from the Great Lakes region in late prehistoric times, which the Cherokee oral tradition also supports. The other is that they had been in the Southeast for thousands of years and that proto-Iroquoian developed there. A Spanish expedition led by Hernando de Soto in 1540–1541 recorded a people called Chalaque around the Keowee River.

From 1710 to 1715 the Cherokee and Chickasaw allied with the British and fought the Shawnee, who were allied with the French, forcing them to move north. After the Cherokee–American wars the Cherokee lands between the Tennessee and Chattahoochee rivers remained independent, but the deerskin trade could no longer support the people on their reduced lands. Ravaged by smallpox and pressed by settlers, they adopted a representative government modelled on that of the United States, with an elected principal chief, senate and house of representatives, and the Cherokee Supreme Court was established by the 1820s. In the 1810s Sequoyah invented a syllabary for the language. Between 1898 and 1906 the federal government dissolved the former Cherokee Nation to make way for the state of Oklahoma.

The Cherokee were mainly farmers living in permanent towns. John Howard Payne, visiting in the 1830s, recorded elders' account of a society with a hereditary, priestly white organization of elders representing the seven clans, and a red organization of younger men responsible for warfare, which the Cherokee considered polluting. Women made decisions for the clan and kept its sacred knowledge. Slavery existed before European colonization, mostly of enemy captives taken in raids, and was seen as a temporary status.

Today three Cherokee tribes are federally recognized: the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band, both headquartered in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, based on the Qualla Boundary in North Carolina.
cherrapunji: Cherrapunji, also called Sohra, stands at an average elevation of 1,430 metres on a plateau in the southern part of the Khasi Hills, facing the plains of Bangladesh. Rain comes from the Bay of Bengal arm of the Indian summer monsoon. The clouds cross about 400 km of plain and then meet the hills, which rise abruptly to about 1,370 metres within 2 to 5 km. Deep valleys funnel the low, moisture-laden clouds together over Sohra, and the steep slopes force them upward, so that the vapour cools and condenses. Sohra holds the record for the most rainfall in a calendar month, 9,300 millimetres in July 1861, and for the most in a year, between August 1860 and July 1861.

The history of the Khasi people, the native inhabitants of Sohra, can be traced from the early 16th century. Between the 16th and 18th centuries they were ruled by their tribal chiefs, the Syiems of Khyriem, and Sohra was the traditional capital of the Khasi kingdom of ka hima Sohra. Khasi society is matrilineal, and children take their mother's surname. The Khasi Hills came under British authority in 1833, when Tirot Sing Syiem, the last of the important Syiems, submitted. The 19th-century British mispronounced the name Sohra as Cherra, and people from the plains later added the Bengali suffix punjee, 'a cluster of villages'. The town has since been officially renamed Sohra.

Sohra is a sub-divisional town in the East Khasi Hills district of Meghalaya. Despite its rainfall it has long had a shortage of drinking water, since heavy rain washes the topsoil from the deforested plateau. Tourism is its main economic activity. The villages near the town are known for living root bridges, which people have grown from the roots of trees over hundreds of years. Each takes 10 to 15 years to grow, and the oldest still in use is over 500 years old.
chesapeake-bay: The Chesapeake Bay lies in the Mid-Atlantic region, separated from the Atlantic Ocean mainly by the Delmarva Peninsula. Its mouth is between Cape Henry and Cape Charles. More than 150 major rivers and streams flow through its drainage basin, which covers parts of six states and all of Washington, D.C. The bay is 2.8 miles (4.5 km) wide at its narrowest and 30 miles (48 km) at its widest, and its average depth is 21 feet (6.4 m). It is the drowned valley of the Susquehanna River, where the river once flowed when sea level was lower. The name comes from an Algonquian word, Chesepiooc, referring to a village at a big river.

Paleoindians may have lived around the bay 11,000 years ago. For thousands of years Native American societies lived in villages of wooden longhouses near the water, where they fished and farmed beans, corn, tobacco and squash. Later, communities formed confederations such as the Powhatan, the Piscataway and the Nanticoke, each led by a central chief.

Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed past the bay in 1524 in the service of the French crown. Spanish Jesuits founded the short-lived Ajacan Mission on a Chesapeake tributary in 1570. In 1781 the bay was the site of the Battle of the Chesapeake, or Battle of the Capes, in which a French fleet defeated the Royal Navy in the decisive naval battle of the American Revolutionary War. The victory allowed George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau to trap Lord Cornwallis's army at Yorktown, Virginia.

The bay forms a link in the Intracoastal Waterway, joined to the Delaware River by the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal. A shipping channel, dredged by the US Army Corps of Engineers since the 1850s, serves the Port of Baltimore. Two bridges span the bay, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge in Maryland and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel in Virginia. It is known for blue crabs, clams and oysters. In the 1970s it was found to contain one of the first identified marine dead zones, and a report of 1983 called it an ecosystem in decline. More than 1,800 wrecks of ships and boats lie on its bed.
cheshire: Cheshire covers 905 square miles (2,344 km2), between Merseyside, Greater Manchester, Derbyshire, Staffordshire, Shropshire and the Welsh counties of Flintshire and Wrexham, with a short coastline on the Dee Estuary. The Cheshire Plain, flat land of glacial till left by the retreat of a Quaternary ice sheet, is dotted with meres, the water-filled kettle holes. To the east the land rises to the Pennines and part of the Peak District. The bedrock is almost entirely red Triassic sandstone, quarried at Runcorn and used for Liverpool Cathedral, Chester Cathedral and Beeston Castle.

The name was first recorded in 980 as Legeceasterscir in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 'the shire of the city of legions', after Chester; the county is thought to have been created by Edward the Elder around 920. After 1066 local resistance was put down in 1069 as part of the Harrying of the North, and the lands of landowners such as Earl Edwin of Mercia were given to Norman barons. William I made Cheshire a county palatine. Hugh d'Avranches, nicknamed Hugh Lupus, became Earl of Chester about 1070, with autonomous powers on the Welsh Marches. Magna Carta did not apply to the shire, so the earl issued his own Chester Charter.

In 1397 Richard II added lands in the Welsh march and raised Cheshire to a principality, in reward for the support of the Cheshire Guard, his standing force of about 500 men. It lost the rank on his fall in 1399.

Cheshire is a ceremonial county of North West England with a population of 1,139,884 in 2024; its largest settlement is Warrington and the city of Chester lies in the west. Four unitary authorities carry out local government: Cheshire East, Cheshire West and Chester, Halton and Warrington. The county council was abolished on 1 April 2009. The county is known for Cheshire cheese, salt and silk, and its farming is based mainly on dairying. Iron Age hill forts and the Roman fortress and walls of Chester survive, and Lewis Carroll named the Cheshire Cat after the county.
chester: Chester lies on the River Dee, very close to the England-Wales border, at the southern end of a two-mile sandstone ridge that rises to 42 metres within a natural S-bend of the river. The eastern and northern parts of the area were heathland and forest, and the western side towards the Dee Estuary was marsh. It is the historic county town of Cheshire.

The Roman Legio II Adiutrix founded Chester in the 70s CE, during the reign of Vespasian, as a fort named Deva Victrix, on land of the Celtic Cornovii. Deva was named for the goddess of the Dee or from the British name of the river, and Victrix came from the Legio XX Valeria Victrix, based there. Its four main roads, Eastgate, Northgate, Watergate and Bridge Street, follow routes laid out then.

After the Romans withdrew, Chester is thought to have become part of the kingdom of Powys. In 689 King Æthelred of Mercia founded the Minster Church of West Mercia, later Chester's first cathedral, and the Angles strengthened the walls against the Danes. It was one of the last cities in England to fall to the Normans, and William the Conqueror ordered a castle built there. It received city status in 1541, and in 1643 the Parliamentarians subdued it in the Civil War.

The city walls of Chester are the most complete in Britain. The circuit measures nearly two miles and is broken only in the south-west, and the walls have Grade I listed status. A footpath runs along the top, and above Eastgate stands Eastgate Clock. Many of the black-and-white buildings are Victorian restorations of the Black-and-white Revival. The Grosvenor Museum holds a collection of Roman tombstones.
chetniks: Small-scale guerrilla warfare has a long history in the South Slav lands that were under Ottoman rule. Bandit companies took part in the First Serbian Uprising, which began in 1804. Chetnik veterans of the fighting since 1904 became leading Serbian patriotic groups in the new Yugoslav state, and in 1921 they organised the Chetnik Association for the Freedom and Honor of the Fatherland in Belgrade.

In April 1940 the Yugoslav General Staff set up a Chetnik Command of six battalions. After the Axis invasion of April 1941, Draža Mihailović began his own movement in May, and its ideology was set out in a series of documents. Stevan Moljević's memorandum Homogeneous Serbia of June 1941 proposed a Greater Serbia of 65 to 70 per cent of Yugoslav territory, with large-scale population transfers.

The Chetniks took part in the uprising in German-occupied Serbia from July to December 1941. The Germans then applied a ratio of 100 hostages executed for every soldier killed, and in October 1941 massacres at Kraljevo and Kragujevac killed over 4,500 civilians, mostly Serbs. Mihailović concluded that attacks on German troops would only bring more deaths, scaled them back and waited for an Allied landing.

The movement drifted into collaboration with the Axis: first with the puppet government in Serbia, then with the Italians in Dalmatia and Montenegro, and after the Italian capitulation in September 1943 with the Germans directly. The Chetniks called this using the enemy. They also fought the Yugoslav Partisans, and the Western Allies eventually withdrew their support.

Chetnik units used terror against Croats, against Muslims in Bosnia, Herzegovina and Sandžak, and against the Partisans. Estimates of the deaths they caused in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina range from 50,000 to 68,000, and about 300 villages and small towns were destroyed. Several historians regard these acts as genocide. Mihailović disapproved of some of them but lacked control over local commanders.

In April and May 1945 many Chetniks retreated towards Italy and Austria. Some were returned by British forces or killed in the Bleiburg repatriations, and many captured members were tried or executed. Mihailović was captured, tried in Belgrade and executed in July 1946. Small Chetnik groups continued an insurgency against the Communist regime until 1950.
cheyenne: The Cheyenne are made up of two tribes, the Tsitsistas and the Suhtai, which merged in the early 19th century; the Suhtai, whose speech and customs differed slightly, travelled with the Tsitsistas and joined them after 1832. The name Cheyenne comes from a Lakota word, Šahíyena, 'little Šahíya', whose meaning is uncertain. Their earliest written record dates from the mid-17th century, when a group visited the French Fort Crevecoeur, near present-day Peoria, Illinois. They then lived between the Mississippi River and Mille Lacs Lake in Minnesota, collecting wild rice and hunting bison. Tribal history says the Assiniboine drove them to Minnesota and North Dakota, where they built villages such as Biesterfeldt on the Sheyenne River. They first reached the Missouri River in 1676.

Pushed west by the Lakota, the Cheyenne formally allied with the Arapaho around 1811, and the alliance helped them expand their territory over much of the central Plains. By 1820 traders reported them at present-day Denver and on the Arkansas River. After Bent's Fort was built, a large part of the tribe moved south and became the Southern Cheyenne, while the rest stayed on the North Platte and Yellowstone headwaters as the Northern Cheyenne. Emigrant traffic along the trails from the 1840s increased competition for water and game, and cholera in 1849 killed about 2,000 Cheyenne, one-half to two-thirds of their population.

The Cheyenne fought the United States Army for over two decades from 1856. With the Arapaho and Lakota they fought in Red Cloud's War and the Great Sioux War of 1876, and a peaceful encampment of mostly women, children and elderly was massacred by US soldiers at Sand Creek. A reservation on the Tongue River, now the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation, was created by executive order on 16 November 1884 and extended in 1900. Along with the Lakota and Apache, the Cheyenne were among the last nations forced onto reservations.

Today the Cheyenne are two federally recognised nations: the Northern Cheyenne in Montana and the Southern Cheyenne, who form the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma with the Southern Arapaho. Historical figures include Black Kettle, Dull Knife, Little Wolf, Roman Nose and Two Moons, and the historian George Bent. The Southern Cheyenne artist Oakerhater is a canonised saint of the Episcopal Church.

The Cheyenne were a horse and warrior people. A warrior was also a protector, provider and leader, and men gained rank by counting coups, acts of bravery in battle. Their government was centred on the Arrow Keeper and the Council of Forty-Four, with four delegates from each of ten principal bands; the council also regulated the military societies. Women tanned hides and made lodges and clothing, and gathered roots and berries. The Cheyenne language belongs to the Algonquian family.
chhattisgarh: In ancient times the region was known as Dakshina Kosala, South Kosala, the native place of Rama's mother Kausalya. In the post-Vedic period the Pulinda tribe dominated part of it. The Sitabenga Caves, among the earliest examples of theatre architecture in India, are dated to the Mauryan period of the 3rd century BCE. From the 6th to the 12th centuries the region was split between rival dynasties, and parts of it were briefly under the Chola dynasty in the 11th century. Most of it was then consolidated under the Haihaiyavansi kingdom, whose rule lasted about 700 years until it came under the suzerainty of the Maratha Empire in the 1740s.

The name Chhattisgarh was popularised under the Maratha Empire and was first used in an official document in 1795. The Bhonsles of Nagpur ruled the region until 1845, when the East India Company annexed it. It was then administered until 1947 as the Chhattisgarh Division of the Central Provinces, and Raipur gained prominence over the earlier capital Ratanpur. Some areas that make up the present state were princely states, later merged into Madhya Pradesh.

The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 placed Chhattisgarh in Madhya Pradesh, where it remained for 44 years. A demand for a separate state was first raised in the 1920s, by the Raipur Congress unit in 1924, and was discussed at the Indian Congress at Tripuri. It was put to the States Reorganisation Commission in 1954 and rejected. No well-organised movement was ever started, and the campaigns took the form of petitions, public meetings, seminars, rallies and strikes. Chhattisgarh was granted statehood on 1 November 2000, with Raipur as its capital.

Chhattisgarh is a landlocked state in east-central India with a population of roughly 30 million. Its northern and southern parts are hilly and the centre is a fertile plain, with forests covering a large share of the state. Hindi and Chhattisgarhi are its official languages, and Scheduled Tribes such as the Gond, Halba and Oraon make up about 30 percent of the population, mainly in the forests of Bastar. The state is known as the rice bowl of India and holds large coal reserves, including the open-cast mines at Korba.
chiang-ching-kuo: Chiang was born on 27 April 1910 at Fenghua in Zhejiang, the eldest son of Chiang Kai-shek. In 1925, when the Kuomintang and the Communist Party were allied, he was sent to Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he was placed in a study group with Deng Xiaoping. After his father broke with the Communists in 1927, he publicly denounced him. The Soviet authorities then refused his repeated requests to return home, and he worked in an electrical plant and at the Uralmash heavy machinery plant, where in 1935 he married Faina Vakhreva. Stalin allowed him to return to China in 1937.

In 1948 he was sent to Shanghai to enforce price controls during the gold yuan currency reform, which failed, and he resigned. In 1949 he moved to Taiwan when the Kuomintang lost the Chinese Civil War. He directed the Taiwan Garrison Command, the military secret police, which used arbitrary arrests and torture during the White Terror. He became minister of defence in 1965, premier in 1972 and chairman of the Kuomintang after his father's death in 1975. The National Assembly elected him president on 21 March 1978.

He is credited with the Ten Major Construction Projects, an anti-corruption campaign and the promotion of native Taiwanese into government. After a pro-democracy rally at Kaohsiung on 10 December 1979 turned violent, opposition leaders were tried by a military court. When the Democratic Progressive Party was founded on 28 September 1986, he did not dissolve it. He ended martial law on 15 July 1987 after 39 years, and in the same year lifted the ban on travel to the mainland.

Chiang died of a heart attack on 13 January 1988, aged 77, and Lee Teng-hui succeeded him. Assessments differ. Some credit him with democratising Taiwan and with economic growth. Others point to the White Terror, the Kaohsiung Incident and the 1984 murder in California of the journalist Henry Liu by Taiwanese military intelligence operatives, and argue that his late reforms came mainly under pressure from Taiwanese citizens, the United States and diplomatic setbacks.
chiang-kai-shek: Chiang was born on 31 October 1887 in Xikou, then a small village about 48 km south of Ningbo, into a family of merchants. His father ran the family salt business, and his mother was a devout Buddhist, the daughter of a Buddhist monk. He received a military education in China and Japan, settling in Tokyo for its reputation as the centre of Japanese military science and for its exiled Chinese revolutionaries. There he became close to Chen Qimei, who recommended him for the Tongmenghui; he swore allegiance to the Three Principles of the People in 1908.

In 1920 Sun Yat-sen appointed Chiang chief of staff of the Second Guangdong Army, and from 1924 he was commandant of the Whampoa Military Academy. After Sun died on 12 March 1925, Chiang became one of the principal figures in a struggle for the succession in Guangzhou. He was appointed commander-in-chief of the Northern Expedition in June 1926, and by the end of October its army had occupied Wuhan. On 12 April troops and armed Green Gang groups attacked Communist-aligned workers' organisations in Shanghai, killing resisters and arresting many. Chiang proclaimed a rival Nationalist government at Nanjing on 18 April.

The Xi'an Incident of 1936 forced him into a Second United Front with the Communists. When the Second Sino-Japanese War broke out in July 1937 he sent 600,000 of his best soldiers to defend Shanghai, losing over 200,000 men. Nanjing fell in December, and he moved the government inland, first to Wuhan and later to Chongqing. In 1949 his Kuomintang was defeated by Mao Zedong's Communists and retreated to Taiwan, where he resumed his duties as president on 1 March 1950.

On Taiwan Chiang imposed martial law and a White Terror, which lasted until 1987 and 1992 respectively. He remained president of the Republic of China until his death on 5 April 1975, presiding over land reform and economic growth. Supporters credit him with unifying the nation and leading the resistance against Japan. Critics fault him for early appeasement of Japan, the deliberate flooding of the Yellow River, corruption and authoritarian rule on both the mainland and Taiwan.
chiang-rai: Chiang Rai lies on the flat alluvial plain of the Kok River, a tributary of the Mekong, between the Daen Lao Range in the north and the Phi Pan Nam Range in the south. The Kok flows along the north side of the city and joins the Mekong about 40 kilometres to the north-east. The Lao River, a tributary of the Kok, runs south of the city. Limestone hills rise to the west and north-west, and most of the region's hill peoples, such as the Karen, Akha, Lisu, Miao and Hmong, have their villages in that direction. The Golden Triangle, where the borders of Thailand, Laos and Myanmar meet, is 55 kilometres to the north-east.

King Mangrai founded the city in 1262 as a capital, and it became the seat of the Mangrai Dynasty. Chiang means city, so the name means the city of Mangrai. It was later conquered by Burma and stayed under Burmese rule for several hundred years. In 1786 it became a vassal of Siam. Siam annexed the Kingdom of Chiang Mai in 1893 as a Monthon, which Chiang Rai joined in 1910, and Chiang Rai became a full province of Thailand in 1933.

In 1432, in the reign of King Sam Fang Kaen (1402 to 1441), the Emerald Buddha, the most revered Buddha statue in Thailand, was found at Chiang Rai. According to one account an earthquake split the chedi at Wat Phra Kaeo and revealed a jade figure inside. Another telling says the statue had been hastily covered in mud just before marauders came to pillage, and that the earthquake broke off a piece of the clay. In 1992 the city pillar was moved from Wat Klang Wiang to Wat Phra That Doi Chom Thong, where it is known as Sadue Mueang, the navel of the city.

Chiang Rai is the capital and business centre of Chiang Rai Province and the northernmost major city of Thailand. It lies about 860 kilometres north of Bangkok and about 200 kilometres north-east of Chiang Mai, and Route 1 links it with Mae Sai on the border with Myanmar. Its temples include Wat Phra Kaeo, Wat Phra Sing and Wat Phra That Doi Chom Thong, and the modern Wat Rong Khun, built since 1998 by the artist Chalermchai Kositpipat. Mae Fah Luang University has a campus there. Chiang Rai is recognised as a Design City by the UNESCO Creative Cities Network.
chiapas: Chiapas is the southernmost state of Mexico. It borders Oaxaca, Veracruz and Tabasco and, to the east and south-east, Guatemala, and it has a long Pacific coastline. Its climate is humid and tropical but is moderated by altitude, and several parallel mountain ranges run through the centre, with cloud forests such as that of the El Triunfo biosphere reserve. The state is among the larger in Mexico, with a territory of 74,415 km2. Its capital and largest city is Tuxtla Gutiérrez.

Hunter-gatherers began to occupy the central valley around 7000 BCE, and agricultural villages appeared across the state between 1800 BCE and 300 CE. The coastal Soconusco region holds the oldest sites, including the Mokaya culture, described as the oldest ceramic culture of Mesoamerica, and Paso de la Amada, with the oldest Mesoamerican ballcourt. Later the Maya built Palenque, Yaxchilán, Bonampak and Toniná. The Bonampak murals are the only Mesoamerican murals preserved for over 1,500 years.

The Spanish found Maya and non-Maya peoples, the latter dominated by the Zoques and the Chiapanecas. Hernán Cortés sent tax collectors in 1522, and Luis Marín led the first military incursion in 1523. Many Tzotzils resisted fiercely in the highlands, and under Diego de Mazariegos many natives preferred suicide to submission, as at the Battle of Tepetchia, where some jumped into the Sumidero Canyon. The diocese was founded in 1538, and Bartolomé de las Casas was its best-known bishop. Because it lacked mineral wealth and was remote and rugged, Chiapas was spared the battles of independence.

In the late 19th century Governor Emilio Rabasa took on the regional caciques and in 1892 moved the capital from San Cristóbal de las Casas to Tuxtla. Estates grew coffee and other cash crops, and recruiters used a debt practice called enganche that trapped workers in a kind of indentured servitude. In January 1994 the Zapatista Army of National Liberation began an armed struggle, rooted in rural poverty and in opposition to Mexico's economic liberalisation.

Chiapas is one of the 32 federal entities of Mexico. It has one of the largest indigenous populations in the country, with twelve federally recognised ethnicities. Its rivers supply a large share of Mexican hydroelectric power, and it is a major producer of coffee and cacao. The marimba is its most important instrument, and its Maya sites draw visitors.
chiavenna: Chiavenna is a comune in the Province of Sondrio and the centre of the Alpine Valchiavenna. It lies about 100 kilometres north of Milan on the right bank of the river Mera, some 16 kilometres north of Lake Como. The Valle Spluga leads north to the Splügen Pass and the road to Chur, and the Val Bregaglia leads east. The name was long explained as coming from the Latin clavis, key, for its position on the passes, but it comes from a much older pre-Latin word, klava, meaning fallen rocks of a mountain slip.

Clavenna was conquered in 16 BCE by the troops of Augustus during his Alpine campaigns. The Romans built two roads from it: one up the Valle Spluga to the Splügen Pass, and another up the Val Bregaglia and across the Septimer Pass to Chur. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town marked the northern limit of the Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy, and it was retaken by the Byzantine Empire in the mid-6th century, avoiding capture by the Lombard kingdom until the 7th century. The bishops of Como gave the citizens town privileges in 1030, and counts ruled the valley until 1194, when the district passed to the bishops of Chur. The Visconti of Milan acquired the town and the Valtellina in 1335.

In 1486 the forces of the Three Leagues set Chiavenna ablaze in their fight with the Sforza, and Ludovico Sforza fortified it two years later. The town came under the Three Leagues during the War of the League of Cambrai and became a bailiwick governed by them. A first Protestant parish arose in 1542, and Chiavenna became a centre of the Reformation, sheltering religious refugees from Italy such as Camillo Renato, Bernardino Ochino and Girolamo Zanchi. Three Leagues rule lasted, apart from a loss during the Bündner Wirren of 1620–39, until 1797, when French revolutionaries merged the town into the Cisalpine Republic. From 1815 to 1859 it belonged with Lombardy to the House of Habsburg, and then followed Lombardy into the Kingdom of Italy.

Chiavenna is the chief town of its district. It is crowned by a ruined castle and is a member of the Cittaslow movement. A statue commemorates Peter de Salis, governor of the Valtellina in the 18th century.
chichen-itza: The Maya name means At the mouth of the well of the Itzá. The northern Yucatán Peninsula is karst, and its rivers run underground, so water comes from sinkholes called cenotes. Four visible cenotes could have supplied water all year at Chichen Itza, of which the Sacred Cenote is the best known. According to sources written after the Spanish conquest, in Maya and Spanish, the Maya threw objects and human beings into it as worship of the rain god Chaac. Edward Herbert Thompson dredged it from 1904 to 1910 and recovered gold, jade, pottery and incense, as well as human remains with wounds consistent with sacrifice.

The city's core took shape between 750 and 900, and its final layout dates from after 900. The earliest hieroglyphic date found there corresponds to 832 and the last, in the Osario temple, to 998. The city was founded by local Maya of northern Yucatán. The Itza, a Maya group of debated origins, began arriving around 800. Chichen Itza rose as the major centres of the southern lowlands declined, and in the 10th century it appears to have contributed to the collapse of Yaxuna and Coba. Between 900 and 1050 it was a powerful regional capital, trading by sea through its port of Isla Cerritos, obtaining obsidian from central Mexico and gold from southern Central America, and taking wealth as tribute from cities it conquered.

Archaeologists in the late 1980s proposed that it was ruled by a council of elite lineages, a system called multepal, but that idea has since been questioned. Colonial Maya sources such as the Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel say that Hunac Ceel, ruler of Mayapan, conquered it in the 13th century. Archaeological data indicate instead that it had declined by 1100, before Mayapan rose.

In 1526 Francisco de Montejo obtained a charter to conquer Yucatán. His son Francisco Montejo the Younger reached Chichen Itza, renamed it Ciudad Real and divided the land among his soldiers. The Maya besieged the Spanish among the ruins, and an assault lost Montejo 150 of his remaining troops. He abandoned the city in 1534, and by 1535 the Spanish had been driven from the peninsula.

The site core covers at least 5 square kilometres and has over 80 causeways, called sacbeob. The Temple of Kukulcán, about 30 m high with nine terraces, was built over an older temple found in the 1930s. The buildings were once painted in red, green, blue and purple. John Lloyd Stephens's book of 1843 made the city known, and Mexico's national anthropology institute now cares for the ruins.
chichester: Chichester stands on the River Lavant, a winterbourne, south of its gap through the South Downs. Many ancient routeways converge there, which made it a good site for settlement. The oldest part lies within the medieval walls, which are built on Roman foundations, and the plan of the city, with its North, South, East and West streets radiating from a central market cross, is inherited from the Romans. It is the county town of West Sussex and its only city.

There is no recorded evidence of a settlement of any size before the Romans. The area is believed to have played a significant part in the Roman invasion of 43, and military storage structures have been found near Fishbourne Roman Palace. The city centre stands on the foundations of Noviomagus Reginorum, capital of the Civitas Reginorum. Stane Street ran from its east gate to London, and an amphitheatre was built outside the walls around 80.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says Ælle of Sussex and his three sons annexed the area late in the fifth century and that the city was renamed after his son Cissa. Historians regard this as a myth, since no evidence shows reoccupation before the 9th century. Alfred the Great rebuilt Chichester as a burh, probably in 878 or 879, and it was one of the larger burhs, rated at 1500 hides in the Burghal Hidage.

After the Norman Conquest the cathedral founded at Selsey in 681 was moved to Chichester after the Norman Council of London of 1075 decreed that sees should be centred in cities. Domesday Book of 1086 records 300 dwellings and a population of 1,500. Roger de Mongomerie, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, received the town and built Chichester Castle soon after 1066. The city was besieged at Christmas 1642 during the First English Civil War.

Chichester Cathedral, the Cathedral Church of the Holy Trinity, is the seat of the Anglican Bishop of Chichester and has a separate bell tower, unusual in Britain. It holds a shrine to Saint Richard of Chichester, and Leonard Bernstein's Chichester Psalms were commissioned for it. Chichester Cross, built in 1501 as a covered marketplace, stands where the four main streets meet. The Novium museum, opened in 2012, preserves the Roman baths.
chief-seattle: His name is an anglicisation of the Lushootseed siʔaɬ, also spelled Si'ahl or Sealth. He was born around 1780 to Schweabe, a Suquamish leader, and Sholeetsa, a Duwamish woman. His birthplace is disputed: Suquamish tradition and Seattle himself said Blake Island, while the Duwamish say his mother's village on the Black River. In his youth he received the thunderbird as a spirit power in a vision quest. In 1792, when he was about six, he met the ships of George Vancouver. He had two wives and seven children, the best known being Kikisoblu, also called Princess Angeline.

Seattle gained a reputation as a strong warrior. Around 1810 he led an ambush on raiders coming down the Green River, in which the occupants of three of five canoes were killed or enslaved, and like many of his contemporaries he enslaved captives. In 1847 he helped lead the Suquamish war against the Chemakum, who were nearly wiped out. One of his sons was killed in it, and Seattle then sought baptism in the Catholic Church, taking the name Noah.

He afterwards cooperated with American settlers, guiding them, supplying labour to sawmills and farms and befriending Doc Maynard. As first signatory for the Suquamish he signed the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliot, ceding roughly 2.5 million acres to the United States, though it has been argued that he had no authority to sign for the upriver peoples. The unpopular treaty led many Duwamish to renounce his leadership. In the Puget Sound War he supported the Americans and afterwards sought clemency for Native leaders such as Leschi. In 1865 the town of Seattle banned Native Americans unless housed and employed by a settler, and he moved to the Suquamish reservation.

Seattle died on 7 June 1866 on the Port Madison Reservation and was buried with both Catholic and Suquamish rites. A speech given in 1854 to Isaac Stevens has been attributed to him. It is known only from a text reconstructed in 1887 from notes taken by Henry A. Smith; the historian Walt Crowley says it was filtered and embellished, and there is no corroboration for the exact words. Later versions added text and influenced environmentalists and Native American rights activists in the 1960s. The Suquamish hold Chief Seattle Days each August.
chieti: Chieti is a city and comune in Abruzzo, 200 kilometres east of Rome, and the capital of the province of Chieti. It lies about 10 kilometres from the Adriatic Sea, with the Majella and Gran Sasso mountains in the background. The old town, Chieti Alta, stands on a hill surrounded by the Pescara and Alento rivers. Its inhabitants are called teatini, and the English form of that name survives in the Theatines, a Catholic religious order.

Legend says the city was founded by the companions of Achilles and named for his mother Thetis, and according to Strabo it was founded by Arcadians as Thegeate. Around the 10th century BCE the Marrucini, an Italic tribe probably from Sabina, took the territory from the Osci, and Teate Marrucinorum was their chief town. After defeat by Rome the Marrucini became loyal allies. They received Roman citizenship and municipal status after the Social War, in which the Teate general Herius Asinius was killed. Teate flourished in the first century BCE as a municipium.

In 801 Pepin of Italy, son of Charlemagne, destroyed the town, which remained a fief of the Duchy of Spoleto for two centuries. In the 16th century Venice opened a consulate there in 1555, and Gian Pietro Carafa, the future Pope Paul IV, was bishop and archbishop. In 1861 it became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

Chieti has Roman remains: three temples, a theatre, baths with mosaics, underground cisterns, and a citadel with an amphitheatre of the first century CE. The National Archaeology Museum of Abruzzo houses the Warrior of Capestrano. The cathedral, dedicated to Saint Justin, was probably founded in the 8th century and keeps parts of a Romanesque crypt. Its Good Friday procession is held by some historians to have taken place since 842.
chihuahua-city: The city began with nearby silver. The Spanish captain Diego del Castillo founded the mining settlement of Santa Eulalia in 1652, but the climate and constant attacks by indigenous people halted work. Rich discoveries in 1707 brought immediate settlement. On 12 October 1709 Blas Cano de los Rios and Antonio Deza y Ulloa founded El Real de Minas de San Francisco de Cuéllar.

It became a villa in 1718 (some sources say 1715) as San Felipe el Real de Chihuahua, for Philip V of Spain, and the name was shortened in 1823. A tax on Santa Eulalia's silver paid for the parish church that is now the cathedral. The meaning of the name is variously given as between two waters, place of the holed rock and, in Rarámuri, dry and sandy place.

News of Mexico's independence movement was slow to reach Chihuahua, and royalists chose it for the trial of the insurgents seized at Acatita de Baján. Ignacio Allende, Mariano Jiménez, Juan Aldama and Manuel Santamaría were shot on 26 June, and Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla on 30 July.

Benito Juárez briefly made it capital of Mexico in 1864, during the second French intervention. In the Mexican Revolution it was a centre of the Madero movement and of Villismo, with figures including Abraham González, Pascual Orozco and Francisco Villa.

Chihuahua is the capital of the Mexican state of the same name, with 925,762 inhabitants in 2020, and its economy rests mainly on industry. Much colonial building was destroyed in the 1970s to widen streets, but the Temple of San Francisco, begun in 1717 and completed in 1789, survives, and the former Federal Palace, now a museum, holds Hidalgo's jail cell.
childebert-i: Childebert was the third of the four sons of Clovis I and was born at Reims. When the kingdom of the Franks was divided on his father's death in 511, he received Paris, the country to the north as far as the Somme, the land to the west as far as the English Channel, and Brittany. His brothers ruled elsewhere: Theuderic I at Metz, Chlodomer at Orléans and Chlothar I at Soissons.

In 523 Childebert joined his brothers in a war against Godomar of Burgundy, in which Chlodomer died in 524. According to tradition, Childebert and Chlothar then sent scissors and a sword to their mother Clotilde, giving her the choice of seeing Chlodomer's sons shorn of their long hair, a symbol of royal power, or killed. The two elder boys were murdered, the youngest, Clodoald, escaped to a monastic life, and Childebert annexed Chartres and Orléans. In 534 he conquered Burgundy with Chlothar and Theuderic's son Theudebert I and received Mâcon, Geneva and Lyons, and Arles and Marseille were guaranteed to him when Provence was ceded to the Franks in 535.

In 531 his sister Chrotilda, a Catholic married to the Arian king Amalaric of Hispania, appealed to him against her husband's mistreatment. Childebert defeated Amalaric, who was assassinated at Barcelona. In 542 he took Pamplona and besieged Zaragoza but had to retreat.

From Spain he brought back to Paris the tunic of Saint Vincent, and in its honour built the monastery later known as St-Germain-des-Prés. He died in December 558 and was buried there, and the abbey remained the royal necropolis of the Neustrian kings until 675. He left two daughters by his wife Ultragotha. He fought in more foreign wars than any of his brothers, in Burgundy, Spain and Provence, and was an acquisitive king.
childeric-i: Childeric was a Frankish ruler in what is now northern France, in the period when this part of Roman Gaul was cut off from the central Roman government in 461 and the last emperor based in Italy was deposed in 476. Gregory of Tours, writing in the 6th century, names his father as Merovech, after whom the Merovingian dynasty was named. Medieval sources disagree about his ancestry.

Gregory is the only near-contemporary source and mentions him twice. One passage tells a story of exile: Childeric dishonoured the daughters of his fellow Franks, was driven out and stayed in Thuringia with King Basinus and his wife Basina. After eight years he received a signal to return, and Basina left her husband to come with him. Modern scholars are sceptical of the claim that the Franks chose the Roman commander Aegidius as king meanwhile, though some think it preserves a memory of real events.

Childeric is called a king, rex, on the seal ring buried with him, though scholars interpret the term differently for northern Gaul at this time. Modern scholars generally assume he was allied with Aegidius, Roman military commander in Gaul from around 457, though there is little evidence of it. Gregory's second passage gives a compressed account of conflicts near the Loire, where the Visigoths were expanding. It places Childeric at a battle at Orléans, usually equated with the battle of about 463 in which Frederic, brother of the Visigothic king Theoderic II, was killed fighting Aegidius and the Franks, though other sources do not name Childeric.

Gregory also reports that Odovacrius allied with Childeric and that they subdued the Alamanni. Many scholars take this as an alliance with Odoacer, who ruled Italy after 476, but others dispute it. The Life of Saint Genevieve shows Childeric holding military control of the countryside around Paris.

He is generally considered to have died in 481 or 482, because Gregory says Clovis had ruled thirty years when he died about 511. Clovis I, his son, went on to unite much of Roman Gaul under Frankish rule.

His tomb was found in 1653 near the church of Saint-Brice in Tournai, now in Belgium. It held gold and garnet jewels, gold coins, a ring with the king's name and some 300 golden winged insects, usually viewed as bees or cicadas, laid on his cloak. The treasure was stolen from the royal library on the night of 5–6 November 1831 and melted down; a few pieces, including two bees, were recovered from the Seine. Napoleon later adopted the bees as a symbol of the French Empire.
chilperic-i: On the death of his father Chlothar I in 561, Chilperic tried to take the whole kingdom, seized the treasure at Berny and entered Paris. His brothers compelled him to divide it. Soissons, with Amiens, Arras, Cambrai, Thérouanne, Tournai and Boulogne, fell to him, while Charibert received Paris, Guntram Burgundy and Sigebert Austrasia. When Charibert died in 567 the brothers divided his kingdom and agreed to share Paris and the territory around it.

Chilperic soon went to war with Sigebert. While Sigebert was away fighting the Avars, Chilperic attacked Reims and took it, but Sigebert returned, retook the city, defeated him at Soissons and imprisoned his eldest son Theudebert. The war flared again in 567 and in 573, when Guntram first allied with Chilperic and then changed sides, and Chilperic lost both times.

Sigebert married Brunhilda, daughter of the Visigothic king Athanagild. Chilperic, who had repudiated his first wife Audovera and taken a serving-woman, Fredegund, as concubine, dismissed Fredegund and married Brunhilda's sister Galswintha. She was soon found strangled in her bed, and a few days later Chilperic married Fredegund.

The murder led to long wars between the brothers. In December 575 two assassins working for Fredegund killed Sigebert, when he had Chilperic at his mercy. Chilperic then took Tours, Poitiers and places in Aquitaine from Austrasia and fostered discord there during the minority of Childebert II.

In 578 he sent an army against the Breton ruler Waroch II of the Bro-Wened, who submitted after three days of fighting, did homage for Vannes, gave his son as hostage and agreed to pay tribute. He later broke his oath, but Chilperic's dominion over the Bretons was relatively secure.

Most of what is known of Chilperic comes from the History of the Franks by Gregory of Tours, who detested him, calling him the Nero and Herod of his time. He had provoked Gregory by taking Tours from Austrasia, seizing church property and appointing as bishops counts of the palace who were not clerics. Gregory also objected to his attempts to teach a new doctrine of the Trinity, although some scholars dispute how far Gregory disliked him, and he reports a forced conversion of Jews. His reign in Neustria saw the introduction of the Byzantine punishment of eye-gouging.

Chilperic was also a musician of some talent, wrote verse modelled on that of Sedulius, tried to reform the Frankish alphabet, and worked to reduce the worst effects of Salic law upon women. He was stabbed to death by an unknown assailant on his return from hunting at Chelles and buried in the Saint Vincent Basilica of Paris. His son Chlothar II succeeded him in Neustria and later became sole king of the Franks.
chimborazo: Chimborazo stands in the Cordillera Occidental of the Andes, in the Chimborazo Province, 150 km south-southwest of Quito, and rises about 2,500 metres above the surrounding highlands. It is a double volcano with four summits, of which Whymper (6,263 m) is the highest. In Quechua, chimba means on the other side and razu means ice or snow, one proposed origin of the name. Its glaciers supply water to people in the Bolívar and Chimborazo provinces, and local ice-gatherers, the hieleros, have sold its ice in the markets of Guaranda and Riobamba.

About 35,000 years ago a collapse produced a debris avalanche that underlies the city of Riobamba. The volcano erupted several times in the Holocene, the last about 550 CE, give or take 150 years. Until the early 19th century Chimborazo was thought the highest mountain on Earth, which drew many attempts on its summit. In 1746 French academicians of the French Geodesic Mission explored it. In June 1802 Alexander von Humboldt, with Aimé Bonpland and Carlos Montúfar, was forced back by altitude sickness at 5,875 m, higher than any European had recorded. On 4 January 1880 the English climber Edward Whymper reached the summit, and when critics doubted it he climbed it again later that year by another route with David Beltrán and Francisco Campaña.

At 6,263 m Chimborazo is the highest mountain in Ecuador. Because the Earth bulges at the Equator, its summit, one degree south of the line, is widely reported to be the farthest point on the surface from the Earth's centre, about 2.1 km farther than the summit of Mount Everest, though Everest is higher above sea level. A faunal reserve for vicuña, llama and alpaca surrounds it, and it appears on the coat of arms of Ecuador. Simón Bolívar's poem Mi delirio sobre el Chimborazo was inspired by it, and Frederick Edwin Church painted it in 1864.
china: China covers 9.6 million square kilometres, the third largest country by area, with a dry and mountainous west and both mountains and wide river valleys in the east. Chinese civilization was traditionally centred in the lowlands around the two longest rivers, the Yangtze and the Yellow River, both of which originate on the Tibetan Plateau. Mount Everest, the world's highest point, lies on the border with Nepal. The climate is dominated by dry seasons and wet monsoons, and the Yellow River's perennial floods have devastated the surrounding plains throughout recorded history.

Modern Homo sapiens are attested in China from around 50,000 years ago, and pottery-making Neolithic cultures emerged after about 8,000 BCE. After 2000 BCE the Erlitou culture emerged in the Central Plain, controversially identified with the Xia, the traditionally accepted first dynasty; no written records confirm this. The Shang dynasty purportedly succeeded the Xia around 1600 BCE, and its late phase is attested by oracle bone script, the earliest known writing in China. The Zhou overthrew the Shang c. 1046 BCE, and centralised authority collapsed in 771 BCE. The Eastern Zhou saw the Spring and Autumn period and then the seven Warring States, and schools of thought such as Confucianism and Daoism.

In 221 BCE the Qin ruler Qin Shi Huang proclaimed himself the first emperor, but the dynasty lasted only fifteen years. It was followed by the Han dynasty, and two millennia of imperial rule across periods of unity and division followed. The empire was succeeded by the Republic of China after the 1911 Revolution. The Warlord Era and the Chinese Civil War followed, interrupted by the Second Sino-Japanese War. In 1949 the Chinese Communist Party proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan; both sides still claim political legitimacy. The party's attempts to advance its political program faltered through famine and political turmoil, and the reform and opening-up that began in 1978 moved China towards a socialist market economy.

The 2020 census recorded a population of 1,411,778,724, and Beijing is the capital. China is a unitary state with the Chinese Communist Party as its sole ruling party. It maintained a one-child policy from 1979 to 2015.

The Han are the dominant ethnicity, and 55 minorities are recognised, including the Hui, Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Zhuang. It has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the Great Wall and the Grand Canal.
chinese-civil-war: After the 1911 Revolution China fell into a power struggle following Yuan Shikai's death in 1916. Sun Yat-sen's Kuomintang (KMT) set up a government in Guangzhou to rival the warlords. When Western countries ignored his requests for aid, Sun turned to the Soviet Union, and in 1923 the Sun–Joffe Manifesto pledged Soviet assistance. In 1926 and 1927 the KMT and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), allied in the First United Front, carried out the Northern Expedition against the warlords. After the Shanghai massacre of 1927 the CCP launched an uprising at Nanchang on 1 August 1927, the date from which armed conflict continued intermittently.

The first phase lasted from 1927 to 1937. In October 1934 the CCP broke out of the ring of blockhouses that encircled it, beginning the Long March, which lasted a year. When Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, Chiang Kai-shek held to a policy of 'first internal pacification, then external resistance'. From 1937, when Japan launched its full-scale invasion, hostilities were mostly put on hold under the Second United Front, though cooperation was minimal and clashes remained common.

As Japan's defeat approached, both sides rushed to take over occupied areas. In 1945 the Communists had 1.2 million troops with 2 million militia, and Soviet forces handed them Northeast China and captured Japanese weapons. On 20 July 1946 Chiang launched a large assault on Communist territory in the north with 113 brigades. The CCP gave up territory to preserve its forces, and after a year the balance had shifted. The Liaoshen, Huaihai and Pingjin campaigns ended in Communist victory in January 1949.

The Communists proclaimed the People's Republic of China in October 1949, and the Republic of China government retreated to Taiwan on 7 December 1949. Historians explain the Communist victory by the hyperinflation, corruption and loss of trust under the Nationalist government, and by the CCP's land reform, which won peasant support. Both sides committed atrocities in which millions of non-combatants were killed. After 1927 the Kuomintang killed between 300,000 and one million people, mainly peasants, in the White Terror, and the Communists executed 2,000 to 3,000 members of the Futian battalion in December 1930. After 1949, official figures of 1954 give at least 2.6 million arrested and 712,000 executed in the Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries.
chinese-communist-party: The October Revolution and Marxist theory inspired the founding of the party. Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao were among the first to support Leninism and world revolution in public, and both regarded the October Revolution as heralding a new era for oppressed countries. In 1921 they founded the party with the help of the Far Eastern Bureau of the Russian Communist Party and that of the Communist International. In its first years it was aligned with the Kuomintang. The rise of the Kuomintang's right wing under Chiang Kai-shek, and massacres of tens of thousands of party members, led to a split and a prolonged civil war.

On 15 July 1927 the Wuhan government of the Kuomintang expelled all communists. The party answered by founding the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army of China, and a battalion under General Zhu De took the city of Nanchang on 1 August 1927 in the Nanchang uprising. During about ten years of guerrilla warfare Mao Zedong became the most influential figure in the party, which built a strong base among the rural peasantry with its land reform policies.

Support continued to grow during the Second Sino-Japanese War, and after the Japanese surrender in 1945 the party defeated the Nationalist government. Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China before a large crowd at Tiananmen Square on 1 October 1949, and the remnants of the Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan.

Mao remained the most influential member until his death in 1976. Under him the party completed its land reform, launched five-year plans and split with the Soviet Union, and in the Cultural Revolution he tried to purge the party of elements deemed capitalist or reactionary. After his death Hua Guofeng removed the Gang of Four from power, and Deng Xiaoping won a power struggle with Hua to become paramount leader in 1978. Deng, with Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang, led the policies of reform and opening up, and argued that a socialist state could use a market economy without itself being capitalist.

The party seeks officially to adapt Marxism–Leninism to Chinese conditions, a process it calls socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is organised on democratic centralism, which allows open discussion of policy on condition of unity once a decision is made. Its highest body is the National Congress, convened every five years. When the Congress is not in session the Central Committee is the highest body, but because it usually meets only once a year, most duties lie with the Politburo and its Standing Committee. The party's leader holds the office of general secretary, and also chairs the Central Military Commission.
chingiz-aitmatov: Chinghiz Torekulovich Aitmatov was born on 12 December 1928 to a Kyrgyz father and a Tatar mother, both civil servants in Sheker. He grew up as Kyrgyzstan was transformed from one of the most remote lands of the Russian Empire into a republic of the USSR. In 1937 his father was charged in Moscow with bourgeois nationalism, and he was arrested and executed in 1938. Aitmatov worked from an early age, as assistant to the secretary of the village soviet at fourteen and later as a tax collector and a loader.
