He studied animal husbandry at Frunze, then literature at the Maxim Gorky Literature Institute in Moscow.

His first publications appeared in 1952, in Russian, and his first work in Kyrgyz, White Rain, in 1954. The novella Jamila, published in 1958, proved his talent: seen through the eyes of an adolescent boy, it tells of a village girl, separated from her soldier husband by the war, who falls in love with a disabled former soldier. He received the Lenin Prize in 1963 for the collection Tales of the Mountains and Steppes. Later works include Farewell, Gyulsary!, The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years of 1980 and The Place of the Skull of 1987.

His writing draws on folklore, recreating oral tales in contemporary settings, and nearly every story refers to a myth, legend or folktale. In The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years a legend of a young captive turned into a mankurt serves as a tragic allegory. He also wrote of the closeness of people to animals, such as a man and his stallion in Farewell, Gyulsary!. Most of his early works were in Kyrgyz, but from 1966 he wrote in Russian, which he said was as much a native language for him as Kyrgyz.

Aitmatov worked for Pravda for eight years, joined the Soviet Communist Party in 1959 and endorsed Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost. From 1990 to 1993 he was Soviet ambassador to Luxembourg, then accredited by Russia, and from 2000 to 2008 he represented Kyrgyzstan to the European Union, NATO, UNESCO and the Benelux countries. He died of pneumonia on 10 June 2008 in a hospital in Nuremberg, aged 79.
chinguetti: Chinguetti is a ksar and medieval trading centre in northern Mauritania, on the Adrar Plateau east of Atar. A wadi divides it into an old sector and a new one. The region was once a broad savannah, and rock paintings at Agrour Amogjar in the nearby Amogjar Pass show giraffes, cows and people in a green landscape. The older houses are built of reddish dry-stone and mud-brick with flat roofs timbered from palms, and many have hand-hewn doors cut from ancient acacia trees that have long disappeared from the area. Narrow streets lead to the central mosque.

The name means spring of horses in the Azer dialect, an extinct dialect of Soninke heavily mixed with Berber. By the 11th century the town was a trading centre for the Sanhaja, a confederation of Berber tribes that merged with the Almoravids, who spread the Malikite rite of Sunni Islam across the western Maghreb. The town's stark architecture is said to reflect their strict beliefs.

After two centuries of decline the town was effectively re-founded in the 13th century as a fortified trading centre for nomadic trans-Saharan caravans, connecting the Mediterranean with Sub-Saharan Africa. The walls have disappeared, but many buildings in the old sector date from this period. For centuries it was a gathering place for pilgrims of the Maghreb on their way to Mecca and was regarded as a holy city in its own right. Its schools taught rhetoric, law, astronomy, mathematics and medicine, and for many centuries all of Mauritania was commonly known in the Arab world as Bilad Shinqit, the land of Chinguetti.

UNESCO designated Chinguetti, with Ouadane, Tichitt and Oualata, a World Heritage Site in 1996. The Friday Mosque, a dry-stone building of the 13th and 14th centuries with a square minaret topped by five ostrich egg finials, is widely considered by Mauritanians to be the national symbol. The old quarter has five important manuscript libraries of scientific and Qur'anic texts, many from the later Middle Ages. The desert threatens the town: high dunes mark its western edge and several houses have been abandoned to the sand.
chinon: Chinon is a commune in the Indre-et-Loire department of the Centre-Val de Loire region, 47 kilometres south-west of Tours. It lies on both banks of the river Vienne, about 10 kilometres from where the Vienne joins the Loire, with the historic town mainly on the northern bank at the foot of the medieval castle. Rivers were the main trade routes in the Middle Ages, and the Vienne links the fertile Poitou and the city of Limoges to the Loire. The rocky outcrop above the town gave both a natural fort and protection from floods.

Settlement dates from prehistoric times, and by the 5th century a Gallo-Roman castrum stood on the site. About the middle of that century Saint Mexme, a disciple of Saint Martin, founded a hermitage and then a monastery east of the town. Chinon grew especially under Henry II, Count of Anjou and, from 1154, King of England, who rebuilt the castle as his administrative centre and favourite residence. He died there in 1189, and it passed to Richard I and then to John, who lost it in 1205 in a siege by Philip II of France.

In 1307 Jacques de Molay, Grand Master of the Knights Templar, and other dignitaries of the order were held in the castle before their trial. During the Hundred Years' War the heir apparent, the future Charles VII, installed his court at Chinon in 1425. In 1429 the seventeen-year-old Joan of Arc came there to meet him, and after she was questioned and given men and arms she broke the siege of Orléans, and Charles was crowned at Reims. François Rabelais was born in the commune. From the 16th century Chinon was no longer a royal residence, and its fortifications were pulled down in the 1820s.

Chinon is known for its castle, its historic town and its Cabernet Franc-based red wines, kept in caves cut into the banks of the Vienne. The historic centre, a conservation area since 1968, has half-timbered houses of the 14th and 15th centuries and town houses of local tufa stone with slate roofs. The Romanesque collegiate church of Saint-Mexme keeps a nave and first façade from about the year 1000. This part of the Loire Valley has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.
chinvat-bridge: The Avestan name, Cinvatô Peretûm, is rendered as bridge of judgement or as beam-shaped bridge; other forms of the name are Chinwad, Cinvat, Chinvar and Chinavat. How the bridge appears depends on the asha, the righteousness, of the soul that comes to it. Three divinities are thought to be its guardians: Sraosha, who stands for conscience, Mithra, for covenant, and Rashnu, for justice. Believers hold that the souls that cross successfully are united with Ahura Mazda. The Yasna describes the bridge in its 71st chapter and the Vendidad in its nineteenth fargard.

The bridge has often been identified with the rainbow or with the Milky Way, as in C. P. Tiele's History of Religion. Other scholars, among them C. F. Keary and Ferdinand Justi, reject this reading, citing descriptions of the bridge as rising straight upward and not in a curve.

Cyrus Niknam, a mobad and writer on ancient Iranian culture, denies that Zoroaster taught a bridge at all. In his reading the phrase in the hymns means a passage concerned with how to live, a questioning of the conscience, with no material crossing for the soul. He holds that the priests of the Sasanian era adapted beliefs about heaven, hell and the afterlife from other cultures that had reached Iran, and that the picture of a bridge wide for the righteous and thin as a hair for sinners belongs to that later development, as does the Book of Arda Viraf, and not to the Gathas.

The most notable of the Sogdian depictions is on the east wall of the funerary couch of the sabao Wirkak, excavated at Xi'an; a fragmentary one is on the couch in the Miho Museum. As-Sirat in Islam is a similar idea. In Yazidism the Silat Bridge at Lalish leads to the holiest Yazidi shrine, marks the passage from the profane world to the sacred, and is held to play a part at the end of times as well. In modern literature Charles Olson refers to the bridge in The Maximus Poems, and Dimitris Lyacos alludes to it in With the People from the Bridge.
chioggia: Chioggia lies on a small island at the southern entrance to the Venetian Lagoon, about 25 kilometres south of Venice. Causeways connect it to the mainland and to its quarter of Sottomarina. It is a comune of the Metropolitan City of Venice in the Veneto region. It is often called Little Venice because of its few canals, chief among them the Canale Vena, and its narrow streets, known as calli.

Chioggia and Sottomarina were not prominent in antiquity. Pliny mentions the place as the fossa Clodia, and a local legend attributes the name to a founder called Clodius, though the origin of the belief is not known. The name later appears as Clugia, Chiozza and finally Chioggia. The oldest documents naming it date from the 6th century, when it was part of the Byzantine Empire. King Pippin of Italy destroyed it in the 9th century, and it was rebuilt around a new industry based on salt pans. In the Middle Ages the town proper was Clugia major, while Clugia minor was a sand bar about 600 metres further into the Adriatic.

A free commune and an episcopal see from 1110, Chioggia played an important part in the War of Chioggia between Genoa and Venice. Genoa conquered it in 1378 and Venice took it finally in June 1380. The town remained largely autonomous but was always afterwards subordinate to Venice. On 14 March 1381 it made an alliance with Zadar and Trogir against Venice. The town's churches were much reworked in the 16th and 17th centuries, the period of its highest prosperity. The cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, founded in the eleventh century, became a cathedral in 1110 and was rebuilt from 1623 by Baldassare Longhena.

Fishing has historically been the livelihood of the port and remains a significant economic sector, alongside textiles, brick-making and steel, while Sottomarina is largely given over to seafront tourism. The bell tower of the Church of Sant'Andrea, dating from the 11th or 12th century, is said to hold the oldest functioning tower clock in the world. Chioggia is known for bobbin lace and was the setting of Carlo Goldoni's play Le baruffe chiozzotte. It also gives its name to a variety of beetroot and of radicchio. Its most common surname is Zennaro, and the comune officially records the nicknames known as detto that distinguish branches of one family.
chisinau: Chișinău stands on the river Bâc, a tributary of the Dniester, in the middle of Moldova, on a relatively level landscape with very fertile ground. It is roughly equidistant between the borders with Romania, 58 km away, and Ukraine, 54 km away, and very close to the geographic centre of the country. The city proper covers 120 km2 and the municipality 635 km2. Its climate is humid continental, with hot summers and cold, windy winters.

The origin of the name is unclear. One theory derives it from the archaic Romanian chișla, meaning spring or source of water, and nouă, new, because the town grew around a small spring. Another, attributed to the historian Ștefan Ciobanu, holds that it was formed like the name of Chișineu in western Romania, from the Hungarian kis, small, and Jenő, one of the seven Hungarian tribes. A third, by the linguist Kiss Lajos, derives it from a Cuman word for a grave or kurgan.

Chișinău was founded in 1436 as a monastery village and belonged to the Principality of Moldavia, which from the 16th century was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire while retaining its autonomy. At the beginning of the 19th century it was a small town of 7,000 inhabitants. In 1812, after the Russo-Turkish War of 1806-1812, the Ottomans ceded the eastern half of Moldavia to the Russian Empire. The new territory became known as Bessarabia, and Chișinău became the capital of its oblast.

A generous development plan gave the city broad, long roads by 1834 and divided it roughly into an old part with irregular buildings and a newer centre and station. Between 1830 and 1836 the architect Avraam Melnikov built the Nativity Cathedral with a bell tower, and in 1840 the Triumphal Arch, planned by Luca Zaushkevich, was completed. The belfry was demolished in Soviet times and rebuilt in 1997. After the Russian Empire the city belonged to the Moldavian Democratic Republic in 1917-1918, to the Kingdom of Romania in 1918-1940 and 1941-1944, and to the Soviet Union in 1940-1941 and 1944-1991.

Chișinău has been the capital of Moldova since 1991. It is the country's main industrial and commercial centre and its largest transport hub, and the municipality holds nearly a third of the population. The city was significantly damaged in the Second World War and by earthquakes. The architect Alexander Bernardazzi designed many buildings, including the City Hall and the Church of Saint Theodore, and much of the city is built of limestone quarried at Cricova. The house where Alexander Pushkin lived in exile is now a museum.
chittagong: Chittagong lies in south-eastern Bangladesh, between the Chittagong Hill Tracts and the Bay of Bengal, on the banks of the Karnaphuli River, which enters the bay through an estuary 12 kilometres west of the city centre. The city straddles the coastal foothills of the hill tracts. The highest peak in the district is Mount Sitakunda, at 351 metres. Several lakes were created under Mughal rule. The etymology of the name is uncertain, and the city has been known as Chatigaon, Chattagrama, Islamabad and Porto Grande de Bengala.

Stone Age fossils and tools show that the region has been inhabited since Neolithic times, and the port has a recorded history reaching back to the 4th century BCE. Its harbour appears on Ptolemy's world map of the 2nd century. The region belonged to the ancient Bengali kingdoms of Samatata and Harikela. In the 7th century the Chinese traveller Xuanzang described the area as a sleeping beauty rising from mist and water. In the 9th century merchants from the Abbasid Caliphate established a trading post there, and the port fell to the Muslim conquest of Bengal in the 14th century. A royal mint stood there under the Delhi Sultanate, the Bengal Sultanate and the Mughal Empire.

Between the 15th and 17th centuries Chittagong was also a centre of administrative, literary, commercial and maritime activity in Arakan, a strip of land along the eastern coast of the Bay of Bengal that was under strong Bengali influence for 350 years. In the 16th century the port became a Portuguese trading post. The Mughal Empire expelled the Portuguese and the Arakanese in 1666. The port was later reorganised, in 1887, and declared a Major Port of British India in 1928.

During the Second World War Chittagong was a critical base for the Allied forces in the Burma Campaign. The Partition of British India in 1947 made it the chief port of East Pakistan, and in 1971 it was the site of the Bangladeshi declaration of independence.

Chittagong, officially Chattogram, is the second-largest city of Bangladesh after Dhaka and the seat of the Chittagong Division. Its port is the busiest in Bangladesh and in the Bay of Bengal. The city is also the business capital of Bangladesh, and the Chittagong Stock Exchange and the Chittagong Tea Auction are based there. The Anderkilla Shahi Jame Mosque is a well-known Mughal property.
chlodio: Very little is known about Chlodio, who is also called Cloio or Chlogio, and he is mentioned only briefly in a small number of records. His name is a short form of Frankish names such as Hlodowig and Hlodhari, from a Germanic root hlod-. A popular proposal among modern scholars makes him a descendant of the Salian Franks whom the Romans allowed to settle in Texandria in the 4th century.

In his time northern Gaul was changing from a Roman border province into an area where several powers lived side by side. It was formally Roman, but the empire largely let the region go, and the general Flavius Aëtius campaigned there mainly through negotiation, temporary garrisons and allies among the Huns.

The poet Sidonius Apollinaris, in a panegyric for the emperor Majorian, describes Franks overrunning the Atrebates under Cloio while Aëtius commanded in Gaul, and tells how Majorian fought under Aëtius in an attack on a Frankish wedding at Vicus Helena. Gregory of Tours, writing much later, says Chlodio attacked from a fort called Dispargum, sent spies to Cambrai, crushed the Romans and captured the town, then occupied the country up to the Somme. Its location is uncertain: Duisburg, a place of that name near Brussels, and Diest have all been proposed.

The Liber Historiae Francorum, a later and generally unreliable work, adds that he pushed west through the Silva Carbonaria and took Tournai before moving south to Cambrai. One study suggests the conquest of Tournai and Cambrai probably happened between 445 and 450. His advance carried Frankish rule deeper into the empire, far from the Rhine border where the Franks had long been established.

Gregory of Tours reports that some people said Merovech, father of Childeric, was descended from Chlodio, and in his own time it was believed that the Merovingian dynasty descended from him somehow. Later chronicles give conflicting parentage, naming Pharamond or Theudemer as his father, and these pedigrees are considered unreliable. No contemporary records mention Merovech, so modern scholars find the link difficult to judge. Childeric was buried in Tournai, which later writers associated with Chlodio, and Childeric's son Clovis I first took power in the same area.
chlodomer: Chlodomer, also spelled Clodomir or Clodomer, was one of the four sons of Clovis I and his wife Clotilde. On his father's death in 511 he divided the kingdom of the Franks with his brothers Theuderic I, Childebert I and Chlothar I, and became king at Orléans. His kingdom included the bishoprics of Tours, Poitiers and Orléans. He married Guntheuc, and they had three sons: Theodebald, Gunthar and Clodoald.

In 523 and 524 Chlodomer and his brothers invaded Burgundy, possibly at the instigation of his mother Clotilde, who wished to avenge the death of her parents, allegedly murdered by her uncle Gundobad, the father of Sigismund of Burgundy. Gregory of Tours tells this story of Clotilde's revenge, but it is assumed to be apocryphal. After capturing Sigismund, Chlodomer returned to Orléans and had Sigismund and his sons Gisald and Gondebaud killed in May 524. Sigismund's brother Gondomar then returned in triumph at the head of troops sent by his ally, the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, and massacred the garrison the Franks had left behind. Chlodomer led a second expedition and was killed in June 524 at the Battle of Vézeronce.

After his death his kingdom was divided: Chlothar I received Touraine and Poitou, and Childebert I the lands on both banks of the Loire with Orléans. His widow married Chlothar, and Chlodomer's three sons were taken to Paris and entrusted to their grandmother Clotilde. Two of them, Theodebald, aged ten, and Gunthar, aged seven, were murdered so that they would not claim a share of their father's inheritance. Only the youngest, Clodoald, was saved by a few loyal followers. Better known as Saint Cloud, he gave up his hair, the symbol of Frankish royalty, rather than his life, and later became abbot of Nogent.
chlodwig-zu-hohenlohe-schillingsfurst: Chlodwig Carl Viktor of Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst was born on 31 March 1819 at Rotenburg an der Fulda, in Hesse, the second of six sons. His father was a Catholic and his mother a Lutheran, and the sons were brought up as Catholics according to the custom of the time. As the younger son of a cadet line he needed a profession. He considered a commission in the British army through his aunt, a half-sister of Queen Victoria, but chose the Prussian civil service. The years of training confirmed his liberalism: he favoured a free press and German unity under Prussia, but opposed the Prussification of Germany.

After the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 he argued for closer union with Prussia. On 31 December 1866 he was appointed minister of the royal house and of foreign affairs and president of the council of ministers of Bavaria, reportedly at the urging of Richard Wagner. He reorganised the Bavarian army on the Prussian model, brought about a military union of the southern states and became a vice-president of the customs parliament in 1868. He opposed the ultramontane party over the First Vatican Council, and the combination of ultramontanes and Bavarian patriots forced him to resign on 7 March 1870.

He was elected to the Reichstag in 1871 and became its vice-president. He helped found the Imperial Liberal Party and supported Bismarck's Kulturkampf. Bismarck made him ambassador in Paris in 1873, and in 1880 he served briefly as head of the Foreign Office in Berlin. As governor of Alsace-Lorraine from 1885 he carried out the coercive measures of 1887 and 1888, though he largely disapproved of them, and his conciliatory manner did much to reconcile the population to German rule.

In October 1894 Emperor Wilhelm II, at his urgent request, made the aged Hohenlohe Imperial Chancellor in succession to Leo von Caprivi. He rarely appeared in the Prussian or German parliaments and left great independence to his secretaries of state, among them Bernhard von Bülow. Wilhelm's reshuffles of 1897, which brought Bülow to the Foreign Office and Alfred von Tirpitz to the Naval Office, in effect disempowered him.

He could not halt the turn to imperialist world policy and naval armament. He attempted a reform of the Prussian Military Law in 1898 and a Law on Associations in 1899, and the Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch was adopted in 1896. He resigned on 17 October 1900, was succeeded by Bülow, and died on 6 July 1901 at Bad Ragaz, aged 82.
chlothar-i: Chlothar was one of the four sons of Clovis I who inherited shares of their father's kingdom in 511. His brothers were Theuderic, Chlodomer and Childebert I. Chlothar received Soissons, which he made his capital, with Laon, Noyon, Cambrai, Maastricht and the lower Meuse, and a second part in Aquitaine. Merovingian custom divided an inheritance evenly among sons, so the kingdom was often split. Chlothar had five wives, more from political expediency than personal motive, among them Radegund, a Thuringian princess later canonised, and Ingund, by whom he had most of his sons. He was a less than enthusiastic Christian and introduced taxes on church property.

Chlothar spent most of his life expanding his territory at the expense of relatives and neighbours, while his brothers avoided open war with him by joining his attacks and sharing the spoils. In 524 Chlodomer was killed at the Battle of Vézeronce. Chlothar and Childebert then took Chlodomer's kingdom of Orléans, and two of Chlodomer's young sons, Theodebald and Gunthar, were killed, according to the account given, by Chlothar himself. A third, Clodoald, escaped and became a monk. With Theuderic he conquered Thuringia, and in 534, with Childebert and Theudebert, he overran the Burgundian kingdom, which was divided among the three.

When Theudebald died childless in 555, Chlothar took Metz, and he put down a Saxon revolt. On 23 December 558 Childebert died without heirs, and Chlothar reunited the whole Frankish kingdom. His son Chram, who had set himself against him with Childebert's encouragement, was captured and put to death with his wife and daughters.

Chlothar died at the end of 561, at the age of 64, of acute pneumonia, and was buried at Soissons. His kingdom then covered all of Gaul except Septimania and part of present-day Germany. It was divided again among his four surviving sons: Charibert received Paris, Guntram Burgundy, Sigebert the kingdom of Metz and Chilperic Soissons.
chlothar-ii: Chlothar was born in May or June 584, the son of Chilperic I and Fredegund. His parents, who suspected that their four older sons had been murdered, raised him in secret at Vitry-en-Artois. In September 584 Chilperic was murdered after a hunt near Chelles, and Fredegund asked King Guntram of Burgundy to adopt the child and protect him. A meeting of Greater Neustria recognised the boy, though some doubted his paternity, and named him Clothar; he was baptised on 23 October 585 with Guntram as godfather.

He took power on Fredegund's death in 597. His realm was rich but one of the smallest in Francia, and in 599 his nephews Theuderic II of Burgundy and Theudebert II of Austrasia defeated him at Dormelles and reduced it to the regions of Beauvais, Amiens and Rouen.

The brothers soon fought each other, and Theuderic died of dysentery at Metz in 613 while preparing to invade Neustria. The mayors of the palace Warnachar and Rado abandoned his heir's cause and nobles deserted the army of the old queen Brunhilda and her great-grandson Sigebert II. Chlothar's soldiers caught them near Lake Neuchâtel, and he had Brunhilda tried and put to death by being dragged behind a horse. Sigebert and his brother Corbo were executed too. Chlothar was sole ruler of the Franks.

In 614 he issued the Edict of Paris, which reserved many rights to the nobles, required officials to come from the region they administer, and excluded Jews from civil employment for the Crown. Historians interpret it in different ways. In 617 he made the office of mayor of the palace a lifetime appointment. In 623 he gave Austrasia to his son Dagobert I, repaying the support of Bishop Arnulf of Metz and Pepin I, who were in effect granted semi-autonomy.

Chlothar died in 629, aged 45, and was buried in the Saint Vincent Basilica of Paris. Dagobert succeeded him in Neustria and Burgundy, and Charibert became king of Aquitaine. Unusually for a Merovingian he practised monogamy, though early deaths meant he had three wives, and he was generally an ally of the church. His reign was long but saw royal power erode in favour of the nobility and the church.
choco-department: The Chocó Department lies in the west of Colombia and is the only Colombian department with coastlines on both the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic. It contains all of Colombia's border with Panama and makes up most of the ecoregion known as El Chocó, which extends from Panama to Ecuador. The Baudó Mountains on the coast and the inland Cordillera Occidental are cut by low valleys, under 1,000 metres in altitude, that form most of the territory, and most of the land is thick rainforest. Three large rivers drain it: the Atrato, the San Juan and the Baudó.

The first city founded by conquistadors on the American mainland, Santa María la Antigua del Darién, was established by Vasco Núñez de Balboa in 1510 and disestablished in 1524. Spanish colonizers brought enslaved Africans to the area, and their descendants make up most of the department's population today. In the late 19th century the Chocó's gold drew miners from many countries. The department was created in 1944.

Its low population, mountainous and inhospitable terrain and distance from Bogotá meant that it received little attention from the Colombian government. Under the military dictator Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, his administration proposed to abolish the Chocó and divide its territory between the departments of Antioquia and Valle del Cauca. The coup of 1957 by General Gabriel París Gordillo overthrew Rojas Pinilla and ended these plans.

Quibdó is the capital and largest city. The department produces much of Colombia's platinum and is its top gold-producing region, and much of the wood used inside the country is harvested there. Afro-Colombians form the large majority of its people, followed by the Embera, an Indigenous people more than half of whose Colombian population lives in the Chocó. Its rainforests are a Key Biodiversity Area, with a high proportion of endemic plant and bird species.
chogha-zanbil: Chogha Zanbil, typically translated as 'basket mound', is an Elamite complex in the Khuzestan province of Iran, about 30 km southeast of Susa. Its construction date is unclear because the chronology of the reign of Untash-Napirisha is uncertain, but it falls in the 14th or 13th century BCE. Its original name was Dur Untash, 'town of Untash', and it was built mainly to honour the great god Inshushinak. It is unlikely that many people besides priests and servants ever lived there. Some scholars infer from its many temples that Untash-Napirisha tried to create a new religious centre, possibly meant to replace Susa, uniting the gods of highland and lowland Elam.

Three concentric walls protect the complex. Inscriptions record that the outer wall had seven gates, of which only two have been found. Between the outer and middle walls stood a temple shared by Napirisha and Inshushinak, the middle area held eleven temples for other gods, and the outer area royal palaces and a funerary palace with five subterranean royal tombs. Most of the innermost area is taken up by the great ziggurat, which originally measured 105.2 metres on each side and about 53 metres in height, in five levels, and was crowned with a temple. It has a mud-brick core faced with baked bricks, many inscribed with the names of deities in Elamite and Akkadian. It now stands 24.75 metres high.

Building continued after Untash-Napirisha's death, and the site was occupied until the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal destroyed it in about 645 BCE, though some researchers place the end of occupation in the late 12th century BCE. A geologist doing oil exploration found an inscribed brick and took it to the excavators at Susa. Roland de Mecquenem excavated the site from 1935, and Roman Ghirshman excavated it in six seasons between 1951 and 1962. In all 5,257 inscribed bricks were found, most in Elamite. In 1979 Chogha Zanbil became the first Iranian site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, and UNESCO considers its ziggurat the best preserved example of the stepped pyramidal monument.
chongzhen-emperor: Zhu Youjian was born on 6 February 1611, the fifth son of Zhu Changluo, the Taichang Emperor, and a low-ranking concubine, Lady Liu. When he was four his father had his mother executed, for reasons unknown, and she was buried in secret. He was raised by his father's other concubines in a lonely but quiet environment. All the Taichang Emperor's sons but two died before adulthood, and after his father's death in 1620 his elder brother Zhu Youjiao became the Tianqi Emperor and made him Prince of Xin.

The Tianqi Emperor died in October 1627 without a surviving heir, and Zhu Youjian, about sixteen years old, took the throne as the Chongzhen Emperor, helped by Empress Zhang. He quickly eliminated Wei Zhongxian and Madam Ke and others held to belong to the Wei-Ke conspiracy, and tried to stem the dynasty's decline, concentrating his reforms on the top ranks of the civil and military establishment. Corruption and an empty treasury left few capable ministers, and he was suspicious of his officials and feared factions. He executed dozens of field commanders, among them Yuan Chonghuan, who had directed the northern defence against the Manchu.

Drought and famine drove two great uprisings, led by Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng, both poor men from Shaanxi. Meanwhile Hong Taiji, whose father Nurhaci had united the Manchu tribes, declared himself emperor of the Qing dynasty in 1636. From 1633 to 1644 the Great Plague of Jingshi devastated northern China. Li Zicheng took Luoyang in 1641 and Kaifeng the next year, and on the lunar New Year of 1644 he proclaimed himself king of the Shun dynasty. The emperor refused repeated proposals to move the court south to Nanjing.

Li Zicheng's forces attacked Beijing on 24 April 1644. Rather than face capture, the emperor gathered the imperial household, killed Consort Yuan and Princess Zhaoren with his sword and severed the arm of Princess Changping. On 25 April he is said to have gone to the hill of Meishan, in present-day Jingshan Park, where he took his own life. Accounts differ on whether he left a note.

The Qing declared their aim to be avenging the emperor and defeated Li Zicheng at the Battle of Shanhai Pass. Because the emperor had not moved the court south, they took over a largely intact Beijing bureaucracy. A Southern Ming court was set up at Nanjing, and its last emperor was executed in 1662. A modern account holds that the Chongzhen Emperor was not especially incompetent by the standards of the later Ming, but that his suspicion, impatience and stubbornness doomed a dynasty already far gone.
chretien-de-troyes: Little is known of Chrétien's life, but he seems to have come from Troyes or to have been closely tied to it. Between 1160 and 1172 he served at the court of Marie of France, Countess of Champagne, a daughter of King Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine, who married Count Henry I of Champagne in 1164. Gaston Paris speculated that he may have served as a herald-at-arms. Later he served at the court of Philippe d'Alsace, Count of Flanders. His name means literally Christian from Troyes, and Urban T. Holmes, Jr., proposed that it might be a pen name of a convert from Judaism to Christianity, also known as Crestien li Gois.

Chrétien wrote five major poems in rhyming eight-syllable couplets, in vernacular Old French marked by the regional Champenois dialect. Four are complete: Erec and Enide (c. 1170), Cligès (c. 1176), and Yvain, the Knight of the Lion and Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, written together between 1177 and 1181. Yvain is generally considered his most masterful work. The fifth, Perceval, the Story of the Grail, was written between 1181 and 1190 and dedicated to Philip of Flanders. He completed only about 9,000 lines; four successors added 54,000 more in the Four Continuations. The last thousand lines of Lancelot were written by Godefroi de Leigni, apparently by arrangement with Chrétien.

Among his lesser works is Philomela, the only one of four poems based on Ovid's Metamorphoses to survive. In the introduction to Cligès he mentions a treatment of King Mark and Iseult, presumably related to the Tristan legend, which he says was not well received and has not survived. His immediate sources are uncertain, since he speaks of them only vaguely; Geoffrey of Monmouth or Wace may have supplied some names, and Lancelot makes repeated use of the customary law of his day.

Chrétien was the first writer to mention the Holy Grail, in Perceval, and Camelot and the love affair of Queen Guinevere and Lancelot, in Lancelot. His romances survive in many copies and were adapted widely: Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival and Hartmann von Aue's Erec and Iwein follow Perceval, Erec and Yvain, and the Welsh romances Peredur, Geraint and Enid, and Owain derive from the same three, though not directly. Karl Uitti argues that Yvain, with its clear beginning, middle and end, helped initiate the vernacular novel.
christchurch: Christchurch lies near the centre of the east coast of the South Island, east of the Canterbury Plains and near the southern end of Pegasus Bay. The Pacific Ocean bounds it to the east and the ancient volcanic complex of Banks Peninsula to the south. Apart from the Port Hills, the city is flat, on average about 20 metres above sea level. The Avon River, Ōtākaro, winds through the centre, with a large urban park along its banks. Gravel layers beneath the plains form an artesian aquifer, which feeds numerous spring-fed streams, including the Avon and the Heathcote. The city has a reputation as an English city, and its nickname is the Garden City.

Before European settlement the land was swampland, with marsh, grassland, scrub and patches of tall forest of kahikatea, mataī and tōtara. The Māori iwi Waitaha first inhabited the area in the mid-thirteenth century. Kāti Māmoe invaded in the sixteenth century, and Kāi Tahu absorbed the Waitaha a century later. Ōtautahi was inhabited seasonally, and a major trading centre was established at Kaiapoi Pā.

European settlement was influenced by the brothers William and John Deans, who farmed at Riccarton Bush from 1843 and showed that the swampy ground could be farmed. The name Christchurch was adopted at the first meeting of the Canterbury Association on 27 March 1848, most likely after Christ Church, Oxford, the college of some of its members. The First Four Ships chartered by the association brought the Canterbury Pilgrims to Lyttelton Harbour in 1850, and the plan of the central city, with its grid of streets, squares and parkland, was laid out by 1850. Christchurch became a city by letters patent on 31 July 1856, the first in New Zealand, and from 1853 to 1876 it was the seat of the Province of Canterbury.

Between 1871 and 1876 nearly 20,000 immigrants arrived in Canterbury, and in the 1880s frozen meat joined wool as a main export. Many Gothic Revival stone buildings by the provincial architect Benjamin Mountfort date from the period. In the early twentieth century the city grew with industry and state housing, and it has been recognised as an Antarctic gateway since 1901. It hosted the 1974 British Commonwealth Games.

Christchurch is the largest city of the South Island and the second largest in New Zealand by urban area, with an urban population of 407,800. It is home to the University of Canterbury. A magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck the region on 4 September 2010. The most destructive of the following earthquakes, on 22 February 2011, killed 185 people and brought down many central buildings. On 15 March 2019 two mosques in the city were the target of the deadliest terrorist attack in New Zealand history.
christiaan-huygens: Christiaan Huygens, Lord of Zeelhem, was born in The Hague on 14 April 1629, the second son of Constantijn Huygens, a diplomat and adviser to the House of Orange who was also a poet and musician. Constantijn corresponded with Galileo Galilei, Marin Mersenne and René Descartes. Christiaan was educated at home until sixteen, studying languages, music, history, geography, mathematics, logic and rhetoric, alongside dancing, fencing and horse riding. From 1645 to 1647 he studied law and mathematics at Leiden University, where Frans van Schooten taught him the work of Viète, Descartes and Fermat. Mersenne compared him to Archimedes in a letter of 3 January 1647.

Between 1651 and 1657 Huygens published works showing his mastery of classical and analytical geometry, beginning with Theoremata de Quadratura Hyperboles, Ellipsis et Circuli in 1651. He questioned Descartes's laws of collision, which were largely wrong, and derived the correct ones; his De Motu Corporum ex Percussione, completed in 1656, was published only in 1703. In 1655 he began grinding lenses with his brother Constantijn to build refracting telescopes, discovered Titan, and explained Saturn's appearance as due to a thin, flat ring, nowhere touching, inclined to the ecliptic. He patented the pendulum clock, manufactured in Paris by Isaac II Thuret, and analysed pendular motion in Horologium Oscillatorium (1673).

In 1666 Huygens moved to Paris on an invitation to a leadership position at Louis XIV's new Académie des sciences, with Jean-Baptiste Colbert as his patron. After serious depressive illness he moved back to The Hague in 1681. He could not return to France in 1685 because of the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. On his third visit to England he met Isaac Newton on 12 June 1689. He died in The Hague on 8 July 1695, never having married, and was buried in an unmarked grave at the Grote Kerk.

Huygens described his wave theory of light in the Traité de la Lumière (1690). It was initially rejected in favour of Newton's corpuscular theory until Augustin-Jean Fresnel adapted Huygens's principle in 1821, and it is now known as the Huygens–Fresnel principle. In 1659 he derived the formula for centrifugal force, a decade before Newton. In 1662 he developed the Huygenian eyepiece. His work on games of chance, published in Latin in 1657, used expected values and later inspired Jacob Bernoulli's work on probability theory. He had no taste for grand philosophical systems and was the leading European natural philosopher between Descartes and Newton.
christian-i-of-denmark: Christian was born in February 1426 in Oldenburg in northern Germany, the eldest son of Count Dietrich of Oldenburg and his second wife, Hedvig of Holstein. The House of Oldenburg was a comital family established since the 12th century west of the River Weser, which had gradually extended its rule over the neighbouring Frisian tribes. When Dietrich died in 1440 Christian and his brothers jointly succeeded him as counts of Oldenburg and Delmenhorst. Christian was raised by his childless uncle Adolphus, who wished him to be his heir and had him elected his successor in the Duchy of Schleswig.

In January 1448 King Christopher of Denmark, Sweden and Norway died without heirs. The Council of the Realm offered the Danish throne first to Duke Adolphus, who declined and recommended Christian. Christian had to promise to obey the Constitutio Valdemariana, which barred one person from ruling both Schleswig and Denmark, and to marry the dowager queen Dorothea of Brandenburg. He was elected at Viborg on 1 September 1448 and crowned at Copenhagen on 28 October 1449, when his marriage was also held.

In Norway the Council of the Realm was divided between Christian and Karl Knutsson, whom Sweden had elected in June 1448. In 1450 the Swedish Council forced Karl to give up his Norwegian claim, and Christian was crowned at Trondheim on 2 August. A treaty signed at Bergen on 29 August made Denmark and Norway elective monarchies sharing one king in perpetuity. Karl was driven into exile in 1457, and Christian was elected king of Sweden, restoring the Kalmar Union for a short time. His reign there ended in 1464, and his attempt to regain Sweden ended in defeat by the regent Sten Sture the Elder at the Battle of Brunkeberg in October 1471.

In 1460, after Adolphus's death, Christian became Duke of Schleswig and Count of Holstein-Rendsburg, his succession confirmed by the estates at Ribe on 5 March 1460. Emperor Frederick III raised him to Duke of Holstein in 1474. Many parts of his realm sought to govern themselves, and there were constant struggles. With the permission of Pope Sixtus IV given in 1475, he inaugurated the University of Copenhagen on 1 June 1479.

Christian died at Copenhagen Castle on 21 May 1481, aged 55, and was buried at Roskilde Cathedral in the Chapel of the Magi. The dynasty he founded went on to rule Denmark, and it held the throne of Norway until 1818 and again from 1905.
christian-ii-of-denmark: Christian was born at Nyborg Castle on 1 July 1481, the son of King John of Denmark and Christina of Saxony. He took part in his father's conquest of Sweden in 1497 and in the Dano-Swedish War of 1501–1512. In 1506 he became viceroy of Norway, where he kept control but quarrelled with the privy council by trying to reduce the nobility's traditional influence.

He succeeded his father in 1513. In 1515 he married Isabella of Austria, a granddaughter of the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I. His mistress Dyveke Sigbritsdatter remained with him until her death in 1517, and her mother, Sigbrit Willoms, became his chief counsellor.

Believing that the magnate Torben Oxe had poisoned Dyveke, Christian had him tried by a common jury, not the Council of State, and executed in November 1517, which deepened the division between king and aristocracy. His attempts to take Sweden from the regent Sten Sture the Younger failed in 1517 and 1518 but succeeded in 1520 with French, German and Scottish mercenaries. Christian was crowned king of Sweden in November.

On 8 and 9 November the Stockholm Bloodbath took place: after an ecclesiastical court condemned Sture's followers for heresy, they were executed at Stockholm castle, among them the bishops of Skara and Strängnäs. The killings provoked a rising led by Gustav Vasa, and Sweden left the Kalmar Union. In Denmark Christian issued a Town Law and a Land Law in 1521, strengthening tradesmen and peasants at the nobility's expense and allowing clergy to marry. Nobles and bishops saw them as a threat, and after rebellion began in Jutland the crown was offered on 20 January 1523 to his uncle Frederick.

Christian left Denmark in April 1523 and lived in exile at Lier in the Netherlands, where he corresponded with Martin Luther and for a time became a Lutheran. By 1531 he was Catholic again and sailed to Norway, but failed to take Akershus Castle and accepted a promise of safe conduct from Frederick I. It was broken, and he was held for 27 years, first at Sønderborg and from 1549 at Kalundborg, where he was treated as a nobleman. His supporters were defeated in the Count's Feud of 1536. He died at Kalundborg in January 1559 and is remembered in Sweden as Christian the Tyrant.
christian-iii-of-denmark: Christian was born on 12 August 1503 at Gottorf Castle in Schleswig, the eldest son of the future Frederick I of Denmark and Anna of Brandenburg. After his father was elected king in 1523 he was made stadtholder of Holstein and Schleswig in 1526 and viceroy of Norway in 1529, and showed considerable administrative ability. His teachers Wolfgang von Utenhof and Johann Rantzau were zealous reformers. In 1521 he travelled to the Diet of Worms to hear Martin Luther speak, and he made no secret of his Lutheran views, which brought him into conflict with the State Council. In 1528 he made the Lutheran Church the state church of Schleswig-Holstein by a Church Ordinance.

After Frederick I died in 1533, Christian was proclaimed king at an assembly in Rye in 1534. The Rigsraad, dominated by Catholic bishops and nobles, refused to accept him and turned to Count Christopher of Oldenburg to restore Christian II, which led to the two-year civil war known as the Count's Feud. Christian found his support among the nobles of Jutland. When peasants under Skipper Clement rose in northern Jutland, Christian sent Johan Rantzau north with Protestant German mercenaries, who stormed Aalborg. Gustav Vasa of Sweden sent armies to Scania and Halland. Count Christopher's forces held out in Malmø and Copenhagen until they surrendered in July 1536.

On 12 August 1536 Christian had three bishops of the State Council arrested, and some Catholic bishops were later executed. On 30 October 1536 the reconstituted council adopted the Lutheran Ordinances designed by Johannes Bugenhagen, making Lutheranism the Danish national church. Monasteries, nunneries and priories were closed and their property taken by the crown, which helped pay his large debt from the war. In 1537 he made Lutheranism the state religion of Norway as well, which remained joined to Denmark until 1814. In Iceland the suppression of the Catholic Church disrupted poor relief.

The first six years of his reign were a contest between the Danish Rigsraad and German counsellors, who had led his armies. He declared war on Charles V in 1542 and allied with German Protestant princes and France. In 1544 he and his half-brothers John the Elder and Adolf partitioned Holstein and Schleswig. He built Landskrona Citadel from 1549 and rebuilt Sønderborg Castle in Renaissance style between 1549 and 1557. Christian died at Koldinghus on 1 January 1559 and was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. His son Frederick II succeeded him.
christian-iv-of-denmark: Christian was born at Frederiksborg Castle on 12 April 1577, the eldest son of King Frederick II and Sofie of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. Denmark was then an elective monarchy, so he was not automatically heir, but in 1580 his father had him elected prince and successor. He was ten when his father died on 4 April 1588, and a regency council led by the chancellor Niels Kaas governed until he came of age. On 17 August 1596 he signed his haandfæstning, a curtailment of the monarch's power comparable to Magna Carta, and he was crowned in Copenhagen on 29 August 1596.

Christian pursued domestic reforms and rearmament. Dutch engineers directed the building of new fortresses, and the navy grew from twenty-two vessels in 1596 to sixty in 1610. He relied mainly on hired mercenaries for his army. Until the early 1620s the economy profited from boom conditions in Europe, and he expanded overseas trade, founding merchant cities such as Christianstad in 1614, Glückstadt in 1617 and Kongsberg in 1624. He rebuilt the Norwegian capital Oslo as Christiania, a name used until 1925. In 1620 a treaty with the Nayak of Tanjore gave Denmark the village of Tranquebar in India.

In 1611 he went to war with Sweden for supremacy of the Baltic, which ended in the Treaty of Knäred of 20 January 1613 with no decisive gains. He entered the Thirty Years' War as war leader of the Lower Saxon Circle, a war that devastated much of Germany, undermined the Danish economy and cost Denmark–Norway some of its conquered territories. In 1643 Sweden attacked again in the Torstenson War, and by the end of January 1644 all of Jutland was in Swedish hands. Christian spent more time in Norway than any other Oldenburg monarch, and founded four cities there.

His last years were embittered by quarrels with his sons-in-law, especially Corfitz Ulfeldt. His obsession with witchcraft led to public executions, among them the burning of Maren Spliid at Ribe on 9 November 1641. He died in Copenhagen on 28 February 1648 and was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. His reign of 59 years and 330 days made him the longest-reigning monarch in Scandinavian history, and he remains popular in both Denmark and Norway.
christian-social-union-in-bavaria: The Christian Social Union in Bavaria, founded in 1945, is regarded as the de facto successor of the Catholic Bavarian People's Party of the Weimar period. It is a Christian democratic and conservative party with a regionalist identity, and it operates only in Bavaria, while its larger counterpart, the Christian Democratic Union, operates in the other states. The CSU has led the Bavarian state government since 1946, except from 1954 to 1957, when the Social Democrat Wilhelm Hoegner formed a coalition government. The separatist Bavaria Party had at first competed for the same voters, since both saw themselves as successors to the Bavarian People's Party; the CSU won this contest, and in 1966 the Bavaria Party left the state parliament.

Franz Josef Strauß left the strongest legacy. He led the party from 1961 until his death in 1988, held four federal ministerial posts between 1953 and 1969, and was Minister-President of Bavaria from 1978. In 1980 he was the first CSU leader to stand for the chancellorship, but lost to the incumbent Helmut Schmidt. No chancellor has ever come from the CSU. Edmund Stoiber, leader from 1999, ran for chancellor in 2002 and also lost.

Before 2008 the CSU regularly won absolute majorities in Bavaria, a dominance unique among the German states. In 2003 it won 60.7 per cent of the vote and 124 of 180 seats, the first two-thirds majority in a German state parliament. It lost its majority in 2008, when its share fell to 43.4 per cent, and governed in coalition with the Free Democratic Party.

In the Bundestag the CSU forms a common group with the Christian Democratic Union, known as the Union. Below the federal level the two parties are entirely independent. The CSU and the state of Bavaria did not sign the Grundgesetz of the Federal Republic, as they could not agree with the division of Germany into two states after the Second World War. The party is divided into ten district associations, 105 county associations and almost 3,000 local associations.
christian-viii-of-denmark: Prince Christian Frederick was born on 18 September 1786 at Christiansborg Palace in Copenhagen, the eldest son of Hereditary Prince Frederick and Duchess Sophia Frederica of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. His mother died in 1794. He was raised conservatively under the minister Ove Høegh-Guldberg, with a broad education, and a love of science and art stayed with him all his life.

In 1806 he married his cousin Charlotte Frederica of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. Their son, the future Frederick VII, was born in 1808, the year Christian Frederick became heir presumptive to his cousin Frederick VI, who had no sons. He divorced her in 1810 after her alleged affair with her singing teacher. In 1815 he married Caroline Amalie of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Augustenburg; they had no children.

In May 1813 he was sent to Norway as governor-general to strengthen loyalty to the House of Oldenburg. When the Treaty of Kiel forced the king to cede Norway to Sweden, he placed himself at the head of the Norwegian party of independence. An assembly of notables elected him regent on 16 February 1814, and after the Constituent Assembly at Eidsvoll he was unanimously elected king of Norway on 17 May, when the constitution was signed. He failed to win the great powers to Norway's cause.

A short campaign followed in which the Swedish crown prince Charles John defeated the Norwegian army. By the Convention of Moss of 14 August 1814 Christian transferred executive power to the Storting, abdicated and returned to Denmark. On 4 November the Storting elected Charles XIII of Sweden king of Norway.

Christian became king of Denmark on 3 December 1839. The Liberal party had high hopes of him as the giver of constitutions, but he had grown conservative and rejected every Liberal project, promising only administrative reform. On the national unrest in Schleswig and Holstein he often seemed hesitant, and not until 1846 did he clearly support the idea of Schleswig as a Danish area. In 1845 the last remnants of Danish India, Tranquebar and Serampore, were sold to the British. He died of sepsis at Amalienborg Palace in 1848 and was buried at Roskilde Cathedral. Some historians believe he would have given Denmark a free constitution had he lived longer.
christina-queen-of-sweden: Christina was born on 18 December 1626 in the royal castle Tre Kronor, the daughter of Gustavus Adolphus and his German wife Maria Eleonora. When Gustavus Adolphus left for Germany in June 1630 to defend Protestantism in the Thirty Years' War, he secured her right to inherit the throne and ordered that she receive the education normally given only to boys. She succeeded him at five, after his death at the Battle of Lützen, but began to rule only in 1644, when she was declared an adult at eighteen.

Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna soon found that her political views differed from his. At the Peace Congress in Osnabrück in 1645 his son argued against peace with the Holy Roman Empire, while Christina, who wanted peace at any cost, sent her own delegate. She patronised scholars and artists and founded the newspaper Ordinari Post Tijdender in 1645. The philosopher René Descartes arrived at her invitation on 4 October 1649, but the two did not get on. She was crowned on 22 October 1650. On 26 February 1649 she had announced that she would not marry and named her cousin Charles Gustav as heir.

In the summer of 1654 she left Sweden in men's clothing and travelled through Denmark as Count Dohna. She entered Rome on 20 December in a sedan chair designed by Bernini, was confirmed by the pope and settled in the Palazzo Farnese, where she opened the Academy of Arcadia on 24 January 1656.

At Fontainebleau in 1657 Christina had her master of the horse, Gian Rinaldo Monaldeschi, whom she suspected of betraying her, stabbed to death by her servants. The act cost her popularity. In 1660, after Charles X Gustav's death, she returned to Sweden hoping to regain the throne if his young son died, but as a Catholic she could not, and she submitted to a second renunciation. She died on 19 April 1689 in the Palazzo Corsini and is one of the few women buried in the Vatican Grottoes. Her life inspired Strindberg's play Kristina (1901) and the film Queen Christina (1933). Historians still discuss her unconventional dress and her letters to Ebba Sparre.
christoph-martin-wieland: Wieland was born on 5 September 1733 at Oberholzheim, half of which belonged to the Free Imperial City of Biberach an der Riss and half to Gutenzell Abbey. His father was a pastor, first at Oberholzheim and then at Biberach, and took great pains with his son's education. At twelve Wieland went to the Kloster Berge gymnasium near Magdeburg, and by 1749 he was widely read in the Latin classics and the leading French writers. In 1750 he went to the University of Tübingen to study law, but gave most of his time to literature.

The Swiss reformer J. J. Bodmer invited him to Zürich in 1752, but the two soon parted. Wieland stayed in Switzerland until 1760, spending the last year as a private tutor in Bern. He then returned to Biberach as director of the chancery, where the library of Count Stadion at Warthausen gave him access to French and English literature.

He married Anna Dorothea von Hillenbrand on 21 October 1765, and they had 14 children. Between 1769 and 1772 he was professor of philosophy at the University of Erfurt. His pedagogic work Der goldene Spiegel (1772) drew the attention of Duchess Anna Amalia of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, who appointed him tutor to her sons Karl August and Constantin at Weimar, which remained his home until his death.

In 1773 he founded Der teutsche Merkur, which under his editorship until 1789 became the most influential literary review in Germany. Goethe attacked him in the satire Götter, Helden und Wieland, and Wieland answered with good nature. Goethe and Herder were soon drawn to Weimar, where Anna Amalia formed a circle later joined by Schiller. Wieland died in Weimar on 20 January 1813.

Geschichte des Agathon (1766 to 1767) is regarded as the first Bildungsroman. Under the guise of a Greek fiction it describes his own spiritual and intellectual growth. He translated twenty-two of Shakespeare's plays into prose (1762 to 1766), the first attempt to present Shakespeare to the German public in something close to full. His light verse romances, such as Musarion (1768) and Der neue Amadis (1771), served as an antidote to the sentimental excesses of Sturm und Drang.

Die Abderiten (1774) satirises German provinciality, and his poetic masterpiece, the romantic epic Oberon (1780), became the basis of operas by Friederike Sophie Seyler and Carl Maria von Weber. Politically he was a moderate liberal who advocated constitutional monarchy and a free press, and his thought was cosmopolitan: only a true cosmopolitan, he remarked, can be a good citizen.
christoph-willibald-gluck: Gluck was born in the Upper Palatinate, probably on 2 July 1714, the date he himself gave on a document requested from Paris in 1785, and was baptised on 4 July. His father Alexander was a forester. In 1727 the family moved to Eisenberg in Bohemia, where Alexander became head forester to Prince Philipp Hyazinth von Lobkowitz. About 1727 or 1728 Gluck went to Prague, left without a degree, and probably reached Vienna in 1734. In 1737 he arrived in Milan and studied with Giovanni Battista Sammartini. His first opera, Artaserse, was performed on 26 December 1741, and he went on to write for Milan, Turin and Venice, mostly to texts by Metastasio.

After posts in London and with touring companies, Gluck married Maria Anna Bergin on 15 September 1750 and settled in Vienna as Kapellmeister. Pope Benedict XIV made him a Knight of the Golden Spur in 1756. With the choreographer Gasparo Angiolini he wrote the ballet Don Juan (1761). Orfeo ed Euridice, first performed on 5 October 1762 to a libretto by Ranieri de' Calzabigi, subordinated star singers to drama and did away with dry recitative. The preface to Alceste (1767) set out the principles: no da capo arias, no virtuoso display, simpler melodic lines and an overture linked to the action.

Under the patronage of Marie Antoinette he wrote eight operas for Paris. Iphigénie en Aulide, premiered on 19 April 1774, set off a quarrel between Gluckists and supporters of the Italian composer Niccolò Piccinni. Iphigénie en Tauride (1779) was a great success, but Echo et Narcisse failed after twelve performances, and he returned to Vienna.

Gluck died on 15 November 1787, a few hours after a heart arrhythmia struck while he lunched with friends, at the age of 73. Only half of his work survived a fire in 1809. It includes about 35 full-length operas and numerous ballets and instrumental works. His reforms influenced Mozart, particularly Idomeneo (1781), and left a school of disciples in Paris, among them Antonio Salieri, Cherubini, Méhul and Spontini. Berlioz was his most devoted French admirer, and his example influenced Weber and Wagner.
christopher-columbus: Scholars agree that Columbus was born in the Republic of Genoa, between 25 August and 31 October 1451; theories placing his origin in Aragon or Portugal are discounted by most of them. His father, Domenico Colombo, was a wool weaver who worked in Genoa and Savona and owned a cheese stand where the boy worked. His mother was Susanna Fontanarossa. In 1470 the family moved to Savona, where Domenico took over a tavern. Columbus wrote that he went to sea at the age of 14, and he later settled in Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew ran a cartography workshop.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1453, the Silk Road was closed to Christian traders. In 1474 the Florentine astronomer Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli suggested to King Afonso V of Portugal that sailing west across the Atlantic would reach Asia faster than the route around Africa, but the king rejected the idea. Columbus and his brother proposed such a plan in the 1480s, and Bartolomeu Dias's rounding of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 complicated it. After the Granada War and years of lobbying, Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand II of Spain agreed to sponsor the voyage.

Columbus left the Port of Palos in August 1492 with three ships and made landfall on 12 October on an island in the Bahamas known to its inhabitants as Guanahani. He then visited Cuba and Hispaniola, where he founded the short-lived fort of La Navidad, and returned to Castile in early 1493 with captured American Indians. Three further voyages took him to the Lesser Antilles in 1493, to Trinidad and the northern coast of South America in 1498, and to the east coast of Central America in 1502. He never clearly renounced his belief that he had reached the Far East, and he called the people he met indios.

As colonial governor Columbus was accused by some contemporaries of significant brutality, and he was arrested and removed from Hispaniola in 1500. He afterwards demanded the tenth of the new lands' wealth promised in the Capitulations of Santa Fe, and after his death his heirs pursued the claim in the protracted lawsuits known as the pleitos colombinos. His remains were moved several times, between Valladolid, Seville, Santo Domingo and perhaps Havana, and DNA tests on those in Seville in 2003 led researchers to conclude that they are his.

His voyages began lasting contact between the two hemispheres and the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, diseases and ideas. Diseases and warfare introduced from the Old World contributed to the decline of Hispaniola's American Indians, who were also enslaved and mistreated under Columbus's government. Once idealized as a heroic discoverer, he is now examined more critically.
christopher-marlowe: Christopher Marlowe was the second of nine children of the Canterbury shoemaker John Marlowe and his wife Katherine, daughter of William Arthur of Dover. He was baptised at St George's Church, Canterbury, on 26 February 1564, and was probably born a few days earlier, about two months before William Shakespeare. Little is known of his adult life beyond legal records. In 1587 the Privy Council ordered Cambridge to award him his Master of Arts, denying rumours that he meant to go to the English Catholic college at Rheims and saying he had been engaged in matters touching the benefit of his country. Some writers conclude that he was a government spy, though that is speculation.

Six dramas have been attributed to Marlowe, alone or in collaboration: Dido, Queen of Carthage, Tamburlaine, The Jew of Malta, Doctor Faustus, Edward the Second and The Massacre at Paris. Tamburlaine, first performed on a regular London stage in 1587, was the first English play in blank verse and, with Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy, is seen as the start of the mature phase of Elizabethan theatre. His plays formed the foundation of the repertoire of the Admiral's Men, and the haughty roles of Tamburlaine, Faustus and Barabas were probably written for the tall actor Edward Alleyn. Doctor Faustus is the first dramatised version of the Faust legend, and its hero is carried off by demons.

His poetry includes The Passionate Shepherd to His Love and the unfinished Hero and Leander, completed by George Chapman and printed in 1598, as well as translations of Ovid's Amores and of the first book of Lucan's Pharsalia. In 1599 the Ovid translation was banned and copies were publicly burned.

In May 1593 bills threatening Protestant refugees were posted in London, one signed Tamburlaine. The next day Thomas Kyd was arrested, and a heretical tract found in his lodgings was said by Kyd, under torture, to be Marlowe's. A warrant for Marlowe's arrest was issued on 18 May, and he presented himself on 20 May. He was killed on 30 May 1593, and scholars still dispute the circumstances. George Peele called him the Muses' darling, and Ben Jonson wrote of Marlowe's mighty line.
chugoku-region: The Chūgoku region, also called the San'in-San'yō region, is the westernmost region of Honshū. It consists of the prefectures of Hiroshima, Yamaguchi, Shimane, Tottori and Okayama, and neighbours Kyūshū, Shikoku and Kansai. The land is characterised by irregular rolling hills and limited plains, and mountains running east and west divide it in two. San'in, the yin of the mountains, is the northern part facing the Sea of Japan, and San'yō, the yang of the mountains, the southern part facing the Seto Inland Sea.

Chūgoku literally means middle country, but the origin of the name is unclear. Japan was divided into provinces called koku, classified by distance from the administrative centre in Kansai into near, middle and far countries. One explanation is that Chūgoku first referred to the middle countries west of the capital, but only five of the provinces normally counted in the region were so classified. An alternative is that it meant the provinces between Kansai and Kyūshū, historically the link between Japan and mainland Asia. Historically the name covered the 16 provinces of the San'indō and San'yōdō, though some of the easternmost were later absorbed into prefectures based in Kansai.

Hiroshima, regarded as the capital of the region, was rebuilt after being destroyed by an atomic bomb in 1945 and is now an industrial city of more than one million people. Okayama is the other large centre. The San'yō coast is a zone of heavy industry, while the San'in is less industrialised, with an agricultural economy.
chulalongkorn: Chulalongkorn was born on 20 September 1853, a son of King Mongkut and Queen Debsirindra, and was made heir presumptive as the first son born to Debsirindra. He learned Buddhism, Pali, chronicles and royal ritual, and also science, English and French from Western teachers, among them Anna Leonowens. In 1868 he went with his father to observe a solar eclipse; both caught malaria, and Mongkut died on 1 October 1868. A council headed by Chuang Bunnag chose the fifteen-year-old Chulalongkorn, and Chuang acted as regent. After visits to Singapore, Java and British India he was crowned in his own right on 16 November 1873.

His first reform, in 1873, was an Auditory Office to take tax collection from nobles such as the Bunnag family. After armed Front Palace troops came to a palace fire in December 1874, reducing the nobility's power became a chief aim, and he abolished the Front Palace, the seat of a second king, in 1885. He founded a military academy in 1887, replaced the old government with ministries in 1888–1892, introduced a Western legal code with the Belgian adviser Gustave Rolin-Jaequemyns, and set up the monthon system of provinces in 1897, which ended the power of local dynasties. Rebellions against it in 1901 were crushed in 1902.

He abolished slavery by steps, wishing to avoid the bloodshed he associated with abolition in the United States. A law of 1874 freed at twenty-one those born as household slaves after 1867, and the Slave Abolition Act of 1905 ended slavery in all forms. The first railway, from Bangkok to Korat, opened in 1901.

In 1893 French demands for Lao lands east of the Mekong led to the Franco-Siamese crisis: French gunboats entered the Chao Phraya, Siam refused an ultimatum, and the matter ended with the cession of Laos. In 1906 France also received Inner Cambodia, and in 1909 four Malay sultanates came under British influence. Chulalongkorn visited Europe in 1897 and 1907, the first Siamese monarch to do so.

He died of kidney disease on 23 October 1910 and was succeeded by his son Vajiravudh. His reforms aimed to secure Siam's independence against Western encroachment, and he is honoured as Phra Piya Maharat, the Great Beloved King. Chulalongkorn University, founded in 1917, bears his name.
chur: Chur lies in the Grisonian Rhine Valley, where the Rhine turns north, on the right bank of the Plessur at 594 m above sea level, almost entirely surrounded by the Alps. It is reputedly the oldest town in Switzerland, with settlement going back to the Pfyn culture. It stands where the roads from several Alpine passes, among them the Lukmanier, Splügen and San Bernardino, come together and continue down the Rhine.

Rome conquered the area in 15 BCE as the province of Raetia. In the late 3rd century Curia Raetorum, later Chur, became the capital of Raetia prima. In the 4th century it became the seat of the first Christian bishopric north of the Alps, and the first known bishop is Asinio in 451. Otto I granted the right to collect tolls in 952, and in 1170 the bishop became a prince-bishop. The League of the House of God was formed in Chur in 1367 to resist the bishopric and the House of Habsburg. After a fire in 1464, Emperor Frederick III freed the city from the bishop's power, and in 1465 the citizens gave all government to the guilds.

The League joined the Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions in 1471 to form the Three Leagues. From 1523 Johannes Comander preached the Reformation in St Martin's Church, and by 1525 the bishop had fled. The Ilanz Articles of 1524 and 1526 allowed each resident of the Three Leagues to choose a religion and sharply reduced the bishop's power. The Three Leagues became the canton of Graubünden in 1803, with Chur as its capital.

Chur is the capital and largest town of the canton of Graubünden, or Grisons, and lies 120 km by rail from Zürich. German is the main language, with Italian and Romansh also spoken. The cathedral of the Assumption was built between 1154 and 1270 on the site of a church of the first half of the 5th century. The church of St Luzi, first recorded in 821, became a Premonstratensian monastery in 1149.
church-of-england: The Church of England traces its history to the Christian hierarchy recorded in Roman Britain by the 3rd century and to the Gregorian mission to Kent. In 597 Pope Gregory I sent missionaries led by Augustine, who became the first archbishop of Canterbury, and the church counts 597 as the start of its formal history. In Northumbria Celtic and Roman missionaries disagreed over the date of Easter and the monks' tonsure. King Oswiu summoned the Synod of Whitby in 664 and decided that Northumbria would follow the Roman tradition.

In 1527 Henry VIII asked Pope Clement VII to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. When the Pope refused, Henry used Parliament to assert royal authority over the church. The Act in Restraint of Appeals of 1533 allowed the Archbishop of Canterbury to annul the marriage without reference to Rome, and in November 1534 the Act of Supremacy declared Henry Supreme Head of the Church of England. Archbishop Thomas Cranmer shaped its doctrine and developed the Book of Common Prayer. Papal authority was briefly restored under Mary I, and Elizabeth I renewed the breach. The Elizabethan Settlement of 1559-1563 concluded the English Reformation.
Struggles over the church under James I and Charles I led to the First English Civil War in 1642, and the Puritans abolished the Book of Common Prayer and episcopacy until 1660.

The monarch is Supreme Governor. The church is organised in dioceses under bishops, with parishes within each, and its legislative body is the General Synod. Its doctrine rests on scripture, informed by the Church Fathers and the creeds, and is expressed in the Thirty-Nine Articles, the Book of Common Prayer and the Ordinal. James I ordered the translation published in 1611 as the King James Version. The church describes itself as a via media between Lutheranism and Calvinism, with Anglo-Catholic, high church, central church and low church strands.
church-of-jesus-christ-of-latter-day-sai: The church arose during the Second Great Awakening. Joseph Smith formally organised it as the Church of Christ on 6 April 1830 in western New York. Early converts were drawn in part by the newly published Book of Mormon, a self-described chronicle of Indigenous American prophets that Smith said he had translated from golden plates. After Smith's death, Brigham Young and the largest body of his followers incorporated the church in 1851 under the name The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Members hold that after the death of Jesus and his apostles the authority of the original church was lost, and that it was restored through Smith.

Under Smith the church's headquarters moved to Ohio, Missouri and Illinois. In Missouri fear of its political and military power led to the Mormon War of 1838 and Governor Lilburn Boggs's Mormon Extermination Order. In 1844 the Nauvoo Expositor criticised plural marriage and other doctrines. Smith took a leading part in destroying its press, was charged with treason and jailed, and was shot dead by a mob that stormed the jail. After the succession crisis most followers sided with Brigham Young, who led them to Nebraska and in 1847 to what later became the Utah Territory. About 80,000 settlers arrived between 1847 and 1869. Plural marriage, announced publicly in 1852, was curtailed in 1890 and officially rescinded in 1904.

The church is led by a president, regarded by members as a prophet, seer and revelator, over a hierarchy of areas, stakes and wards led by volunteer bishops. Its canon consists of the Bible, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. Members believe in Jesus Christ as the Son of God but reject the ecumenical creeds and the Trinity, holding that God the Father, Jesus and the Holy Ghost are three distinct beings united in purpose. Members observe the Word of Wisdom, which forbids alcohol, coffee, tea and tobacco, and give a tenth of their income. Young men are expected to serve a two-year mission.
church-of-the-holy-sepulchre: After the siege of Jerusalem in 70 the city lay in ruins. In 130 the emperor Hadrian began building the Roman colony of Aelia Capitolina, and about 135 he ordered a cave containing a rock-cut tomb to be filled in as a flat foundation for a temple of Venus or Aphrodite. When Constantine the Great began to favour Christianity, Bishop Macarius of Jerusalem asked permission to dig for the tomb. With the help of Eusebius, three crosses were found near a tomb, and one that was said to have cured the dying was taken to be the True Cross.

The church, planned by the architect Zenobius, was built as two separate structures: a rotunda called the Anastasis, or Resurrection, over the tomb, and the great basilica known as the Martyrium, across a colonnaded courtyard to the east, with the traditional site of Calvary in one corner. The New Testament places the tomb outside the city wall.

After Jerusalem came under Islamic rule the early Muslim rulers protected its Christian sites. On 18 October 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered its complete destruction, as part of a wider campaign against Christian and Jewish places of worship, and Christian Europe reacted with shock. His son allowed Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos to rebuild it, and the work was completed in 1048.

The knights of the First Crusade took the church on 15 July 1099, and it was modified into a structure that departs greatly from the original. It was lost to Saladin in 1187, though the treaty after the Third Crusade allowed Christian pilgrims to visit. Emperor Frederick II regained it by treaty in the 13th century, and the Khwarezmians and Ayyubids captured it in 1244. An Ottoman decree of 1757 helped establish the Status Quo, confirmed by a firman of Sultan Abdülmecid I in 1852 and 1853.

The church is the seat of the Armenian, Greek Orthodox and Latin Catholic patriarchates of Jerusalem, and it has been a major pilgrimage site since the fourth century. The main communities sharing it are the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox, Armenian Apostolic, Coptic, Syriac and Ethiopian Orthodox. Inside lie the last four stations of the Cross and Calvary, and the tomb is enclosed in the Aedicule, a 19th-century shrine. Disputes between the communities have at times led to violence: in 1902, 18 friars were hospitalized after a dispute over who could clean a step.
chutia-people: The origin of the name Chutia is not known; the chronicles written in the Ahom language called the kingdom Tiora, while those in Assamese used Chutia. The historic Chutias are thought to have had some Shan admixture, and their ruling families are estimated to have been originally matrilineal or not entirely patrilineal. They worshipped a primordial male deity and a primordial female deity, Kechaikhati, whose worship was conducted by a priestly section identified today as the Deori people. The settlement of Brahmins in the kingdom led to the Hinduisation of its rulers, and inscriptions of the late 14th century suggest that the kings then followed the Vaishnava tradition.

After the annexation the capital region became a frontier province of the Ahom kingdom under an officer called the Sadiya-khowa Gohain, and the Chutia nobles were widely dispersed in Upper Assam. Those Chutias who had not been Hinduised were initiated in the 17th century into the Ekasarana dharma under the Mayamara Satra by Aniruddhadev. After the fall of the kingdom a new Hindu lineage was constructed, tracing the Chutias to the legendary King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha.

The community divided into several groups. The Hindu Chutias were a large section. The Ahom Chutias intermarried with the Ahoms, held high offices in the Ahom administration and were mostly absorbed. The Borahi Chutias had religious rites of their own, and the Miri Chutias fled to the Miri hills and intermarried with the Mishing. According to one chronicle, the Ahom court adopted muga silk by employing a thousand producers and weavers from the Chutia community.

Most Chutias live in Upper Assam, mostly in the interior on the banks of rivers, in villages of about 60 to 140 families. They generally live in joint families headed by the father, which at times exceeded one hundred members. Their original Tibeto-Burman language has disappeared; a British colonial officer of the 19th century wrongly identified it with the Deori language, but the Deori community is not related to the Chutias ethnically or linguistically.

Their rituals have a tribal and tantric base influenced by Hinduism and Vaishnavism. Those called Kesa-ponthi accept restrictions on meat and alcohol in their rites, while the Poka-ponthi keep the older customs. The Government of India recognises the Chutias as an Other Backward Class, and there is a political movement to include them in the list of scheduled tribes.
chuvash-people: There is no universally accepted etymology of the name Chuvash.
