One theory derives it from Common Turkic jăvaş, 'friendly' or 'peaceful'; another from Tabghach, the name of the Xianbei clan that founded the Northern Wei dynasty, which Gerard Clauson showed could become Chuvash through regular sound changes. Two schools place the people's origin differently: a mixing of the Sabir tribes with Finno-Ugrians, or descent from the Volga Bulgars. After Old Bulgaria broke up in the second half of the 7th century, the Sabirs and other Oghuric tribes migrated to the Volga-Kama region and founded Volga Bulgaria.

The Mongols destroyed Volga Bulgaria in 1236, and the Golden Horde and then the Kazan Khanate ruled the Chuvash. The modern name appears in records from the sixteenth century. Russia conquered the Kazan Khanate in 1552; the Chuvash had to pay yasak and gradually lost much of their land, and many farmers became bonded laborers in the timber industry or worked on barges. Most were not converted to Orthodox Christianity until the mid-19th century.

A written script was created in 1871. The Chuvash Autonomous Region was established on 24 June 1920 and became a Soviet republic on 21 April 1925. Soviet authorities redrew its borders, leaving many Chuvash in neighbouring republics, and the language vanished from education and public use for most of the Soviet period. A cultural revival began in 1989.

Chuvash is the only surviving member of the Oghur branch of Turkic, marked by r for Common Turkic z and l for š. It was first thought a Turkified Finno-Ugric language until August Ahlqvist's fieldwork of 1856. UNESCO considers it endangered. Most Chuvash are Eastern Orthodox Christians; a minority are Sunni Muslims or follow Vattisen Yaly, a revival of the ethnic religion. Some pre-Christian traditions survive, including prayer and goose sacrifice at shrines called keremet, and distinctive embroidery on traditional clothing. A 2017 genome study found a largely Finno-Ugric genetic component beside a Turkic one shared with the Bashkirs and Volga Tatars.
chyhyryn: Chyhyryn lies on the banks of the Tiasmyn river, not far from where it enters the Dnieper, in central Ukraine. Its name appears in Polish as Czehryń. From 1320 to 1569 the area was part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and it passed to the Kingdom of Poland before the Union of Lublin.

In 1589 King Sigismund III of Poland allowed Aleksander Wiśniowiecki, starosta of Cherkasy, to found a town and build a castle on a deserted site called Czehryn. The castle stood on a hill surrounded by the Tiasmyn, and in 1592 the town received Magdeburg rights and a coat of arms with three arrows. Cossacks settled there from the start, and in 1638 the Polish Sejm created the Chyhyryn Regiment of registered Cossacks.

After Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossack rebels defeated Crown forces, he chose Chyhyryn as his main seat. From 1648 to 1669 it was the hetman's residence, and after the Ruthenian Orthodox metropolitan see was forcibly moved from Kyiv in 1658 it became a full capital of the Cossack Hetmanate. Petro Doroshenko took it about 1665 and accepted Turkish protection; he was given a small principality there, but the land was devastated and Chyhyryn became a Tatar slave market.

In 1676 Russian and Cossack forces besieged the city and Doroshenko surrendered. A Turkish siege in August 1677 was repelled by the Russians, but another a year later, led by Kara Mustafa, succeeded: the Turks destroyed the city and dismantled the fortress. Under a Polish-Russian treaty of 1686 the land around it was to stay uninhabited, so it was not rebuilt. People returned after peace in 1714, and Russia annexed the town in 1793.

Since the 17th century Chyhyryn has shrunk to a semi-rural settlement. The Trinity Monastery, built near it in 1627, was destroyed by the Soviet authorities, together with the town hall and Khmelnytsky's palace. After Ukraine regained independence the hetman's residence was restored and became a museum.
cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born on 3 January 106 BCE in Arpinum, a hill town 100 kilometres south-east of Rome, into a wealthy family of the equestrian order. His father was in poor health and could not enter public life, so he studied extensively to compensate. The cognomen Cicero comes from the Latin for chickpea, cicer. Plutarch explains that it was first given to an ancestor with a cleft in the tip of his nose resembling a chickpea, and says that Cicero refused to change the name when he entered politics.

His first major appearance in the courts came in 81 BCE, at 26. In 80 BCE he defended Sextus Roscius of Ameria on a charge of parricide in Pro Roscio Amerino, his first criminal case. He accused Chrysogonus, a freedman of the dictator Sulla, of fabricating the proscription of Roscius's father to obtain the family's property, while tactfully avoiding any charge against Sulla himself. He won and gained a good reputation as an orator.

Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE with the support of every unit of the centuriate assembly. He suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy, but because he had executed five of the conspirators without trial he was exiled in 58 BCE and recalled the next year. In 60 BCE he refused Julius Caesar's invitation to join the partnership of Caesar, Pompey and Marcus Licinius Crassus, fearing it would undermine the Republic.

In 51 BCE he reluctantly took the proconsulship of Cilicia, where he restored calm by mild government and recovered public property embezzled by previous governors. In Caesar's civil war he favoured Pompey and followed the Pompeian forces to Pharsalus, but after Caesar's victory there on 9 August 48 BCE he refused to take command and returned to Rome in 47 BCE.

After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE Cicero opposed Mark Antony in a series of speeches called the Philippics, and he praised Caesar's heir Octavian to play him against Antony. When Octavian and Antony joined with Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, Cicero was proscribed and executed in late 43 BCE, on 7 December, while trying to escape Italy. On Antony's order his head and hands were displayed on the Rostra.

Cicero is considered the master of Latin prose. He coined much of Latin's philosophical vocabulary. Of his speeches 88 were recorded and 52 survive. Petrarch's rediscovery of his letters is often credited with starting the 14th-century Renaissance, and his authority peaked in the 18th-century Enlightenment.
cidade-velha: Cidade Velha lies on the south coast of Santiago, at the mouth of the river Ribeira Grande de Santiago, 10 kilometres west of Praia. Abundant water from the river gave the site an advantage over the other settlement on the island, Alcatrazes. The Portuguese changed the name from Ribeira Grande to Cidade Velha, old city, in the late 18th century after relocating the capital to Praia.

The island of Santiago was discovered in 1460 by António da Noli, a Genoese in Portuguese service, who settled at Ribeira Grande in 1462 with family members and colonists from the Algarve and Alentejo. The settlement became a key port of call for Portuguese colonisation in Africa and South America, and in the 16th and 17th centuries a centre of maritime trade. Its closeness to the African coast made it an essential platform for the trade in enslaved Africans. Vasco da Gama called there in 1497, Christopher Columbus in 1498 and Ferdinand Magellan's expedition in 1522. In 1533 it became the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Santiago de Cabo Verde.

Privateers attacked it, among them Sir Francis Drake in 1585 and Jacques Cassard in 1712. The fort Forte Real de São Filipe, built in 1587-93, did not end its vulnerability, and the town declined. The capital was moved to Praia in 1770.

Restoration began in the 1960s, and in 2009 Cidade Velha was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Surviving parts of the original planned layout include the royal fortress, a 16th-century town square, and Nossa Senhora do Rosário, built in 1495 and described as the oldest colonial church in the world. The pillory in the main square, erected in 1512 or 1520, was where rebellious enslaved people were publicly punished.
cieszyn: Cieszyn stands on the east bank of the Olza River, a tributary of the Oder, in the western Silesian Foothills north of the Silesian Beskids. It lies in the historical region of Cieszyn Silesia, the south-easternmost part of Upper Silesia. Because of several major fires and later rebuilding, the last in the late 18th century, its old town combines Polish and Old Austrian styles and is sometimes called Little Vienna.

West Slavic peoples have lived in the area since at least the 7th century, and it became part of the emerging Polish state in the 10th century. According to legend, three sons of a prince, Bolko, Leszko and Cieszko, met here in 810 and founded a settlement, naming it from the words cieszym się, 'we are happy'. Cieszyn was the capital of the Duchy of Cieszyn from 1290. The Piast dynasty ruled the duchy until 1653 and the Habsburg dynasty until 1918. In May 1779 Maria Theresa and Frederick II signed the Peace of Teschen there, ending the War of the Bavarian Succession.

In July 1920 the Spa Conference divided the town. Its smaller western suburbs became Český Těšín in Czechoslovakia, and the larger part joined Poland as Cieszyn. Poland annexed the Trans-Olza area together with Český Těšín in October 1938. Germany occupied the town from 1939 to 1945. In 1939 and 1940 the Germans arrested local Poles in the Intelligenzaktion campaign and imprisoned them in a new Nazi prison, and many teachers, priests and activists were deported to concentration camps and murdered. Almost the entire Jewish community was murdered. After the war the 1920 border was restored.

Cieszyn is a border town in southern Poland and the seat of Cieszyn County. Three bridges connect it to Český Těšín. Its sites include a Romanesque rotunda of St Nicholas from the 11th century, a Piast castle tower mostly of the 14th century and the Gothic Church of St Mary Magdalene, the burial site of the Cieszyn line of the Piast dynasty. The Museum of Cieszyn Silesia is housed in the former Larisch palace.
cilicia: Cilicia lies on the southern coast of Anatolia. It historically extended from Coracesium or the river Melas in the west to the Amanus Mountains in the east, and was bounded on the north by the Taurus Mountains, passable in very few places such as the Cilician Gates. The name derives from the Akkadian Ḫilakku, used by the Neo-Assyrian Empire for the western part. Rough Cilicia in the west is a rugged mountain district whose small harbours made the coast a string of havens for pirates in classical times. Plain Cilicia in the east has a large coastal plain of rich soil, praised by Xenophon, and formed an important link between Syria and the Anatolian highlands.

Plain Cilicia has been intensively settled since the Neolithic. After the Bronze Age Collapse ended Kizzuwatna, two main states emerged: Ḫiyawa in the east, called Que in Neo-Assyrian sources, and Ḫilakku in the west. The ancient inhabitants were largely Luwian speakers. Alexander the Great entered through the Cilician Gates unopposed after the Battle of Issus. In 102 BCE the Roman Republic set up a command there against the Cilician pirates, and between 78 and 74 BCE Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus conquered Rough Cilicia, which made a lasting Roman presence possible.

The Muslim Arabs invaded in the 7th century, and under the Abbasid Caliphate Cilicia became a fortified frontier zone, with Tarsus, rebuilt in 787/788, as its largest settlement. In 1080 Ruben, a relative of the last king of Ani, founded a small principality in the Cilician Taurus that grew into the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, a Christian state that lasted about 300 years and supported the Crusaders. The Mamluks took the whole region by 1375, and Selim I incorporated the Ramadanid beylik into the Ottoman Empire in 1516.

Modern Cilicia, in Turkey, includes the provinces of Mersin, Adana, Osmaniye and Hatay, and its population is concentrated mostly on the Cilician plain, Çukurova. The Armistice of Mudros in 1918 gave Cilicia to France, and the region became part of the Republic of Turkey in 1921 with the Treaty of Ankara. Among its sites are Kizkalesi, a fort built in the early 12th century by the Armenian kings of the Rubeniyan dynasty, and the Roman town of Soloi-Pompeiopolis.
cimbri: Ancient authors described the Cimbri variously as a Celtic-Gaulish, Germanic or even Cimmerian people. Several ancient sources place them in Jutland, which some classical texts call the Cimbrian peninsula. Augustus's Res gestae records that his fleet sailed east from the mouth of the Rhine to the lands of the Cimbri, who sent envoys seeking his friendship. Archaeologists, however, have found no clear sign of a mass migration from Jutland in the early Iron Age. There is no direct evidence for their language: their chiefs bore Celtic names such as Boiorix and Lugius, while northern Jutland has only Germanic place names.

Some time before 100 BCE many of the Cimbri, with the Teutons and Ambrones, migrated south-east and appeared about 113 BCE in Noricum, where they invaded the lands of the Taurisci, a Roman ally. At the Battle of Noreia they defeated the Romans under Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, saved from annihilation only by a storm. They turned west into Gaul, defeating Roman armies in 109 and 107 BCE. In 105 BCE discord between the proconsul Quintus Servilius Caepio and the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus let them rout the Romans at the Battle of Arausio, where Livy reports as many as 80,000 Romans lost.

Rome was in panic, and Gaius Marius was elected consul five years in a row, from 104 to 100 BCE. The Cimbri pillaged the Iberian Peninsula until Celtiberians confronted them. In 101 BCE Marius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus destroyed them at Vercellae.

At Vercellae the chieftains Lugius and Boiorix died, Caesorix and Claodicus were captured, and the women killed themselves and their children to avoid slavery. Some captives may have had sons among the rebel gladiators of the Third Servile War. Julius Caesar held that the Belgic Atuatuci descended from the Cimbri and Teutones. The people of Himmerland in Denmark claim to be their heirs, and the Danish author Johannes V. Jensen told their story in 1922.
cimmerians: The Cimmerians were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people from the Pontic-Caspian steppe. They were culturally Scythian and related to the Scythians, but ethnically distinct, and the Scythians later displaced and replaced them. The Cimmerians left no written records. Most information comes from Neo-Assyrian records of the 8th to 7th centuries BCE and from Greek and Roman authors from the 5th century BCE onward.

Their early homeland lay in the Caspian and Ciscaucasian steppes, north and west of the Caspian Sea, with the Volga as the eastern border separating them from the Scythians and the Kerch Strait at the west. The early Scythians began to arrive from Central Asia in the 9th century BCE, driven west by the Massagetae or the Issedones.

In the second half of the 8th century BCE and the 7th century BCE the Cimmerians moved south into West Asia, crossing the Caucasus by the Alagir, Darial and Klukhor passes. Mesopotamian sources call their first land in Transcaucasia māt Gamir, near the Kuros river, north of Lake Sevan. They later became active in the Iranian Plateau and Anatolia, and split into a western horde in Anatolia and an eastern horde that moved into Mannai and later Media.

Three kings are recorded: Teušpâ, who ruled until 679 BCE, Dugdammî, from 679 to 640 BCE, and Sandakšatru, from 640 to about the 630s BCE. The inroads of the Cimmerians and the Scythians upset the balance between Assyria, Urartu and Phrygia, and contributed to the decline of several of them and the rise of the Medes and the Lydians.

The Cimmerians were a tribal confederation, possibly ethnically mixed under an Iranic aristocracy, ruled by a supreme king whose power passed within a single dynasty. Military assemblies could be convened by the king, and warlords could rebel against him. They lived as mounted pastoralists like the Scythians, with the same weapons, horse harness and Animal Style art.

The western Cimmerians in Anatolia became settled, in fortified and other settlements, with a capital called Ḫarzallē. There they adopted chariot warfare and infantry, and appear to have taken up the worship of the Anatolian god Šanta. Homer's Odyssey gives the first mention of the Cimmerians in Greek literature, placing them in a misty land at the entrance of Hades.
cinnamon: Cinnamon is obtained from the inner bark of several tree species of the genus Cinnamomum. Cinnamomum verum, known as Ceylon cinnamon after its origin in Sri Lanka, is considered true cinnamon, but most cinnamon in international commerce comes from four other species, more correctly called cassia. The stems are processed while the inner bark is still wet: the outer bark is scraped off and the inner bark pried off in long rolls, which curl into quills as they dry. Ceylon cinnamon is lighter and finer than the thicker, harder cassia.

The English word comes through Latin and medieval French from the Greek kinnámōmon, which was borrowed from a Phoenician word similar to the Hebrew qinnāmōn. Cinnamon was imported to Egypt as early as 2000 BCE, and it was so prized that it was regarded as a gift fit for monarchs. Its source was kept a trade secret in the Mediterranean world for centuries by traders protecting their monopoly. In Ancient Egypt it was used to embalm mummies. Herodotus and Aristotle named Arabia as its source and recounted that giant cinnamon birds gathered the sticks for their nests; Pliny the Elder called this a traders' fiction made up to raise prices.

According to Pliny, a Roman pound of cassia or cinnamon cost up to 1,500 denarii, the wage of fifty months' labour. Through the Middle Ages the cinnamon-based cameline sauce was among the most common at tables in Western Europe, though the origin of the spice remained a mystery. The first mention that it grew in Sri Lanka is in al-Qazwini about 1270. Venetian traders held a monopoly in Europe, distributing it from Alexandria, and the disruption of this trade by the Mamluk sultans and the Ottoman Empire was one of many factors that led Europeans to search for other routes to Asia.

The Portuguese controlled Sri Lankan cinnamon in the 1500s. Dutch traders established a trading post on the island in 1638, took control of the manufactories by 1640 and expelled the remaining Portuguese by 1658. The British seized control of Ceylon from the Dutch in 1796.
circassians: The Circassians, also called the Cherkess or the Adyghe, are a Northwest Caucasian people native to Circassia in the North Caucasus. Dolmens in the northwest Caucasus point to a megalithic culture. Feudalism began to emerge among them by the 4th century. Christianity spread through the Caucasus between the 3rd and 5th centuries, and the Circassians, then known as Kassogs, began to accept it without abandoning every older belief. They founded several states, among them the medieval kingdom of Zichia, but could not achieve political unity. Around the end of the first millennium they were integrated into the Kingdom of Alania. In the 17th century, under Crimean Tatar and Ottoman influence, large numbers converted to Islam, and most Circassians are now Sunni Muslim.

In 1714 Peter I drew up a plan to occupy the Caucasus, and Catherine II began to carry it out. Circassian resistance lasted until 1864, in the Russo-Circassian War. Most Circassians were then exiled to the Ottoman Empire, in what is described as the Circassian genocide; the Russian and Ottoman governments negotiated the process, and the Circassians were moved or pressed to the Black Sea coast, from where Ottoman boats took them to Anatolia. In the 1860s and 1870s the Ottoman government settled them in what are now Turkey, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Israel, Iraq and parts of the Balkans.

Circassians had lived outside the Caucasus since the Middle Ages. Most leaders of the Burji Mamluk dynasty of Egypt (1382–1517) were of Circassian origin, and Qaitbay was sultan from 1468 to 1496. In Jordan, Circassian refugees founded Amman in 1878. About 800,000 Circassians live in historical Circassia, in Adygea, Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia and Krasnodar Krai, and some 4,500,000 live elsewhere, mostly in Turkey.

Before the Russian conquest Circassian society was highly stratified, with a caste of princes, then lesser nobility, commoners, serfs and slaves, though a few mountain tribes were fairly egalitarian. Custom was governed by Adyghe khabze. The people are divided into twelve tribes, among them the Abzakh, Besleney, Kabardians, Shapsugh and Ubykh, which the twelve stars of the Circassian flag represent. They speak two mutually intelligible languages, Adyghe, or West Circassian, and Kabardian. The Ubykh language became extinct in 1992 with the death of its last speaker.
circe: In Greek mythology Circe is a witch and goddess, in most accounts a daughter of the sun god Helios and the Oceanid Perse; the Orphic Argonautica names her mother Asterope instead. Some sources call her a nymph. Her brother was Aeëtes, keeper of the Golden Fleece and father of Medea, and Pasiphaë, wife of King Minos, is sometimes listed as her sister. Dionysius Scytobrachion and Diodorus Siculus make her and Medea daughters of Hecate, whom they treat as a mortal woman who discovered drugs. She was known for her knowledge of potions and herbs, and with these and a wand or staff she changed her enemies, or those who offended her, into animals. Her Homeric epithet is polypharmakos, knowing many drugs or charms.

In Homer's Odyssey, Circe lives in a palace in a dense wood on her island of Aeaea, where strangely docile lions and wolves prowl. She lures visitors with her singing as she weaves, then drugs them and changes their shape. When Odysseus visits her on the way home from the Trojan War she turns most of his crew into swine, but he persuades her to restore them, and he stays with her for a year. Hesiod's Theogony says she bore him three sons, Agrius, Latinus and Telegonus. In the lost Telegony she gave Telegonus a poisoned spear, and he killed his father unknowingly, after which Circe made Penelope and Telemachus immortal.

In the Argonautica, Apollonius has her purify Jason and Medea of the murder of Absyrtus with the blood of a piglet and send them away. Other tales say she turned the Italian king Picus into a woodpecker for resisting her advances, and that she poisoned the water where the nymph Scylla bathed, out of jealousy over the sea-god Glaucus, turning her into a monster. Circe was venerated at a tomb-shrine on one of the Pharmacussae islands and at Mount Circeo in Italy, which was said to be named for her. The gens Mamilia of Latium claimed descent from her.

Early philosophers asked whether being changed from a reasoning human into a beast might be preferable, a debate that affected the Renaissance; Giovan Battista Gelli's La Circe of 1549 gave it dialogue form. Socrates had explained the transformation as gluttony overcoming self-control, while Andrea Alciato's Emblemata of 1546 made Circe a type of the prostitute. Renaissance epics gave her heirs in the sorceresses Alcina, Armida and Acrasia. Later Christian opinion saw her as an abominable witch.

She is common in ancient vase painting, usually stirring a potion or threatened by Odysseus. Stradella's cantata La Circe was first performed in 1667, and Martha Graham's ballet Circe appeared in 1963.
cirebon: Cirebon is the only coastal city of West Java, about 40 km west of the provincial border with Central Java and about 297 km east of Jakarta. Because it lies on the border of the Sundanese and Javanese cultural regions, many residents speak a dialect mixing the two, known as Jawareh, and linguists treat Cirebonese as a language area of its own. The name may derive from the Javanese word caruban, meaning mixed, a reference to the city's blend of Sundanese, Javanese, Chinese and Arabic elements, or from the Sundanese ci, water, and rebon, shrimp.

According to the manuscript Purwaka Caruban Nagari, Cirebon began in the 15th century as a small fishing village named Muara Jati that attracted foreign traders. Its port master, Ki Gedeng Alang-Alang, was appointed by the king of Galuh and later moved the port to Lemahwungkuk. A prince of Pajajaran, Walangsungsang, converted to Islam, became duke of Cirebon with the title Cakrabumi, and declared independence from Sunda and Galuh. This marked the first Islamic rule in western Java. Under Sunan Gunungjati in the early 16th century the sultanate was independent, and Tomé Pires named Cirebon around 1513 as one of the trade centres of Java.

After the Sunda kingdom collapsed, Banten and Mataram fought over Cirebon, which declared its allegiance to Sultan Agung of Mataram. His grandson Amangkurat II ceded the city to the Dutch in 1677, the year the sultanate split into four royal houses, each with its own palace. In 1705 a treaty made the area west of the Cisanggarung River a Dutch protectorate jointly administered by three sultans. Under the Dutch Culture System, trade in cash crops attracted Chinese entrepreneurs, and a famine struck in 1844 after drought and the shift from subsistence farming to indigo and sugarcane.

Cirebon had 333,303 inhabitants at the 2020 census, and a large ethnic Chinese community that dates from immigration since the 17th century. Four palaces of the former sultanate remain as cultural institutions: Kasepuhan, Kanoman, Kaprabonan and Kacirebonan. The city is known for batik, whose Megamendung pattern resembles Chinese cloud imagery, for glass painting and for the Topeng Cirebon mask dance. The Sunan Gunung Jati complex lies about 24 km west of the city centre.
cisalpine-gaul: Cisalpine means on this side of the Alps from the Roman point of view, as opposed to Transalpine Gaul beyond them. The region was also called Gallia Citerior, Hither Gaul, and Gallia Togata, toga-wearing Gaul, a name that points to its early Romanization. It was divided into Gallia Cispadana, south of the Po, and Gallia Transpadana, north of it, and the Roman province of the 1st century BCE ran from the Alps to the Apennines, the Rubicon and the Adriatic Sea.

The Canegrate culture of the 13th century BCE may represent a first migration of proto-Celtic people over the Alps into the western Po valley, bringing cremation. It later merged with the native Ligurians to give rise to the Golasecca culture. According to Livy, a group led by Bellovesus occupied the area between Milan and Cremona in the time of Tarquinius Priscus, and Milan itself was presumably founded by Gauls in the early 6th century BCE.

In 391 BCE, according to Diodorus Siculus, Celts from beyond the Alps seized the land between the Apennines and the Alps, and the Senones sacked Rome in 390 BCE. A Celtic army was crushed at the Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE. In the Second Punic War the Boii and Insubres allied with the Carthaginians, and after Hannibal's victories all the Gauls except the Cenomani joined the revolt; Rome withdrew until Carthage was defeated in 202 BCE. Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica completed the conquest of the Boii in 191 BCE, and the Ligurians were finally subdued in 155 BCE.

The province was probably established about 81 BCE and governed from Mutina, where in 73 BCE forces under Spartacus defeated the governor's legion. In 49 BCE all its people received Roman citizenship, and Julius Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon that year began the civil war. It was merged into Italia about 42 BCE. Virgil, Catullus and Livy were born there.
cisleithania: Cisleithania, officially the Kingdoms and Lands Represented in the Imperial Council, was the northern and western part of Austria-Hungary. Its capital was Vienna, the residence of the Emperor of Austria, and in 1910 it had a population of about 28.6 million. It reached from Vorarlberg in the west to Galicia and Bukovina in the east, and from Bohemia in the north to Dalmatia in the south. Its name comes from the Leitha River, a tributary of the Danube that formed the historical boundary between the Archduchy of Austria and the Kingdom of Hungary. The official name was used by politicians and officials but had no official status until 1915, and the public usually just called the lands Austria.

Cisleithania consisted of 15 crown lands, each with a regional assembly, the Landtag, that made laws on matters of mostly minor importance. The Reichsrat in Vienna was its parliament. From 1873 its lower house was directly elected on a four-class franchise, and equal and universal suffrage for men came only with the reform of 1907. The government handled everything except the common army, navy and foreign ministry. German-speaking deputies dominated at first, but as the franchise widened the Slavs gained a majority, and conflict between German and Slavic politicians, notably over the Czech National Revival, often paralysed politics. After 1893 no government could rely on a parliamentary majority, and the emperor sometimes ruled by decree.

The December Constitution of 1867 declared all languages equal, but German kept a privileged position in administration, courts, army and education and never became the legal state language. In April 1897 Minister-President Kasimir Felix Badeni issued ordinances making Czech equal to German in Bohemia and Moravia. German deputies answered with a filibuster, there were street demonstrations, and on 28 November 1897 Emperor Franz Joseph dismissed Badeni. Riots followed in German and Czech towns, and martial law ended four days of rioting in Prague. The ordinances were withdrawn in 1899. The Reichsrat was prorogued in March 1914 and did not meet again until May 1917.

Cisleithania covered the present territory of Austria except Burgenland, most of the Czech Republic and Slovenia, southern Poland, and parts of Italy, Croatia, Montenegro, Romania and Ukraine. Roman Catholics made up about 79 per cent of its population, and almost 60 per cent were ethnically Slavic. Its economic growth after the Compromise was significantly faster than in the preceding half-century.
cistercians: In 1098 Robert of Molesme left Molesme Abbey in Burgundy with around twenty supporters, who felt that the Cluniac communities had abandoned the rigour and simplicity of the Rule of Saint Benedict. They founded Cîteaux Abbey near Dijon, whose Latin name, Cistercium, gave the order its name. The first three abbots were Robert, Alberic and Stephen Harding, a monk from England. The Cistercians are also called White Monks, after the colour of their cowl, in contrast to the black cowl of the Benedictines.

Their life returned to literal observance of the Rule, including manual labour and especially work in the fields, and at times went beyond it in austerity. Bernard entered Cîteaux in the early 1110s, and his charisma greatly enlarged the order. In 1115 Count Hugh of Champagne gave the order forested land east of Troyes, where Bernard founded the Abbey of Clairvaux with twelve other monks.

By the end of the 12th century the order had spread through most of Europe. Houses included Waverley Abbey in Surrey (1128), Rein Abbey in Styria (1129), Mellifont Abbey in County Louth (1142) and Alcobaça Monastery in Portugal (1153). The first community of nuns, Tart, was founded in 1125. In the early 13th century there were about five hundred abbeys.

For a hundred years, until the first quarter of the 13th century, the Cistercians were the most powerful order and chief religious influence in western Europe, replacing Cluny. Bernard became mentor to popes and kings, and in 1145 one of his monks was elected Pope Eugene III. Afterwards the initiative passed to the mendicant orders. Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries confiscated every monastery in England, while in Germany abbeys such as Loccum and Amelungsborn adopted the Lutheran faith. A reform at La Trappe Abbey in 17th-century France produced the Trappists.

The Cistercians were the main force in spreading technology in fields such as agriculture and hydraulic engineering. They developed an organised system for selling produce, cattle and horses, and fostered the wool and cloth trade. Their architecture avoided decoration as a sign of poverty and simplicity, yet the order helped to spread Gothic construction across Europe. The abbeys of Fontenay, Fountains, Alcobaça, Poblet and Maulbronn are recognised as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
ciudad-bolivar: Ciudad Bolívar lies where the Orinoco River narrows to about 1 mile (1.6 km) in width. It is the site of the first bridge across the river and a major river port for the eastern regions of Venezuela. Moriche palms and scrub oaks grow on the shores of the river, and the local fauna include capybaras, turtles, herons, parrots and iguanas. The climate is tropical savanna, with a dry season from December to April and a wet season from May to early November.

The settlement began as a Spanish fortified port called Santo Tomé de Guayana, which had to be moved on three occasions because Carib peoples and European rivals, such as the Dutch and English, kept attacking it. The first settlements lay downstream from the present city. Dutch forces destroyed the town in 1579. A second settlement was founded in 1595 by Don Antonio de Berrío. One of Walter Raleigh's expeditions sacked it in 1617, and Raleigh's son Watt died in the fighting. Fernando de Berrío refounded the town in 1620, but English and Dutch pirates destroyed it in 1629 and the Dutch burned it again in 1637.

The fourth and present city was officially founded in 1764 by Don Joaquín Moreno de Mendoza, with names that included San Tomé de Angostura, after its diocese and its position at the first narrows of the Orinoco. Angostura became the capital of Guayana Province and the seat of the Congress of Angostura from 1819 to 1821, which was responsible for the creation of Gran Colombia. Angostura bitters were invented in the city in 1824, although the company that made them later moved to Trinidad and Tobago. The city took the name Ciudad Bolívar in 1846, in honour of Simon Bolívar.

Ciudad Bolívar is the capital of Bolívar State. Its well-preserved historic centre has a cathedral and other colonial buildings around the Plaza Bolívar. The Jesús Soto Museum of Modern Art, designed by the Venezuelan architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva and opened in 1973, honours the sculptor and painter Jesús Soto, a native of the city. The guitarist and composer Antonio Lauro was also born there. The state economy rests on agriculture and animal husbandry, and the city has several universities, among them the Universidad de Oriente's Bolívar campus, created in 1960.
ciudad-real: Ciudad Real lies in the southern half of the Inner Plateau, in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula, at about 625 metres above sea level. It belongs to the Campo de Calatrava, a transitional region between the Montes and La Mancha that is unusual in the peninsula for its volcanic origin; the Plaza del Pilar is built at the centre of a shallow volcanic maar. No major river passes through the city, which lies between the Guadiana to the north and its tributary the Jabalón to the south. It stands at the crossroads of the Madrid–Andalusia and Levante–Portugal routes but did not particularly prosper from this.

Villa Real, the Royal Town, was founded in 1255 under Alfonso X as a royal demesne town, with a charter modelled on that of Cuenca, over the hamlet of Pozuelo de San Gil. As an independent royal enclave within the dominion of the Order of Calatrava, it struggled at first to attract settlers, and the Order set up a rival market at nearby Miguelturra. Friction reached its climax about 1323 in armed conflict. A middle-sized jewry was documented by 1290, and the local aljama was largely dismantled in the pogroms of 1391. The town hosted the Cortes of Castile in 1346.

Juan II of Castile made it a city in 1420, with probably no more than 2,000 inhabitants. It became capital of the province of La Mancha in 1691, and many of the buildings that followed were destroyed by the Lisbon earthquake of 1755. French troops occupied it in 1809. After the territorial division of 1833, Almagro and Manzanares challenged its status as provincial capital without success. Much of the centre was destroyed in the Spanish Civil War.

Ciudad Real is the capital of its province in Castile–La Mancha. Only two parts of the medieval wall stand, including the Toledo Gate. The Church of Santiago dates from the end of the 13th century and the Church of San Pedro from the 14th and 15th centuries. The cathedral, built in the 16th century, has the second-largest nave in Spain.
cividale-del-friuli: Cividale del Friuli, in Friulian Cividât and in Slovene Čedad, lies in the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region of north-eastern Italy, 135 metres above sea level in the foothills of the eastern Alps and close to the Slovenian border. It stands on the river Natisone, which forms a picturesque ravine and splits the town in two. In the Iron Age the area was settled by Veneti and Celts.

Because of its strategic position on the north-eastern frontier of Roman Italy, the Romans founded a castrum there in 50 BCE, which Julius Caesar transformed into a forum named Forum Iulii. After Aquileia was destroyed in 452, Forum Iulii became the chief town of the district, which took its name from it. In 568 it was the first major centre occupied by Alboin's Lombard invasion of Italy, and Alboin gave it to his nephew Gisulf as capital of the Lombard Duchy of Friuli. After the Franks defeated the Lombards in 774, the town was renamed Civitas Austriae, Charlemagne's City of the East.

The patriarchs of Aquileia resided there from 773 to 1031, and it became the capital of the Patriarchal State of Friuli when that was founded in 1077. When the patriarchs moved on to Udine in 1238, a rivalry began between the two towns that ended only when they surrendered to Venice, Cividale in 1419 or 1420. A church council held there in 1409 by Pope Gregory XII was poorly attended and achieved nothing. After the Napoleonic Wars Cividale became part of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia, and it passed to the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.

Cividale is a quiet small town that attracts visitors with its medieval centre, which holds the National Archaeological Museum and the Duomo, built in the 15th century over an 8th-century building. A silver altarpiece of Patriarch Pellegrino II, made between 1195 and 1204, is inscribed with individual letter punches. The Oratorio di Santa Maria in Valle, also called the Lombard Temple, shows strong Byzantine influence. The part of the historical centre dating from Lombard times was added to the UNESCO list in 2011.
civil-disobedience: The practice is older than the term. An early depiction is in Sophocles' play Antigone, in which Antigone defies King Creon of Thebes, who forbids her to give her brother Polynices a proper burial, and says she must obey her conscience rather than human law. The earliest recorded collective incident took place under the Roman Empire, when unarmed Jews gathered in the streets to prevent the installation of pagan images in the Temple in Jerusalem. Conrad Grebel and the Anabaptists advocated civil disobedience to oppression, and Étienne de La Boétie, in his Discours de la servitude volontaire of 1552, was one of the first to propose non-cooperation as an effective weapon.

Henry David Thoreau's essay Resistance to Civil Government, first published in 1849 and published after his death in 1866 as Civil Disobedience, popularized the term in the United States. Mahatma Gandhi wrote in 1935 that he had not drawn the idea from Thoreau, since resistance to authority in South Africa was well advanced before he read the essay, and that he came to prefer the phrase civil resistance.

Civil disobedience is the active and professed refusal of a citizen to obey certain laws, demands or orders of a government or other authority. Some definitions require it to be nonviolent, as Black's Law Dictionary does, while others, such as that of Christian Bay, require only carefully chosen and legitimate means. Howard Zinn noted that some campaigns classed as nonviolent, such as the Birmingham campaign, included elements of violence. Writers also distinguish revolutionary from non-revolutionary disobedience, and collective from solitary acts such as Thoreau's.

It concerns a citizen's relation to the state, not a conflict between two public bodies. Those who practise it can expect arrest, charge and punishment. Martin Luther King Jr. held that a person who breaks a law that conscience tells him is unjust, and accepts the penalty, expresses the highest respect for law. Acts that avoid punishment by concealment or flight, or a test case brought only to challenge a law's constitutionality, are generally not counted.

Governments have generally not recognized civil disobedience as legitimate. The law usually distinguishes criminal motive from criminal intent, so a protester with admirable motives may still have a criminal intent, and the saying goes that any justification must come from outside the legal system. It has been used by many movements: Susan B. Anthony in the late 19th century, Saad Zaghloul in the 1910s, Gandhi in 1920s British India, and the civil rights movement in the United States in the 1960s, in which King and James Bevel led protests. The term has also been stretched; in Marshall Cohen's words it has been used to describe everything from bringing a test case in court to taking aim at a federal official.
civita-castellana: Civita Castellana is a town and comune in the province of Viterbo, 65 kilometres north of Rome. Mount Soracte lies about 10 kilometres to the south-east. The site was settled in the Iron Age by the Italic Falisci, who called it Falerii.

After the Faliscan defeat by the Romans, the Romans built a new city about 5 kilometres away, Falerii Novi. The abandoned city was repopulated from the early Middle Ages and took the name Civita Castellana, meaning City of the Castle, first mentioned in 994. In the following centuries it was a flourishing independent commune, often disputed between the Pope and the Holy Roman Empire. Emperor Otto III died on 23 January 1002 at the castle of Paterno, whose ruins survive.

Pope Paschal II captured the city at the beginning of the 12th century, and it was later given as a fief to the Savelli by Pope Gregory XIV. Pope Sixtus IV assigned it to Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia, the future Pope Alexander VI, who began the Rocca, the citadel, designed by Antonio da Sangallo the Elder. It was completed under Pope Julius II and enlarged under him and Pope Leo X.

The town became an important road hub with its connection to the Via Flaminia in 1606 and with the Ponte Clementino, built after the Battle of Civita Castellana. In that battle, on 5 December 1798, a French army defeated a Neapolitan army while the town was part of the Roman Republic of 1798 to 1799.

The cathedral of Santa Maria Maggiore has a Cosmatesque portico erected in 1210 by Laurentius Romanus, his son Jacobus and his grandson Cosmas, with ancient columns and mosaic decoration. Its interior was modernised in the 18th century, and the high altar is made from a Paleo-Christian sarcophagus of the 3rd or 4th century. The church of Santa Chiara has a Renaissance portal of 1529, and the belltower of Santa Maria del Carmine, of the 12th century, incorporates ancient Roman spolia. The National Museum of the Faliscan Countryside houses finds from ancient Falerii and the surrounding area.
cizre: Cizre lies on the Tigris by the Syria–Turkey border, in the historical region of Upper Mesopotamia. It was founded in the 9th century as Jazirat Ibn ʿUmar by Al-Hasan ibn Umar, Emir of Mosul, on a manmade island in the river, and the name means island of the son of Umar. Its position as a river crossing and port, at the end of an old Roman road to the Mediterranean, made it an important commercial and strategic centre.

By the 12th century the town had an intellectual and religious role, with Christian and Jewish communities, four Shafi'i madrasas and two Sufi lodges outside the walls. Badr al-Din Lu'lu' acknowledged Mongol suzerainty as early as 1252. The town suffered several sackings in the 15th century, and the Aq Qoyunlu leader Uzun Hasan took it in 1456. After the Ottoman victory at Chaldiran in 1514, Idris Bitlisi persuaded the emir of Bohtan to submit to Sultan Selim I, and in 1515 Bohtan became an autonomous territory in the province of Diyarbekir.

In 1836 an Ottoman army retook the town from Muhammad Pasha of Rawanduz and replaced the emir of Bohtan with Bedir Khan Beg, who reportedly set up a munitions factory there. By the end of the 19th century Cizre had shrunk to a small district centre dominated by ruins. Its Christian population was destroyed in 1915 in the Armenian genocide and the Sayfo, and its Jews left for Israel in 1951.

Cizre is a city in Şırnak Province in Turkey, in the cultural region of Turkish Kurdistan, and is predominantly inhabited by Kurds. It received electricity and running water in the mid-1950s, and its population grew greatly from 1984 as people fled the Kurdish–Turkish conflict. As the capital of the Bohtan emirate, it was an important Kurdish cultural centre in which music, poetry and science flourished under the emirs' protection.
clara-schumann: Clara Josephine Wieck was born in Leipzig on 13 September 1819 to Friedrich Wieck and Mariane, born Tromlitz, who sang and played piano at the Gewandhaus. Her parents divorced in 1825, and five-year-old Clara stayed with her father. After her mother left he taught her daily in piano, violin, singing, theory, harmony, composition and counterpoint, followed by two hours of practice, to the detriment of her general education. She began touring at eleven and succeeded in Paris and Vienna, among other cities.

Robert Schumann, a little more than nine years older, proposed in 1837. Friedrich Wieck refused his permission, so the couple sued him, and the judge allowed the marriage, which took place on 12 September 1840, the day before her 21st birthday. They had eight children. Clara premiered many of Robert's works and earned money by giving concerts, and the burden of family duties narrowed her scope as a composer. After his early death she toured Europe for decades, often with the violinist Joseph Joachim, and gave sixteen winter-spring tours of England between 1865 and 1888. From 1878 she taught piano at Dr. Hoch's Konservatorium in Frankfurt and edited her husband's works.

More than 1,300 programmes of her concerts between 1831 and 1889 survive. Her early repertoire, chosen by her father, was showy; later she played Scarlatti and Bach, and above all contemporaries such as Chopin, Mendelssohn, her husband and Johannes Brahms. Her Op. 1, the Quatre Polonaises, dates from 1831, and she wrote her Piano Concerto in A minor at fourteen. After marriage she turned to songs and choral works, and published one joint work with Robert in 1841, settings of Friedrich Rückert. She died on 20 May 1896 after a stroke and was buried in Bonn beside her husband, as she wished. Interest in her compositions revived in the late 20th century.
classic-of-poetry: The collection holds the oldest chronologically authenticated Chinese poems. Most date to the Western Zhou period, 1046 to 771 BCE, and the latest song was dated by Zheng Xuan to about 700 BCE. It falls into the Airs of the States and the Hymns and Eulogies. The Airs are shorter lyrics in simple language, generally ancient folk songs on love, soldiers on campaign, farming and political satire. The Hymns and Eulogies are longer ritual songs, courtly praise and dynastic hymns for the founders of the Zhou dynasty. About 95 per cent of the lines have four syllables.

Tradition says officials collected verses current in the various states so that the king could understand the condition of the common people. Tradition also says Confucius selected the 300 songs that best conformed to ritual propriety from some 3,000. The Han historian Sima Qian was the first to attribute the work to Confucius directly, and the view is now generally discredited, since the Zuo Zhuan records the Classic of Poetry already existing in definitive form when Confucius was a child. The Analects does record Confucius telling his son that without studying the Odes there was nothing to say to him.

The Odes became a classic in the canonical sense when the Han dynasty adopted Confucianism officially. Three versions had chairs at the Imperial Academy under Emperor Wu, but the Mao tradition became dominant in the Eastern Han, and by the 5th century it alone survived as the received text. Scholars long read the songs as moral and political allegory, a tradition first doubted by Zheng Qiao in the 12th century. Since the Qing dynasty the rhymes have been studied to reconstruct Old Chinese pronunciation, and the Odes remain a source of four-character idioms still used in Chinese.
classical-greece: Classical Greece is a period of around 200 years, the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. It is marked by much of the eastern Aegean and northern Greek regions, such as Ionia and Macedonia, gaining autonomy from the Persian Empire, by the peak of democratic Athens, by the Peloponnesian Wars, by the Spartan and then Theban hegemonies, and by the expansion of Macedonia under Philip II. Much of the early defining mathematics, science, architecture, sculpture, theatre, literature, philosophy and politics of Western civilisation derives from it. In the history of Greek art it follows the Archaic period and is succeeded by the Hellenistic period.

The Athenian democracy grew out of the reforms of Cleisthenes, which made the deme the basic civic unit and gave power to an assembly of citizens headed by a council of 500 chosen at random. Only men were citizens. The Ionian Greeks rose against Persia in 499 BCE, and in 490 BCE an Athenian army of 9,000 hoplites and 1,000 Plataeans defeated the Persians at Marathon. After Thermopylae the Persians were beaten at Plataea in 479 BCE. In 477 BCE Athens became leader of the Delian League, which became a front for Athenian hegemony in the Aegean.

War broke out between Athens and Sparta in 431 BCE. Plague killed many in besieged Athens, including Pericles, and the Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE brought a pause. Athens was decisively defeated in 404 BCE. The Treaty of Antalcidas in 387 BCE handed the Greek cities of Ionia and Cyprus to Persia. Thebes under Epaminondas won at Leuctra in 371 BCE, and Philip II of Macedon was drawn into Greek affairs in 346 BCE.

In 334 BCE Alexander the Great crossed the Hellespont and conquered the Achaemenid empire in less than a decade. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and the period conventionally ends there, as his empire was divided among the Diadochi. Post-Renaissance European elites saw themselves as the spiritual heirs of Greece, and Will Durant wrote in 1939 that, excepting machinery, there is hardly anything secular in our culture that does not come from Greece.
claude-lorrain: He was the third of five sons of Jean Gellée and Anne Padose, born at Chamagne in the Duchy of Lorraine. The early biographers disagree about his youth. Baldinucci has him orphaned at twelve and taught drawing by an elder brother before he went to Naples and then to Agostino Tassi in Rome. Sandrart says he was apprenticed to a pastry baker and reached Rome as a servant and cook to Tassi, who made him an apprentice. Modern scholars generally prefer Sandrart or combine the two. Most agree that he trained with Goffredo Wals around 1620 to 1622 and with Tassi from about 1622 or 1623 to 1625, and by 1627 he had settled in Rome near the Spanish Steps for life.

Sandrart reported that in the late 1620s he already sketched outdoors, especially at dawn and dusk. His first dated painting is of 1629. Commissions came from the French ambassador in Rome in 1633 and from Philip IV of Spain, and Cardinal Guido Bentivoglio recommended him to Pope Urban VIII, who ordered four pictures. By the end of the 1630s he was the leading landscapist in Italy. About 1636 he began the Liber Veritatis, a book of drawings of his finished pictures with the purchasers' names on the back, whose 195 drawings are now in the British Museum. He died in Rome on 23 November 1682.

His landscapes grew larger, with fewer figures. He was not generally an innovator, except in placing the sun and its streaming light in many paintings, which had been rare before. His grand temples and palaces are mostly imagined from real buildings, and his harbour scenes show up-to-date merchant ships whatever the period of the subject. Figures were his weak point, and according to Baldinucci he joked that he charged for the landscape and gave the figures for free. After his death he became very popular with English collectors, and the UK still holds many of his works. The Claude glass, a tinted mirror used by tourists to frame views, was named after him.
claude-monet: Monet was born in Paris on 14 November 1840 and baptised Oscar-Claude. His family moved to Le Havre in 1845, where his mother, a singer, supported his wish to become an artist. In 1862 he joined the studio of Charles Gleyre, where he met Frédéric Bazille, who became his closest friend.

He married Camille on 28 June 1870, shortly before the Franco-Prussian War, and lived in London and the Netherlands to avoid conscription. In London he met the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, an encounter decisive for his career, and admired the works of John Constable and J. M. W. Turner. Back in France he joined Renoir, Pissarro, Sisley, Paul Cézanne, Edgar Degas and Berthe Morisot in exhibiting independently as the Anonymous Society of Painters, Sculptors and Engravers. At their first exhibition in 1874 he showed Impression, Sunrise, The Luncheon and Boulevard des Capucines, and the critic Louis Leroy's hostile review coined the term Impressionism. In 1883 Monet and his family rented a house and gardens at Giverny.

Monet made light the central subject of his paintings. He sometimes finished a canvas in one sitting, often without preparation, and wished to show how light alters colour and perception. He believed his only merit lay in having painted directly in front of nature, seeking to render the most fleeting effects, and he wanted to paint the air. His method of painting a scene many times produced the haystacks of 1890 to 1891 and the paintings of Rouen Cathedral of 1892 to 1894.

In his garden at Giverny the water lilies, the pond and the Japanese bridge became his chief subject. An exhibition of 1909 showed 42 canvases of the Water Lilies, and he eventually made over 250 paintings of them. Around 1905 he began to abandon the pond's edge, and by the mid-1910s his style had become fluid and nearly abstract. In his later years the first signs of cataracts appeared, and they darkened his later paintings and altered his perception of colour.

Monet died of lung cancer on 5 December 1926, aged 86, and is buried in the church cemetery at Giverny. At his funeral Clemenceau removed the black cloth from the coffin, saying: No black for Monet. His Giverny paintings are said to link Impressionism with twentieth-century art and modern abstraction, and he is now the best known of the Impressionists.
claude-of-france: Claude was born on 13 October 1499 at Romorantin-Lanthenay and named after Claudius of Besançon, a saint her mother had invoked on a pilgrimage so that she might bear a living child. Of Anne of Brittany's at least fourteen pregnancies, only Claude and her sister Renée, born in 1510, survived to adulthood. Because Anne had no surviving sons, Claude was heir presumptive to Brittany, while the French crown could pass only through male heirs under Salic Law.

Queen Anne sought to keep Brittany separate from the crown by marrying Claude to the future Emperor Charles V, and the contract was signed at Lyon on 10 August 1501. The first Treaty of Blois of 1504 gave Claude a large dowry if her father died without male heirs, including Brittany, Milan, Burgundy, Blois and Asti. In 1505 the ailing Louis XII cancelled the engagement at the Estates General of Tours, after Louise of Savoy had obtained a secret promise that Claude would marry her son.

Claude became Duchess of Brittany on 9 January 1514, when her mother died, and on 18 May, at fourteen, she married her cousin Francis. Louis XII died on 1 January 1515, less than three months after marrying Mary of England, and Francis and Claude became king and queen. She was crowned at the Basilica of St Denis on 10 May 1517.

She never ruled Brittany: in 1515 she gave its government to her husband in perpetuity. She refused his repeated suggestion that Brittany be incorporated into France and named her eldest son, Francis, heir to the duchy. At court she was eclipsed by her mother-in-law, Louise of Savoy, and had little interest in politics, preferring religion. Anne Boleyn was in her household until late 1521. She spent almost all her marriage in annual pregnancies.

Claude died on 26 July 1524 at the Château de Blois, aged twenty-four, and was buried at St Denis. Sources disagree on the cause: childbirth or miscarriage, exhaustion after many pregnancies, or bone tuberculosis, as her mother had. Her eldest son, Francis, succeeded her as Duke of Brittany, with his father as guardian, and after his death in 1536 her second son, Henry, became Dauphin and Duke of Brittany. He later became King of France as Henry II.
claudio-monteverdi: Monteverdi was baptised in Cremona on 15 May 1567, the first child of the apothecary Baldassare Monteverdi. There is no clear record of his early training. His first published work, the three-voice motets Sacrae cantiunculae, was issued in Venice in 1582 when he was fifteen, and in it he calls himself the pupil of Marc'Antonio Ingegneri, maestro di cappella at Cremona Cathedral, who by one account gave him a solid grounding in counterpoint and composition.

In 1590 or 1591 Monteverdi entered the service of Duke Vincenzo I Gonzaga of Mantua as a player of the vivuola, working beside the maestro di cappella Giaches de Wert. He married the court singer Claudia de Cattaneis in 1599. In his last five years at Mantua he completed L'Orfeo (1607) and L'Arianna (1608), and wrote the Messa in illo tempore and the Vespro della Beata Vergine (both 1610). In 1613 he became maestro di cappella of San Marco in Venice, where he found the choir neglected and had to recruit and manage about 30 singers and six instrumentalists. Much of his Mantuan stage music is lost, perhaps in the wars of 1630. His last years were largely given to opera for Venice.

He published nine books of madrigals between 1587 and 1638, moving from the style of his teacher to more expressive settings influenced by Wert. He defended novel techniques as a seconda pratica, as against the older prima pratica, and used the basso continuo of the Baroque. In Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria and L'incoronazione di Poppea (1643) he helped turn opera from a private entertainment of the nobility into a commercial genre; how much of the surviving Poppea is his is debated. He died on 29 November 1643 and was given a funeral of royal pomp at the Frari. After the 1650s his name faded, and his music was largely forgotten until its rediscovery around the beginning of the twentieth century.
claudius: Claudius was born on 1 August 10 BCE at Lugdunum in Roman Gaul, where his father Nero Claudius Drusus was stationed as a military legate, and so was the first Roman emperor born outside Italy. His mother was Antonia Minor, a granddaughter of Octavia Minor, the sister of Augustus, and his elder brother was Germanicus. Because of a limp, a stammer and a tremor, which he suffered after an illness in youth, his family kept him from public office until his consulship with his nephew Caligula in 37. His infirmity probably saved him from the purges of Tiberius and Caligula. He also wrote history, including a work on the Civil Wars that offended Augustus's circle and a twenty-book Etruscan history.

Caligula was assassinated on 24 January 41 in a conspiracy involving the tribune Cassius Chaerea and several senators. Claudius, the last adult male of his family, was declared emperor by the Praetorian Guard. He took pains to please the Senate, allowing it to issue its own bronze coinage and returning Macedonia and Achaea to it as senatorial provinces. He relied heavily on freedmen, dividing the secretariat into bureaus led by Narcissus (correspondence), Pallas (the treasury) and Callistus (justice).

In his reign the Empire began its conquest of Britain. A census in 48 counted 5,984,072 adult male citizens. He finished the Aqua Claudia and the Aqua Anio Novus and built Portus, a new harbour near Ostia, which reduced flooding in Rome. He sat in judgment on many cases, and ancient writers complained that he was easily swayed. Several plots against him led to the deaths of many senators. He married four times, last to his niece Agrippina the Younger.

Ancient historians agree that Claudius was poisoned and died in the early hours of the 13th of October in the year 54, and nearly all blame Agrippina, who wished to secure the throne for her son Nero before Claudius's own son Britannicus could gain power. Nero and the Senate deified him almost at once, though many of his edicts were later disregarded. The Flavians later contrasted him favourably with Nero. Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio, who favoured the Senate, painted a poor picture of him, and more recent historians have revised that view.
claudius-gothicus: Marcus Aurelius Claudius was born on 10 May 214, according to most historians, though some suggest 219 or 220. His birthplace is unknown; he may have been born near the Danube. The only source for his early life is the Historia Augusta, which is full of fabrications and flattery. In the 4th century he was declared a relative of Constantius Chlorus, the father of Constantine the Great; historians regard this as a genealogical fabrication meant to connect Constantine's family with a respected emperor. Before coming to power he served in the army and reached the highest military posts.

In the 260s the empire was split into the core Roman Empire, the Gallic Empire and the Palmyrene Empire. In the summer of 268, probably between July and October, the emperor Gallienus was killed in a conspiracy of senior officials, and the army outside Milan chose Claudius to succeed him. Accounts differ on whether he took part in the plot. He asked the Senate to spare Gallienus's family and supporters and had the dead emperor deified. He was the first of a series of tough soldier emperors who eventually restored the empire after the crisis of the third century.

The most pressing threat was a Gothic invasion of Illyricum and Pannonia. At the Battle of Naissus Claudius and his legions, with his cavalry commander, the future emperor Aurelian, routed a huge Gothic army, took thousands of prisoners and destroyed the Gothic cavalry as a force. The victory earned him the surname Gothicus, and the Goths did not pose a serious threat again for nearly a century. He also routed the Alamanni at the Battle of Lake Benacus in the late autumn of 268, and won victories against the Gallic Empire, regaining Hispania and the Rhône valley.

Claudius went to Sirmium late in 269 to prepare for war against the Vandals, who were raiding Pannonia. He fell victim to the plague, possibly the Plague of Cyprian, and died in 270; historians date his death to January, April, August or September, as the sources conflict. He is thought to have named Aurelian as his successor, though his brother Quintillus briefly seized power. The Senate deified him as Divus Claudius Gothicus.

His victories made him a hero in Latin tradition. A medieval legend links him to Saint Valentine, said to have refused to deny Christ before an Emperor Claudius and to have been beheaded; historians agree that the accounts cannot be verified.
claudius-ptolemy: Ptolemy's date and place of birth are both unknown. A 14th-century astronomer, Theodore Meliteniotes, gave his birthplace as Ptolemais Hermiou in the Thebaid, but the testimony is late and nothing supports it. He lived in or around Alexandria in the Roman province of Egypt and died there. His Latin name Claudius is generally taken to mean that he was a Roman citizen. He wrote in Koine Greek and used Babylonian observations and lunar theory. Later Arabic sources often called him the Upper Egyptian.

Astronomy took most of his effort. The Almagest, originally the Mathematical Treatise, is the only surviving comprehensive ancient treatise on astronomy. Following Hipparchus, Ptolemy derived geometrical models for the Sun, Moon and planets from observations, and supplied tables for computing their positions. It also contains a star catalogue with forty-eight constellations. The planetary models were geocentric and almost universally accepted until heliocentric models reappeared in the Scientific Revolution. Robert R. Newton argued in 1977 that Ptolemy fabricated data, a charge that Owen Gingerich and others rejected.

His Geography is a handbook on drawing maps from coordinates, based on earlier work by Marinus of Tyre. Its second part catalogues some 8,000 localities, of which about 6,300 have coordinates. He also wrote the Tetrabiblos, an astrological treatise, and the Harmonics, on the mathematics of musical scales.

For over a thousand years the Almagest was the authoritative text on astronomy across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. It was preserved in Arabic manuscripts and translated twice into Latin in the 12th century, once in Sicily and once in Spain. Plato of Tivoli first translated the Tetrabiblos from Arabic into Latin in 1138. Many abridged introductions to his astronomy circulated among Arabs and Byzantines, which suggests that few truly mastered the mathematics.
claus-von-stauffenberg: Claus Philipp Maria Justinian Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg was born on 15 November 1907 at Stauffenberg Castle in Jettingen, the third of four sons of Alfred Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg, the last Oberhofmarschall of the Kingdom of Württemberg. He married Nina von Lerchenfeld on 26 September 1933, and they had five children. Though he did not join the Nazi Party, in 1932 he voiced tentative support for Hitler. His views wavered, and the Night of the Long Knives and Kristallnacht led him further from the party.

Stauffenberg served in the invasion of Poland, on the general staff of the 6th Panzer Division in the Battle of France and in Tunisia in 1943 with the 10th Panzer Division. On 7 April 1943 he was wounded near Mezzouna and lost his left eye, his right hand and two fingers of his left hand. In September 1943 the conspirators brought him to the Replacement Army headquarters on the Bendlerstrasse in Berlin, where Friedrich Olbricht was one of his superiors. The Replacement Army was to carry out Operation Valkyrie, a contingency plan that was secretly changed to sweep the Nazi regime from power if Hitler died.

With Henning von Tresckow on the Eastern Front, Stauffenberg became the driving force of the plot. He knew that under German law he was committing high treason. After General Hellmuth Stieff declined to act on 7 July 1944, he decided to kill Hitler himself and also run the coup in Berlin.

On 20 July 1944 at the Wolf's Lair, Stauffenberg armed one of two small bombs in a briefcase and left it under the conference table. Four people were killed, but Hitler, shielded by the table leg, was only slightly wounded. After Goebbels announced on the radio that Hitler had survived, the coup in Berlin failed. General Friedrich Fromm held an impromptu court martial, and Stauffenberg, Werner von Haeften, Olbricht and Albrecht Mertz von Quirnheim were shot in the Bendlerblock courtyard before 1:00 on 21 July.

His brother Berthold was executed at Plötzensee on 10 August. More than 200 were condemned in show trials, and over 20,000 Germans were killed or sent to concentration camps in the purge. The Bendlerblock now houses the Memorial to the German Resistance.
clausthal-zellerfeld: Clausthal-Zellerfeld lies on the Upper Harz Plateau in the south-western part of the Harz mountains, at an altitude between 390 and 821 metres. The surrounding area is less mountainous than most of the Harz, with less woodland and more pasture. Numerous dams and streams of the Upper Harz Water Regale are scattered in and around the town. A depression between Clausthal and Zellerfeld marks a natural borderline between them. Its population is about 15,000, and it is the largest town in the area that lies in the mountains rather than at their edge.

The town originally consisted of two towns, Clausthal and Zellerfeld, which were merged in 1924 into one administrative unit. Mining in the area began in the 16th century. The German mining engineer Wilhelm Albert invented modern wire rope between 1831 and 1834 for use in the Harz mines at Clausthal. It proved superior to ropes of hemp or metal chains and soon found wide application, notably in suspension bridges. The Clausthal mint operated from 1617 to 1849. A railway, the Innerste Valley Railway, was opened in 1877 and extended to Altenau in 1914, and it closed in 1976.

The Clausthal University of Technology was established in 1775 to educate mining engineers. An air raid on 7 October 1944 destroyed the large station building and 70 other buildings, and 92 people died. Mining halted in 1930 because the ore deposits were exhausted.

The university is now a technical university teaching engineering, natural science, computer science and business studies, and it is of great importance to the town. The rebuilt station of 1961 to 1963 houses the tourist information and the municipal library. Among the surviving buildings are the Market Church in Clausthal, begun in 1639, which is the largest wooden church in Germany with 2,200 seats, the Bergapotheke of 1674 in Zellerfeld, the Salvator Church, also begun in 1674, and the Oberbergamt building. The microbiologist Robert Koch was born in the town, and the Upper Harz Mining Museum and the university's GeoMuseum are open to visitors.
cleisthenes: Historians estimate that Cleisthenes was born around 570 BCE. He belonged to the aristocratic Alcmaeonid clan and was the younger son of Megacles and Agariste, which made him the maternal grandson of the tyrant Cleisthenes of Sicyon. When Pisistratus took power in Athens as a tyrant, he exiled his opponents and the Alcmaeonidae. After Pisistratus died in 527 BCE, Cleisthenes returned and became the eponymous archon, but Pisistratus's successors Hipparchus and Hippias exiled him again. He then turned to the Oracle of Delphi, which accepted his plea for help against the tyranny because his family had earlier helped rebuild the sanctuary after a fire.

With Spartan help and the support of his clan, Cleisthenes took part in overthrowing Hippias in 510 BCE. He then rivalled Isagoras, who gained the upper hand by appealing to the Spartan king Cleomenes I, and Cleisthenes went into exile. Isagoras tried to dissolve the Boule, the council of citizens that ran the city's daily affairs. The council resisted and the people backed it. Isagoras and his partisans were besieged on the Acropolis and left the city on the third day. Cleisthenes and the exiles were recalled, and he took the lead in Athens.

He replaced the four traditional tribes, based on family ties, with ten tribes drawn from residence in demes. The demes, perhaps 139 in number though this is debated, were grouped in thirds called trittyes, one each from the city, coastal and inland regions. He had citizens named by their deme rather than by their father's name, and he reorganised the Boule from 400 members to 500, fifty from each tribe. Appointment to office by lot is also credited to him. Cleisthenes called his reforms isonomia, equality before the law, rather than demokratia.

Cleisthenes may also have introduced ostracism, first used in 487 BCE, by which a vote of at least 6,000 citizens could exile a man for ten years. In 507 BCE, probably at his instigation, Athens sent envoys to Artaphernes, the Persian satrap at Sardis, seeking help against Sparta. According to Herodotus, the envoys agreed to give earth and water as a sign of submission and were censured on their return. No ancient text mentions Cleisthenes after his reforms, and his later life is unknown. Historians call him the father of Athenian democracy.
clemens-brentano: Clemens Brentano was born on 9 September 1778 into a wealthy merchant family in Frankfurt, the son of Peter Anton Brentano and Maximiliane von La Roche. His maternal grandmother was the writer Sophie von La Roche, and his sister Bettina von Arnim corresponded with Goethe as a young girl and published the letters in 1835. He studied in Halle and Jena and lived afterwards at Heidelberg, Vienna and Berlin. He was close to Wieland, Herder, Goethe, Friedrich Schlegel, Fichte and Tieck.

From 1798 to 1800 he lived in Jena, the first centre of the Romantic movement, and in 1801 he moved to Göttingen, where he befriended Achim von Arnim. In 1804 he moved to Heidelberg and worked with Arnim on Des Knaben Wunderhorn, a collection of folk songs published from 1805 to 1808 on which Gustav Mahler later drew. In 1818 he returned to the practice of the Catholic faith and withdrew to Dülmen, where he became secretary to the visionary nun Anne Catherine Emmerich, copying her dictation until her death in 1824.

He then prepared an index of her visions, The Dolorous Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, published in 1833. Investigations in 1923 and 1928 made it uncertain how much of the books he attributed to her was his own creation. He spent his later years in Regensburg, Frankfurt and Munich, promoting the Catholic faith.

Brentano belonged to the Heidelberg group of German Romantic writers, and his works are marked by fantastic imagery and abrupt, bizarre modes of expression. His first publications were Satiren und poetische Spiele (1800) and the romance Godwi (1801). His finest work is generally held to be the Romanzen vom Rosenkranz, published posthumously in 1852, and his short story Geschichte vom braven Kasperl und dem schönen Annerl (1817) was very popular. His collected works, edited by his brother Christian, appeared in nine volumes from 1851 to 1855. He died in Aschaffenburg.
clement-attlee: Clement Richard Attlee was born on 3 January 1883 at Putney, then in Surrey, the seventh of eight children of Henry Attlee, a solicitor, and Ellen Bravery Watson. He attended Haileybury College and the University of Oxford and became a barrister. From 1906 he volunteered at Haileybury House, a charitable club for working-class boys in Stepney. The poverty he saw there convinced him that only direct action by the state would help, and he joined the Independent Labour Party in 1908. He served in the First World War in the South Lancashire Regiment at Gallipoli, became mayor of Stepney in 1919 and was elected Member of Parliament for Limehouse in 1922.

Attlee was Under-Secretary of State for War in the first Labour government of 1924. At the 1931 election Labour lost over 200 seats, and he kept Limehouse by 551 votes and became deputy to George Lansbury. When Lansbury resigned on 8 October 1935, Attlee became interim leader and then leader. He took Labour into Winston Churchill's coalition in May 1940, as Lord Privy Seal and from 1942 as deputy prime minister.

Labour won a landslide at the 1945 election. The government aimed to maintain full employment, a mixed economy and an enlarged system of social services. It nationalised public utilities and major industries, passed the National Insurance Act 1946 and the National Assistance Act 1948, and formed the National Health Service in 1948. It oversaw the partition of India in 1947, the independence of Burma and Ceylon and the end of the British mandate in Palestine, and Attlee and Ernest Bevin supported the Marshall Plan and in 1949 promoted NATO. Shortages of food, housing and resources persisted, and the 1950 election cut Labour's majority to five seats. The Conservatives took power in 1951, although Labour won the most votes.

Attlee stayed on as leader until 1955, in years marked by quarrels between Hugh Gaitskell's right wing and Aneurin Bevan's left. He then became Earl Attlee. In 1958 he helped to found the Homosexual Law Reform Society. He died on 8 October 1967 at Westminster Hospital, and his ashes were buried at Westminster Abbey. He remains the longest-serving Labour leader.
clement-of-alexandria: Titus Flavius Clemens, known as Clement of Alexandria, was born to pagan parents, and neither his birthdate nor his birthplace is certain. Epiphanius of Salamis says Athens, but there is also a tradition of an Alexandrian birth. He rejected paganism as a young man because of its perceived moral corruption and travelled in Greece, Asia Minor, Palestine and Egypt, a journey that was mainly religious. He met an Ionian theologian in Greece, identified as Athenagoras of Athens, and in the east he was taught by an Assyrian, sometimes identified with Tatian, and by a Jew, possibly Theophilus of Caesarea.

Around 180 he reached Alexandria and met Pantaenus, who taught at the Catechetical School. Clement studied under him and was ordained to the priesthood by Pope Julian before 189. Little else is known of his life in Alexandria.

Three major works survive in full, as a trilogy: the Protrepticus, an exhortation to the Greeks to adopt Christianity, written around 195; the Paedagogus, or Tutor, written around 198; and the Stromata, or Miscellanies, written between about 198 and 203. His Salvation for the Rich, written around 203, argues that Jesus's words about the rich are not to be taken literally and that wealth is not wrong in itself if it is used charitably.

Clement was influenced by Hellenistic philosophy, especially Plato and the Stoics, more than any other Christian thinker of his time. He held that philosophy was a preparation for Christianity among the Greeks and sought to harmonize its insights with biblical teaching. Faith, in his view, was the basis of salvation and of gnosis, spiritual knowledge, a word he took from the Gnostics he opposed. He is often regarded as one of the first Christian universalists.

Clement died around 215. Eusebius gave the first account of his life and works, and Jerome called him the most learned of men. He is usually regarded as a Church Father and is venerated as a saint in Coptic Christianity, Eastern Catholicism, Ethiopian Christianity and Anglicanism. In the West he was revered until his name was removed from the Roman Martyrology in 1586 on the advice of Baronius.
cleopatra-selene-ii: Cleopatra Selene was raised and educated in Alexandria as a Ptolemaic princess. Her second name means "moon" in Greek, matching that of her twin Alexander Helios, "sun". Mark Antony acknowledged the twins in 37 BCE, and in 34 BCE, at the Donations of Alexandria, he bestowed kingdoms on the children before huge crowds. Selene was made ruler of Cyrenaica and Libya, though she was too young to rule.

After the defeat at Actium in 31 BCE her parents sent the children away, but Roman soldiers captured them on the road to Thebes, and their parents killed themselves as Octavian invaded Egypt. Octavian paraded the twins in his triumph in golden chains so heavy that they could not walk in them, which drew sympathy from onlookers.
