Augustus gave them to his sister Octavia to be raised on the Palatine Hill. Selene is the only known surviving member of the Ptolemaic dynasty, and her brothers are not recorded again.

Octavia arranged her marriage to Juba II, a learned prince raised in Octavian's household. It likely took place in 25 BCE, when Augustus made the couple co-rulers of the client kingdom of Mauretania, and they renamed their capital Caesarea, now Cherchell in Algeria, in the emperor's honour. Selene is said to have had great influence on Juba's policies. She brought scholars and artists from Alexandria, introduced the cult of Isis to Caesarea and imported sculptures from Egypt.

The kingdom exported fish, grapes, pearls, figs, grain, wooden furniture and a purple dye from shellfish to Spain and Italy. Selene minted coins in her own name as Queen Cleopatra, and the couple also issued a joint coinage. Building at Caesarea and Volubilis mixed Egyptian, Greek and Roman styles and included a lighthouse like the Pharos of Alexandria and a seafront palace.

The couple had a son, Ptolemy of Mauretania, born in 10 BCE and named for her dynasty and her younger brother, who succeeded Juba, and probably a daughter whose name has not survived. Selene's death is placed about 5 BCE, and the country became extremely wealthy during the couple's reign.
cleopatra-vii: Cleopatra VII was born in Alexandria in early 69 BCE, the daughter of Ptolemy XII Auletes and an uncertain mother, presumably his wife Cleopatra V Tryphaena. She belonged to the Macedonian Greek Ptolemaic dynasty, descended from Ptolemy I Soter, a general and companion of Alexander the Great. Earlier Ptolemaic rulers refused to learn Egyptian; she was the first known to have done so, and Plutarch implies that she spoke several other languages as well.

Her father tried to ward off Roman annexation by lavish gifts to statesmen such as Pompey and Julius Caesar, which bankrupted him, and in 58 BCE he was exiled from Egypt. Before he died, some time before 22 March 51 BCE, he named her his heir.

Cleopatra began to reign alongside her brother Ptolemy XIII. Her first act as queen was installing a sacred Buchis bull at Hermonthis, and she faced famine caused by drought and a low Nile flood. A falling-out with her brother led to civil war. When Pompey fled to Egypt after losing at Pharsalus in 48 BCE, Ptolemy XIII had him ambushed and killed, and Caesar then occupied Alexandria and was besieged with Cleopatra in the palace. After Ptolemy XIII drowned in the Nile, Caesar made Cleopatra and her brother Ptolemy XIV joint rulers; her son Caesarion was born of her affair with Caesar. After Caesar's assassination she named Caesarion co-ruler.

In the civil war of 43–42 BCE she sided with the Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Mark Antony and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. After meeting Antony at Tarsos in 41 BCE she had three children with him, and he came to rely on her for funds and military aid. The Donations of Alexandria declared their children rulers of territories under his authority, and Octavian presented this as treason and declared war on Cleopatra. She ruled as an absolute monarch and chief religious authority.

After Octavian defeated the fleet of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE, his forces invaded Egypt in 30 BCE and Antony killed himself. Cleopatra reportedly killed herself too, probably by poison, to avoid being paraded in a Roman triumph. Her three surviving children were sent to Rome in the care of Octavian's sister Octavia.

Plutarch's Life of Antonius gives the fullest surviving account and draws on eyewitness sources as well as the Augustan view. Roman historiography and Latin poetry produced a generally critical view of the queen that shaped medieval and Renaissance literature.
clermont-ferrand: Clermont-Ferrand lies on the plain of Limagne in the Massif Central, surrounded by the chain of volcanoes called the Chaîne des Puys, which includes the dormant Puy de Dôme, 10 kilometres away. The mountains put the city in a rain shadow, so it has one of the driest climates in metropolitan France outside the Mediterranean coast, with cold winters and hot summers. The old part of Clermont follows the line of the ramparts as they stood at the end of the Middle Ages, and the city's cathedral is built of black lava stone.

The first known mention is by Strabo, who called it the metropolis of the Arverni, then named Nemessos, a Gaulish word for a sacred forest, on the mound where the cathedral now stands. Vercingetorix was born somewhere near it around 72 BCE and repulsed the Roman assault at Gergovia in 52 BCE. After the Roman conquest it was Augustonemetum, Latin for sanctuary of Augustus. It became a bishop's seat in the 5th century under Namatius, and the emperor Julius Nepos ceded it to the Visigoths in 475. The Franks took it a generation after the Visigoths lost it in 507. Vikings ravaged it in 862 and 864 and again around 898.

The castle of Clarus Mons gave its name to the town in 848. Pope Urban II called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095. In 1120 the counts of Auvergne founded the rival town of Montferrand next to Clermont's walls to counter the bishops' power. Clermont became a royal town in 1551, and the Edict of Troyes of 1630 joined the two towns, confirmed in 1731 by Louis XV. Montferrand demanded independence three times, in 1789, 1848 and 1863.

The Michelin factories and the city gardens built in the 20th century united the two towns, though two distinct downtowns survive and Montferrand keeps a strong identity. Clermont-Ferrand is the prefecture of Puy-de-Dôme and had a population of 146,351 in 2023. It is the headquarters of Michelin and hosts an international short film festival. Its Romanesque church of Notre-Dame du Port was nominated as a World Heritage Site in 1998, and the cathedral, in Gothic style, was built between the 13th and 19th centuries.
clodius-albinus: Albinus was born at Hadrumetum in the province of Africa, to an aristocratic Roman family. The unreliable Historia Augusta gives his parents' names, which modern historians doubt. He entered the army young and served with distinction, especially in 175 during the rebellion of Avidius Cassius against Marcus Aurelius, who is said to have written that without Albinus the legions in Bithynia would have gone over to Cassius and that he intended to have him made consul.

Commodus gave Albinus commands in Gallia Belgica and then in Britain. When a false rumour spread that Commodus had died, Albinus denounced him before his soldiers as a tyrant and argued that the Empire would benefit from restoring the Senate's ancient dignity and power. The Senate was pleased, the emperor was not, and he sent Junius Severus to relieve Albinus of his command. Albinus kept it until after the murders of Commodus and Pertinax in 193.

In the Year of the Five Emperors the legions in Syria proclaimed Pescennius Niger, those in Illyricum and Pannonia proclaimed Septimius Severus, and the armies in Britain and Gaul proclaimed Albinus. Albinus first allied with Severus, who had taken Rome. He added the name Septimius to his own, accepted the title of Caesar. With three British legions and one Spanish, he remained effective ruler of much of the western Empire. After Severus defeated and killed Niger in 194 and took Byzantium in 196, he resolved to be absolute master of the Empire.

In autumn 196 Albinus heard that Severus had named his elder son Caracalla as successor with the title of Caesar and had persuaded the Senate to declare Albinus an enemy of Rome. He proclaimed himself emperor, crossed from Britain to Gaul with a large part of the British garrison and defeated Severus's legate Virius Lupus. He made Lugdunum his headquarters, but he could not win over the Rhine legions.

On 19 February 197 Albinus met the army of Severus at the Battle of Lugdunum, where according to Cassius Dio 150,000 troops stood on each side. Albinus was defeated and died. Severus had the naked body laid out so that he could ride his horse over it. Albinus's wife and two sons were at first pardoned and then beheaded, and their bodies and his headless body were thrown into the Rhône. Severus sent the head to Rome with a letter mocking the Senate for its loyalty to Albinus. Lugdunum was plundered, and Albinus's adherents were persecuted.
cloves: Cloves are the aromatic flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum, an evergreen tree of the family Myrtaceae that grows up to 8 to 12 metres tall, with large leaves and crimson flowers grouped in terminal clusters. The buds are pale at first, turn green and then bright red when ready for harvest, and are picked at 1.5 to 2 centimetres in length. The tree is native to the Maluku Islands, or Moluccas, in Indonesia. The word clove first appears in English in the 15th century and derives, through Old French clou de girofle, from the Latin clavus, meaning nail. A major component of the taste is the chemical eugenol, which makes up 72 to 90 per cent of the essential oil.

Until the colonial era cloves grew only on a few islands in the Moluccas, historically called the Spice Islands, among them Bacan, Makian, Moti, Ternate and Tidore. They were first traded by the Austronesian peoples in their maritime trade network, which began around 1500 BCE and later became the Maritime Silk Road and part of the Spice Trade. The archaeologist Giorgio Buccellati found cloves at Terqa in Syria, in a burned house dated to 1720 BCE, the first evidence of their use in the west before Roman times. They reached Rome by the first century CE.

A Chinese book of about 200 BCE, the Han Guan Yi, says that ministers should suck cloves to sweeten their breath before speaking to the emperor. During the Song dynasty private ventures imported cloves from Austronesian polities such as Java, Srivijaya, Champa and Butuan, and during the Yuan dynasty Chinese merchants began sending ships directly to the Moluccas. Some early mentions of cloves in China, South Asia and the Middle East from before Southeast Asian maritime trade are thought to be misidentifications of other plants such as cassia buds, cinnamon or nutmeg.

Cloves flavour meats, curries, marinades, fruit and hot drinks, and are common in spice blends such as the Malay rempah empat beradik. They are added to betel quids, and in Indonesia they are used in a type of cigarette called kretek. Clove oil is used in traditional medicine as an anodyne, chiefly for dental emergencies. In Europe cloves were used in burial and embalming practices from the late Middle Ages. The earliest known macro-botanical cloves in northwest Europe come from the wreck of the Danish-Norwegian flagship Gribshunden, which sank in June 1495.

In the 17th century the Dutch East India Company sought a monopoly in cloves as it had in nutmeg. In 1770, on the instruction of Pierre Poivre, seedlings of an old tree on Ternate were taken to the Isle de France, now Mauritius, and the Seychelles, and later spread to Martinique and Saint-Domingue. Indonesia is today the largest producer.
clovis-i: Clovis was the son of Childeric I, a king of the Salian Franks, and Basina, a Thuringian princess. The dynasty he founded is named after his supposed grandfather Merovech. Historians believe that Childeric and Clovis were both commanders of the Roman military in the province of Belgica Secunda. Childeric died in 481 and Clovis succeeded him, aged fifteen. Imperial power in Gaul had declined since the death of Aetius in 454, and the lands held by Syagrius, son of Aegidius, formed the Kingdom of Soissons.

In 486 Clovis allied with his relative Ragnachar of Cambrai and another Frankish king, Chararic, and defeated Syagrius at Soissons, ending the last remnant of the Western Roman Empire outside Italy. Clovis made Paris his capital and married Clotilde, a Burgundian Catholic princess, to win the clergy's support. In 496 he narrowly defeated the Alamanni at Tolbiac. In 507 he defeated the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse at Vouillé, where King Alaric II died.

Clovis was born a pagan. Clotilde persuaded him to accept Catholic Christianity, and he was baptised on Christmas Day near the later abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims; scholars debate the year. After Vouillé he removed the other Frankish kings, among them Chararic and Ragnachar. Under him Salian Frankish law was first written down.

Shortly before his death Clovis called the First Council of Orléans, which passed decrees establishing equality between Franks and Romans. He died in 511 and was buried at the Abbey of Saint Genevieve in Paris. His kingdom was divided among his four sons, a practice that led to disunity until the Merovingian dynasty ended in 751. Many French people regard him as the founder of the French state. In later centuries he was venerated as a saint in France, though never formally canonised.
cluny-abbey: William I, Duke of Aquitaine, founded the abbey in 910 on a modest scale as the motherhouse of the Congregation of Cluny and chose as its first abbot Berno, abbot of Baume and of Gigny. The deed of gift stipulated that the monastery would be free from local authorities, lay or ecclesiastical, and subject only to the pope, who could not appoint an abbot without the consent of the monks. William gave up his hunting preserve in Burgundy and released the abbey from all obligations to him and his family other than prayer, whereas patrons normally kept a proprietary interest and installed their kinsmen as abbots.

Odo, abbot from 926, travelled from monastery to monastery to consolidate the reform, and in 931 obtained the right to reform other abbeys. Majolus directed Cluny from 954 until 994 and was nicknamed the arbiter of kings. Odilo, abbot for 55 years from 994, supported the Peace and Truce of God, and at his death the order had 70 houses. Under Hugh of Semur, abbot from 1049, it extended into Spain, Italy and England and numbered 10,000 monks.

Cluny III was financed largely by the annual payment set by Ferdinand I of León, which Alfonso VI doubled in 1090. When payments in gold later lapsed, the Order fell into a financial crisis. The foundation of the more austere Cîteaux Abbey in 1098 challenged Cluny's supremacy, and the Cistercians and the Mendicants later weakened its standing. With the Concordat of Bologna in 1516 the king of France gained the power to appoint the abbot. The order was suppressed in France in 1790, the library and archives were burned in 1793, and the monastery was mostly demolished in 1810.

Cluny created a highly centralised federated order, foreign to Benedictine tradition, in which the heads of subsidiary houses, styled priors, answered to the abbot of Cluny and met at Cluny once a year. By the twelfth century 314 monasteries paid allegiance to it. Its central work was the liturgy: monks recited 138 psalms each day, rising to 215 in Lent, and hired workers did the labour that monks had traditionally done.

Cluny was not known for the severity of its discipline, and its monks ate well and used silver candelabras and gold chalices set with gems. Four monks of Cluny became popes: Gregory VII, Urban II, Paschal II and Urban V. Little remains of the buildings, only about 10 per cent of the floor space of Cluny III.
cnut-the-great: Cnut was a son of Swein Forkbeard and came from a line of Scandinavian rulers central to the unification of Denmark. His grandfather Harald Bluetooth was king at the time of the Christianization of Denmark. Neither the place nor the date of his birth is known. He was already a Christian before he was king, and was named Lambert at his baptism. In September 1015 he landed at Sandwich, sailed round Kent to Wessex and harried Dorset, Wiltshire and Somerset, beginning a campaign of an intensity not seen since the days of Alfred the Great.

On 18 October 1016 Cnut's army defeated Edmund Ironside's at the Battle of Assandun in Essex, where Eadric Streona withdrew his forces and brought about a decisive English defeat. Cnut ruled England for nearly two decades. He quickly eliminated possible challengers from the Wessex dynasty: Eadwig Ætheling was killed on his orders, and Edmund Ironside's sons fled abroad. In July 1017 he married Queen Emma, widow of Æthelred. In 1018 he collected a Danegeld of £72,000, with another £10,500 from London, paid off his army and kept 40 ships as a standing force.

When Harald II died in 1018, Cnut went to Denmark to secure the throne. At Easter 1027 he attended the coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor Conrad II in Rome, where he sought lower costs for the pallium of English archbishops and better conditions for pilgrims. On the way back he wrote that he was king of all England and Denmark and the Norwegians and of some of the Swedes. He claimed the crown of Norway at Trondheim in 1028. He repaired churches and monasteries that Viking raids had plundered and was a patron of monastic communities, though his marriage to Emma while he was married to Ælfgifu of Northampton conflicted with Church teaching.

Cnut died on 12 November 1035 at Shaftesbury in Dorset and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. His son Harthacnut succeeded him in Denmark, while Harold Harefoot, his son by Ælfgifu, became regent in England and claimed the throne in 1037. The medieval historian Norman Cantor called Cnut the most effective king in Anglo-Saxon history. Henry of Huntingdon, in the early twelfth century, first recorded the story of Cnut commanding the tide not to wet him, which has become the best-known story about him. In modern readings he is usually a wise man who knew from the start that he could not control the waves.
coahuila: Coahuila borders Nuevo León to the east, Zacatecas to the south and Durango and Chihuahua to the west. To the north it holds a 512 km stretch of the border with the United States, along the Rio Grande opposite Texas. With an area of 151,563 km2 it is the third-largest state in Mexico. The Sierra Madre Oriental crosses it from north-west to south-east, and west of the range the land lies in the Chihuahuan Desert. The state is largely arid or semi-arid, but its rivers support irrigated farming, especially of cotton, and the Parras district produces wine and brandy.

The Spanish explored the north some decades after their victory over the Aztecs, and the harsher climate and the absence of gold delayed them. The first Spanish settlement in the region was at Minas de la Trinidad in 1577, and Saltillo was settled in 1586 as part of the province of Nueva Vizcaya in New Spain. Tlaxcalan settlers founded a community beside Saltillo, San Esteban de Nueva Tlaxcala.

Under the Constitution of 1824 Coahuila y Tejas became a state of independent Mexico, first with Nuevo León, which was detached later that year, and with Texas, which stayed until it seceded in 1836. Monclova was the capital from 1833 to 1835. In 1840 Coahuila was briefly part of the Republic of the Rio Grande. In the mid-19th century the Sánchez Navarro family owned a ranch of 6,700,000 hectares, mostly in Coahuila, the largest privately owned property in the Americas, and Comanche raiders attacked the state often in the 1840s and 1850s. On 19 February 1856 Santiago Vidaurri annexed Coahuila to Nuevo León, and it regained separate status in 1868. In the Mexican Revolution Francisco Villa attacked Torreón.

Coahuila de Zaragoza, named for General Ignacio Zaragoza, who was born there, is one of the 31 states of Mexico. Its capital is Saltillo, and its other main cities are Torreón, Monclova, Piedras Negras and Ciudad Acuña. The state has two biosphere reserves, Maderas del Carmen and the Cuatro Ciénegas Basin. Venustiano Carranza and Francisco I. Madero, both presidents of Mexico, came from Coahuila.
coal: The word coal took the form col in Old English, from a reconstructed Proto-Germanic root meaning live coal, and has cognates in Old Norse kol, Dutch kool and German Kohle. The oldest intentional use of black coal documented is at Ostrava, Petřkovice, in an Old Stone Age settlement on the top of Landek Hill. Radiocarbon dating places the site between 25,000 and 23,000 BCE. Coal has been known and used for thousands of years, but its use was limited until the Industrial Revolution, and with the invention of the steam engine consumption increased.

Coal is a combustible black or brownish-black sedimentary rock that forms in layers called coal seams. It is mostly carbon, with variable amounts of hydrogen, sulfur, oxygen and nitrogen. It formed when plants decayed into peat, which the heat and pressure of deep burial over millions of years converted into coal. Vast deposits formed from wetlands, the coal forests that covered much of the tropics during the late Carboniferous and early Permian. The process is called coalification: dead plant matter was protected from oxidation, usually by mud or acidic water, and became peat, which was then buried by sediments and lost water, methane and carbon dioxide, so that its proportion of carbon rose.

The grade of coal depends on the maximum pressure and temperature reached. Lignite, or brown coal, forms under relatively mild conditions and is the lowest rank. Sub-bituminous coal, bituminous coal and anthracite follow with increasing temperature and pressure. Bituminous coal is the more abundant of the two main black coals, and anthracite has the highest percentage of carbon; some anthracite deposits contain pure carbon in the form of graphite.

Most coal is used as fuel. Bituminous coal, known as steam coal in the UK, was historically used to raise steam in locomotives and ships, and coal later fired power stations, where it is burned in a furnace to make the steam that turns turbines. Coke is made by baking metallurgical coal in an oven without oxygen at temperatures as high as 1,000 °C, and it serves in blast furnaces as a fuel and as the agent that reduces iron ore to iron.

Chemicals have been made from coal since the 1940s, mainly by gasification to produce syngas, from which methanol, hydrogen, ammonia, urea and many other products derive. Coal can also be converted into synthetic fuels equivalent to gasoline or diesel; the chemical company Sasol of South Africa used gasification combined with the Fischer–Tropsch process to make chemicals and motor fuels from coal. The deadly London smog was caused chiefly by the heavy use of coal.
coburg: Coburg lies on the River Itz at the foot of the Thuringian Highlands, about 90 kilometres south of Erfurt and 100 kilometres north of Nuremberg. During the Cold War, as part of West Germany, it bordered East German Thuringia on three sides. The origin of the name is unclear; the first element may be the German kuh, cow, giving a literal meaning of cow borough.

Coburg was first mentioned in a monastic document of 1056, although a settlement called Trufalistat already stood there. The name at first referred to a property centred on the hill where Veste Coburg was later built. The castle passed to the House of Henneberg in 1248 and to the House of Wettin in 1353. During the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 Martin Luther spent six months there, since his lord John, Elector of Saxony, feared he would be imprisoned and burned as a heretic if he attended, and he continued his translation of the Bible into German. In 1547 the princely residence moved to the Ehrenburg, a former monastery rebuilt as a Renaissance palace.

Coburg became capital of the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg in 1596 and of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha from 1826 to 1918. Dynastic marriages tied the ducal family to the royal houses of Belgium, Bulgaria, Portugal and Britain. Leopold of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld became King of Belgium in 1831, and Prince Albert married Queen Victoria in 1840. The last duke, Charles Edward, abdicated in November 1918. The Free State of Coburg then voted by an 88 per cent majority to join Bavaria rather than Thuringia, and the merger took place on 1 July 1920.

Coburg is in Upper Franconia, Bavaria, with a population close to 41,500. It was not much damaged in the Second World War and keeps many historic buildings. Veste Coburg is one of Germany's largest castles, and its museum includes the collection of copperplate engravings begun by the duke in the early 19th century.
cockburn-town: Cockburn Town stands on Grand Turk, the largest island in the Turks Islands archipelago, and spreads across most of it. Historic Bermudian architecture of the 18th and 19th centuries lines Duke and Front Streets, and the town is known for its long, narrow streets and old street lamps. The nearest anchorage is Hawk's Nest Anchorage, which is sheltered but should be entered only in good light because of reefs near the entrance.

Cockburn Town was the first permanent settlement on any of the islands, founded in 1681 by salt collectors. It is supposed to lie where Juan Ponce de León first landed on the island. It has been the seat of government ever since 1766, and it is named for Francis Cockburn, a former Governor of the Bahamas. It reportedly has ties to the Burrowes family, whose proclivity aided the naming of the town.

Her Majesty's Prison on Pond Street was built in the 1830s and stayed in operation until 1994. It has a main cell block, offices for prison officials and a bell tower, and today it hosts its own museum.

Cockburn Town is the capital of the Turks and Caicos Islands. The Turks & Caicos National Museum is in Guinep House on Front Street, a colonial-era house believed to be over 180 years old, built largely from the timber of local shipwrecks, including a ship's mast that is one of its main supports. The museum's collections include the Molasses Reef Wreck, dated 1505, the oldest known European shipwreck in the Americas, and exhibits on the Lucayans, slavery and the slave trade, and the sisal and salt industries.
code-of-hammurabi: The Code is a Babylonian legal text in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian, purportedly by Hammurabi, sixth king of the Amorite First Dynasty of Babylon, who ruled from around 1792 to around 1750 BCE by the middle chronology. When he inherited the throne Babylon held little sway, and the local power was Rim-Sin of Larsa. Hammurabi conquered his territory in one campaign. His letters suggest an interest in law and justice, and he often calls himself his people's shepherd. The Code was not the first Mesopotamian law collection: the Code of Ur-Nammu, the Code of Lipit-Ishtar and the Laws of Eshnunna are earlier, and they too claim a ruler as author.

The main copy is a basalt stele 2.25 m tall, with a relief at the top of Hammurabi with Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. Below are about 4,130 lines of cuneiform, one fifth a poetic prologue and epilogue and four fifths the laws. In the prologue Hammurabi says the gods chose him to rule in order to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak. The laws are conditional sentences, if one thing happens then another follows, and cover criminal, family, property and commercial law, including rules on medical treatment. They apply the principle of lex talionis: law 196 prescribes an eye for an eye, and law 229 requires the death of a builder whose house collapses and kills its owner.

Nobles had greater protection than commoners and enslaved people. Scholars dispute what the text was. Some treat it as legislation, others as a law report of past cases, and others as an abstract work of jurisprudence, a view that has gained support among Assyriologists.

The stele was found in 1901 at Susa in present-day Iran, where it had been taken as plunder about 600 years after it was made. It was found in three large fragments and now stands in the Louvre. Seven columns near the bottom were polished away in antiquity, but over 50 manuscripts of the laws are known, from Susa, Babylon, Nineveh, Assur and other sites, and they fill in most of the erased text. Scribes copied the text for over a millennium. Father Jean-Vincent Scheil published the first edition in 1902, and editions in German, English and Italian followed. Scholars compared its provisions with the Mosaic Law, but the consensus is that the similarities come from shared traditions and not direct borrowing.
codex: The word codex comes from the Latin caudex, meaning a trunk of a tree, a block of wood or a book. The Romans used reusable wax-covered wooden tablets for notes, and two polyptychs excavated at Herculaneum used a connecting system that anticipates the later sewing of leaves with thongs or cords. Around the turn of the 1st century CE a folded parchment notebook called pugillares membranei became common in the Roman Empire.

Martial described three of the books he sent as Saturnalia gifts as codices, praising their compactness and their convenience on a journey. In another poem he advertised an edition of his works as a codex that took less space than a scroll and was easier to hold in one hand.

A codex is a stack of pages bound at one edge. Sheets of papyrus or parchment were folded, gathered into quires, most often of four folded sheets making sixteen pages, and sewn through the fold, so that both sides of each leaf could be used. Scribes pricked the parchment and ruled lines to guide the text.

The form was compact and sturdy and allowed a reader to turn to any page at once, where a scroll had to be read in sequence. Used parchment could be scraped and written on again, producing a palimpsest in which the older text can often be recovered.

There is evidence that by the early 2nd century a codex, usually of papyrus, was the preferred format among Christians. Whether they led its development, or adopted it to distinguish themselves from Jews, cannot be settled from the evidence. The earliest surviving fragments come from Egypt and include the Rylands Library Papyrus P52, containing part of the Gospel of John, perhaps from between 125 and 160.

The codex reached numerical parity with the scroll around 300 CE and had replaced it by the 6th century. Many works not copied from scroll to codex between the 4th century and the 8th were lost. Maya and Aztec codices were long strips folded like a concertina, and in China folded-leaf books developed from the 9th century. Judaism still keeps the Torah scroll for ceremonial use.
coimbra: Coimbra stands on a hill beside the Mondego River in central Portugal. It lay historically at a junction between Braga and Lisbon, and the river gave a route between the interior and coastal towns such as Figueira da Foz, 40 km to the west. Lisbon is 197 km and Porto 116 km away.

In Roman times the city was Aeminium. The Romans founded its civitas at the time of Augustus, and it came under the protection of nearby Conímbriga. Its walls followed an orthogonal plan, with the main streets crossing at the forum, and it had an aqueduct. When the Sueves and Visigoths sacked Conímbriga in the 460s and it was abandoned, Aeminium became the seat of the bishopric in its place. Coimbra capitulated to the Muslim commander Musa bin Nusair in 714, and as Qulumriyah in Al-Andalus it was the largest settlement along the northern Tagus valley, with a walled enclosure of 10 hectares and between 3,000 and 5,000 inhabitants.

Ferdinand I of León and Castile reconquered it in 1064. In 1096 Alfonso VI placed the counties of Portucale and Coimbra under Henry of Burgundy, who married his daughter Theresa. Their son Afonso Henriques made his home at Coimbra. The city was the capital of Portugal from 1131 to 1255, and Afonso Henriques and Sancho I are buried in the Santa Cruz Monastery.

After it lost its political role Coimbra became a cultural centre, and the first Portuguese university, founded at Lisbon in 1290, is the oldest academic institution in the Portuguese-speaking world. In the 15th and 16th centuries Manuel I and the local bishops patronised artists who left Manueline and Renaissance works. In 1772 the Marquis of Pombal reformed the university and strengthened the sciences, but his plans led to the demolition of the medieval walls and castle.

Coimbra is the largest city of its district and of Portugal's Central Region. UNESCO classified the university's historical buildings as a World Heritage site in 2013. The old and new cathedrals, the Roman aqueduct and cryptoporticus survive, and Coimbra fado is a distinct form of the music that grew there.
colchester: Colchester lies on the River Colne in north-eastern Essex, about 80 kilometres north-east of London. The gravel hill on which it stands was formed in the Middle Pleistocene, and Palaeolithic flint tools, including at least six Acheulian handaxes, have been found there, along with Mesolithic tools and many sherds of Neolithic, Bronze Age and early Iron Age pottery. It is surrounded by Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments, among them a henge at Tendring and large barrow cemeteries at Dedham, Langham and Brightlingsea.

Colchester is said to be the oldest recorded town in Britain because Pliny the Elder, who died in 79, mentioned it. Its Celtic name, Camulodunon, meaning the fortress of the war god Camulos, appears on coins minted by the chieftain Tasciovanus in 20–10 BCE. Before the Roman conquest it was a centre of power for Cunobelin, king of the Catuvellauni, known to Shakespeare as Cymbeline, who minted coins there. Roman writers called him king of the Britons.

Soon after the conquest of 43 a legionary fortress, the first in Britain, was set up there. When the twentieth legion moved west around 49, Camulodunum became a colonia, named in a second-century inscription as Colonia Victricensis. It had a large Temple to the Divine Claudius, the largest classical-style temple in Britain. Tacitus describes how the settlement of ex-soldiers was burned in the Iceni rebellion. Its walls, built between 65 and 80, shortly after Boudicca destroyed the undefended colonia, stayed in use until after the Siege of Colchester in 1648. The Balkerne Gate is the earliest and most complete Roman gateway in the United Kingdom.

Colchester Castle, an 11th-century Norman keep, was built on the vaults of the old Roman temple. In 1648, during the Second English Civil War, a Royalist army under Lord Goring was surrounded by Thomas Fairfax and Henry Ireton for eleven and a half weeks from 13 June. After the surrender on 27 August, Charles Lucas and George Lisle were executed in the castle grounds.

Colchester has been an important military base since Roman times. The Castle Museum has an extensive exhibit on Roman Colchester, and the town also has the ruins of St Botolph's Priory and the gateway of St John's Abbey. Colchester claims to be Britain's first city, as the site of Camulodunum, the first major city and first capital of Roman Britain.
cold-war: Animosity between the Allies of the Second World War predated its end. After the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt in April 1945, the administration of Harry Truman took a harder line, and diplomats disputed how to read the Yalta agreements, the composition of the Polish government and the running of the United Nations. In February 1946 George F. Kennan's Long Telegram from Moscow helped shape American strategy, and on 5 March Winston Churchill gave his Iron Curtain speech at Fulton. The term itself was used by George Orwell in 1945 and applied to the confrontation by Bernard Baruch on 16 April 1947.

The United States declared the Truman Doctrine of containment in 1947, launched the Marshall Plan in 1948 and founded NATO in 1949; the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact followed in 1955. Early confrontations were the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953, which ended in a stalemate. The Soviet Union tested its first nuclear weapon in 1949. After Joseph Stalin died in 1953, Nikita Khrushchev denounced him in 1956, the year the Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian Revolution. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is widely considered the closest the war came to nuclear conflict.

Both powers courted the newly decolonised states, and the Vietnam War of 1955 to 1975 ended in a North Vietnamese victory. In Indonesia from 1965 to 1966 the military, with the aid of the United States and other Western governments, led the mass killing of more than 500,000 members and sympathisers of the Indonesian Communist Party. The Soviet Union invaded Czechoslovakia with the Warsaw Pact in 1968, and a period of détente in the 1970s brought treaties limiting nuclear arsenals. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 renewed tensions.

Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985. In June 1987 he announced perestroika, an agenda of economic restructuring, and introduced glasnost, or openness. These reforms contributed to the revolutions of 1989 in the Eastern Bloc and to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, which ended the Cold War.

By 1989 the United States had military alliances with 50 countries and 526,000 troops stationed abroad. Nearly 100,000 Americans died in the Korean and Vietnam Wars, and millions died in the proxy wars around the globe, most of all in eastern Asia. Historians have disagreed over who was responsible for the breakdown of relations: orthodox accounts blame the Soviet Union, revisionists place more responsibility on the United States, and post-revisionists see a more nuanced pattern.
collectivity-of-saint-martin: The Collectivity of Saint Martin occupies the northern 60% of the island of Saint Martin in the Leeward Islands, together with smaller islands, the largest of which is Tintamarre. Its land area is 53.2 km2. The southern 40% of the island is Sint Maarten, so this is the only place in the world where France borders the Netherlands. The terrain is generally hilly, with Pic Paradis, at 424 m, the highest point on the island.

Archaeological evidence shows that Amerindian peoples lived on the island from as early as 2000 BCE. Saladoid people from the Orinoco basin arrived around 550 BCE and brought agriculture and pottery, and the Kalinago arrived around 1300 to 1400 CE and began to displace the earlier Arawak inhabitants. Christopher Columbus is commonly said to have named the island after Saint Martin of Tours on 11 November 1493, but he gave that name to the island now called Nevis, and confusion among the poorly charted Leeward Islands moved it to this one.

The island was nominally Spanish and was contested by France and the United Provinces, while the Amerindian population fell sharply from diseases brought by Europeans. In 1631 the Dutch built Fort Amsterdam, and the Spanish captured the island in 1633. When the Eighty Years' War ended in 1648 the island lost its value to Spain, which left. The French and Dutch then agreed in the Treaty of Concordia to divide it, and the boundary settled in its present position by 1817.

In the 18th century cotton, tobacco and sugar plantations brought many African slaves, who came to outnumber the European settlers. France abolished slavery on 28 May 1848, and the Dutch did so on 1 July 1863. The French part was merged into the Guadeloupe colony in 1763 and became an arrondissement of Guadeloupe in 1946, and tourism grew from the 1960s. In 2007 it was detached from Guadeloupe and became an overseas collectivity.

The capital of the collectivity is Marigot, and French is the official language, although English is widely spoken. It uses the euro and remains an outermost region of the European Union. Tourism is its main economic activity.
college-of-cardinals: The word cardinal comes from the Latin cardo, meaning hinge. The office evolved slowly during the first millennium from the clergy of Rome. The term first appears in the Liber Pontificalis in the biography of Pope Stephen III, where a Roman synod of 769 decided that the pope should be elected from among the cardinal priests and deacons.

The three classes of the College began to form under Pope Stephen V (816-817), who bound the cardinal bishops to sing Mass in rotation at the high altar of St. Peter's Basilica. In 845 the Council of Meaux-Paris required bishops to establish cardinal titles or parishes in their towns, and the popes began using cardinal priests as legates and special envoys.

The College gained its weight through the Gregorian Reform. Before the mid-11th century the papacy was fought over by Roman aristocratic families such as the Theophylacti and Colonna, and the Holy Roman Emperor held a special power to appoint the pope.

After the death of Henry III in 1056 left a child on the throne, reformers took advantage of the king's weakness, and in 1059 Pope Nicholas II reserved papal elections to the clergy of Rome by the bull In nomine Domini. This was part of the wider Investiture Controversy. From the start of the 12th century the three orders met as one College. The last non-cardinal to be elected pope was Urban VI, who died in 1389.

Its size was a recurring dispute. From the 13th to the 15th centuries it never exceeded thirty, and John XXII (1316-1334) limited it to twenty. Popes also enlarged the College to raise money, win allies or dilute its strength as a counterweight to papal supremacy: in 1517 Leo X added 31 cardinals, bringing the total to 65. In 1586 Sixtus V fixed the number at 70.

The College advises the pope when he summons it to a consistory and has no ruling power except during a papal vacancy, when its powers are limited by law. The dean and vice-dean are chosen from the cardinal bishops, with papal confirmation, and act as first among equals. Paul VI barred cardinals over 80 from voting in conclaves from 1971 and set the number of electors at 120 in 1975.
colmar: Colmar lies 64 km south-south-west of Strasbourg, on the River Lauch, a tributary of the Ill, immediately east of the Vosges and linked by canal to the Rhine. The mountains hold back moisture from the west, so the city is one of the driest in France, a sunny setting for the vineyards of Alsace. Colmar sits on the Alsatian Wine Route and calls itself the capital of Alsatian wine.

Colmar was first mentioned in the 9th century, and the Carolingian emperor Charles the Fat held a diet there in 884. Frederick II made it a free imperial city in 1226, and in 1354 it joined the Décapole, a league of Alsatian cities. It adopted the Protestant Reformation in 1575, long after Strasbourg and Sélestat to the north. In the Thirty Years' War the Swedish army took it in 1632 and held it for two years, and in 1635 imperial forces spoiled its harvest while the townspeople shot at them from the walls.

Louis XIV conquered the city in 1673, and the Treaties of Nijmegen formally ceded it in 1679. It kept a distinct German character because of its location, language and culture. A cholera epidemic killed many people in 1854, and the Franco-Prussian War brought Colmar, with the rest of Alsace, to the new German Empire in 1871, in the province of Alsace-Lorraine. It returned to France under the Treaty of Versailles in 1919, was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1940, and was again French after the battle of the Colmar Pocket in 1945. A hoard of precious objects hidden by Jews during the Black Death, the Colmar Treasure, was found in the city in 1863.

Colmar is the seat of the prefecture of the Haut-Rhin department and the third-largest commune of Alsace. Its old town was largely spared by the French Revolution and the wars of 1870 to 1871, 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945, and its buildings show eight centuries of German and French architecture in timber framing and Vosges sandstone. The area of canals along the Lauch is called Little Venice. The Unterlinden Museum holds the Isenheim Altarpiece. The sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, creator of the Statue of Liberty, was born there, and the Municipal Library owns more than 2,300 incunabula, many from monasteries dissolved during the Revolution.
cologne: Cologne is centred on the left bank of the Rhine, about 35 kilometres south-east of Düsseldorf and 22 kilometres north-west of Bonn, in the Cologne Lowland of the central Rhineland. The city's highest point is 118 metres above sea level and its lowest 37.5 metres. It is regularly affected by flooding from the Rhine, and its flood control system was redesigned after a flood in 1993 that caused heavy damage.

The first urban settlement on the site was the Oppidum Ubiorum, founded in 38 BCE by the Ubii, a Germanic tribe. In 50 CE the Romans founded Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, named after Emperor Claudius and his wife Agrippina the Younger, who was born here. It became capital of the province of Germania Inferior in 85, and from 260 to 271 was the capital of the Gallic Empire under Postumus, Marius and Victorinus. Emperor Constantine I had a bridge built over the Rhine at Cologne in 310. The Franks occupied the city in 462. Its population is put at about 40,000 in 100–200 CE, 20,000 in 1000 and 50,000 in 1200.

Cunibert, made bishop of Cologne in 623, advised the Merovingian King Dagobert I. In 795 Charlemagne's bishop Hildebold was promoted to archbishop, and the Treaty of Verdun of 843 placed the city in Lothair I's Middle Francia.

Its position on major trade routes between eastern and western Europe made it a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire and a major member of the Hanseatic League, and one of the largest European cities of the medieval and Renaissance periods. French forces occupied it in 1794, and the Treaty of Lunéville of 1801 made the left bank of the Rhine part of the French Republic. The Napoleonic Code, introduced under French rule, remained in use there until 1900. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave Cologne to the Kingdom of Prussia.

Cologne is the fourth-most populous city of Germany and the largest city of North Rhine-Westphalia, with over one million inhabitants. It was one of the most heavily bombed cities in Germany during the Second World War, which reduced its population by 93%, mainly through evacuation, and destroyed around 80% of the old city centre. Most major historic landmarks were restored, among them Cologne Cathedral, built to house the Shrine of the Three Kings and the world's tallest building from 1880 to 1890, and the Romanesque churches. Eau de Cologne has been produced in the city since 1709.
colombo: Colombo lies on the west coast of Sri Lanka. It is the most populous city of the country and its financial centre, with 752,993 inhabitants within the municipal limits. The name was introduced by the Portuguese in 1505 and is believed to come from the classical Sinhala Kolon thota, port on the river Kelani. Another belief derives it from Kola-amba-thota, harbour with leafy mango trees.

The traveller Ibn Battuta, who visited the island in the 14th century, called it Kalanpu. Arabs began to settle in Colombo around the eighth century, mostly because the port helped them control much of the trade between the Sinhalese kingdoms and the outside world. Portuguese explorers led by Dom Lourenço de Almeida arrived in Sri Lanka in 1505 and made a treaty with Parakramabahu VIII, King of Kotte, which let them trade in cinnamon and establish a trading post. Within a short time they expelled the Muslim inhabitants of Colombo and began to build a fort in 1517.

The Dutch captured Colombo in 1656 after a long siege, at the end of which 93 Portuguese survivors were given safe conduct out of the fort. It served as capital of the Dutch maritime provinces under the Dutch East India Company until 1796. The British captured it in 1796, but it remained a military outpost until the Kandyan Kingdom was ceded to them in 1815, when they made it the capital of the crown colony of British Ceylon and built houses and civilian structures around the fort. Ceylon became independent in 1948.

Colombo is Sri Lanka's executive and judicial capital and its commercial capital, since plans of the 1980s moved Parliament and several ministries to Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, though the move was never completed. Its harbour is the largest and one of the busiest ports in Sri Lanka. The Fort area keeps the name of the old fortifications, whose ramparts the British demolished in the late 19th century. Few buildings survive from the Dutch period, among them the former Dutch Hospital.
colon-panama: Colón lies beside the Caribbean Sea near the Atlantic entrance to the Panama Canal. The city proper stands on the Manzanillo Peninsula, a former island surrounded by Limon Bay, Manzanillo Bay and the Folks River. It was founded on the western end of a marshy islet, Manzanillo Island, which was joined to the mainland by a causeway built for the railroad, with part of the island drained for permanent buildings.

The city was founded in 1850 as the Atlantic terminal of the Panama Railroad, built to meet the demand during the California Gold Rush for a fast route to California. For some years the community of emigrants from the United States called the town Aspinwall, after the railroad's promoter William Henry Aspinwall, while Hispanic residents called it Colón in honour of Christopher Columbus. Its population grew from 3,001 in 1900 to 31,203 by 1920 with the building of the canal.

Fires destroyed much of the city in 1885, during the Colombian Civil War, in 1915, and on 13–14 April 1940, when one third of it burned. A boundary treaty of 1914 made Colón an exclave surrounded by the Canal Zone, and the Hull–Alfaro Treaty of 1936 ceded a strip, the Colón Corridor, for a road linking it to the rest of Panama. In 1948 part of Manzanillo Island was designated the Colón Free Trade Zone. Riots in the 1960s destroyed the municipal palace and began a decline.

Colón is the capital of Colón Province and has traditionally been known as Panama's second city, with around 204,000 people in 2000. Most are of West Indian or mixed mestizo ancestry. The Panama Canal Railway and Enrique Adolfo Jiménez Airport serve it. Henryk Sienkiewicz's novella Latarnik is set in the lighthouse at Aspinwall.
colorado: Colorado is a landlocked state in the Mountain West. It shares the Four Corners region with Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is bordered by Wyoming to the north, Nebraska to the northeast, Kansas to the east and Oklahoma to the southeast. It takes in most of the Southern Rocky Mountains, the northeastern portion of the Colorado Plateau and the western edge of the Great Plains, and its landscape includes alpine mountains, high plains, deserts with huge sand dunes and deep canyons.

In 1861 the United States Congress defined the boundaries of the new Territory of Colorado exclusively by lines of latitude and longitude, from 37°N to 41°N and from 102°02′48″W to 109°02′48″W. After 165 years of government surveys the borders were officially defined by 697 boundary markers and 697 straight lines. Colorado, Wyoming and Utah are the only states whose borders are defined solely by straight lines with no natural features. The Four Corners Monument is the only place in the United States where four states meet.

The region has been inhabited by Native Americans and their Paleo-Indian ancestors for at least 13,500 years and possibly more than 37,000. The Lindenmeier site contains artifacts dating from approximately 8720 BCE. The Ancient Pueblo peoples lived in the valleys and mesas of the Colorado Plateau in the far southwest, and the Ute Nation inhabited the mountain valleys of the Rocky Mountains. The Apache and Comanche lived in the east and southeast. In the 17th century the Arapaho and Cheyenne moved west from the Great Lakes region to hunt across the High Plains.

The United States acquired the territorial claim to the eastern Rocky Mountains with the Louisiana Purchase from France in 1803. In 1806 Zebulon Pike led an army reconnaissance expedition into the disputed region. Spanish cavalry arrested him and his troops in the San Luis Valley the following February, took them to Chihuahua and expelled them from Mexico in July.

In 1848 much of the Nuevo México region was annexed to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The Pike's Peak Gold Rush of 1858-1862 brought an influx of settlers. On 28 February 1861 President James Buchanan signed the act creating the Territory of Colorado, and on 1 August 1876 President Ulysses S. Grant signed Proclamation 230, admitting Colorado as the 38th state.

Denver is the capital, the most populous city and the centre of the Front Range Urban Corridor. Colorado Springs is the second-most populous city. The state is the eighth-largest by area. Its economy rests on government and defense, mining, agriculture, tourism and manufacturing.
colossus-of-rhodes: In the late fourth century BCE Rhodes, allied with Ptolemy I of Egypt, resisted an invasion by Antigonus I Monophthalmus. His son Demetrius I of Macedon besieged the city for a year, and in 304 BCE a relief force sent by Ptolemy arrived and he abandoned the siege, leaving most of his equipment. The Rhodians sold it for 300 talents and decided to build a colossal statue of their patron god Helios. Chares of Lindos directed the work, which began in 292 BCE. His teacher Lysippos had made a 22-metre bronze statue of Zeus at Tarentum.

Most descriptions give the statue a height of about 70 cubits. It stood on a white marble pedestal near the harbour entrance, though other sources place it on a breakwater. Accounts describe an iron frame with bronze plates as a skin, filled with stone blocks as work proceeded. Philo of Byzantium wrote that Chares cast it in horizontal courses, burying each section in earth. The image of the statue straddling the harbour mouth is a medieval invention, and engineering analysis indicates that a bronze statue with legs apart would have collapsed. Its true location remains in dispute.

The statue stood for 54 years. An earthquake in 226 BCE snapped it at the knees. Ptolemy III offered to pay for rebuilding, but the Oracle of Delphi led the Rhodians to fear they had offended Helios, and they declined. The remains lay for over 800 years and drew visitors. Strabo called it the best of the city's votive offerings, and Pliny the Elder wrote that few men could clasp its thumb in their arms. Theophanes the Confessor records that in 653 an Arab force sold its bronze to a Jewish merchant, who loaded it on 900 camels; he is the only source, and L. I. Conrad considers the story likely propaganda.
columba: Columba was born to Fedlimid and Eithne of the Cenél Conaill at Gartan, in Tír Chonaill, mainly modern County Donegal. His name in Irish, Colmcille, means dove. He studied at the monastic school of Movilla and then at Clonard, where he was one of twelve students of Finnian of Clonard known as the Twelve Apostles of Ireland. He became a monk and was ordained priest. Several important monasteries are attributed to him in the following years, among them Derry, Durrow, Kells and Swords.

Traditions link him with a quarrel over a psalter and with the Battle of Cúl Dreimhne in 561, though Richard Sharpe warns against accepting the many references that connect the battle with his leaving Ireland. One account says that a synod threatened him with excommunication and that he resolved to expiate his sense of offence by leaving Ireland, a departure described as exile or, more often, as pilgrimage.

In 563 he crossed to Scotland with twelve companions in a currach of wicker covered with leather. The island of Iona was given to him by his kinsman Conall mac Comgaill, king of Dál Riata, who perhaps invited him. The Ulster Gaels had lived on the Scottish west coast for a couple of centuries, so he was in a sense not leaving his own people. Iona was the only centre of literacy in the region, and his reputation as a holy man gave him a role as a diplomat among the tribes. He visited the pagan King Bridei of Fortriu at Inverness and won his respect but, according to Adomnán, not his conversion.

Columba founded several churches in the Hebrides and turned Iona into a school for missionaries. He is credited with transcribing 300 books, and two Latin hymns, Altus Prosator and Adiutor Laborantium, are attributed to him.

According to traditional sources he died on Iona on Sunday, 9 June 597, and was buried by his monks. His relics were removed in 849 and divided between Scotland and Ireland. The main source for his life is the Life of Columba by Adomnán, one of his successors at Iona. He is one of the patron saints of Ireland with Patrick and Brigid, and patron of Derry, and was venerated by both the Gaels of Dál Riata and the Picts.
columbanus: Columbanus, the Latinised form of Colmán, meaning little dove, was born in the Kingdom of Leinster in Ireland. He was first educated under Abbot Sinell of Cluaninis, whose monastery stood on an island of the River Erne in modern County Fermanagh, and under Sinell he composed a commentary on the Psalms. He then moved to Bangor Abbey to study as a teacher of the Bible, learning grammar, rhetoric and geometry, and Abbot Comgall taught him Greek and Latin. He stayed at Bangor until about 590, when Comgall reluctantly allowed him to travel to the continent.

Columbanus sailed with twelve companions, among them Gallus, and landed at Saint-Malo in Brittany. In Burgundy King Guntram welcomed them and granted land in the Vosges Mountains, where they turned a ruined Roman fortress into a school. It drew so many students that they moved to Luxeuil and founded a second school at Fontaines, all under his authority and following the Celtic tradition in which he had been educated. In 603 he and his followers quarrelled with the Frankish bishops over the date of Easter, since the Irish used their own calculation, and the bishops also objected to the Irish tonsure.

In 611 he reached the court of Theudebert II at Metz and travelled up the Rhine to preach to the Suebi and Alemanni, settling at Bregenz on Lake Constance, where Gallus preached and a monastery was founded. When war in 612 gave Theuderic II control of Austrasia and some of his students were murdered, he crossed the Alps. In Milan he was welcomed by King Agilulf and Queen Theodelinda of the Lombards and wrote against Arianism. In 614 Agilulf gave him land at Bobbio. At the king's request he also wrote to Pope Boniface IV about the controversy over the Three Chapters.

In his last year King Chlothar II invited him to return to Burgundy, but he declined and asked the king to protect his monks at Luxeuil. He retired to a cave above the Trebbia river and died at Bobbio on 21 November 615. His Rule embodied the customs of Bangor and other Irish monasteries and was much shorter than the Rule of Saint Benedict, with ten chapters beginning with absolute obedience. His teaching on penance stressed private confession to a priest, followed by penances imposed in reparation. Gallus stayed in the Alps until his death, and the Abbey of Saint Gall was founded at the site of his cell about seventy years later.
columbia-university: Columbia University is a private university in New York City. Its main campus lies in the Upper Manhattan neighbourhood of Morningside Heights, on more than six city blocks, about 32 acres. It was designed on Beaux-Arts principles by the architects McKim, Mead and White, following the vision of Seth Low, a campus where all disciplines could be taught in one place. In 2007 the university bought most of a 17-acre site in Manhattanville for a second campus.

Classes began in July 1754 under the first president, Samuel Johnson, and the college was officially founded on 31 October 1754 as King's College by royal charter of George II, on the grounds of Trinity Church in Manhattan. After the American Revolution it was renamed Columbia College in 1784, and in 1787 it was placed under a private board of trustees headed by Alexander Hamilton and John Jay. In 1857 it moved to a Gothic Revival campus at 49th Street and Madison Avenue. Barnard College was created in 1889 in response to the refusal to admit women. In 1896 President Seth Low moved the campus to Morningside Heights, and the name became Columbia University.

Columbia is organised into 17 schools, with two affiliated colleges, Barnard College and Teachers College, and two seminaries. It is a member of the Ivy League and was the first school in the United States to grant the MD degree. Scientists there took part in the first nuclear fission reaction in North America and in the invention of the laser and of FM radio. The university administers the Pulitzer Prize and the Bancroft Prize in history, and a prize for the translation of Japanese literature, the oldest of its kind.
columbian-exchange: The term was first used in 1972 by the American historian Alfred W. Crosby in his book The Columbian Exchange, which mapped the biological and cultural transfers between the Old and New Worlds and was rapidly adopted by other historians. Before 1492 there is little evidence of contact between the two hemispheres. The Norse visits to Greenland, Newfoundland and Vinland in the late 10th and 11th centuries had no known impact on the Americas, and many scientists accept that contact between Polynesians and coastal South Americans around 1200 explains the sweet potato in Polynesia. The exchange began with the first voyage of Christopher Columbus in 1492.

Plants moved in both directions. Potatoes, grown only in South America before 1500, were widely eaten in Europe by the 18th century and are estimated to have contributed 12 to 25 per cent of the population growth in Afro-Eurasia between 1700 and 1900. The Portuguese brought cassava to Africa in the 16th century, and it gradually replaced sorghum and millet as the most important food crop there. Spanish colonizers brought maize and sweet potatoes to Asia, and the Portuguese took chili peppers to India. In the other direction rice, wheat, sugar cane, citrus fruits and coffee became important in the Americas, and enslaved Africans brought rice-growing skills to Georgia, South Carolina, Cuba and Puerto Rico.

Horses, donkeys, mules, pigs, cattle, sheep, goats, chickens and bees were rapidly adopted by native peoples; the Plains Indians used horses for hunting and the Mapuche adopted them in the Arauco War. The turkey and the Muscovy duck went to Europe. Diseases were far deadlier toward the Americas. Hispaniola's pre-contact population was probably at least 500,000, and fewer than 500 remained by 1526. Smallpox, first recorded in the Americas in 1518, is estimated to have killed 40 per cent of the 200,000 people of Tenochtitlan in 1520.

An estimated 80 to 95 per cent of the Native American population died in epidemics within 100 to 150 years of 1492. The Mexican population fell from an estimated 20 million to barely more than a million in the 16th century. The need for labour and the decline of Indigenous peoples was linked to the Atlantic slave trade, which brought 11.7 million Africans to the Americas, far more than the about 3.4 million Europeans who migrated between 1492 and 1840. The Old World also gained from the discovery of quinine, the first effective treatment for malaria. Syphilis may have been carried to Europe by Columbus's crew, though historians debate its origin.
comanche: The Comanche call themselves Nʉmʉnʉʉ, 'the people'. Their language is a Numic language of the Uto-Aztecan family, closely related to Shoshone. It was originally a Shoshone dialect but diverged after the Comanche adopted a nomadic horse culture in the early 18th century. The movement of Proto-Comanche groups onto the Plains was part of the wider Shoshonean expansion, and the Kotsoteka were probably among the first. Contact with the Shoshone of Wyoming lasted until the 1830s, when advancing Cheyennes broke it. The name Comanche comes from the Ute word kɨmantsi, 'enemy', which the Spanish adopted. It is first recorded in 1706.

After the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 various Plains peoples acquired horses. The horse made hunting, war and moving camp easier, a man's wealth was measured by his herd, and the Comanche came to be regarded as among the finest light cavalry in history. They built a vast territory across what is now north-western Texas, eastern New Mexico, south-eastern Colorado, south-western Kansas and western Oklahoma, which colonists called Comanchería. It was not a centralised state, but a set of politically autonomous divisions linked by kinship. At its peak their language was the lingua franca of the southern Great Plains.

Their large raids of the 1840s and 1850s reached hundreds of miles into Mexico, where they took livestock that they mostly sold in Texas. They also took many captives, whom they used as slaves, sold to the Spanish and later to Mexican settlers, or adopted. In 1844 Sam Houston, president of the Republic of Texas, almost reached a peace treaty at Tehuacana Creek, but in 1845 the Texas Legislature refused to fix a boundary with Comancheria. Epidemics, the destruction of the bison herds and warfare and massacres by the United States Army forced the Comanche onto reservations in Indian Territory in the mid-1870s.

Bison supplied most of the Comanche's tools, household goods and weapons, and nearly 200 utilitarian items were made from its horn, hide and bone. They moved so often that they used no pottery. Men hunted bison, elk, pronghorn and deer, and hunting was a main source of prestige.

In the later 19th century Quanah Parker, appointed paramount chief by the United States government, argued for better terms for his people and became a wealthy cattleman. He also campaigned for the right to practise the rites of the Native American Church. Many Comanche children were placed in boarding schools, where they were discouraged from speaking their language. The Comanche Nation today is headquartered in Lawton, Oklahoma.
comayagua: Comayagua lies in a valley 80 km north-west of Tegucigalpa on the highway to San Pedro Sula, 594 metres above sea level, and is the capital of the Comayagua department. Hondurans call it La Antañona, the old one, because it keeps much of its colonial architecture. The name is indigenous: most agree it combines the Lenca words koma, a huge amount of land, and jawa, water, meaning abundant land of water. The Spaniards called the place Valladolid and the Country of the Fig Trees. The Lenca people have lived in the valley since approximately 1,000 BCE, as remains at Yarumela and Tenampúa show.

Captain Alonso de Cáceres founded the city in 1537, on the instructions of Francisco de Montejo, to find a site for a city between the two oceans. It was first called Santa María de la Concepción de Comayagua. King Philip II granted it the title of city in 1557, and in 1561 the episcopal see moved there from Trujillo because of its central position and its closeness to the gold and silver mining regions. It remained the capital of Honduras throughout the colonial period, and in 1788 it became an intendancy that absorbed Tegucigalpa, which had grown as a mining centre. This fed a rivalry between the two cities.

Honduras became part of the United Provinces of Central America in 1823, and Comayagua stayed its capital. On 4 April 1827 federal troops under Colonel Justo Milla laid siege to the city to overthrow the head of state, Dionisio de Herrera, and much of it was burned and looted. A decree of June 1849 to move the capital to Tegucigalpa was not carried out. On 30 October 1880 President Marco Aurelio Soto decided to transfer it, after which the population, commerce and importance of Comayagua fell notably, though it remained the seat of the diocese of Honduras.

Comayagua has some of the oldest buildings in Central America, among them the churches of La Merced, San Francisco and San Sebastián, built in the 16th century. The cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, built in the colonial period, holds a clock that is said to be the oldest in the Americas. The Caxa Real, built between 1739 and 1741, stored the tribute and the silver and gold of the Spanish crown. Museums cover colonial religious art, the Lenca and the republican period.
comecon: Comecon was founded in 1949 by the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland and Romania. It was the Eastern Bloc's response to the Marshall Plan and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation in Western Europe. Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland had remained interested in Marshall aid, but its conditions of a convertible currency and market economies would have tied them more closely to free European markets than to the Soviet Union. In July 1947 Joseph Stalin ordered these governments to withdraw from the Paris Conference on the European Recovery Programme.

After Stalin's death in 1953 the members began again to discuss complementary specialisation, and in 1956 ten permanent standing committees were set up. The Soviet Union began to trade oil for goods made in Comecon countries. A charter modelled on the 1957 Treaty of Rome followed in 1959. Until 1967 Comecon worked only by unanimous agreement, which usually meant failure. That year it adopted the interested party principle, under which any country could opt out of a project while the others still used Comecon's machinery. This was aimed partly at letting Romania chart its own economic course without leaving.

From the early 1970s Soviet oil and gas were transferred within Comecon at below-market rates, which many Western commentators saw as a politically motivated subsidy. In the 1980s, under Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet influence grew and there were attempts to give Comecon some supranational authority. East Germany withdrew on 2 October 1990, after reunification.

Comecon's official hierarchy had a Session, an executive committee, a Secretariat, four council committees and twenty-four standing commissions. The Session was the highest organ and usually met in a member's capital each year. Each country had one vote, and the charter of 1959 proclaimed the sovereign equality of members. In practice the Soviet Union dominated, holding about 90 per cent of the members' land and energy resources and 70 per cent of their population, and many committees had their headquarters in Moscow. Members traded by barter, using world prices as a reference but keeping prices stable for years, which suited central planning. Albania stopped taking part in 1961, and Yugoslavia had associate status from 1964.
comilla: Comilla, officially spelled Cumilla, lies on the banks of the Gumti River in the east of Bangladesh. It is the seat of Comilla District and the second largest city in Chittagong Division. The district is bounded by Tripura to the north, and the rivers that pass through it include the Gomati and the Little Feni. Comilla was one of the cities of ancient Bengal and was once the capital of the Tripura kingdom. Its city corporation covers 53.04 square kilometres.

In ancient times the region was under Gangaridai and Samatata. In the 9th century CE it came under the kings of Harikela, and Lalmai Mainamati was ruled by the Deva dynasty in the 8th century and by the Chandra dynasty in the 10th and mid-11th centuries. In 1732 the area became the centre of the Bengal-backed domain of Jagat Manikya. A peasants' movement against the king of Tripura, led by Shamsher Gazi, rose in 1764, and in 1765 the area came under the East India Company. It was made the Tripura district in 1790 and renamed Comilla in 1960.

Under British rule Comilla saw unrest during the partition of Bengal in 1905, and on 21 November 1921 Kazi Nazrul Islam composed patriotic songs there to protest the visit of the Prince of Wales. The Avay Ashram was a revolutionary institution of this time, and Rabindranath Tagore and Mahatma Gandhi visited the town. In 1931 about 4,000 peasants at Mohini village in Chauddagram revolted against a land revenue tax, and Gurkha soldiers fired on the crowd, killing four; in 1932 police fired at a peasant gathering at Hasnabad, killing two.

Comilla Cantonment, the oldest military base in East Bengal, was widely used by the British Indian Army in the Second World War and was the headquarters of the British 14th Army. The Maynamati War Cemetery, kept by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, commemorates Allied soldiers who died in both world wars and also holds Japanese graves. In the war of 1971 Pakistan formed an ad hoc division in mid-November to hold the Comilla and Noakhali districts, and its forces surrendered on 16 December 1971, a day commemorated in Bangladesh as Bijoy Dibos.

Comilla Victoria Government College in the city is named after Queen Victoria. Archaeological finds from the district, especially of the 7th and 8th centuries, are kept in the Mainamati Museum. The professional cricket team Comilla Victorians is based in the city.
commentarii-de-bello-gallico: Caesar's victories in Gaul had increased the alarm and hostility of his aristocratic enemies at Rome, the optimates, who intended to prosecute him for abuse of his authority once he laid down his imperium. A conviction would have stripped him of wealth and citizenship and undone the laws he had passed as consul. The Commentaries are understood as an effort to address the plebeians and the Tribunes of the Plebs directly, bypassing the Senate, and to present the wars as just and pious, fought in self-defence.

The classicist Ruth Breindal thinks Caesar probably dictated much of the work to a scribe, while keeping an overwhelming hand in it, and regards its main purpose as propaganda to protect his reputation. The last chapters of Book 8 were written after Caesar's death in 44 BCE by the consul Aulus Hirtius, who died in 43 BCE.

The work opens with the often quoted Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres, "Gaul is a whole divided into three parts". It is divided into eight books of roughly 5,000 to 15,000 words. Gaul here means the Celtic regions outside the province of Gallia Narbonensis, which Rome already held. The narrative begins in 58 BCE with the migration of the Helvetii, whom neighbouring allies asked Caesar to resist, and draws in further tribes and the Germanic Suebi.

Among the Gallic leaders, Diviciacus of the Haedui (Aedui) is shown as the one man in whom Caesar had absolute confidence, and his appeals led Caesar to act against the German leader Ariovistus. Book 6 describes the Germans, the Druids and their sacrifices. Book 5 tells of the centurions Lucius Vorenus and Titus Pullo, rivals who saved each other's lives when the garrison of Quintus Tullius Cicero was besieged in a revolt of the Belgae led by Ambiorix.

Most contemporaries and later historians took the account as truthful until the 20th century. After the Second World War historians began to question it, above all its claim that the Romans faced Gallic forces of up to 430,000, a size thought impossible for an army of the time, and suffered no deaths against them. From the 1970s some critics read the work less as history than as literature.

Its clear, direct Latin has made it a mainstay of Latin teaching. About 240 medieval manuscripts preserve it, the oldest written at Fleury Abbey in the later ninth century, and the first printed edition was published by Giovanni Andrea Bussi at Rome in 1469. Caesar appears in the Astérix albums, whose jokes include his speaking of himself in the third person.
committee-of-public-safety: A widespread belief held that revolutionary France was in immediate peril, threatened by foreign armies, the revolts in the Vendée and foreign agents plotting from within. The Girondin leader Maximin Isnard proposed a nine-member committee, supported by Georges Danton, who called it "a hand to grasp the weapon of the Revolutionary Tribunal". The National Convention created it on 6 April 1793, after a proposal by Bertrand Barère. It supplemented the Committee of General Defence of early January 1793, and at first it was called the Danton Committee. Danton was not included when it was recomposed on 10 July 1793.

Maximilien Robespierre was elected to the committee on 27 July 1793. It governed the war, named the judges and juries of the Revolutionary Tribunal, provisioned the armies and the public and oversaw the state bureaucracy. It applied the Convention's decrees and so carried out some of the harshest policies of the Terror, among them the levée en masse of 23 August 1793 and the Law of Suspects of 17 September. The Law of 14 Frimaire on 4 December 1793 codified its powers.

The Hébertists were arrested and executed in March 1794, and Danton and Camille Desmoulins, who had turned the newspaper Le Vieux Cordelier against the committees, went to the guillotine on 5 April 1794. The Law of 22 Prairial, enacted on 10 June 1794, limited the legal recourse of the accused and made death the punishment for all the crimes it covered. Discord grew within the government, and Robespierre quarrelled with Collot d'Herbois and Billaud-Varenne and almost stopped attending in June 1794 because of illness.

On 26 July 1794 Robespierre told the Convention that the committees needed purifying. The next day, 9 Thermidor, Saint-Just was interrupted by Jean-Lambert Tallien and Billaud-Varenne, and the Convention ordered the arrest of Robespierre, his brother Augustin, Saint-Just and their supporters. Philippe Le Bas killed himself, and the others were guillotined on 28 July 1794. The Thermidorian Reaction that followed repealed many of the year's most unpopular laws and restricted the committees. The committee's influence diminished over 15 months, and it disappeared on 25 October 1795, the day the National Convention ended, under the Constitution of the Year III, which began the Directory.
commodus: Commodus was born on 31 August 161 at Lanuvium, the son of Marcus Aurelius and Faustina the Younger. His twin brother died in 165 and a younger brother in 169, leaving him his father's only surviving son. He was the first emperor born in the purple, during his father's reign. He was with the army at Carnuntum in 172 and received the title Germanicus, and in 175, when Avidius Cassius declared himself emperor in Syria, he assumed the toga virilis on the Danube front. On 27 November 176 his father gave him the title Imperator, and on 1 January 177 he became consul at fifteen, the youngest up to that time.

Marcus Aurelius died on 17 March 180, leaving Commodus sole emperor at eighteen. He soon made peace with the Danubian tribes. He had little interest in administration and left it to favourites: the chamberlain Saoterus, the praetorian prefect Perennis and the freedman Cleander. He devalued the denarius and paid for handouts and shows partly by taxing the senators. Cassius Dio, a contemporary, saw his accession as a descent from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust; the Historia Augusta is unreliable.

Conspiracies followed. In 182 his sister Lucilla plotted against him; her accomplices were executed and she was exiled to Capri and later killed. Cleander sold senate seats and commands, and in 190 appointed a record 25 suffect consuls; a food shortage and a riot brought his fall. Commodus presented himself as Hercules. After a fire damaged Rome in 191 he declared himself a new Romulus in early 192, renamed the city Colonia Lucia Annia Commodiana and renamed the months after his twelve names. He also fought as a gladiator in the arena.

In late 192 Commodus announced that he would take office on 1 January as both consul and gladiator. His mistress Marcia found a list of people he meant to execute, with her own name, the prefect Laetus and the chamberlain Eclectus on it. On 31 December she poisoned his food; he vomited it, and the conspirators sent his wrestling partner Narcissus to strangle him in his bath. The Senate declared him a public enemy and demolished his statues. His death ended the Nerva–Antonine dynasty, and Pertinax succeeded him. In 195 Septimius Severus had the Senate deify him. His sole reign is commonly thought to mark the end of the Pax Romana.
common-law: The common law was so named because it was common to all the king's courts across England.
