It originated in the practices of the courts of the English kings in the centuries following the Norman Conquest of 1066. Before the Conquest much legal business took place in local folk courts of the shires and hundreds, boroughs, fairs and large landholders held courts of their own, and the Catholic Church ran a separate system for canon law. How far the common law drew on Anglo-Saxon traditions such as the jury, ordeals and writs is still much discussed.

King Henry II is regarded as its establisher. He wanted to preserve public order, though providing law was also profitable, since fines and forfeitures brought the government large sums. He developed the practice of sending judges from the Curia Regis, the king's court, to hear disputes round the country, and as these circuits spread, a law emerged that was common to all England.

Common law is the body of law developed mainly through judicial decisions rather than statutes. It rests on the principle of stare decisis, to stand by things decided: courts follow the precedents set in earlier similar cases, and in a case of first impression the judge resolves the issue and sets a new one. Supporters value the predictability this gives commercial parties. Common law courts usually use an adversarial system, in which two sides present their cases to a neutral judge.

Equity developed beside it. From the 15th century litigants who felt cheated by the common law petitioned the king, and the resulting system was administered by the Lord Chancellor in the courts of chancery. The two often conflicted, and in England the courts were merged by the Judicature Acts of 1873 and 1875, with equity prevailing in a conflict.

In the 12th and 13th centuries continental European countries began receiving Roman law, including the Corpus Juris Civilis, but England already had the common law in place, so common law and civil law jurisdictions differ in judicial reasoning and sources of law. England spread its system to Wales, Ireland and overseas colonies, and the British Empire continued this; the laws of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh are largely based on it from the period of the British Raj. Many former colonies kept it after independence. Today about one third of the world's population lives in common law jurisdictions or in mixed systems that combine common and civil law.
commonwealth-of-independent-states: In March 1991, amid perestroika, Mikhail Gorbachev, president of the Soviet Union, proposed a referendum to preserve the Union as a federation of sovereign republics. The new treaty was never signed, because Communist Party hardliners staged a coup attempt in Moscow in August. After it collapsed, many republics declared independence. A week after the Ukrainian independence referendum, the leaders of Belarus, the Russian SFSR and Ukraine met at the Belovezhskaya Pushcha Natural Reserve and on 8 December 1991 signed the Belovezha Accords, declaring that the Union had effectively ceased to exist and proclaiming the CIS in its place. On 21 December these three republics and eight others signed the Alma-Ata Protocol.

The Charter of the CIS, signed on 22 January 1993, set up its institutions and rules. All who had ratified the creation agreement were founding states, but only those ratifying the Charter became member states. Ukraine, which never ratified the Charter, therefore remained a founding state and not a member. The CIS Interparliamentary Assembly was established on 27 March 1992 in Kazakhstan, and in 1995 the CIS adopted a Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

In May 1992 six post-Soviet states signed the Collective Security Treaty, also called the Tashkent Pact; it took effect in 1994. An Agreement on the Economic Union was signed on 24 September 1993. Three organisations later originated from the CIS: the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the Eurasian Economic Union and the Union State of Russia and Belarus.

A joint CIS team, the Unified Team, competed in the 1992 Winter and Summer Olympics. Between 2003 and 2005 three member states experienced changes of government in the colour revolutions: Eduard Shevardnadze was overthrown in Georgia, Viktor Yushchenko was elected in Ukraine and Askar Akayev was toppled in Kyrgyzstan. Georgia left the CIS after the Russo-Georgian War.
commonwealth-of-nations: On 18 January 1884 Lord Rosebery, visiting Adelaide, described the changing British Empire as a Commonwealth of Nations, as some of its colonies became more independent. Conferences of British and colonial prime ministers began in 1887 and led to the Imperial Conferences created in 1911. In the Balfour Declaration at the 1926 Imperial Conference, the United Kingdom and its dominions agreed that they were autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status and in no way subordinate one to another, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations. The term Commonwealth was officially adopted for the community, and the United Kingdom formalised it by the Statute of Westminster in 1931.

The Commonwealth and Empire took part in every major theatre of the Second World War, and the governments of Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom set up the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan for pilots from across the Empire. After the war the Empire was gradually dismantled, and most of its components became independent countries and members of the Commonwealth.

Membership at first required dominionhood. On 18 April 1949 Ireland formally became a republic and so left the Commonwealth, although it had not taken an active part since the early 1930s. Other members wished to become republics without losing their ties, and at a meeting of prime ministers in London in April 1949 the London Declaration, drafted by V. K. Krishna Menon, allowed India to remain a member when it became a republic in January 1950, accepting the British sovereign as a symbol of the free association and as Head of the Commonwealth. The word British was dropped from the title.

In 1961 respect for racial equality became a requirement, which led to the withdrawal of South Africa's re-application, and the Singapore Declaration of 1971 committed members to world peace, liberty, human rights, equality and free trade. Mozambique in 1995 and Rwanda in 2009 were admitted without any constitutional link to Britain.

The main decision-making forum is the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, successor to the Imperial Conferences, and the Commonwealth Secretariat, established in 1965, is the main intergovernmental agency. The Commonwealth Foundation works with civil society. Members have no legal obligations to one another, and their countries are represented to one another by high commissions rather than embassies. The headship is symbolic. The Commonwealth Games, begun in 1930 as the Empire Games and first held at Hamilton, Canada, were designed to be the Friendly Games. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission, founded in 1917 as the Imperial War Graves Commission, maintains the graves of 1.7 million service personnel who died in the two world wars.
communist-international: The Communist International descended from the First International (1864 to 1876) and the Second International (1889 to 1914), which collapsed in the First World War. On 24 January 1919 Moscow sent a wireless invitation to thirty-nine communist parties and groups, timed to pre-empt a conference of reformist socialists in Berne. The founding congress met in the Kremlin from 2 to 6 March 1919. Of fifty-one delegates only nine came from abroad, because of the Allied blockade of Russia. Its aim was a world party for the armed overthrow of capitalist private property, and its founding split the labour movement between communists and social democrats.

The Comintern first expected revolutions in post-war Europe, especially Germany. When these failed in 1920 and 1921, Lenin concluded that revolution was not on the immediate agenda, and a united workers front was adopted in December 1921. After Lenin's death in January 1924 the Comintern was increasingly marked by Russian dominance. In China it directed the Communist Party to enter the Kuomintang in August 1922, forming the First United Front. From 1928 to 1933 it denounced social democrats as social fascists; after the Nazi seizure of power it turned to the Popular Front, ratified in 1935, and helped organise support for the Spanish Republic.

During the Great Purge many Comintern officials and foreign communists in Moscow were arrested and shot, and the Communist Party of Poland was dissolved in 1938. After the Nazi–Soviet Pact of August 1939 the Comintern called the war an imperialist war until Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941.

Stalin unilaterally dissolved the Comintern on 15 May 1943 as a gesture to the Allies. Its formal structures were dismantled, but Soviet control over the international communist movement persisted and was partly revived through the Cominform, which existed from 1947 to 1956.
communist-party-of-the-soviet-union: The party began in 1898 as part of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. In August 1903 a split opened between the followers of Julius Martov, called Mensheviks, meaning the minority, and those of Vladimir Lenin, called Bolsheviks, meaning the majority, although the two factions were of fairly equal size. Before the February Revolution of 1917 the party worked underground, and many of its leaders, Lenin among them, were in exile. The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution of 1917, and the party took the name Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) on 8 March 1918 and All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) on 31 December 1925.

After Lenin's death Joseph Stalin, the general secretary, and Leon Trotsky struggled for power. Trotsky argued for permanent revolution abroad, Stalin for building socialism in one country. By 1929 Stalin was leader, and he formalised Marxism-Leninism as the guiding ideology. The party pursued state socialism, with nationalised industries and a command economy, and Stalin's rule was marked by an extensive cult of personality.

After Stalin's death Nikita Khrushchev won the struggle for the top post and began the Thaw, which ended the mass terror of the earlier decades. At the 20th Congress in 1956 he denounced Stalin's crimes. Mikhail Gorbachev became general secretary on 11 March 1985, and his policies of perestroika and glasnost, with multi-candidate elections, weakened the party. In 1990 the Congress of People's Deputies changed Article 6 of the 1977 constitution, which had given the party a monopoly of the political system. Its activities were suspended on 29 August 1991, after a failed coup by conservative party leaders, and Boris Yeltsin banned it by decree on 6 November 1991.

The party was based on democratic centralism, conceived by Lenin: policy was discussed openly, but once the party line was agreed discussion had to cease, and dissent could mean expulsion. The 10th Congress approved a ban on factions. The Congress met every five years and was nominally the highest body, though under Stalin it became largely symbolic. Between congresses the Central Committee was the highest body, and daily business fell to the Politburo and the Secretariat. The party leader was General Secretary, a title renamed First Secretary from 1953 to 1966. Below them stood a nested system of regional, city and district committees and workplace organisations. The Komsomol was the party's youth wing.
communist-party-of-vietnam: The party traces its history to 1925, when Nguyen Ai Quoc, later Ho Chi Minh, established the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League. Its aims were to end French colonial rule, win national independence and redistribute land to working peasants, and the Comintern supported the groundwork financially. In 1928 the Kuomintang destroyed the League's headquarters in Guangdong, China, and the group was driven underground and split. On 17 June 1929 more than twenty delegates from cells in the Tonkin region met in Hanoi and declared the League dissolved and a Communist Party of Indochina established. The League's other faction, based in Cochinchina, declared itself the Communist Party of Annam in late 1929.

In 1941 the party set up the Viet Minh as a coalition front. In March 1945 Japan overthrew the French colonial regime in Indochina, and by August Japan had surrendered. The Viet Minh used the power vacuum to launch a nationwide uprising, and Emperor Bao Dai abdicated on 25 August. Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945, but no country recognised it at first. The party led the First Indochina War, after which it became the ruling party in the north in 1954.

The third party congress, held in Hanoi in 1960, set the task of building socialism in North Vietnam and committed the party to the liberation of the south. After the party took power in the whole country in 1975, it unified Vietnam as the Socialist Republic in 1976. It had run a command economy in the north since 1954 and introduced the market reforms known as Đổi Mới in 1986. In 1988 it became the only political party when it absorbed its two sister parties, the Socialist Party and the Democratic Party.

The party is organised on the principle of democratic centralism. Its National Congress, held every five years, elects a Central Committee, which in turn elects the Politburo and the Secretariat and appoints the general secretary, the highest party office. The supremacy of the party is guaranteed by Article 4 of the constitution. The party holds to Marxism-Leninism and to Ho Chi Minh Thought, which became its official ideologies in 1991. At its 10th National Congress in 2006 it amended its statutes to let members engage in private business. It describes its economic system as a socialist-oriented market economy.
comoro-islands: The Comoro Islands are a group of volcanic islands in the Mozambique Channel, to the north-west of Madagascar and facing Mozambique, covering a total area of 2,034 square kilometres. They are Ngazidja (Grande Comore), the largest and the seat of the capital Moroni, Ndzuwani (Anjouan), Mwali (Mohéli) and Mayotte (Maore). Mayotte is the oldest island still above sea level, while Grande Comore is the youngest and still volcanically active; its shield volcano Karthala rises to 2,361 metres. The climate is tropical maritime, with a hot and humid season from November to April and a dry season from May to October.

The islands may have been settled as early as the 6th century. Among the peoples who crossed the sea to populate them were Bantu-speaking peoples, Austronesian peoples including Malagasy, Arabs, Somalis, Portuguese, French and Indians. Islam probably arrived during the 10th century. With Zanzibar, Pemba, Lamu and the coastal towns of Kenya and Tanzania, the Comoros formed a prosperous region of Swahili culture, trading in local goods that were exported to the African coast, Madagascar, the Middle East and India, and political power lay with local rulers. The Portuguese made landfall in 1505; the Arabic word qamar means moon, hence the name Islands of the Moon.

French settlers later established plantations, first for sugar, which depended on the labour of numerous Africans, and in the 20th century for perfume plants and spices such as ylang-ylang, vanilla and cloves. In 1946 France redefined the islands as an overseas territory. In a referendum of 1974 the population voted overwhelmingly for independence, except in Mayotte, and after a unilateral declaration of independence in 1975 France kept sovereignty over Mayotte. The three other islands formed the Etat Comorian, later the Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros Islands, and in 2001 became the Union of the Comoros under a new constitution. Mayotte became a French department on 31 March 2011.

The archipelago is divided between the Union of the Comoros, formed by Grande Comore, Anjouan and Mohéli, and the French department of Mayotte, which the Union's constitution also claims. The islands hold eight native land mammal species, among them two lemurs and the endemic Livingstone's fruit bat, and the coelacanth, a deepwater fish known from fossils over 300 million years old, lives in their waters.
companions-of-the-prophet: The Arabic word sahaba, the companions, comes from a verb meaning to accompany or keep company with. The term covers the disciples of Muhammad who saw or met him in his lifetime and embraced Islam while he lived. The last of them, Abu al-Tufayl, died in 110 AH (728 CE). Their followers are named by generation: the Tābi'ūn knew at least one companion, and the next generation knew at least one of them.

Companions are also classed in groups: the Muhajirun, the migrants who left Mecca with Muhammad when he was persecuted, the Ansar, the people of Medina who protected them, and the Badriyyun who fought at the Battle of Badr. Lists of prominent companions usually give 50 or 60 names, but al-Qurtubi's work holds 2,770 biographies of men and 381 of women.

The companions played a major part in the Muslim battles, in hadith narration and in governance after Muhammad's death. According to the History of the Prophets and Kings, Abu Bakr, Umar, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah and the Ansar of Medina held consultations and chose Abu Bakr as the first caliph, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Uthman then selected Umar as the second. Later scholars accepted the companions' testimony about Muhammad's words and deeds and about the occasions of the Quran's revelation. Passed down through chains of trusted narrators, it became the basis of the developing Islamic tradition, from which the way of life (sunnah), the code of conduct (sharia) and jurisprudence (fiqh) are drawn.

The most widespread Sunni definition, given by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, holds that a companion is one who met Muhammad while believing in him and died a Muslim, however long or short the time. Anyone who later left Islam is not counted. Sunni scholars assume all companions to be just unless proven otherwise. The Shia, and some modern Sunni scholars, follow a stricter definition requiring substantial contact, such as living with Muhammad, joining his campaigns or preaching. The Shia therefore judge each companion individually, assess righteousness by loyalty to Muhammad's family after his death, and hold that some companions bear responsibility for the loss of the caliphate by Ali's family.
conakry: Conakry was originally settled on the small Tombo Island, one of the Îles de Los, and later spread to the neighbouring Kaloum Peninsula, a stretch of land 36 km long and between 0.2 and 6 km wide. The expanding urban area has since spread north-eastwards to occupy the whole of the peninsula. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a wet season of very heavy rainfall, more than 1,100 mm in both July and August, and a dry season dominated between December and April by the harmattan wind.

The city was essentially founded after Britain ceded the island to France in 1887. In 1885 the two island villages of Conakry and Boubinet had fewer than 500 inhabitants between them. Conakry became the capital of French Guinea and prospered as an export port, particularly after a railway to Kankan, now closed, opened the interior of the country to the large-scale export of groundnuts.

After Guinea gained independence in 1958 the population boomed, from 50,000 in 1958 to 600,000 in 1980. The city's small land area and relative isolation from the mainland, an advantage to its colonial founders, created an infrastructural burden after independence. In 1970 the conflict between Portuguese forces and the PAIGC independence fighters in neighbouring Portuguese Guinea spilled into the Republic of Guinea, when 350 Portuguese troops and Guinean loyalists landed near the capital, attacked the city and freed 26 Portuguese prisoners of war held by the PAIGC before withdrawing. Camp Boiro, a feared concentration camp, stood in Conakry during the rule of Sekou Touré.

Conakry is the capital and largest city of Guinea and its administrative, communications and economic centre. It forms a region and a prefecture of its own, the Conakry Special Zone, divided into communes. Its port ships alumina and bananas, and its manufactures include food products, cement and metal goods. Among its buildings are the Grand Mosque and the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Sainte-Marie, and the Sandervalia National Museum and the National Library of Guinea are in the city. Its population is roughly one fifth of that of Guinea, more than eight times that of the next city, Kankan.
concentration-camp: The English term concentration camp comes from the reconcentration camps (Spanish: reconcentrados) set up by the Spanish military in Cuba during the Ten Years' War of 1868–1878. Spain used such camps again in the Cuban War of Independence of 1895–98, when Valeriano Weyler's Reconcentration policy moved rural Cubans into them. The label was later applied to camps run by the United States during the Philippine–American War, by the British during the Second Boer War, and by the German Empire during the Herero and Nama genocide of 1904–1907, in which the death rate in the camps was 45 per cent, twice that of the British camps. Civilian internment may be older still, since a first example may date to the 1830s.

A concentration camp is a prison or other facility used to intern political prisoners or politically targeted groups, such as national or ethnic minorities, on grounds of national security, exploitation or punishment. The term covers systems that differ greatly in severity, mortality and architecture. What they share is that the inmates are held outside the rule of law. Extermination camps, whose main purpose is killing, are also loosely called concentration camps, and historians debate whether other cases of civilian internment should be called concentration camps or internment camps.

In the Russian Empire, katorga was a punishment for the most serious crimes; about 6,000 convicts were serving it in 1906 and 28,600 in 1916. During the Russian Civil War the Bolsheviks created separate prison camps under the Cheka. In 1929 the camps were put under the Joint State Political Directorate and expanded into the Gulag, which held some 18 million people from 1929 until 1953.

During the Armenian genocide, deported Armenians reaching Aleppo from mid-1915 were sent into camps across Syria and Upper Mesopotamia, including Ras al-Ayn and Deir ez-Zor, where hunger, disease and killings followed. It is estimated that up to 700,000 Armenians were killed in these camps between 1915 and 1918.

Nazi Germany opened camps in 1933 for tens of thousands of political prisoners, mainly members of the Communist Party and the Social Democratic Party, then arrested so-called anti-socials from 1937 and Jews increasingly from 1938. About 1.65 million people were registered as prisoners, and about a million of them died.
concepcion-chile: Concepción was founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1550 north of the Bío Bío River, at the site now known as Penco. It was named Concepción de María Purísima del Nuevo Extremo. The settlement lay a few kilometres north of La Frontera, the boundary between Spanish territory and the land of the Mapuche, who remained independent until the 1870s. Spanish authorities formally recognised it as a town two years later by royal decree and gave it a coat of arms still in use today. When the Spanish arrived, the chronicler Jerónimo de Vivar noted that local Mapuche wore gold and silver bracelets and crown-like ornaments, interpreted either as Incan gifts, war spoils or the adoption of Incan metallurgy.

The city was the capital of the Kingdom of Chile between 1565 and 1573 and kept the unofficial position of military capital for the rest of the colonial period. After a serious earthquake in 1751 it moved to the Valle de la Mocha, where the city centre and historic district now stand. Its inhabitants are still called penquistas, after Penco. The city was an important site in the struggle for Chile's independence, and the declaration of independence was held at the Plaza de la Independencia. Until the election of Manuel Montt as president in 1851, executive power in independent Chile was dominated by Concepción elites.

Concepción is the capital of the Biobío Region and of Concepción Province, about 500 km south of Santiago. It is the core of the Greater Concepción metropolitan area, the second largest city in Chile by urban area, and sits in the most heavily industrialized region of the country. It is known as the university city, with the Universidad de Concepción, the Universidad del Biobío and the Catholic University of the Most Holy Conception. Like most of Chile it is seismically active: an earthquake in 1939 destroyed much of the city, one in 1953 damaged 15 per cent of its buildings, and a major earthquake in 1960 had a nearby epicentre.
concordat-of-worms: The Investiture Controversy began in the middle of the 11th century, when a reforming movement in the Church sought to reassert the rights of the Holy See. Pope Gregory VII forbade secular rulers to make clerical appointments, and Emperor Henry IV, who habitually invested the bishops and abbots of the Empire, rejected the claim. The dispute outlasted both men. In 1111 Henry V made an agreement with Pope Paschal II at Sutri, but when it was not carried out he imprisoned the pope, who then yielded under duress and later went back on his promises.

Callixtus II resumed talks, and in autumn 1119 the emperor agreed in principle at Strasbourg to give up investing bishops and abbots with ring and crosier. A planned summit at Mouzon broke down, and Henry was excommunicated at the council at Reims. Afterwards most of the clergy became willing to compromise. In 1121 a faction of nobles led by Archbishop Adalbert I of Mainz pressed Henry to make peace, and in February 1122 Callixtus wrote to him in a conciliatory tone.

The talks seem to have taken place at nearby Mainz while Henry waited at Worms. The papal delegation was led by Cardinal Bishop Lamberto Scannabecchi of Ostia, the future Pope Honorius II. On 23 September 1122 delegates signed the documents outside the walls of Worms, which had no room for the crowd. The agreement was issued as two charters, the Calixtinum, addressed to the emperor, and the Henricianum, addressed to God. Neither was signed.

Henry renounced investiture with ring and staff, opened ecclesiastical appointments in his realm to canonical election, recognised the papal patrimony and promised to return church lands he or his father had seized. Callixtus allowed the emperor or his officials to be present at elections and to judge disputed ones, and let him invest bishops and abbots with a sceptre representing their temporal lands. In Germany this came before consecration, elsewhere in the Empire within six months. The charters were deliberately brief, and the word regalia meant different things to each side.

The First Lateran Council confirmed the concordat in March 1123 with nearly 300 bishops and 600 abbots present. Some followers of Paschal II cried non placet, and Callixtus told them that they had not to approve but to tolerate it. Henry V died in 1125. Historians disagree about how decisive the settlement was. Some stress that it ended the Ottonian and Salian imperial church system and showed that the emperor held no religious authority; others note that the king was left in possession of the field and that the controversy over investiture continued for at least another decade. Successive emperors found its terms favourable enough that it remained almost unaltered until the Empire was dissolved in 1806.
conde-sur-lescaut: Condé-sur-l'Escaut is a commune of the Nord department on the border with Belgium, 12 km north-east of Valenciennes. It lies at the confluence of the Haine and the Scheldt. The name comes from the Celtic word Condate, meaning confluence. A Romanised form, Condatum, was in use in the Roman period, and Condé was in use by the 14th century. The present name dates from 1886. The region is noted for its coal mines, which made it a strategic objective in both world wars.

The meeting of two rivers gave the site military importance from before Roman times. It was first occupied by the Nervians, then was the site of a Roman military camp and later a settlement of Franks. Saint Wasnulf preached at Condé and died there around 650, and Vikings held the town from 855 to 889. During the Middle Ages and the Renaissance it changed hands many times, falling to the Flemish forces of Jacques van Artevelde, to Louis XI of France, to Les Gueux in the Eighty Years' War and to Turenne.

Louis XIV seized the town in 1676, and it became part of France in 1678 with the Treaty of Nimègue. Vauban improved its fortifications. Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld captured it after a 92-day siege in 1793, and forces of the Seventh Coalition took it from Napoleon in 1815 and returned it to French control three years later. Germans occupied the town in the Second World War and used its people to run the adjacent coal mines. The U.S. 5th Armored Division liberated it on 2 September 1944.

Coal mining ended in 1989. The population peaked at 13,994 in 1975 and has since declined. The town is the eastern member of the Valenciennes metropolitan area, which administers 35 communes. It is known in music history as the home, retirement place and burial place of the Renaissance composer Josquin des Prez, who was provost of the church of Notre-Dame, which had one of the most sumptuous musical establishments in Hainaut. His house stood on the market square, and the church, with his tombstone, was destroyed in 1793.
condor-legion: After the military coup of 17 July 1936 began the Spanish Civil War, the Nationalists asked Germany and Italy for support. The first request for German aircraft, on 22 July, was for ten transport planes. Adolf Hitler decided to help on 25 or 26 July, though he was wary of provoking a wider European war. The first mission, Operation Magic Fire, used Junkers Ju 52 aircraft to carry the Spanish Army of Africa from Spanish Morocco to Spain, and German involvement was hidden through a dummy company and funded with three million Reichsmarks. The first contingent of 86 men left Germany on 1 August 1936, many of them believing they would only train the Nationalists.

The Legion was commanded by Hugo Sperrle, with Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma leading its ground element, which included small armoured units of Panzer I tanks. It had bomber, fighter, reconnaissance, anti-aircraft and signals groups. In 1937 it supported the Nationalist offensive in Biscay, a Basque region of northern Spain. Its aircraft attacked Otxandio and Durango, where the Basques said 250 civilians died on 31 March, and on 26 April it bombed Guernica in Operation Rügen. Casualties there are disputed: perhaps 200 or 300 people were killed, while the Basques reported 1,654 dead. The Times reporter George Steer wrote the first full account, noting German involvement.

The Legion also fought at the Battle of Brunete and in the campaign that ended with the fall of Santander and of Gijón on 21 October 1937. After the Nationalist conquest of Asturias, much of its industrial and mineral output was shipped to Germany as repayment for the Legion's service. Its maritime unit attacked Republican shipping and ports. The Legion left Spain in May 1939, sailing from Vigo to Hamburg, where crowds and ceremonies awaited it.

Many have regarded the intervention as a proving ground for the Second World War. Hermann Göring said at Nuremberg that he urged Hitler to help Franco partly to test the young Luftwaffe. The Messerschmitt Bf 109 entered service in Spain from about January 1937, and Wolfram von Richthofen, who commanded the Legion, later led ground-attack units in Poland, France and Operation Barbarossa. Adolf Galland, however, held that the value of the lessons was exaggerated and the wrong conclusions drawn. In 1997 German President Roman Herzog apologised to survivors of the Guernica raid, and in 1998 the German parliament had the names of former Legion members removed from military bases.
confederation-of-the-rhine: The Final Imperial Recess of 1803 transformed the Holy Roman Empire. About 112 immediate territories east of the Rhine were absorbed by larger states, all ecclesiastical territories but one were secularised, and most free imperial cities were mediatised. The Emperor lost important political support, and in 1804 Francis II took the title of Emperor of Austria to offset the loss of prestige. When the War of the Third Coalition began in 1805, Bavaria, Baden and Württemberg allied with Napoleon, and after Austerlitz Francis II had to assent to raising Bavaria and Württemberg to kingdoms.

The formation was not altogether voluntary. On 12 July 1806 Talleyrand summoned the princes' envoys in Paris and compelled them to sign a treaty whose terms were far harsher than expected. King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria was aghast that foreign policy would pass to Napoleon, the Protector of the Confederation, but his envoy was detained at the border until all the others had signed. Sixteen German states joined. On 1 August 1806 they seceded from the Holy Roman Empire, and on 6 August, after an ultimatum from Napoleon, Francis II declared the empire dissolved.

The treaty provided for common constitutional bodies, but the larger states wanted unlimited sovereignty. The highest office was held by Karl Theodor von Dalberg as Prince-primate, who presided over a Diet that never assembled. After Prussia's defeat in 1806, 23 more states joined, and in 1808 the confederation reached 36 states, ruling over some 14.5 to 15 million people. It served as a buffer between France and the two largest German states, Prussia and Austria.

It was above all a military alliance. Members had to keep substantial armies and supply France with troops, and found themselves more subordinated to Napoleon than they had been to the Habsburgs. Its states were of three kinds: model states ruled by Napoleon's relatives, such as the Kingdom of Westphalia under Jérôme Bonaparte; reform states, among them Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse-Darmstadt; and smaller states that joined after 1806, in which change was minimal. After Napoleon's failed invasion of Russia many members changed sides at the Battle of Leipzig, and the allies dissolved the confederation on 4 November 1813.

On 30 May 1814 the Treaty of Paris declared the German states independent. The Congress of Vienna abolished Napoleonic creations such as the Kingdom of Westphalia and the Grand Duchy of Berg, and most members in central and southern Germany survived with minor border changes. With Prussia and Austria they formed the German Confederation, created on 8 June 1815.
confucianism: Chinese has no term that corresponds directly to Confucianism. The nearest catch-all is rú, which in modern Chinese means scholar or learned man and in Old Chinese carried meanings such as to tame, to mould and to educate. Confucius regarded himself as a transmitter of cultural values from the earlier Xia, Shang and Western Zhou dynasties. The Zhou made their claim to rule rest on moral power, the Mandate of Heaven, which Tian, Heaven, gave to virtuous rulers. By the 6th century BCE the Zhou system of rites had become diffuse and was claimed by different rulers in the Zhou states.

Tradition held that Confucius wrote or edited the Five Classics, whose received versions were edited about 500 years later by the Imperial Librarian Liu Xin. The scholar Yao Xinzhong adds that nothing can be taken for granted about their early versions. Philosophers of the Warring States period built on his legacy, which is compiled in the Analects.

Confucianism seeks the unity of the individual self and Tian, and extends self-cultivation to family and society. Its ethics are summed up in the Five Constants worked out by Han scholars: ren, benevolence; yi, righteousness; li, propriety or rites; zhi, wisdom; and xin, sincerity. The junzi, literally son of a lord, became in the Analects a person of noble character, a model any individual may reach through discipline of mind and action. Confucius also taught the rectification of names, holding that disorder stems from failing to call things by their proper names.

Social harmony requires everyone to play their part, as when Confucius tells Duke Jing of Qi that there is government when the prince is prince, the minister minister, the father father and the son son. A ruler governs by his own virtue rather than coercion. Confucius admitted students of different classes, and the Analects has him say that in teaching there should be no distinction of classes.

Confucianism was suppressed under the Legalist Qin dynasty and flourished under the Han, becoming the dominant ideological framework. Neo-Confucianism arose in response to the rising influence of Buddhism and Taoism and became central to the imperial examination system and the scholar-official class of the Song. The examination system was abolished in Korea in 1894, in China in 1905 and in Vietnam in 1919. Critics were present from the start, among them Mozi and the Legalist Han Fei. Jesuit missionaries translated Confucian texts in the 17th century, and the translations influenced Enlightenment thinkers, including Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.
confucius: The name Confucius is a Latinized form of the Mandarin Kǒngfūzǐ, meaning roughly Great Master Kong, coined in the late 16th century by early Jesuit missionaries to China. His family name was Kong and his given name Qiu, meaning hill or mound. His courtesy name was Zhongni, the Zhong indicating that he was the second son in his family.

It is thought that he was born on 28 September 551 BCE in Zou, in modern Qufu, Shandong. The area was formally controlled by the kings of Zhou but effectively independent under the local lords of Lu. His father Kong He, an elderly commandant of the local Lu garrison, died when Confucius was three years old, and his mother Yan Zhengzai raised him in poverty.

Traditional accounts trace the family back through the dukes of Song to the Shang dynasty, though not all modern scholars accept this descent. He was born into the class of shi, between the aristocracy and the common people, and was educated at schools for commoners. At 19 he married Qi Guanshi, and a year later their son Kong Li was born. He is said to have held various government jobs in his early 20s and to have mourned his mother for three years.

In the Analects, Confucius presents himself as a transmitter who invented nothing. He put the most emphasis on study and wanted his disciples to master older classics rather than build a systematic theory. Tradition credits him with authoring or editing the Five Classics, but modern scholars are cautious about attributing particular assertions to him, since some of the texts and philosophy associated with him are more ancient, and the Analects were compiled many years after his death. His ethics stress self-cultivation and emulation of moral exemplars over rules, and he taught a negative form of the Golden Rule, sometimes called the Silver Rule.

His disciples and his grandson Zisi continued his school, and Mencius in the 4th century BCE and Xunzi in the 3rd century BCE elaborated his ideas in different ways. The Qin state, which conquered all of China in 221 BCE, adopted Legalism as its official doctrine. Under Emperor Wu of Han, works attributed to Confucius were made the official imperial philosophy and required reading for civil service examinations in 140 BCE, a practice continued nearly unbroken until the end of imperial China in 1912.
congo-basin: The Congo Basin is the sedimentary basin of the Congo River, a massive depression within the Congo Craton, in a region of Central Africa known as west equatorial Africa. It begins in the highlands of the East African Rift system, with the Chambeshi, the Uele and Ubangi rivers in the upper reaches and the Lualaba River draining wetlands in the middle reaches, and it ends where the Congo River empties into the Gulf of Guinea. The basin covers a total of 3.7 million square kilometres. Rainfall is between 1,500 and 2,000 millimetres a year and temperatures usually lie between 20 and 30 degrees.

The first inhabitants of the basin are believed to have been hunter-gatherers, whose small numbers reflect the dense forests and wet climate; remnants of their culture survive. Bantu peoples later migrated into the region and founded the Kingdom of Kongo. By the late 19th century Belgium, France and Portugal had established colonial control over the whole region. The General Act of the Berlin Conference of 1885 gave a precise definition to the conventional basin of the Congo, which included the entire actual basin plus some other areas, and bound its signatories to neutrality there, though this was not respected during the First World War.

Countries wholly or partly in the Congo region include Angola, Gabon, Burundi, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Tanzania and Zambia. The basin holds some of the largest undisturbed stands of tropical rainforest on Earth, with humid forests covering 1.6 million square kilometres, and large wetlands. Its animals include the okapi, African forest elephant, bonobo, chimpanzee and western lowland gorilla. Eight sites in the basin are on the World Heritage List, among them national parks such as Virunga, Salonga and Garamba.
congo-crisis: Colonial rule in the Congo began in the late 19th century with the Congo Free State, the personal colony of King Leopold II of Belgium, recognised internationally in 1885. Violence by its officials against Congolese and its system of economic extraction brought diplomatic pressure on Belgium, which took control in 1908 and created the Belgian Congo. A nationalist movement grew among the évolués in the 1950s, divided into parties along ethnic and regional lines. The largest was the Mouvement National Congolais, in which Patrice Lumumba became a leading figure.

At a Round Table Conference in Brussels in January 1960 Belgium, which had hoped for at least thirty years before independence, was pressed into fixing 30 June 1960. Delegates did not agree on federalism, ethnicity or Belgium's future role. Few preparations had been made, and white technical experts stayed in post, which many Congolese resented.

In the first week of July 1960 the army mutinied and violence broke out between black and white civilians. Belgium sent troops to protect fleeing whites. On 11 July Moïse Tshombe declared Katanga independent, saying 'We are seceding from chaos', and South Kasai also seceded. On 14 July the United Nations Security Council called for Belgian withdrawal and a UN force, but Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld would not use it against the secessionists. Lumumba then asked the Soviet Union for help, which split the government. On 5 September President Joseph Kasa-Vubu dismissed him, and Colonel Joseph-Désiré Mobutu took control in a coup.

Lumumba was captured on 1 December 1960 and handed to Tshombe's forces, who executed him on 17 January 1961 with the help of Belgian officers. Hammarskjöld was killed in a plane crash in late 1961, and the UN then took a firmer line. With UN troops the central government ended the secessions of Katanga and South Kasai by the start of 1963. In 1964 Maoist-inspired Simba rebels took territory in the east. Belgium and the United States intervened at Stanleyville in November 1964, and mercenaries helped the army retake the ground. About 100,000 people are believed to have died.

After elections in March 1965 a new stalemate between Tshombe and Kasa-Vubu paralysed the government, and on 25 November 1965 Mobutu seized power in a bloodless coup. He centralised the state, created a single party in 1967 and renamed the country Zaire in 1971. He remained in power until 1997. A Belgian inquiry led to an official apology in 2001 for moral responsibility, though not direct involvement, in Lumumba's killing. Historians usually portray the crisis as a time of intense disorder, and it was also a proxy conflict of the Cold War. Its turmoil helped to ignite the Portuguese Colonial War in neighbouring Angola.
congo-free-state: Until the middle of the 19th century the Congo lay at the heart of independent Africa, since fierce local resistance, rainforest and diseases such as malaria and sleeping sickness kept Europeans from settling the interior. In 1876 Leopold II of Belgium hosted the Brussels Geographic Conference and founded the International African Association, which he presented as a humanitarian enterprise but used to promote his plans to seize central Africa. At the Berlin Conference, convened by Otto von Bismarck in November 1884, he persuaded the powers that he would do philanthropic work and not tax trade. On 29 May 1885 he announced the name Congo Free State. Leopold ruled it from Brussels and never visited.

Leopold held the title Sovereign of the Congo Free State. He could not meet the costs of the state and set up a system to maximise revenue. Land without a habitation or cultivated plot was declared vacant and belonged to the state, and communities had to deliver set quotas of rubber and ivory. By the late 1890s wild rubber far surpassed ivory as the main revenue, and it peaked in 1903. Failure to meet rubber quotas was punishable by death, and soldiers of the Force Publique had to bring in the hand of each person they shot, so that quotas were in part paid in severed hands.

A reduction of the population between the start of Leopold's control and 1908 is noted by all who compared the two dates, but estimates of the death toll vary considerably. Some contemporary observers suggest a decrease by half. Roger Casement named war, starvation, reduced births and disease as the main causes. Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, published in 1899, and the Congo Reform Association, founded by Casement and E. D. Morel, drew international opposition.

Under international pressure the Belgian Parliament reluctantly annexed the state on 15 November 1908 as the colony of the Belgian Congo, and Leopold died in Brussels on 17 December 1909. The state included the entire area of the present Democratic Republic of the Congo. Whether the killing amounts to genocide is debated: Adam Hochschild wrote that it was of genocidal proportions but not strictly speaking a genocide, while Robert G. Weisbord argued that the conditions would qualify under the UN convention.
congo-river: The Congo River, formerly also called the Zaire, is the only major river to cross the equator twice. Its basin covers about 4 million square kilometres and ten countries, around 13 percent of Africa. The Chambeshi River in Zambia is generally taken as its source, and the Lualaba is the river upstream of the Boyoma Falls. From Kisangani it flows north-west, then south-west to Pool Malebo, where Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other. Below the Pool it falls through the Livingstone Falls, a series of 32 falls and rapids, to the sea at Muanda. Its flow is stable because its basin lies on both sides of the Equator, and it is one of the deepest rivers in the world.

The whole basin is populated by Bantu peoples, whose expansion is estimated to have reached the middle Congo by about 500 BCE. The name Congo comes from the Kingdom of Kongo, once on the southern bank, formed in the late 14th century. The name Zaire is a Portuguese adaptation of the Kikongo nzere, river. European exploration began in 1482, when the Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão found the estuary and made contact with the Kingdom of Kongo. The full course remained unknown throughout the early modern period.

Henry Morton Stanley's expedition of 1876-77 proved that the Lualaba fed the Congo and not the Nile. It reached Boma on 9 August 1877, having most probably lost 132 people to disease, hunger, drowning, killing and desertion. Stanley founded Kinshasa as a trading post in 1881, named Léopoldville for Leopold II of Belgium, who claimed the basin privately as the Congo Free State in 1885.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo are both named after the river. Although the Livingstone Falls block access from the sea, nearly the whole river above them is navigable in sections, especially between Kinshasa and Kisangani, and it remains a lifeline in a land with few roads or railways. Its basin holds the Congo rainforest, the second-largest rainforest area in the world, and almost 800 fish species have been recorded there, many found nowhere else.
congress-of-berlin: The Treaty of San Stefano of March 1878, which ended the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878, created a large Principality of Bulgaria as an autonomous vassal of the sultan. This extended Russian influence over the Balkans and alarmed the other powers. Britain saw the entire Mediterranean as its sphere of influence, and Austria-Hungary wanted Habsburg control over the Balkans. Otto von Bismarck therefore called the Congress and presided over it as an impartial mediator, since Germany stood to gain nothing from the crisis. Before it opened, Britain concluded the Cyprus Convention on 4 June 1878, a secret alliance with the Ottomans that let Britain occupy Cyprus.

The Congress met from 13 June to 13 July 1878 at Bismarck's Reich Chancellery in Berlin. Britain, Austria-Hungary, France, Germany, Italy, Russia and the Ottoman Empire were members. Delegates from Greece, Romania, Serbia and Montenegro attended only the sessions that concerned their states. The Congress revised or eliminated 18 of the 29 articles of the Treaty of San Stefano.

Romania, Serbia and Montenegro were recognised as independent. Romania received Northern Dobruja but had to give Southern Bessarabia to Russia. Bulgaria was divided into the Principality of Bulgaria, with nominal autonomy under the Ottomans, and Eastern Rumelia, an autonomous province under a Christian ruler. Macedonia stayed under the Ottoman Empire. Austria-Hungary was given the administration of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the right to garrison the Sanjak of Novi Pazar, and Britain took over the administration of Cyprus.

The result was at first hailed as a success for peace, but most participants were dissatisfied. Russia, which had won the war, felt humiliated, and Gorchakov called the Treaty of Berlin the darkest page of his life. Bulgaria was left with less than half the territory planned at San Stefano. The Serbs resented Russia's consent to the Austrian administration of Bosnia, and Bismarck was hated by Russian nationalists. The League of the Three Emperors was destroyed. Historians see the settlement as having sown the seeds of the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 and the First World War.
congress-of-vienna: The Congress of Vienna was a series of diplomatic meetings held from September 1814 to June 1815 to agree a new layout for the European order after the fall of Napoleon Bonaparte. It was chaired by the Austrian statesman Klemens von Metternich. Its aim was a long-term peace: the main powers were to be resized so that they could balance each other. Conservative leaders such as Metternich also wished to restrain Bonapartist, republican and liberal movements. More than 200 states and princely houses were represented, and much business was done informally at salons, banquets and balls.

The four victorious powers, Austria, the United Kingdom, Prussia and Russia, hoped to exclude France, but Talleyrand made himself part of the inner councils. The hardest question was the Polish-Saxon crisis, since Russia wanted most of Poland and Prussia all of Saxony. Austria and Britain opposed this, and on 3 January 1815 they and France signed a treaty promising war on Russia and Prussia if necessary. The Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before the Battle of Waterloo.

Russia received most of the Duchy of Warsaw, Prussia three-fifths of Saxony and land on the Rhine, and Austria Lombardy-Venetia. A German Confederation of 39 states replaced the nearly 300 states of the former Holy Roman Empire. The Netherlands and the Southern Netherlands were united as a kingdom under the House of Orange-Nassau. The Congress gave rise to the Concert of Europe. Critics have judged the settlement a reaction that ignored national and liberal movements. Others, among them Henry Kissinger and Paul Schroeder, credit it with preventing a widespread European war from 1815 to 1914.
connecticut: Connecticut is bordered by Long Island Sound to the south, New York to the west, Massachusetts to the north and Rhode Island to the east. It is named after the Connecticut River, the longest in New England, which roughly bisects the state. The river's name derives from anglicized spellings of Quinnetuket, a Mohegan-Pequot word for long tidal river. Many coastal towns lie less than 20 feet above sea level, and because the coast is on Long Island Sound, an estuary, it is relatively protected from high storm waves.

Evidence of human presence dates back 10,000 years. The peoples were semi-nomadic and shared Algonquian languages. In the early 17th century about 8,000 Pequots lived in the south-east, a number roughly halved by the smallpox epidemic of 1633–34, and 1,500 to 2,500 Mohegans lived west of the Thames. Their economies combined hunting, shellfishing, gathering and maize agriculture, and wampum from quahog and whelk shells served as currency and as a record of agreements.

In 1633 the Dutch West India Company established a short-lived settlement, House of Hope, in Hartford. The Dutch colony of New Netherland initially claimed half of Connecticut, but the English founded the first major settlements at about the same time. Thomas Hooker led followers from the Massachusetts Bay Colony to form the Connecticut Colony, and the Saybrook and New Haven Colonies, founded by other settlers from Massachusetts, had both merged into it by the mid-1660s. The Fundamental Orders of 1638–39 framed its first government, and King Charles II granted a charter in 1662.

Connecticut was one of the Thirteen Colonies that rejected British rule. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 its delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth proposed the Connecticut Compromise, a bicameral Congress with proportional representation in the House and equal representation of the states in the Senate. In January 1788 Connecticut became the fifth state to ratify the Constitution. Hartford became the sole capital in 1875; before then New Haven and Hartford alternated.

Hartford is the capital and Bridgeport the most populous city. Connecticut is the third-smallest state by area. Its nickname, the Constitution State, was adopted in 1959. Yale University stands in New Haven, and the United States Coast Guard Academy in New London.
connecticut-river: The Connecticut River flows roughly south for 406 miles (653 km) through four states. It rises from Fourth Connecticut Lake, a small pond 300 yards south of the Canadian border in Pittsburg, New Hampshire, and for 255 miles forms the border between New Hampshire and Vermont. After the last ice age the middle valley lay at the bottom of Lake Hitchcock, and its rich, almost rockless soil comes from that lake's sediments. The name is a corruption of the Mohegan word quinetucket and the Nipmuc kwinitekw, meaning beside the long, tidal river. Because of large shifting sandbars at its mouth, it is the only major river in the northeastern United States without a port there.

Archaeology shows human habitation of the valley for 6,000 years before the present. The Pequots dominated the southern part, from the river's mouth to just below Middletown, and kept an uneasy stand-off with their rivals the Mohegans. In 1614 the Dutch explorer Adriaen Block became the first European to chart the river, which he called the Fresh River and claimed for the Netherlands as the northeastern border of New Netherland. Dutch traders built a fortified post at the site of Hartford in 1623. Puritan groups followed: settlers from Plymouth Colony founded Windsor after 1632, a group from Watertown in the Massachusetts Bay Colony founded Wethersfield in 1633, and Hartford and Springfield were established in 1635 and 1636.

The valley's fertile soil and central position made it the object of centuries of border disputes. Springfield broke away from the Connecticut Colony in 1641, which brought the Massachusetts Bay Colony to the river. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 set the border between New Hampshire and the Province of Canada at the northwesternmost headwaters of the Connecticut. Several streams fit that description, and the dispute produced the short-lived Indian Stream Republic, from 1832 to 1835.

The river's numerous falls powered mills and waterwheels, and industry grew up on its banks, especially at Springfield and Hartford. From about 1865 the river carried massive logging drives to sawmills, and these spring drives stopped after 1915, with a final drive in 1918. In March 1936 a flood destroyed numerous bridges. Its watershed of 11,260 square miles covers parts of five states and one Canadian province, and its valley holds some of the most productive farmland in the northeastern United States.
conques: Conques lies at the confluence of the rivers Dourdou de Conques and Ouche, in a valley, and takes its name from the Occitan word conca, meaning basin, which comes from the Latin concha, a shell. The village is built on a hillside with narrow medieval streets, so that large vehicles cannot enter the historic centre and most day visitors arrive on foot. It was largely passed by in the nineteenth century and was saved from oblivion by the efforts of a small number of dedicated people. The historic core therefore has very little construction dating from between 1800 and 1950.

The first monastery building at Conques was an eighth-century oratory built by monks fleeing the Saracens in Spain. In the eleventh century the original chapel was destroyed to make way for a much larger church, since the arrival of the relics of Saint Faith, a young woman martyred in the fourth century, had shifted the pilgrimage route from Agen to Conques. A second phase, finished by the end of the eleventh century, added five radiating chapels. A third phase, completed early in the twelfth century, was inspired by the churches of Toulouse and Santiago de Compostela, with galleries over the aisles and a western aisle for the increased pilgrim traffic.

The Abbey Church of Sainte-Foy was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1998, as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France. Conques is counted among Les Plus Beaux Villages de France. On 1 January 2016 it was merged into the new commune of Conques-en-Rouergue. The American author Hannah Green wrote Little Saint, a book about the town and its church, after visiting in 1975.
conrad-i-of-germany: Conrad, called the Younger, was the son of Duke Conrad of Thuringia, called the Elder, and his wife Glismoda, who was probably related to Ota, wife of the Carolingian emperor Arnulf of Carinthia. The Conradines, counts in the Franconian Lahngau region, had been loyal supporters of the Carolingians, and they competed with the sons of the Babenberg duke Henry of Franconia for predominance in Franconia. In 906 the two parties fought near Fritzlar. Conrad the Elder was killed, as were two of the three Babenberg brothers, and King Louis the Child took the Conradines' side. Conrad then became the undisputed duke of all Franconia. He failed, however, to extend Conradine rule over western Lotharingia.

After the death of Louis the Child, Conrad was elected king of East Francia on 10 November 911 at Forchheim by the rulers of Saxony, Swabia and Bavaria. He was the first king not of the Carolingian dynasty, the first elected by the nobility and the first to be anointed. The dukes kept Charles the Simple, king of West Francia, from the throne. Only Reginar, duke of Lotharingia, refused allegiance and joined West Francia.

Because he was himself one of the dukes, Conrad found it hard to establish his authority over them. Henry of Saxony rebelled against him until 915, and Burchard II of Swabia demanded and received more autonomy. Erchanger of Swabia revolted in 913, defeated the royal army near Lake Constance and was executed on 21 January 917 with his brother Berthold. Arnulf of Bavaria called on the Magyars for help. His campaigns against Charles the Simple to regain Lotharingia and Aachen failed. The Magyar raids, continuing since the Bavarian defeat at the Battle of Pressburg in 907, further weakened his authority.

Severely injured in one of his battles with Arnulf, Conrad died on 23 December 918 at Weilburg Castle and was buried in Fulda Cathedral. According to the chronicler Widukind of Corvey, he persuaded his brother Eberhard of Franconia on his deathbed to offer the crown to Henry the Fowler, duke of Saxony and one of his main opponents, whom he thought the only duke able to hold the kingdom together against the rivalries of the dukes and the Magyar raids.

Eberhard and the Frankish nobles accepted this advice in May 919, and Henry was elected king at the Diet of Fritzlar. Kingship passed from the Franks to the Saxons. Eberhard succeeded Conrad as duke of Franconia and was killed in 939 at the Battle of Andernach during a rebellion against Otto I; the duchy then became a direct possession of the Ottonian dynasty until 1024.
conrad-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Conrad was the son of the Franconian count Henry of Speyer and Adelaide of Metz, and as a child he inherited the titles of count of Speyer and Worms. He was a great-great-grandson of Otto the Great. In 1016 he married Gisela of Swabia, a twice-widowed duchess whose son Ernest II was a minor duke. Conrad hoped to act as regent in Swabia, but Emperor Henry II gave the guardianship to Archbishop Poppo of Trier, which strained relations between the Salian family and the Ottonian house.

Henry II died childless in 1024, and on 4 September an assembly of princes at Kamba chose Conrad as king. He toured the kingdom to win recognition, gaining the Saxon nobles at Minden by promising to respect their customs and laws, while the princes of Lorraine rejected his claim. In Italy many nobles considered the throne vacant, and the Lombard cities offered the crown to Robert II of France and then to Duke William V of Aquitaine, who both refused. On 26 March 1027 Pope John XIX crowned Conrad and Gisela in Rome, in the presence of Cnut the Great and Rudolph III of Burgundy.

His stepson Ernest II rebelled in Swabia and rose again during the Italian expedition. Conrad continued the Ottonian system of using bishops and abbots as imperial servants but ended the favouritism once shown to churchmen. From his second Italian expedition in 1036 he won the lesser nobles, the valvassores, against the bishops. When Rudolph III died childless in 1032, Conrad claimed Burgundy and incorporated it into the empire, so that Germany, Italy and Burgundy formed the royal triad.

In 1038 Conrad went to southern Italy to settle a dispute over Capua, took the city and gave it to Guaimar IV of Salerno. An epidemic then killed many of his troops on the return. He died of gout at Utrecht on 4 June 1039 and was buried at Speyer Cathedral, which he founded and which holds the Salian emperors. His son Henry, elected and anointed king in 1028, succeeded as Henry III. His chaplain Wipo of Burgundy wrote a biography in chronicle form.
conrad-iii-of-germany: Conrad was the son of Duke Frederick I of Swabia and Agnes, a daughter of Emperor Henry IV. After his father's death in 1105 his elder brother Frederick II inherited Swabia. In 1116 their uncle, Emperor Henry V, made Conrad Duke of Franconia. When Henry V died in 1125, Conrad unsuccessfully backed Frederick for the kingship.

Frederick was banned and Conrad lost Franconia. With the support of the imperial cities, Swabia and Austria he was elected anti-king at Nuremberg in December 1127, was crowned King of Italy at Monza but achieved little there, and in 1135 acknowledged Lothair III as emperor. After Lothair died in December 1137, Conrad was elected king at Coblenz on 7 March 1138 and crowned at Aachen six days later. Henry the Proud, the most powerful prince in Germany, refused to accept this, and Conrad stripped him of his lands. The civil war that followed is considered the first act of the struggle between Guelphs and Ghibellines. A peace was made at Frankfurt in May 1142.

In 1146 Conrad heard Bernard of Clairvaux preach the Second Crusade at Speyer and joined Louis VII. He had his son Henry Berengar elected king before leaving. His army of about 20,000 men crossed Anatolia rather than taking the coast, and on 25 October 1147 the Seljuk Turks defeated it at Dorylaeum, killing or capturing most of the foot soldiers. Conrad fell ill at Ephesus, recovered at Constantinople, and later took part in the failed Siege of Damascus.

In 1150 Conrad and Henry Berengar defeated Welf VI and his son at Flochberg. Henry Berengar died that year, and the Welfs and Hohenstaufen made peace in 1152. Conrad was never crowned emperor and styled himself King of the Romans until his death on 15 February 1152. According to the account of his last hours, he named his nephew Frederick Barbarossa as successor rather than his six-year-old son Frederick. Barbarossa was elected king at Cologne a few weeks later, and the son received Swabia.
conservatism: The Anglo-Irish statesman Edmund Burke, who opposed the French Revolution, is credited as one of the forefathers of Western conservative thought in the 1790s, along with the Savoyard statesman Joseph de Maistre. Burke served as private secretary to the Marquess of Rockingham and as official pamphleteer to the Rockingham branch of the Whig party, which together with the Tories made up the conservatives of the late 18th century United Kingdom. The first established use of the term in a political context came in 1818 from François-René de Chateaubriand, during the Bourbon Restoration.

Conservatism seeks to promote and preserve traditional institutions, customs and values, and its central tenets vary with the culture in which it appears. In Western countries conservatives have sought to preserve institutions such as the family, organised religion, the nation-state, property rights, aristocracy and monarchy. Political scientist Andrew Heywood names five central beliefs: tradition, human imperfection, organic society, authority and hierarchy, and property. The philosopher Michael Oakeshott wrote that to be conservative is to prefer the familiar to the unknown and the tried to the untried.

The ideology has many variants. Paternalistic conservatism first arose in the United Kingdom under Benjamin Disraeli's One Nation Toryism and stresses the obligation of the privileged towards the poor. Liberal conservatism joins a minimal role for the state in the economy to a strong state for law and order. Reactionary conservatism seeks to return to an earlier state of affairs.

Early European forms of conservatism were often reactionary and romantic, idealising the Middle Ages with their feudal order, aristocratic rule and established church. In the late 19th century conservatism became more progressive, adopting capitalism and nationalism, which until then had been anti-traditionalist forces. In the first half of the 20th century, as socialist movements grew stronger and the Tsarist regime fell in the Russian Revolution, conservatism in Austria, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Spain and Romania moved to the far right and became more authoritarian. After the war it took a more moderate form, with Christian-democratic parties dominating Western Europe. In Latin America conservative elites held power through the Catholic Church and the military.
conservative-party-uk: The Conservative Party was founded in 1834 from the Tory Party and was, with the Liberal Party, one of the two dominant parties of the 19th century. Writers differ about its deeper roots. Some trace it to the Tory Party; others point to a faction rooted in the 18th-century Whig Party that gathered around William Pitt the Younger in the 1780s, known as Pittites, who never used the terms Tory or Conservative. From about 1812 the name Tory was commonly used for a new party that, in the historian Robert Blake's words, are the ancestors of Conservatism.

Under the Earl of Derby and Benjamin Disraeli the party carried the Reform Act 1867. In 1886 it allied with the Liberal Unionist Party and, under Lord Salisbury and Arthur Balfour, held power for all but three of the next twenty years, until a heavy defeat in 1906 when it split over free trade. The Liberal Unionists merged with it in 1912.

After the landslide of 1918 the Conservatives dominated the government of David Lloyd George. In May 1940 a National Government was formed under Winston Churchill, but the party lost the 1945 general election in a landslide to Labour. It returned in 1951. Margaret Thatcher deposed Edward Heath in 1975 and won the 1979 general election. John Major won the 1992 election, the party's fourth successive victory.

The party comprises the voluntary party, the parliamentary party and the professional party. Membership peaked in the mid-1950s at about 3 million. Its factions have included one-nation conservatives, dominant in the 20th century until the rise of Thatcherism in the 1970s, free-market Thatcherites, who sought lower taxes and privatisation, and traditionalists, who support the Church of England, the unitary British state and the family. Historically the party favoured protectionism and the British Empire, and since the 1980s it has generally favoured free markets. It opposes independence for any part of the United Kingdom.
constans-i: Constans was the third and youngest son of Constantine the Great and Fausta. He was educated at Constantinople under the poet Aemilius Magnus Arborius, who taught him Latin. On 25 December 333 his father raised him to caesar. He was engaged to Olympias, daughter of the praetorian prefect Ablabius, but never married.

After Constantine's death, Constans and his brothers Constantine II and Constantius II were proclaimed augusti and divided the empire on 9 September 337. Constans received Italy, Africa and Illyricum, and in 338 he campaigned against the Sarmatians.

Constantine II tried to issue legislation for Africa in 339 and invaded Italy a year later, but was ambushed and killed by Constans' troops, and Constans took over his territories. From 341 to 342 he campaigned against the Franks, after an initial setback ending in victory and a favourable peace. In early 343 he visited Britain, for reasons that remain unclear.

He issued an edict in 341 banning pagan sacrifices but soon legislated against the destruction of temples. His support for Nicene orthodoxy and Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria brought him into conflict with Constantius II. The Council of Serdica of 343 failed to settle it, and by 345 Constans was threatening civil war, until Constantius let Athanasius return. He also used the army against Donatism in Africa.

On 18 January 350 the general Magnentius was proclaimed emperor at Augustodunum (Autun) with the support of court officials such as Marcellinus. Constans, on a hunting trip, tried to reach Hispania but was cornered at Helena (Elne) in the eastern Pyrenees and killed after seeking sanctuary in a temple.

Ancient sources, which may reflect Magnentius' propaganda, blame his fall on corruption, neglect of parts of the empire and contempt for soldiers. Jill Harries and others doubt this and see the revolt as the work of an apprehensive official, noting that Constans often travelled with only a small escort.
constans-ii: Constans was born on 7 November 630 in Constantinople, the son of Constantine III and Gregoria. Constantine III was a son of Emperor Heraclius. When Heraclius died in February 641, Constantine III and his younger half-brother Heraclonas succeeded him, and Constantine III died suddenly after three months. In September 641 the ten-year-old Constans was crowned co-emperor, amid rumours that Heraclonas and his mother Martina had poisoned his father. Around 5 November the general Valentinus deposed Heraclonas, leaving Constans sole emperor. He reigned at first under a regency of senators led by Patriarch Paul II of Constantinople.

His reign coincided with the Arab conquests. The Byzantines withdrew completely from Egypt in 642. A fleet under the admiral Manuel retook Alexandria in 645, but its commander plundered the countryside and was forced to leave. In 647 Arab forces entered Armenia and Cappadocia, and a major offensive in 650 and 651 led Constans to negotiate with Mu'awiya I, the governor of Syria. In 655 Constans led a fleet against the Muslims at the Battle of the Masts, off Lycia. About 500 Byzantine ships were destroyed and the emperor was almost killed. Peace with the Arabs followed in 659, and in 658 he defeated the Slavs in the Balkans.

In religion he tried to steer a middle line between Orthodoxy and Monothelitism, forbidding discussion of the natures of Christ by the Typos of 648, which satisfied few. Pope Martin I condemned both the doctrine and the decree at the Lateran Council of 649. He was arrested in 653, brought to Constantinople, condemned and exiled to Cherson, where he died in 655. Constans also forced his younger brother Theodosius to take holy orders and had him killed in 660.

Having earned the hatred of the people of Constantinople, he left the city for Syracuse in Sicily. From 663 he campaigned in Italy against the Lombard Duchy of Benevento, besieging Benevento without success before withdrawing to Naples. That year he spent twelve days in Rome, the first emperor to visit it since 476, where Pope Vitalian received him with honour. He stripped buildings, the Pantheon among them, of their bronze, and his later demands in Calabria and Sardinia enraged his Italian subjects.

On 15 July 668 Constans was assassinated in his bath by his chamberlain, either with a bucket or with a knife. His son Constantine succeeded him as Constantine IV and quickly suppressed a brief usurpation in Sicily by Mezezius. Chinese histories record an embassy from the Byzantine ruler in 643, which they name Boduoli, to the Tang emperor Taizong.
constantine-algeria: Constantine, also spelled Qacentina, lies about 80 kilometres from the Mediterranean coast on the banks of the Rhumel River. It stands on a plateau 640 metres above sea level, framed by a deep ravine, and is often called the City of Bridges because of the many bridges that connect the hills and ravines it is built on. It is the railhead of an agricultural area and a centre of the grain trade, and is regarded as the capital of eastern Algeria.

In antiquity the city was Cirta, capital of the Berber kingdom of Numidia. In 112 BCE it was the capital of King Jugurtha, and the Roman generals Metellus and Gaius Marius used it as a base against him. In 311 CE it was destroyed in a war between the emperor Maxentius and the usurper Domitius Alexander, and in 313 it was rebuilt and renamed Constantina for Constantine the Great. Under Roman rule it exported wheat. The Vandals captured it in 432 and it returned to the Byzantine Exarchate of Africa in 534. After the Arab conquest of the 8th century it became known as Qacentina.

The city recovered in the 12th century and under the Almohad and Hafsid rulers was a prosperous market with links to Pisa, Genoa and Venice. The Ottoman Empire took it in 1529, and it was ruled by a bey subordinate to the dey of Algiers. Salah Bey, who ruled from 1770 to 1792, built much of the Muslim architecture still visible. The last bey, Ahmed Bey, led a fierce resistance to the French, who captured the city by 13 October 1837. In 1880 Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran, working in its military hospital, discovered that the cause of malaria is a protozoan.

Constantine is the capital of Constantine Province and the third largest city in Algeria, with about 450,000 inhabitants. Its monuments include the Great Mosque of 1136, the El Bey Mosque of 1703, the Ahmed Bey Palace and the ruins of a Roman aqueduct. The Roman city of Tiddis and the mausoleum of the Numidian king Massinissa lie nearby.
constantine-i: Constantine was born on 27 February at Naissus, in Moesia Superior; the day is recorded but not the year, and scholars have proposed dates between 271 and 280, most favouring 272 or 273. His father was Flavius Constantius, an army officer who became one of the four emperors of the Tetrarchy, and his mother Helena was a woman of low birth, probably from Bithynia. He was educated at the court of Diocletian, where he was held as something of a hostage, and served Diocletian and Galerius against the Danube tribes and the Persians. In 305 he left Galerius's court and joined his father in Gaul.

After his father's death in 306 the army at Eboracum proclaimed Constantine augustus. His share was Britain, Gaul and Spain, and he drove back the Picts and the Franks. In 307 he married Fausta, daughter of Maximian, who rebelled against him in 310 and hanged himself that July. Galerius's edict of 30 April 311 ended the persecutions. Constantine then defeated the emperors Maxentius and Licinius in the civil wars of the Tetrarchy, and in 324 became sole ruler of the empire.

Constantine separated civil and military authority, disbanded the Praetorian Guard and introduced the solidus, a gold coin struck in similar weight and purity for seven centuries. He won victories over the Franks, Alamanni, Goths and Sarmatians. He favoured Christianity from 312, had a part in the Edict of Milan of 313, and convoked the First Council of Nicaea in 325, which produced the Nicene Creed. He was baptised by Eusebius of Nicomedia, and some modern scholars debate his beliefs.

He chose the Greek city of Byzantium as capital, founding it in 324 and dedicating it on 11 May 330 as Constantinopolis. He left the empire to his sons, replacing the Tetrarchy with dynastic succession. Eastern Churches venerate him as a saint equal to the Apostles. The Donation of Constantine, a document of the 8th century, was shown by Lorenzo Valla in 1440 to be a forgery.
constantine-i-of-greece: Constantine was born in Athens on 2 August 1868, the eldest son of King George I and Queen Olga. As the first Greek-born member of the royal family, he was greeted with great enthusiasm, and crowds shouted for him to be named Constantine, after the king who in popular legend would reconquer Constantinople. He was educated in the Hellenic Military Academy and in Germany, where he served in the Imperial Guard. In 1889 he married Princess Sophia of Prussia, the sister of Wilhelm II. As crown prince he commanded the Army of Thessaly in the Greco-Turkish War of 1897, which ended in a humiliating defeat.

In the First Balkan War of 1912 Constantine commanded the Army of Thessaly. He defeated the Ottomans at Sarantaporos and Giannitsa, and accepted the surrender of Thessaloniki on 27 October 1912 (Old Style), less than a day before Bulgarian forces arrived. His father, George I, was assassinated at Thessaloniki on 18 March 1913 and Constantine became king. The Balkan Wars doubled Greece's territory and population.
