When the First World War began he rejected Wilhelm II's request to join the Central Powers but also refused to bring Greece in on the Allied side, as Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos wished. He held that neutrality best protected Greece, while his opponents accused him of German sympathies. He dismissed Venizelos twice, and in August 1916 Venizelist officers set up a rival government in Thessaloniki. The division of Greek society between Venizelists and royalists is known as the National Schism. Under Allied pressure and a blockade, Constantine left for Switzerland on 11 June 1917, and his son Alexander became king.

Alexander died on 25 October 1920. Venizelos lost a general election the following month, and a plebiscite in which nearly 99 per cent voted for his return brought Constantine back on 19 December 1920. The war against the Turkish nationalists in Asia Minor continued. In August 1922 the Greek army, overextended after an advance towards Ankara, was driven back to the coast. After a revolt of Venizelist officers he abdicated on 27 September 1922 in favour of his eldest son, George II. He died at Palermo, Sicily, on 11 January 1923. The royalist slogan 'bread, olives and King Constantine' dates from the Allied blockade of 1916 and 1917.
constantine-ii-of-greece: Constantine was born on 2 June 1940 in Psychiko, a suburb of Athens, the only son of Crown Prince Paul and Crown Princess Frederica. His father was the younger brother and heir of King George II. Italy invaded Greece in October 1940 and Germany in April 1941, and the infant Constantine was evacuated with his mother and sister to Crete and then, on 30 April 1941, to Egypt. The family later found refuge in South Africa. They returned to Greece in 1946, during the Greek Civil War, and when George II died on 1 April 1947, Paul became king and Constantine crown prince at the age of six.

He was a keen sailor. At the 1960 Rome Olympics he was helmsman of the yacht Nireus, which won the gold medal in the Dragon class with Odysseus Eskitzoglou and Georgios Zaimis, the first Greek gold medal since 1912.

Paul died of cancer on 6 March 1964, and Constantine, aged 23, succeeded him. Later that year he married Princess Anne-Marie of Denmark. His reign was marked by political instability. In the Apostasia of 1965, the king refused the prime minister Georgios Papandreou's wish to take over the defence ministry after the ASPIDA affair, and Papandreou resigned on 15 July; at least 39 members of parliament then left his Centre Union. Historians suspect the king and his mother were interested in a coup from mid-1965, though the royalist C. M. Woodhouse rejected such evidence as certainly untrue.

The Colonels' Coup of 21 April 1967 left Constantine with no loyal forces to rely on, and he reluctantly agreed to swear in the junta on condition that it include mostly civilian ministers. He disliked the regime from the outset and planned a countercoup, which failed. On 13 December 1967 he fled the country.

He remained head of state in exile until the junta abolished the monarchy on 1 June 1973, a decision confirmed by a referendum in July that he contested. After the junta fell, a second referendum in December 1974, which he was not allowed to return to campaign for, confirmed the abolition by a majority of almost 70 per cent. He publicly accepted the verdict. Archives published later show that between 1975 and 1978 he was involved in a conspiracy against the government of Konstantinos Karamanlis, which never materialised.

He lived for decades in London, returning to Greece only briefly, as for his mother's funeral in 1981, which he was allowed to attend for six hours. A dispute over royal property ended in 2002, when the European Court of Human Rights awarded his family €13.7 million. In 2013 he moved back to Athens, where he died on 10 January 2023 after a stroke, aged 82.
constantine-iii-western-roman-emperor: Little is known of Constantine before he was declared emperor; his date and place of birth are unknown. He was a common soldier, not an officer. In 406 the roughly 6,000 troops of the field army of Roman Britain, unpaid for years, revolted and chose their own leader. They first appointed Marcus and killed him, then Gratian, who was killed after four months. On 31 December 406 the Vandals, Sueves and Alans crossed the Rhine, and in this insecurity the army chose a man named after Constantine the Great. Early in 407 his fellows acclaimed him emperor. A contemporary called Britain a province rich in usurpers.

Constantine crossed the Channel at Bononia with all the mobile troops left in Britain and their commander Gerontius, and set up his headquarters at Lyon. The army in Gaul declared for him, followed by the civil administration in Hispania, and he negotiated agreements with the Franks, Alamanni and Burgundians that secured the Rhine. Honorius sent Sarus the Goth against him, but after Sarus killed Justinianus, one of Constantine's generals, he was forced to retreat to Italy.

By May 408 Constantine had captured Arles and made it his capital, and he raised his oldest son, a monk, to caesar under the name Constans. Late in 408 Honorius, needing to placate him while the Visigoths under Alaric were in Italy, acknowledged him as co-emperor and sent a purple robe. They were joint consuls in 409.

In 409 Gerontius rebelled, proclaiming his client Maximus emperor at Tarraco and inciting the barbarians in Gaul against Constantine. Saxon raids on Britain began in 408, and in 409 the Roman inhabitants expelled his officials. In spring 410 Constantine led an army into northern Italy but withdrew to Arles at the River Po after a false report that the general Allobich was dead. Gerontius defeated and killed Constans at Vienne, probably early in 411, and then besieged Constantine at Arles.

In 411 Honorius's new general Constantius III arrived at Arles. Much of Gerontius's army deserted to him, and Gerontius retreated to Hispania, where he committed suicide. Constantius defeated a relief force in an ambush, and Constantine, whose troops on the Rhine had abandoned him to support the Gallo-Roman Jovinus, surrendered with his son Julian. Despite a promise of safe passage, Constantius had both beheaded in August or September 411, and Constantine's head was presented to Honorius on 18 September.

The historian Peter Heather describes the Roman Army of Gaul as emerging from these wars in tatters. Roman rule never returned to Britain after Constantine stripped its defences. He has been associated with the Constantine of Geoffrey of Monmouth's fictitious Historia Regum Britanniae, who through his son Uther Pendragon becomes the grandfather of King Arthur.
constantine-iv: Constantine IV was the eldest son of the emperor Constans II and Fausta, daughter of the patrician Valentinus. His year of birth is unknown, though often given as around 650. He was made co-emperor with his father in 654 and became emperor in September 668, when news arrived that Constans II had been assassinated in Sicily.

His first task was to suppress the revolt in Sicily, where conspirators had proclaimed an officer named Mizizios emperor. Pope Vitalian withheld recognition and the navy stayed loyal. Constantine landed at Syracuse, captured Mizizios and had him executed.

Constantine faced severe pressure from the Caliphate of Muʿāwiya I. The Arabs captured Cyzicus and used it as a base, and their fleet took Smyrna and other coastal cities. Possession of the fleet allowed Constantine to defend the capital, and the Byzantines gradually regained the initiative, with counteroffensives into Egypt and Syria that helped end fifteen years of continuous raids. Muʿāwiya's death in 680 closed this period. At home Constantine reintroduced the heavy copper follis of Justinian I to restore the currency.

In November 680 he convened the Sixth Ecumenical Council, also called the Third Council of Constantinople, which reaffirmed the doctrines of Chalcedon and ended the Monothelite controversy; it closed in September 681. In 680 the Bulgars under Khan Asparukh crossed the Danube. Constantine besieged their camp in Dobruja but, in poor health, left the army, which panicked and was defeated. In 681 he acknowledged the Bulgar state in Moesia and agreed to pay tribute.

His brothers Heraclius and Tiberius had been crowned with him, and the populace demanded that this stand, but in late 681 Constantine had their noses slit so that they would be ineligible to rule. He died of dysentery on 10 July 685, succeeded by his son Justinian II. The Eastern Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint for calling the council.
constantine-vi: Constantine was born on 14 January 771, the only child of Emperor Leo IV and Irene. His father crowned him co-emperor in 776, and he succeeded as sole emperor in 780 at the age of nine, with his mother and her minister Staurakios as regents. In 788 Irene broke off his engagement to Rotrude, a daughter of Charlemagne.

After the Armeniac troops rebelled against Irene, Constantine came to actual power in 790. After an unsuccessful campaign in the Balkans he restored his mother as co-ruler in 792, the year he was defeated by Kardam of Bulgaria at the Battle of Marcellae. A plot then formed in favour of his uncle, the Caesar Nikephoros. Constantine had his uncle blinded and the tongues of his father's four other half-brothers cut out. He also blinded the Armeniac general Alexios Mosele, and the Armeniacs revolted, a rising he crushed with extreme cruelty in 793.

He then divorced his wife Maria of Amnia, who had borne no male heir, and married his mistress Theodote. The marriage was unpopular and canonically illegal and began the Moechian controversy. Patriarch Tarasios refused to officiate, and Theodote's uncle Plato of Sakkoudion was imprisoned after breaking communion with him. The controversy cost Constantine most of his support in the church, which Irene took care to back in public.

On 19 August 797 supporters of Irene captured Constantine, blinded and imprisoned him, and she was crowned as the first empress regnant. When he died is unknown, but it was before 805, and he may have died of his wounds soon after. He was buried in the Monastery of St Euphrosyne, which Irene had founded. In 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Emperor of the Romans, on the assertion that a woman could not rule in her own right, so Constantine was the last ruler recognised by the eastern empire, the papacy and the Western powers alike.
constantine-vii: Constantine was born in Constantinople on 17 or 18 May 905, the son of Emperor Leo VI by his fourth wife, Zoe Karbonopsina, a marriage the church regarded as uncanonical. To help legitimise him, his mother gave birth to him in the Purple Room of the imperial palace, where legitimate children of reigning emperors were normally born, hence the epithet Porphyrogennetos, born in the purple. His father and uncle raised him to the throne as a two-year-old child on 15 May 908. In early 913 his dying uncle Alexander appointed a seven-man regency council headed by Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos.

Most of Constantine's reign was dominated by others. The patriarch made an unpopular peace with Tsar Simeon of Bulgaria, and Zoe drove him out of the regency, but the Bulgarians defeated her general Leo Phokas in 917. In March 919 the admiral Romanos Lekapenos replaced her as regent and married his daughter Helena to Constantine; he became co-emperor on 17 December 920, and Constantine was eclipsed by a senior emperor. Constantine spent those years studying the ceremonies of the court.

Romanos was deposed by his sons in December 944, and Constantine became sole emperor on 27 January 945, aged 39. He left government largely to bureaucrats, generals and his wife Helena. In 947 he ordered the return of peasant lands without compensation. A fleet sent against the Arab corsairs of Crete in 949 failed, but in the east Nikephoros Phokas took Adata in 958 and John Tzimiskes captured Samosata a year later. Olga of Kiev, regent of the Rus', visited him in 957 and was baptised. Constantine died on 9 November 959 and his son Romanos II succeeded him; it was rumoured that he had been poisoned.

Constantine was a writer and scholar who gathered educated men round him. He wrote or commissioned the Geoponika, a compilation of earlier agronomic works; De Ceremoniis, on court ceremonies; De Administrando Imperio, advice for his son on running the empire and dealing with its enemies; and the Excerpta Historica, selections from ancient historians, of which only six of fifty-three titles survive. A history praising his grandfather Basil I is also attributed to him, though his authorship is uncertain. John Julius Norwich calls him the Scholar Emperor.
constantine-xi-palaiologos: Constantine was born on 8 February 1404, the fourth son of Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos and the Serbian noblewoman Helena Dragaš. Little is known of his youth, but from the 1420s he showed skill as a military commander, and his older brother John VIII Palaiologos twice named him regent in Constantinople. In 1428 he was proclaimed Despot of the Morea, the Peloponnese, which he ruled with his brothers Theodore and Thomas; together they extended Roman rule over almost the whole peninsula for the first time since the Fourth Crusade and rebuilt the Hexamilion wall. A campaign into Central Greece and Thessaly in 1444–1446 failed.

John VIII died childless in October 1448 and Constantine, his preferred heir, was supported by their mother Helena against his brother Demetrios, who had the backing of those opposed to church union. The Ottoman sultan Murad II accepted the succession. Constantine remained unmarried and childless. Like John, he supported the union of the Greek Orthodox and Catholic Churches proclaimed at the Council of Florence, and appealed for help to Pope Nicholas V and to Venice, but the pope required full acceptance of the union and Venice promised aid only if others joined it. In October 1452 the legate Isidore of Kiev arrived with 200 Neapolitan archers to confirm the union, which inflamed its opponents in the city.

In April 1453 Mehmed II led an army of perhaps 80,000 men against Constantinople, defended by probably fewer than 10,000. Constantine had laid a great chain across the Golden Horn to keep out the Ottoman fleet. The city fell on 29 May 1453. No eyewitness to the emperor's death survived, and the sources differ: most, among them Michael Critobulus and Cardinal Isidore, say he died fighting at the gate of Saint Romanus; others report that he was trampled, that he hanged himself, or that he escaped.

His death ended the line of Roman emperors begun by Augustus. In Greek folklore he became the Marble Emperor: an angel was said to have turned him to marble and hidden him beneath the Golden Gate, to be raised when God wills the city restored.
constantinople: The city stood on a peninsula at the south-eastern tip of Thrace, with the Bosporus to the east, the Golden Horn to the north and the Sea of Marmara to the south. Its position between the Aegean and the Black Sea, and between Europe and Asia, gave it command of the trade routes between the two seas. Before Constantine it was Byzantion, settled around 657 BCE by colonists from Megara, and briefly renamed Augusta Antonina by Septimius Severus. Constantine at first called his city New Rome; it soon became known as Constantinople, the city of Constantine.

The land side was protected by the Theodosian walls, a double wall with a moat and palisades in front, and from the fifth century by the Anastasian Wall, a chain of walls about 60 kilometres long across the Thracian peninsula. The city was built to rival Rome, and it was claimed that several of its elevations matched Rome's seven hills.

Constantine chose the site because Rome lay too far from the frontiers and the armies, and because Byzantion could be readily defended, with easy access to the Danube and Euphrates frontiers and supplies from the workshops of Roman Asia. It became the eastern capital in 330 and the sole capital once the western provinces were lost in the fifth century. Its standing grew gradually: it received its first known urban prefect, Honoratus, in 359. Under Justinian I the expedition to reconquer Africa sailed from the city in 533. In 618 Heraclius ended the free grain supply, since Egypt could no longer feed the city during the Persian wars, and the population fell substantially.

From the mid-fifth century to the early thirteenth, Constantinople was the largest and wealthiest city in Europe. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade, diverted against it, sacked the city and set up the Latin Empire, which lasted until Michael VIII Palaiologos retook the city in 1261. It then had about 35,000 people, a number he raised to about 70,000 by the end of his reign. The Black Death reached it in 1347. Mehmed II took the city in 1453; his soldiers had three days to pillage, and he ordered an imam to call the adhan in Hagia Sophia, turning the cathedral into a mosque.

The city remained the Ottoman capital until the empire's dissolution and the founding of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, when the capital moved to Ankara. It is now known internationally as Istanbul and lies in both Europe and Asia. Byzantine architecture, from St Mark's Basilica in Venice to churches across the Slavic East, was widely copied, and Byzantine gold coinage, the bezant, was prized throughout the Middle Ages.
constantius-i: Marcus Flavius Valerius Constantius was born on 31 March in a year that is unknown, probably no later than about 250, in Moesia Superior, a Roman province on the middle Danube. He was of humble origin. The Historia Augusta, an unreliable source, makes him the son of a nobleman named Eutropius and of Claudia, a niece of the emperor Claudius Gothicus; modern historians suspect this link was invented under his son Constantine. The nickname Chlorus, the Pale, was popularised by Byzantine-era historians and was not used in his lifetime.

He served in the guard under Aurelian, fought against the Palmyrene Empire in the east, and later became governor of Dalmatia. By 288 he was praetorian prefect in the west under Maximian, and he took part in campaigns against the Alamanni. Around 289 he divorced Helena, the mother of Constantine, and married Maximian's daughter Theodora.

In 293, under the power-sharing arrangement known as the Tetrarchy, Constantius was appointed caesar to Maximian at Milan on 1 March. His command included Gaul and Britain, and his capital was Trier. He first defeated the forces of the usurper Carausius in Gaul, capturing Boulogne. Carausius was then murdered by his finance officer Allectus, who held Britain until 296. Constantius spent two years against the Franks and Alamanni before launching two fleets across the Channel. The one under his prefect Julius Asclepiodotus landed near the Isle of Wight and defeated and killed Allectus; Constantius occupied London and killed the Frankish mercenaries roaming the province.

He reorganised the British provinces and restored Hadrian's Wall and its forts. In 298 he defeated the Alamanni at Langres and again at Vindonissa, and in 300 he fought the Franks, settling some of them in deserted parts of Gaul. When the Diocletianic Persecution began in 303 he ordered the demolition of churches but made the least effort of the four rulers to enforce the edicts; Eusebius denied that he destroyed any, while Lactantius says he did.

Diocletian and Maximian abdicated on 1 May 305, and Constantius became augustus in the west. His son Constantine, who had been passed over for the rank of caesar, joined him in Gaul as he prepared to campaign in Britain. Constantius advanced into the far north of the island against the Picts and, by 7 January 306, claimed a victory and the title Britannicus Maximus. He wintered at York and died there on 25 July 306, recommending his son to the army, which acclaimed Constantine emperor. This helped bring down the Tetrarchy and began civil wars that ended in 324.

Christian writers made Constantius secretly Christian, and medieval Welsh and Geoffrey of Monmouth's tales gave him a British wife; these have no historical validity, as he had divorced Helena before going to Britain.
constantius-ii: Constantius was born on 7 August 317 at Sirmium in Pannonia, the third son of Constantine the Great and the second by his wife Fausta. His father made him caesar on 8 November 324, when he was seven. In 336 war broke out with Sasanian Persia under Shapur II, and Constantine sent him east to command the frontier. He defeated and killed the Persian general Narses at Narasara, recaptured Amida and strengthened its walls.

When Constantine died in 337, Constantius buried him in the Church of the Holy Apostles. Soon afterwards the army massacred two of his uncles and seven cousins, among them Hannibalianus and Dalmatius. The official account blamed a mutinous army, but Ammianus Marcellinus, Zosimus, Libanius, Athanasius and Julian blamed Constantius himself. He and his brothers Constantine II and Constans then divided the empire at Sirmium, and he received the eastern provinces.

For years Constantius defended the eastern frontier against Shapur II, whose attacks were mostly sieges of Nisibis, Singara and Amida; Shapur won most of these encounters but gained little. In the west, Constantine II died in an ambush in 340, leaving Constans in control until he was killed in 350 by forces loyal to the usurper Magnentius. Constantius made his cousin Gallus caesar in the east and married his sister Constantina to him. He defeated Magnentius at Mursa Major in 351, one of the bloodiest battles between Roman armies, and at Mons Seleucus in 353, after which Magnentius killed himself.

Sole ruler from 353, he had Gallus arrested and executed after reports of his conduct, and on 6 November 355 made his last male relative, Julian, caesar and sent him to Gaul. He campaigned against the Alamanni, and in 357 against the Sarmatians and Quadi across the Danube; that year he visited Rome for the only time. Laws of the 350s forbade pagan sacrifice under penalty of death, though he never disbanded the priestly colleges. He pressed a compromise position between Arianism and the Nicene Creed on the church, and he restricted Jewish ownership of slaves.

When Shapur destroyed Singara and took Amida in 360, Constantius travelled east. Julian's Gallic legions, ordered to send reinforcements, proclaimed him augustus. Constantius could not answer at once and in 361 set out west, but he fell ill with fever and died at Mopsuestia on 3 November 361. Sources say he was baptised by the bishop Euzoius and named Julian his successor. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.

His reputation is divided. Ammianus portrays a conscientious but vain emperor open to flatterers, while orthodox churchmen and Julian saw a heretic and a murderer. Some modern historians think he suffered at the hands of unsympathetic authors, and note that many contemporaries held him in high esteem.
constitution-of-3-may-1791: The Government Act, as the Constitution was titled, was adopted by the Great Sejm that met from 1788 to 1792, in response to the perilous situation of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had been a major European power only a century earlier. Since 1652 the liberum veto had allowed any Sejm deputy to nullify all the legislation of that Sejm, and deputies bribed by magnates or foreign powers had paralysed government for over a century; only a confederated sejm was immune to it. The Great Sejm opened on 6 October 1788 and became a confederated sejm on its second day. Russia and Austria were at war with the Ottoman Empire, and a new alliance with Prussia seemed to offer security.

On 18 April 1791 the Sejm adopted the Free Royal Cities Act, expanding the rights of townspeople after their Black Procession in Warsaw demanded enfranchisement. The Constitution was drafted by King Stanisław August Poniatowski, with contributions from Ignacy Potocki, Hugo Kołłątaj and others. The King is credited with the general provisions and Kołłątaj with the document's final shape.

The Constitution reflected Enlightenment influences, among them Rousseau's social contract and Montesquieu's balance among legislative, executive and judicial branches and a bicameral legislature. It sought a more effective constitutional monarchy, introduced political equality between townspeople and nobility and placed the peasants under the government's protection, mitigating the worst abuses of serfdom. Article I acknowledged the Roman Catholic faith as the dominant religion but guaranteed tolerance and freedom to all religions. Article II confirmed many old privileges of the nobility. Article III made the Free Royal Cities Act integral to the Constitution: personal security was extended to townspeople, including Jews, who also gained the right to acquire landed property and became eligible for officers' commissions and public offices.

The Commonwealth's neighbours reacted with hostility. Magnates opposed to the reform formed the Targowica Confederation and asked Catherine the Great to intervene, and Russian armies allied with them in the Polish–Russian War of 1792, while Frederick William II of Prussia broke the Prussian alliance. The Constitution was in force for less than 19 months. The Grodno Sejm of 1793 declared it null and void, and the Second and Third Partitions of 1793 and 1795 ended the sovereign existence of Poland and Lithuania until 1918.

Over the following 123 years its memory helped sustain Polish and Lithuanian aspirations for independence. Two of its authors, Potocki and Kołłątaj, called it the last will and testament of the expiring Homeland. The holiday of 3 May was banned during the partitions, reinstated in 1919 and restored in April 1990.
constitution-of-india: In 1928 the All Parties Conference convened a committee at Lucknow to prepare a constitution for India, whose report became known as the Nehru Report. The constitution that was eventually adopted drew mainly on the Government of India Act 1935, which was largely drafted by Samuel Hoare. Its framers also borrowed features of earlier legislation: the Government of India Act 1858, the Indian Councils Acts of 1861, 1892 and 1909, the Government of India Act 1919 and the Indian Independence Act 1947. The last of these, which led to the creation of Pakistan, divided the former Constituent Assembly in two, and each new assembly had sovereign power to draft a constitution for its own state.

The Constituent Assembly was elected by the members of the provincial assemblies. It first met on 9 December 1946, and on 11 December appointed Rajendra Prasad as its president and B. N. Rau as constitutional legal adviser. Its 389 members were reduced to 299 after partition. On 13 December 1946 Jawaharlal Nehru presented an Objective Resolution laying down the underlying principles, which later became the Preamble. The assembly took almost three years to draft the constitution, holding eleven sessions over 165 days. Rau's initial draft had 243 articles and 13 schedules; after discussion, debate and amendment the text came to 395 articles and 8 schedules, in 22 parts. A seven-member drafting committee chaired by B. R. Ambedkar considered and amended Rau's draft.

The constitution declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular and democratic republic, though the words socialist and secular were added to the Preamble by the 42nd amendment in 1976. It sets up a parliamentary system in which the Council of Ministers, headed by the prime minister, is collectively responsible to the lower house, the Lok Sabha. Its first article describes India as a Union of States. The states retain important powers and are represented in the Rajya Sabha, but the Union List gives the national government exclusive authority over matters such as defence and international relations. Article 368 sets the procedure for amendment, which needs a two-thirds majority in each house of Parliament.

The framers repealed earlier British acts in Article 395, to ensure constitutional autochthony. The text is deliberately worded in generalities, to ensure flexibility. The American historian Granville Austin called it first and foremost a social document, with its Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as its chief instruments and conscience. It does not limit Parliament's power of amendment, but in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala the Supreme Court held that certain features are so integral to the constitution that they can never be removed, a principle known as the Basic Structure doctrine. The Hindi translation was the first into an Indian language, made by the linguist Raghu Vira.
constitution-of-japan: The Meiji Constitution of 1889, the fundamental law of the Empire of Japan, was modelled on Prussian and British examples and made the prime minister and cabinet accountable to the emperor rather than to the elected Imperial Diet. On 26 July 1945 the United States, the United Kingdom and the Republic of China issued the Potsdam Declaration, which demanded surrender, demilitarisation and democratisation. Japan accepted its conditions, which implied changes to the constitution after the surrender.

General Douglas MacArthur, the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, at first directed Prime Minister Kijūrō Shidehara to prepare a new constitution, but Emperor Hirohito and most of the cabinet were reluctant to replace the 1889 document. In February 1946 MacArthur presented a draft prepared under his own supervision, which Japanese scholars reviewed and modified. To preserve legal continuity, the new text was adopted as an amendment to the Meiji Constitution under Article 73 of that document.

The constitution has a preamble and 103 articles in 11 chapters, and is short at about 5,000 words. The preamble declares that sovereign power resides with the people. The emperor is 'the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people', and his role is entirely ceremonial. Article 9 states that the Japanese people forever renounce war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force to settle international disputes.

Thirty-one articles describe the rights and duties of the people, which the Meiji Constitution had granted only within the limits of law. The constitution sets up a parliamentary system. A bicameral National Diet is made up of a House of Representatives and a House of Councillors, and the old House of Peers, composed of nobles, was abolished. The Cabinet is headed by a Prime Minister and answerable to the Diet. Amendments need a two-thirds vote of each house and a majority in a referendum.

The Diet's two houses made amendments of their own without interference from MacArthur, adding provisions for suits against the State for officials' torts and for wrongful detention. The text took effect on 3 May 1947, after a six-month transitional period. A government body, the Kenpō Fukyū Kai, was established to promote acceptance of the new constitution among the people.

The necessity and extent of Article 9 have been debated in Japan since its enactment, particularly after the Self-Defense Forces were set up in 1954. Some lower courts have found them unconstitutional, but the Supreme Court has never ruled on the question.
constitution-of-the-united-states: The Constitutional Convention assembled at Independence Hall in Philadelphia and sat between 25 May and 17 September 1787. Twelve states were represented, Rhode Island refusing to take part, and 55 of the 74 appointed delegates attended. The convention's mandate was limited to amending the Articles of Confederation, which had proved ineffective, but the delegates soon began considering a replacement. The framers drew on English common law, on Magna Carta for the principle of due process, and on Enlightenment writers such as John Locke and Montesquieu, whose ideas lie behind the separation of powers. Some scholars argue that Haudenosaunee political ideas also influenced the document, a claim other historians dispute.

The text has a Preamble, seven articles and a closing endorsement signed by 39 framers. Articles I to III set up Congress, the presidency and the courts. Articles IV to VI deal with federalism: relations among the states and with the federal government, the amendment process, and the supremacy of the Constitution and federal law over state law, with a ban on religious tests for office. Article VII set the way of ratification. Instead of the unanimous approval that the Articles of Confederation required, it called for conventions in the states and for the approval of nine of the thirteen.

The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, took effect in 1791. They protect freedoms of religion, speech, press and assembly and the right to keep and bear arms. The Eleventh Amendment of 1795 overturned the Supreme Court's decision in Chisholm v. Georgia (1793). Amendments are appended to the document, not written into the original text.

The convention's secretary, William Jackson, signed a note verifying four changes made by hand to the final text. Within three days of the signing the document went to the Congress of the Confederation, which voted unanimously on 28 September 1787 to send it to the states. It replaced the Articles on 4 March 1789. Early justices of the Supreme Court included men who had framed or ratified it, among them John Jay and John Marshall. Marshall's Court held in Barron v. Baltimore (1833) that the Bill of Rights restricted only the federal government, not the states. The Constitution has served as a model abroad, and its amendments and judicial review informed Benito Juárez, José Rizal and Sun Yat-sen, among others.
constitutional-monarchy: A constitutional monarchy is also called a limited, parliamentary or democratic monarchy. The monarch exercises authority in accordance with a constitution and does not decide alone. It differs from an absolute monarchy, in which the monarch is the only decision-maker, because the ruler works within a legal framework. The powers of constitutional monarchs vary widely. Some are hereditary symbolic heads of state with almost no executive power, in what are sometimes called ceremonial monarchies or crowned republics. In executive or semi-constitutional monarchies the monarch keeps significant powers, such as appointing and dismissing ministers or dissolving the assembly. Many constitutional monarchies are democratic, but some are not.

The oldest example from ancient times was, according to this account, that of the Hittites, whose king shared authority with an assembly called the Panku. Herodotus says that Demonax created a constitutional monarchy for King Battus III the Lame of Cyrene in about 548 BCE. In England the first form of constitution came with Magna Carta in 1215, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 furthered limits on the crown through laws such as the Bill of Rights 1689 and the Act of Settlement 1701. In Scotland the Claim of Right Act 1689 placed similar limits.

Queen Anne was the last British monarch to veto an Act of Parliament, on 11 March 1708. George III still blocked Catholic Emancipation, which led to the resignation of William Pitt the Younger in 1801. William IV was the last to dismiss a prime minister, Lord Melbourne, in 1834, and Queen Victoria was the last to exercise real personal power, which declined over her reign. Poland produced the first constitution for a monarchy in continental Europe, the Constitution of 3 May 1791. Hegel gave the concept a philosophical justification in 1820.

The modern form developed mainly in the United Kingdom, where an elected parliament and a government led by a prime minister hold real power while the monarch is bound by convention to act on ministers' advice. In France's July Monarchy Louis-Philippe I was styled King of the French rather than King of France. In the German Empire, shaped by Otto von Bismarck, the Kaiser kept considerable executive power and the Imperial Chancellor needed no parliamentary confidence vote. That model was discredited and abolished after Germany's defeat in the First World War. Italy's monarchy was discredited under Benito Mussolini and abolished in 1946. After the Second World War surviving European monarchies almost always adopted the British model.

The Commonwealth realms keep reserve powers for emergencies, as in November 1975, when the Governor-General of Australia dismissed the prime minister Gough Whitlam. Walter Bagehot named three rights of a constitutional monarch: to be consulted, to encourage and to warn.
constructivism-art: Constructivism was a development of Russian Futurism after the First World War, and particularly of the counter-reliefs that Vladimir Tatlin exhibited in 1915. The term was coined by the sculptors Antoine Pevsner and Naum Gabo, whose Realistic Manifesto of 1920 is its first appearance. Its geometric abstraction owed something to the Suprematism of Kazimir Malevich. As theory and practice it grew out of debates at the Institute of Artistic Culture in Moscow from 1920 to 1922, which defined the style as a combination of faktura, the material properties of an object, and tektonika, its spatial presence.

The key work was Tatlin's proposal for the Monument to the Third International (1919-20), known as Tatlin's Tower, which joined a machine aesthetic to searchlights and projection screens. It was never built, for lack of money after the revolution. Gabo and Pevsner held that the movement had a spiritual core, while Tatlin and Alexander Rodchenko held a utilitarian view. The debates led to Productivism, which demanded direct participation in industry and an end to easel painting.

Constructivists designed street festivals and propaganda for the Bolshevik government during the Civil War, and later advertising during the New Economic Policy. Rodchenko and the poet Vladimir Mayakovsky called themselves advertising constructors. Others worked in theatre, where Vsevolod Meyerhold developed his biomechanical acting, and in cinema, photomontage, book design and poster design, as with the Stenberg brothers.

Tatlin's designs were hailed in Germany, and exchanges between Moscow and Berlin led to a short-lived Constructivist International that met Dadaists and De Stijl artists in 1922. Teachers at the Bauhaus drew on Constructivist ideas and the teaching methods of VKhUTEMAS. Its main early political patron was Leon Trotsky, and after his expulsion in 1927-28 the movement came under suspicion. The Communist Party gradually favoured realist art, and about 1934 Socialist Realism was instituted in its place, although some Constructivists kept working for the state. Naum Gabo carried a version of Constructivism to England, and Joaquín Torres García helped spread it to Latin America.
continental-congress: The idea of a joint colonial body first arose in 1754, at the start of the French and Indian War, when representatives of seven of the thirteen colonies met at the Albany Congress and Benjamin Franklin proposed a confederation. The proposal was rejected. A further step came with the Stamp Act Congress, which met in New York City in October 1765 and sent a Declaration of Rights and Grievances to Parliament. The Stamp Act was repealed in March 1766. The Continental Congress drew its organisation less on Parliament than on that congress, and nine of its delegates sat in the First Continental Congress.

The First Continental Congress met in Carpenter's Hall, Philadelphia, from 5 September to 26 October 1774. Fifty-six delegates from twelve colonies attended, among them George Washington, Patrick Henry and John Adams, with Peyton Randolph of Virginia as president. Georgia did not take part. The delegates organised an economic boycott of Britain, adopted the Continental Association and petitioned the King for redress. Most were not yet ready to break away from Britain.

The Second Continental Congress convened on 10 May 1775 at the State House in Philadelphia, shortly after fighting began. It raised armies, directed strategy, appointed diplomats and made treaties. On 14 June it established the Continental Army and on 15 June appointed Washington its commander. It sent the Olive Branch Petition to King George III, but after the Proclamation of Rebellion of August 1775 some members concluded that peace would not come. It adopted Richard Henry Lee's resolution for independence on 2 July 1776 and, two days later, the Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson. It created standing committees, including a board of war and a navy board, and approved the Articles of Confederation on 15 November 1777.

The Articles came into force on 1 March 1781, and the body became the Congress of the Confederation, a single chamber in which each state had one vote. It could declare war, sign treaties and borrow or print money, but it could not tax. It met in Philadelphia and later in other cities, including Annapolis and New York City, and its authority declined after the war. Its Northwest Ordinance of 1787 placed the land north of the Ohio River under federal control. The Philadelphia Convention of 1787 was authorised to amend the Articles, and the first Congress under the new Constitution replaced the Confederation Congress in 1789.
continental-system: Britain declared war on France in May 1803. Napoleon could not invade because of the Royal Navy's control of the sea, and after the British victory over a Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar on 21 October 1805 he abandoned his plans and turned to economic warfare. On 16 May 1806 the Royal Navy imposed a blockade of French and French-allied coasts. Britain was then Europe's manufacturing and business centre as a result of the Industrial Revolution, and Napoleon believed that, as an island nation, it could be forced to sue for peace if its trade with the continent were cut off.

Napoleon issued the Berlin Decree on 21 November 1806, forbidding the import of British goods into any European country allied with or dependent on France and cutting all connections with Britain, even mail. Britain replied with orders in council in January and November 1807, and Napoleon answered with the Milan Decree of 1807, under which neutral ships using British ports or paying British tariffs were to be treated as British and seized. The embargo was applied intermittently and ended on 11 April 1814, after Napoleon's first abdication.

Enforcement drew Napoleon into further wars. Portugal, allied with Britain, refused to comply. After the Treaty of Tilsit in July 1807 Napoleon failed to capture the Portuguese fleet, which sailed with the court to Brazil, and the Peninsular War began in 1808. Britain bombarded Copenhagen and seized the Danish fleet in 1807, and used bases at Heligoland, Gothenburg and Hanö to smuggle goods into the Baltic. Russia reopened trade with Britain in 1810, which was a motive for Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812.

The blockade did not cause lasting damage to Britain. Smuggling was extensive, and British exports to the continent fell by between 25 and 55 per cent compared with the period before 1806, but trade with the rest of the world rose sharply and covered much of the loss. Britain did suffer high unemployment and inflation from 1810 to 1812, and unrest, including the Luddite movement, was put down by the yeomanry and militia.

The system hurt France and its allies. Shipbuilding and other industries that depended on overseas markets declined, ports such as Marseille and Bordeaux suffered, and food prices rose across the continent. The Dutch economy, built on trade, suffered greatly. The industrial north and east of France and Wallonia gained from the lack of British competition. Napoleon's St Cloud Decree of July 1810 admitted limited British trade, and the resentment of allied governments weakened his coalition. The embargo also contributed to the War of 1812 between Britain and the United States.
continuation-war: The Winter War of 1939 to 1940 ended with the Moscow Peace Treaty. Finland distrusted Germany afterwards, but the fall of France ended any Western orientation in its foreign policy. On 31 July 1940 Hitler ordered planning for an attack on the Soviet Union, and Germany reversed its refusal to sell arms to Finland and allowed its troops to transit through Finland and Sweden. Its leaders said they would fight only to redress the balance of the 1940 treaty and described themselves as co-belligerents rather than allies of Germany, though President Risto Ryti envisioned a Greater Finland and Mannerheim often called the war an anti-Communist crusade. Historians still disagree on whether Finland was an ally of Nazi Germany.

German forces invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, and Finnish troops occupied the demilitarised Åland Islands. After a Soviet air raid on Finnish cities on 25 June, Finland declared war. By September 1941 it had regained the territory conceded in 1940, and it went on into East Karelia, halting some 30–32 km from the centre of Leningrad. Historians debate how far Finland took part in the siege of the city. In Lapland the joint German–Finnish Operation Silver Fox, begun on 29 June, failed to take Murmansk or cut the Kirov Railway.

From 19 July 1941 the Finns ran a military administration in occupied East Karelia, intending to prepare its incorporation into Finland; almost 30% of the remaining Russian civilians were interned in concentration camps. On 9 June 1944 the Soviet Leningrad Front began the Vyborg–Petrozavodsk Offensive. The Red Army retook Viipuri on 20 June and Petrozavodsk by 28 June, though the Finnish army halted the offensive in August.

A ceasefire took effect on 4 September 1944, and the Moscow Armistice was accepted by the Finnish Parliament on 19 September. Finland restored the borders of 1940, ceded Petsamo, leased the Porkkala Peninsula to the Soviets, paid war reparations, held war-responsibility trials and banned fascist groups. A Soviet-led Allied Control Commission oversaw the terms. The demand that German troops leave led to the Lapland War between Finland and Germany. According to Finnish historians, Finnish forces lost 63,204 dead or missing and around 158,000 wounded.

The 1947 Paris Peace Treaty described Finland as an ally of Hitlerite Germany during the war. The Finnish Jewish community of about 2,000 had full civil rights, but in November 1942 officials secretly deported eight Jewish refugees to the Gestapo, of whom only one survived; the government then refused to hand over any more.
copan: Copán lies in a fertile mountain valley in the alluvial basin of the Copán River, on the south-eastern edge of Mesoamerica. The valley made it a trade hub between the Maya lowlands and the non-Maya peoples of southern Central America, and its polity controlled access to the upper Motagua River valley, a main source of jadeite and obsidian. Its ancient name was probably Oxwitik, meaning the Three Witiks.

Little is known of the rulers before a new dynasty with origins at Tikal was installed in the early 5th century. Texts record that a warrior named K'uk' Mo' Ajaw took the throne in 426 as K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', probably sponsored from Tikal; he may have strengthened his claim by marrying into the old Copán royal family. K'ak' Chan Yopaat, the eleventh ruler, was crowned in 578 and reigned until 5 February 628.

Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil became the thirteenth king in July 695. Under him Copán's sculpture developed into the full in-the-round style characteristic of the city, and he ranked his city among the four most powerful Maya states with Tikal, Calakmul and Palenque. In 724 he installed K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat as a vassal on the throne of Quiriguá, but in 738 that ruler captured and beheaded him. Copán lost its domain and the Motagua trade route, though its rulers began building monuments again within a few decades.

At its peak the kingdom had at least 20,000 people. The population fell in the 8th and 9th centuries to fewer than 5,000, and the valley held only a few farming hamlets when the Spanish arrived in the 16th century.

Copán is in western Honduras, near the border with Guatemala. It is known for its portrait stelae, the Acropolis, a ballcourt and the Hieroglyphic Stairway. Altar Q, dedicated by Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat in 776, shows the first sixteen kings of the dynasty. John Lloyd Stephens and Frederick Catherwood described the site in 1841. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1980.
copenhagen: Copenhagen lies on the eastern shore of the island of Zealand, partly on the island of Amager and on a number of natural and artificial islets between the two. It faces the Øresund, the strait that separates Denmark from Sweden and connects the North Sea with the Baltic Sea. The Swedish city of Malmö lies directly across the sound, 42 kilometres away by road.

The Danish name København reflects the city's origin as a harbour and a place of commerce. The Old Norse form was Kaupmannahǫfn, meaning 'merchants' harbour', and the present form developed through sound changes that took place around 1400. The Latin name Hafnia is the source of the name of the element hafnium.

Flint tools show settlement in the Stone Age, and many historians believe the town dates to the late Viking Age, possibly founded by Sweyn I Forkbeard. The first habitations were probably centred on Gammel Strand, 'old shore'. The natural harbour and good herring stocks attracted seasonal fishermen and merchants from the 11th century and more permanent residents in the 13th. Excavations have uncovered the remains of a large merchant mansion from about 1020 near Kongens Nytorv, and a well from the late 12th century in Pilestræde.

Copenhagen became the capital of Denmark in the early 15th century, and the University of Copenhagen was founded in 1479. In the 16th century it served as the de facto capital of the Kalmar Union and its monarchy, and by the 17th century it was the centre of the Danish government and military. The 18th century brought a devastating plague outbreak and urban fires, followed by the building of the district of Frederiksstaden and of institutions such as the Royal Theatre and the Royal Academy of Fine Arts. In this period the city was the centre of the Danish slave trade.

A British fleet bombarded the city in 1807 during the Napoleonic Wars. The Danish Golden Age that followed gave Copenhagen a neoclassical look. After the Second World War the Finger Plan guided the growth of housing and businesses along five urban railway routes running out from the centre.

Copenhagen is the capital and largest city of Denmark and its cultural, economic and governmental centre. Since the completion of the Øresund Bridge it has been increasingly integrated with Malmö and the Swedish province of Scania in the Øresund Region. Its landmarks include Tivoli Gardens, the Amalienborg and Christiansborg palaces, Rosenborg Castle and Frederik's Church, and the University of Copenhagen is the oldest university in Denmark.
copper: Copper is a chemical element with the symbol Cu, from the Latin cuprum, and atomic number 29. It is a soft, malleable and ductile metal with very high thermal and electrical conductivity, second only to silver among pure metals at room temperature. Pure copper is orange-red, one of the few metals with a natural colour other than grey or silver. In air it slowly forms a protective layer of copper oxide, and on old roofs and the Statue of Liberty a green layer of verdigris appears. Copper is also one of the few native metals, found in nature in a directly usable, unalloyed form.

The use of native copper dates to about 9000 BCE in the Middle East, and a native copper pendant found in northern Iraq dates to 8700 BCE. The history of copper metallurgy is thought to run from cold working of native copper to annealing, then smelting, and finally casting. The earliest archaeological evidence of hot metallurgy in Eurasia, in the Balkans and Carpathian Mountains, dates to between 6200 and 5000 BCE. An amulet from Mehrgarh in Pakistan, dated to 4000 BCE, is the earliest example of lost-wax casting in copper. Ötzi the Iceman, who lived between 3300 and 3200 BCE, was found with a copper axehead of 99.7 per cent purity.

Smelting was probably discovered in China before 2800 BCE, in Central America around 600 CE and in West Africa about the 9th or 10th century. Experience with copper helped the development of other metals, and copper smelting likely led to the discovery of iron smelting.

Copper was alloyed with zinc to make brass and with tin to make bronze, and copper-tin bronzes have been used to make bells for centuries, the composition of the alloy affecting the tone. Alloys of copper and nickel, called cupronickel, are used in low-denomination coins. In Japan, shakudō is a decorative alloy of copper with 4 to 10 per cent gold, which can be patinated to dark blue or black. For more than two centuries copper paint has been used on boat hulls to control the growth of plants and shellfish.
coptic-orthodox-church: According to Coptic tradition the church was founded by Saint Mark the Evangelist, a companion of the Apostles, around 42, and it regards itself as the subject of many Old Testament prophecies. The Catechetical School of Alexandria, which Jerome records as founded by Mark himself, is the oldest catechetical school in the world. It became a leading centre of the allegorical method of biblical interpretation and sought a rapprochement between Greek culture and the Christian faith.

In the 4th century an Alexandrian presbyter named Arius began a dispute about the nature of Christ. Emperor Constantine I convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 after Pope Alexander I of Alexandria proposed a council, and it led to the Nicene Creed. After the Council of Chalcedon in 451, disputes over the nature of Christ left the Oriental Orthodox churches in schism.

The Muslim invasion of Egypt took place in 639. Bishop John of Nikiu, whose Chronicle survives in Ge'ez, gives a hostile account of the conquest, though he says that Amr ibn al-As took none of the property of the churches. The population remained mainly Christian at first, but gradual conversion to Islam made Egypt a largely Muslim country by the end of the 12th century. Scholars point to the repression of Coptic revolts, Arab-Muslim immigration and conversion, and to higher Umayyad taxes on Christians, which weakened the church's economic base. The church moved its seat from Alexandria to Cairo in the 12th century.

The position of Copts began to improve early in the 19th century under the Muhammad Ali dynasty, and Sa'id Pasha abolished the jizya tax in 1855. Pope Cyril IV founded the first modern Coptic schools in 1853, including the first Egyptian school for girls, and a printing press. The Theological College of the School of Alexandria was re-established in 1893.

The pope of Alexandria heads the church, which follows the Coptic Rite. The language of its liturgy descends from Ancient Egyptian and uses the Coptic alphabet, derived from the Greek with added letters from the Demotic. Since Coptic was supplanted by Arabic after the Arab conquest, service books carry Arabic in parallel columns. Believers use a breviary called the Agpeya to pray seven times a day, facing east.

The church has long consecrated the archbishops of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose first native head, Abuna Basilios, was crowned patriarch by Pope Cyril VI in 1959. The Eritrean church gained autocephaly in 1998.
copts: The word Copt entered English in the 17th century through Neo-Latin from the Arabic Qubṭ, an Arabization of the Coptic word for Egyptian, itself adapted from the Greek Aigýptios. It originally referred to all Egyptians and became synonymous with native Christians after Egypt's Islamization and Arabization following the Muslim conquest. Copts are descended from the ancient Egyptians and historically spoke the Coptic language, the latest stage of the Egyptian language.

According to sacred tradition Mark the Evangelist introduced Christianity to Alexandria around 42, during the reign of Claudius. A fragment of the Gospel of John in Coptic from the first half of the 2nd century shows it had spread across Egypt. By the beginning of the 3rd century Christians were the majority of the population, and the Church of Alexandria was one of Christendom's four apostolic sees.

The Catechetical School of Alexandria, founded around 190 by Pantanaeus, taught Athenagoras, Clement, Didymus and Origen. The first three ecumenical councils were presided over by patriarchs of Alexandria: Alexander I at Nicaea in 325, Timothy I at Constantinople in 381 and Cyril at Ephesus in 431. The Council of Chalcedon in 451 condemned and deposed the Alexandrian patriarch Dioscorus I. The Egyptian delegation rejected it, and so did most native Egyptians, whose church became the predecessor of the Coptic Orthodox Church, while the church that accepted the council became the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria. Byzantine emperors repeatedly deposed and exiled non-Chalcedonian patriarchs.

After the Arab conquest in the 7th century the Copts were subjected, in the historian Roger S. Bagnall's account, to a system that prioritized fiscal exploitation, particularly through taxation. Their treatment ranged from relative tolerance to open persecution, in cycles that varied with the ruler. Under Islamic rule Copts held important administrative and commercial positions. When Napoleon conquered Egypt in 1798, a Coptic Legion under General Yaqub was raised, and it left for France with the French army in 1801.

Most Copts follow the Coptic Orthodox Church, an Oriental Orthodox church, while a minority belong to the Coptic Catholic Church, which is in communion with Rome. Coptic remained a literary language until the 13th century and was supplanted by Arabic toward the 16th. In the early 19th century it helped Champollion decipher the Egyptian hieroglyphs.

Copts keep the Coptic calendar, based on the ancient Egyptian calendar and reformed under Augustus in 25 BCE to match the Julian calendar. It has twelve months of thirty days and a short thirteenth month, and farmers still use it to follow the agricultural seasons. Coptic music is thought to preserve elements of ancient Egyptian music, with Byzantine and Hebrew influences.
corazon-aquino: María Corazón Sumulong Cojuangco was born on 25 January 1933 in Paniqui, Tarlac, the sixth of eight children of the businessman and former congressman José Cojuangco and Demetria Sumulong, a pharmacist. Both parents came from prominent political families. While studying law in 1953 she met Benigno Aquino Jr., known as Ninoy, and she gave up her studies to marry him on 11 October 1954. They had five children, among them Benigno Aquino III. Her husband became a leading critic of Ferdinand Marcos.

After her husband was assassinated on 21 August 1983 she became a figurehead of the opposition. Marcos announced a snap election on 3 November 1985, held on 7 February 1986. A petition with 1.2 million signatures urged her to run, and she declared her candidacy on 3 December, with Salvador Laurel as her running mate. The Batasang Pambansa proclaimed Marcos the winner, which prompted allegations of fraud and her call for civil disobedience.

On 22 February 1986 Juan Ponce Enrile and General Fidel V. Ramos announced their defection from the Marcos government. Cardinal Sin appealed over the Church's Radyo Veritas, and millions gathered on Epifanio de los Santos Avenue. The People Power Revolution ousted Marcos, and Aquino, who had held no earlier political office, was sworn in on 25 February 1986.

She issued a provisional Freedom Constitution, and the 1987 Constitution limited the presidency to a single six-year term. Her government produced the Family Code of 1987 and the 1991 Local Government Code, and in 1989 created the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao after talks with the Moro National Liberation Front. It faced coup attempts, the deadliest in August 1987 leaving 53 dead and the most serious in December 1989. Marines killed 12 farmers at the Mendiola Massacre in January 1987. Aquino declined to seek re-election and left office in 1992.

She chaired the Benigno S. Aquino Jr. Foundation and spoke abroad on democracy and human rights. She died of colorectal cancer on 1 August 2009, and her family declined a state funeral. Time named her Woman of the Year in 1986, and she received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1998.
corinth-canal: The first to propose cutting through the isthmus was the tyrant Periander of Corinth in the 7th century BCE. He built instead the Diolkos, a stone trackway along which ships were towed from one side to the other, a change of mind attributed to the expense, a lack of labour or fear that a canal would rob Corinth of its role as a trading centre. Caligula commissioned a study in 40 CE, and Egyptian experts wrongly claimed that the Gulf of Corinth was higher than the Saronic Gulf.

Nero was the first to begin work. In 67 CE he broke the ground himself with a pickaxe, and about 6,000 Judean prisoners of war began digging trenches from both sides. According to Suetonius the cut reached about 700 metres, a tenth of the isthmus, before work stopped on his death. Herodes Atticus and the Venetians, after their conquest of the Peloponnese in 1687, considered the project but did not start it. The modern canal follows Nero's course.

The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 gave new impetus, and in 1870 a law authorised construction. A concession of 1881 went to the Société Internationale du Canal Maritime de Corinthe, and work was inaugurated on 23 April 1882 in the presence of King George I of Greece. After eight years the company's money ran out and it went bankrupt. A Greek company resumed work in 1890, and the canal was completed on 25 July 1893.

It is a sea-level channel without locks, 6,343 metres long and 8 metres deep, 24.6 metres wide at the surface and 21.3 metres at the bottom, with near-vertical rock walls rising 90 metres above sea level. It saves ships a journey of 700 kilometres around the Peloponnese.

Traffic fell far below the hoped-for 4 million net tons a year. By 1906 it had reached only half a million net tons, and 1.5 million by 1913. The narrow channel, winds funnelled by its walls and strong tidal currents made navigation difficult, and the unstable limestone walls caused repeated landslides. Between 1893 and 1940 the canal was closed for a total of four years for repairs.

On 26 April 1941 German paratroopers captured the main bridge during the Battle of Greece, but British charges destroyed it. In October 1944 retreating German forces blocked the canal with landslides and wreckage. The United States Army Corps of Engineers began clearing it in November 1947, and it reopened to all traffic by September 1948. Because it is too narrow for most modern ships, it is now used mainly by smaller and tourist vessels.
cornelius-vanderbilt: Vanderbilt was born on Staten Island on 27 May 1794 and left school at eleven to work on his father's ferry in New York Harbor. At sixteen he began his own ferry to Manhattan, and other captains called him the Commodore in jest, a nickname that stuck. In 1817 he began working for Thomas Gibbons, who was fighting a steamboat monopoly granted by the New York legislature. In Gibbons v. Ogden the Supreme Court ruled for Gibbons on 2 March 1824, holding that states could not interfere with interstate commerce.

From 1829 Vanderbilt worked for himself and built steamboat lines around New York, on Long Island Sound and on the Hudson, where in 1834 he competed as The People's Line until the monopoly paid him to stop. By the end of the 1830s he dominated steamboats on the Sound and began to take over connecting railroads. With the gold rush he turned to ocean steamships and founded the Accessory Transit Company to carry passengers across Nicaragua. During the Civil War he gave his largest steamship, the Vanderbilt, to the Union Navy and received a Congressional Gold Medal.

In 1863 he took control of the New York and Harlem Railroad through a stock corner, and in 1864 he sold his last ships to concentrate on railroads. He bought the Hudson River Railroad in 1864 and the New York Central in 1867, and in 1870 merged two lines into the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad, one of the first giant corporations in the United States. His attempt to corner Erie Railway stock led to the Erie War with Jay Gould and James Fisk Jr.

In 1869 he married Frank Armstrong Crawford, and at her urging gave one million dollars, then the largest charitable gift in American history, to found Vanderbilt University in Nashville. He died on 4 January 1877, aged 82, with an estimated fortune of 105 million dollars, 95 per cent of it left to his son William and four grandsons. Two daughters and a son challenged the will in court, and William settled. His biographer T. J. Stiles credits him with expanding the nation's transport infrastructure, while critics call him a robber baron for monopolies helped in part by political manipulation.
cornwall: Cornwall forms the tip of the south-west peninsula of Great Britain and is exposed to the full force of the Atlantic winds. Its only land border is with Devon, formed almost entirely by the River Tamar. The coast is mostly resistant rock and tall cliffs, and the interior is a spine of infertile upland made of granite intrusions, among them Bodmin Moor, Hensbarrow, Carnmenellis and the Penwith peninsula. These are the exposed parts of the Cornubian batholith, which also includes Dartmoor and the Isles of Scilly. The Lizard peninsula is mainland Britain's only ophiolite, a section of oceanic crust now found on land.

The area was inhabited from the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic periods, and in the Late Bronze Age it belonged to a maritime trading culture, the Atlantic Bronze Age system, that reached from Ireland to Portugal. Cornwall had a minor Roman presence and later formed part of the Brittonic kingdom of Dumnonia. The Battle of Deorham in 577 separated Dumnonia from Wales, after which its people often fought the expanding kingdom of Wessex. Centwine of Wessex drove the Britons as far as the sea in 682, and the Annales Cambriae report a British victory at Hehil in 722. King Æthelstan set the boundary at the Tamar in 936.

By the Norman Conquest Cornwall was administered as part of England but kept its own culture. Breton allies of the Normans took many lands, and a new Cornish-Norman ruling class later emerged, some of its members involved in the Stannary Parliament system. Cornwall became a duchy in 1337. In 1548 the college at Glasney was closed and looted, and objections to the English language Book of Common Prayer led to the Prayer Book Rebellion; reprisals have been estimated to account for 10 to 11 per cent of the civilian population and began the slow decline of the Cornish language. During the Industrial Revolution the tin and copper mines expanded and then declined, and china clay became a major industry around St Austell.

Cornwall is a ceremonial county with an area of 1,375 square miles; its only city is Truro. It is recognised by Cornish and Celtic political groups as one of six Celtic nations, and its flag is Saint Piran's, a white cross on a black field. Efforts to revive the Cornish language began in the nineteenth century, and the language is recognised under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages. The Newlyn School and later the artists of St Ives made the county a centre of painting, and the derelict mine workings survive as a World Heritage Site.
coro-venezuela: Coro stands on a coastal plain at the south of the Paraguaná Peninsula, a few kilometres from its port, La Vela de Coro, on the Caribbean Sea. The Médanos de Coro National Park, a field of dunes, lies to the north. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with strong winds. According to tradition the name comes from the Caquetio word curiana, meaning place of winds.

The city was founded on 26 July 1527 by Juan de Ampíes as Santa Ana de Coro. Ampíes agreed to respect Manaure, the leading chief of the Caquetio people, but in 1529 Ambrosius Ehinger arrived as first governor for the Welser, a banking family of Augsburg to whom the emperor Charles V had granted the Province of Venezuela. As Neu-Augsburg it was the first German colony in the Americas, and expeditions set out from it in search of El Dorado. The Welser government ended in 1545. The diocese of Coro, created in 1531, was the first bishopric in South America.

Coro was the first capital of the captaincy general of Venezuela until 1578, when Caracas replaced it because of repeated pirate attacks and its harsh climate. Francis Drake sacked the cathedral in 1567, and in the 17th century a hurricane and more raids struck the city. In 1795 José Leonardo Chirino led a rising of enslaved and other dominated people in the Sierra de Coro that aimed to end slavery and was defeated. In 1806 Francisco de Miranda landed at La Vela de Coro, bringing the tricolour later adopted by Gran Colombia. Coro stayed loyal to Spain in 1810 and joined the independence movement in 1821.

Coro is the capital of Falcón State. Its centre joins the Spanish chequerboard plan with irregular streets of German origin, and its houses are built of adobe and bahareque, an earth and plant-fibre technique unique in the Caribbean. The cathedral is the oldest Catholic church on the South American mainland. Coro and its port were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1993 and have been on the List of World Heritage in Danger since 2005 because rain damages the earthen buildings.
coromandel-coast: The delimitations of the coast vary, but it is generally taken to be bounded by the mouth of the Krishna river to the north, the Bay of Bengal to the east, the cape of Point Calimere to the south and the Eastern Ghats to the west, although some extend its northern boundary to Ganjam. It covers about 22,800 square kilometres, with an average elevation of 80 metres, backed by the low, flat-topped hills of the Eastern Ghats. It is home to the East Deccan dry evergreen forests, whose leathery leaves stay on the trees all year, and to mangrove forests along the low coast and river deltas. Kaliveli Lake and Pulicat Lake are important wetlands for migrating and resident birds.

The name comes from Cōḻamaṇḍalam, Tamil for the realm of the Cholas, from which the Portuguese derived Coromandel. Another derivation is Karaimaṇḍalam, the realm of the shores. In Muslim sources from the 12th century on the coast was called the Maʿbar Coast. An Italian explorer, Ludovico di Varthema, perhaps first gave the name Coromandel in 1510, and the Portuguese then used it on maps.

By late 1530 the coast had three Portuguese settlements, at Negapatão, São Tomé de Meliapore and Paliacate. In the 17th and 18th centuries it was the scene of rivalry among European powers for control of the India trade. The British established themselves at Fort St George, Madras, and at Masulipatnam, the Dutch at Pulicat and Sadras, the French at Pondicherry, Karaikal and Nizampatnam, and the Danish at Dansborg, or Tranquebar. Eventually the British won out, though France kept the small enclaves of Pondicherry and Karaikal until 1954. The Dutch took up serious trading there.

The coast supplied Indian Muslim eunuchs to the court of Siam. In the 18th century Chinese lacquer goods such as boxes, screens and chests became known as Coromandel goods, because many Chinese exports were consolidated at its ports. Two works on its economic history are Merchants, Companies and Commerce on the Coromandel Coast, 1650 to 1740, by Arasaratnam, and The World of the Weaver in Northern Coromandel, by P. Swarnalatha. The name was later given to places elsewhere: the Coromandel Peninsula in New Zealand took it from a Royal Navy ship called HMS Coromandel, and Coromandel Valley in South Australia from a ship that reached Holdfast Bay in 1837 with 156 English settlers.
corpus-christi-feast: The feast resulted from some forty years of work by Juliana of Liège, a Norbertine canoness born in 1191 or 1192, who had been raised by the Augustinian nuns of Mont-Cornillon. She reported a first vision of Christ in 1208, in which she was told to plead for a feast of Corpus Christi, and kept it secret for about twenty years. She then petitioned the Dominican Hugh of St-Cher and Robert of Thourotte, Bishop of Liège, who in 1246 ordered the feast kept each year in his diocese on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday. The first celebration was at St Martin's Church in Liège.

In 1251 Hugh of St-Cher, as Cardinal-Legate, found the feast unobserved at Liège and reinstated it, and the next year he established it across his jurisdiction. Jacques Pantaléon, who had served as archdeacon at Liège, became Pope Urban IV and in 1264 made the feast universal for the Latin Church by the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo. The bull gave as the chief reason that so many other themes crowded Maundy Thursday that the Eucharist was almost lost sight of.

Tradition says that Urban IV was moved by a procession to Orvieto in 1263 after a bleeding host was witnessed at Bolsena. Scholars have questioned this, noting problems in dating the miracle, whose tradition begins in the 14th century. Thomas Aquinas, at Orvieto from 1259 to 1265, is credited with the office and Mass of the feast, including the hymn Pange Lingua.

The feast was not widely kept for half a century. It became truly universal only after the bull was included in the Clementines, promulgated in 1317 by Pope John XXII. The central observance is a procession of the Blessed Sacrament in a monstrance, followed by Benediction, with flower wreaths on doors and windows. In medieval Europe it was also a time for mystery plays: those at York were performed on Corpus Christi Day for some 200 years until the 16th century.

During the Reformation the feast was suppressed in many Protestant churches, especially Calvinist ones, because it affirmed the real presence. Martin Luther condemned processions with the consecrated elements as vain idolatry, yet Lutheran calendars kept the feast until about 1600, and it continues in some Lutheran churches. England abolished it in 1548, and the Church of England has since allowed a Day of Thanksgiving for the Institution of Holy Communion on the same Thursday.
corpus-juris-civilis: Justinian came to the throne in Constantinople in 527. Six months later, to reduce the great number of imperial constitutions and so of lawsuits, he arranged a new collection of them, the Codex Iustinianus. The commission could leave out or change text and delete what was obsolete or contradictory. The first edition was completed on 7 April 529 and replaced all earlier constitutions; it is lost, and a second edition of 534 survives.

A little over a year later Justinian appointed a commission headed by Tribonian to compile the writings of the jurists in a shorter, more contemporary form. It finished the Digest in 533. How far the editors amended their material is not recorded and mostly cannot be known. The text was almost entirely in Latin, though Greek was the language of most citizens.

The work has four parts. The Code collects imperial pronouncements having force of law back to the time of Hadrian; its first law requires all peoples under imperial rule to hold the Christian faith. The Digest is an encyclopedia of brief extracts, mostly from the second and third centuries, from 38 jurists, and was given full force of law.

The Institutes, a student textbook in four books made by Tribonian and the professors Theophilus and Dorotheus, is largely based on the Institutes of Gaius, of which two thirds is literal quotation. It became law on 30 December 533, with the Digest. All three were meant to be the sole source of law, but Justinian had to pass further laws after 534, counted as the fourth part, the Novels.

In the Eastern Empire the Corpus was revised into Greek and remained the basis of law, in the Basilika of the late 9th century, until the 15th century. In the West it took effect in areas regained under Justinian, such as Ravenna, but was otherwise recovered only in the Middle Ages. Historians disagree on how it was recovered in northern Italy about 1070. It was taught at Bologna by Pepo and then Irnerius, whose pupils, the Four Doctors of Bologna, were among the first glossators.

The recovered law became the foundation of law in all civil law jurisdictions and influenced the canon law of the Catholic Church. Its influence on common law is markedly less. The name Corpus Juris Civilis was adopted only in the 16th century, when Dionysius Gothofredus printed it under that title in 1583.
corrientes: Corrientes lies in the Argentine Littoral, on the eastern shore of the Paraná River, near the border with Paraguay. It is about 1,000 km from Buenos Aires and 300 km from Posadas, on National Route 12. Across the river, which marks the natural border with Chaco Province, lies its twin city Resistencia, joined to it by the General Belgrano Bridge. The Guarani name of the city is Taragui, meaning 'Currents'. The climate is humid subtropical, with an annual average temperature of 21.3 °C and annual rainfall of around 1,500 millimetres.

Europeans reached the region early. Sebastian Cabot established the fort of Sancti Spiritu upstream on the Paraná in 1527, and in 1536 Pedro de Mendoza went further north into the river's basin, searching for the Sierras of Silver. Juan Torres de Vera y Aragón founded the city on 3 April 1588 and named it San Juan de Vera de las Siete Corrientes, later shortened to Corrientes.

The seven currents refer to seven peninsulas on the shore at this place, which produced wild currents that made navigation difficult. Its position between Asunción and Buenos Aires made it an important middle point, helped by its land, 55 metres high, which prevents flooding when the river rises. In 1615 Jesuits settled near the Uruguay River. In 1807 the city resisted the British invasions. During the Argentine War of Independence it was in permanent conflict with the centralist government of Buenos Aires, but the Paraguayan War united them after Paraguayan forces attacked the city in 1865.

Corrientes is the capital of the province of Corrientes and had a population of 346,334 at the 2010 census. It combines colonial and modern architecture with several churches, and it is home to one of Argentina's biggest carnival and chamamé celebrations.
corsica: Corsica is the fourth-largest island in the Mediterranean, lying south-east of the French mainland, west of the Italian Peninsula and immediately north of Sardinia. It is 183 km long at its longest and 83 km wide at its widest. It is the most mountainous island in the Mediterranean, a mountain in the sea: a single chain makes up two-thirds of the island, with Monte Cinto the highest peak at 2,706 metres. Its granite backbone on the western side formed about 250 million years ago.

People have lived on Corsica since the Mesolithic, and a permanent presence is documented from the Neolithic. After the western Roman Empire collapsed in the fifth century CE the island was invaded by the Vandals and the Ostrogoths, briefly recovered by the Byzantine Empire, then became part of the Kingdom of the Lombards. Pepin the Short, king of the Franks, expelled the Lombards and nominally granted Corsica to Pope Stephen II.

In the first quarter of the 11th century Pisa and Genoa together freed the island from the threat of Arab invasion, and it then came under the influence of the Republic of Pisa.
