The county had 95,840 people at the 2022 census. Whiskey is distilled at Kilbeggan, and the county has an extensive beef and dairy trade and many stud farms.
county-wicklow: County Wicklow lies in Leinster, bordered by the Irish Sea to the east and by Wexford to the south, Carlow to the southwest, Kildare to the west and Dublin to the north. The county is named after the town of Wicklow, about 50 kilometres south of Dublin, whose name derives from the Old Norse Víkingaló, meaning Vikings' Meadow. The Wicklow Mountains are centred on the Leinster batholith, a mass of granite covering 1,500 square kilometres, the most expansive mass of intrusive igneous rock in Ireland or Britain. The River Liffey, 132 kilometres long, rises near Tonduff mountain. The coastline is relatively short, at 64 kilometres, and Wicklow Head is the most easterly mainland point of the Republic of Ireland.

In 431 Saint Palladius, a bishop from Britain or Gaul sent to the Irish believing in Christ, landed with companions at Wicklow harbour. The local tribe, the Cualann, had a chief named Naithi who opposed the missionaries, but Palladius still founded three churches, at Donard, Tigroney and Colbinstown. After a rather unsuccessful stay he left for Scotland.

Wicklow was the last of the traditional counties of Ireland to be shired, in 1606, from land previously part of Dublin and Carlow. It was established as a distinct county to control local groups such as the O'Byrnes. After the failed Irish Rebellion of 1798, government forces built the Military Road across the mountains, from Rathfarnham to Aghavannagh, to help defeat rebels still active in an area that had been a hotbed of rebellion for centuries. Wicklow was the first county in Ireland to lose the Irish language: only about 2 per cent of people spoke it in the 1770s. Andrew and Hannah Byrne of Glenealy, who both died in 1830, were among the last native speakers in the county.

The county town is Wicklow, though Bray is by far the largest town, and Wicklow County Council is the local authority. The population was 155,258 at the 2022 census. The county is colloquially called the Garden of Ireland for its scenery and woodlands, and the Wicklow Way is the oldest waymarked long-distance walking trail in Ireland. Places of interest include the ruins of the monastic city of Glendalough, Powerscourt Estate and Waterfall, Wicklow Gaol and the Wicklow Mountains National Park.
coup-of-18-brumaire: The French Republic under the Directory had been at war with the major European powers since 1792. Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès, elected to the Directory in May 1799, opposed the Constitution of 1795, which gave the Directory limited powers and no parliamentary control, and saw a coup as the only way to change it. He looked for a strong man who would restore the Republic on his terms and first had General Joubert in mind; when Joubert fell at the Battle of Novi in August 1799, he turned to Napoleon on the advice of General Moreau.

Napoleon reached Paris on 16 October but was under the minimum age of 40 for the Directory. When Paul Barras refused to support a coup on 4 November, Napoleon allied with Sieyès. The coup was planned for 7 November and postponed by 24 hours to Saturday, 9 November.

On 9 November the Council of Elders was summoned to the Tuileries, where Sieyès persuaded it, on the pretext that a Jacobin plot was imminent, to move the legislature to the Château de Saint-Cloud, outside Paris, and gave Napoleon command of the troops in the Paris area. The directors Gohier and Jean Moulin were placed under house arrest, and Talleyrand persuaded Barras to resign. On 10 November Napoleon had the palace at Saint-Cloud surrounded by 6,000 soldiers.

In the Orangery, where the Council of Five Hundred sat, deputies shouted 'Kill him!' and tried to seize him, and Murat and Lefebvre saved him, dazed and bleeding. Lucien Bonaparte told the guards that Napoleon had been attacked, and the chamber was cleared by force. By 2 am Lucien had gathered a quorum of stragglers from the Five Hundred and fifty members of the Elders, who dissolved the Directory and swore allegiance to three provisional consuls: Napoleon, Sieyès and Ducos.

Napoleon moved to isolate Sieyès, who resigned after Napoleon publicly criticised his ideas. Napoleon kept the main features of his draft, with four assemblies able to block one another and ministers answering only to the Consul. The constitution was adopted on 12 December, with Jean-Jacques Cambacérès and Charles Lebrun as co-consuls.

It was put to a referendum, which gave 3,011,007 votes for and 1,562 against. Half a million of these votes were cast by the army without valid ballots, and some 900,000 were forged by Lucien Bonaparte. With a turnout of 25 per cent, Napoleon secured only about 17 per cent of the genuine votes, on this reckoning. Most historians regard the coup as the end of the French Revolution.
courland: Courland, in Latvian Kurzeme, is one of the Historical Latvian Lands. It lies in western Latvia, bordered on the north by the Gulf of Riga, on the west by the Baltic Sea and on the south by Lithuania, and its name means Land of Curonians. The landscape is low and undulating, with marshy coastlands and, inland, wooded dunes of pine, spruce, birch and oak, swamps and lakes. Its largest city is Liepāja. Of nearly a hundred rivers, only the Daugava, the Lielupe and the Venta are navigable.

The Curonians were a Baltic tribe with a strong warrior culture and a reputation for seafaring, living on the Baltic shore from before the 5th century. During the Livonian Crusades they resisted German crusading orders for a long time. After the Samogitians defeated the Livonian Order at the Battle of Durbe in 1260, uprisings followed, but in 1266 the whole of Courland was partitioned between the Livonian Order and the Archbishop of Riga. Curonian nobles in Kuldīga kept their personal freedom and some privileges.

From 1561 until 1795 the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia was a semi-independent state, nominally a vassal of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. The future Empress Anna served as regent from 1711, and after the ducal line died out in 1737 she arranged for the duchy to pass to Ernst Johann von Biron. The duchy was one of the smallest European states to found overseas colonies, on Tobago and Trinidad and on James Island in the Gambia. In 1795 the last duke, Peter von Biron, ceded it to the Russian Empire, and it became the Courland Governorate, where most land was held by nobles descended from German invaders and most Latvians were landless labourers.

German forces took Courland in 1915. After Latvia declared independence on 18 November 1918, Courland became one of its provinces. In 1944–1945 some 200,000 German troops were trapped in the Courland Pocket until their surrender on 8 May 1945.

Courland is part of Latvia but is no longer an administrative unit; the Kurzeme Planning Region covers much of it. Its population has long been predominantly Lutheran, with Orthodox, Catholic and Jewish communities.
court-of-justice-of-the-european-union: The Court began as a single court, the Court of Justice of the European Coal and Steel Communities. When the Euratom and the European Economic Community were founded in 1957, its name changed to the Court of Justice of the European Communities. In 1988 the Court asked the Commission to create a Court of First Instance, and in 2004 a Civil Service Tribunal was added to deal with cases brought by EU staff. That Tribunal was later ended, its competence passing to the Court of First Instance, which was renamed the General Court. The Treaty of Lisbon in 2009 gave the system its present name and renamed the older court simply the Court of Justice.

The institution is seated in the Kirchberg district of Luxembourg City and consists of two courts. The Court of Justice hears applications from national courts for preliminary rulings on the interpretation of EU law, direct actions against member states for failure to fulfil an obligation, direct actions against EU institutions, and appeals from the General Court. It has one judge from each member state, assisted by Advocates General, each of whom prepares an independent, non-binding opinion in the cases assigned to them.

The General Court hears actions brought by individuals or companies against acts of EU institutions and agencies, claims for damages, intellectual property cases and employment disputes between institutions and their staff. It has two judges from each member state. Judges and Advocates General are appointed by national governments jointly, for a renewable term of six years. The working language of the Court is French.

The Court's mission is to ensure that the law is observed in the interpretation and application of the Treaties. It reviews the legality of the actions of EU institutions, enforces compliance by member states with their obligations and interprets EU law, working with national courts so that the law is applied uniformly. It is described as a sui generis court system, of its own kind, and as a supranational institution.
coxs-bazar: Cox's Bazar lies on a coastal plain in the south-eastern corner of Bangladesh, about 150 km south of Chittagong, bounded by the Bakkhali River on the north and east and by the Bay of Bengal on the west. Along the shore is an extensive area of beach and dunes, one of the longest natural sea beaches of South-East Asia. Most of the town stands on a floodplain, so it is exposed to flooding from cyclones and storm surges.

In the early 9th century the greater Chittagong area, including Cox's Bazar, was under the Arakan kings until the Mughals conquered it in 1666. When the Mughal prince Shah Shuja passed through the hills on his way to Arakan he is said to have camped there; a place named Dulahazara, meaning one thousand palanquins, recalls his retinue. After the Mughals the area came under the Tipras and the Arakanese, then the Portuguese and then the British.

The name comes from Captain Hiram Cox, an officer of the British East India Company who was superintendent of the outpost of Palonki. He took on the settlement of Arakanese refugees and died in 1799 before finishing the work, and a market named after him commemorated this. The town was first established in 1854 and became a municipality in 1869. During the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971 Pakistani soldiers killed many people in the town. The subdivision became a district in 1984, and in 2017 hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees from Myanmar arrived in the district.

Cox's Bazar is a fishing port and tourism centre and the headquarters of its district; its population was 196,385 in the 2022 census. Nearby are Himchari National Park, established in 1980, and the Buddhist monastery of Aggmeda Khyang. The town is linked by road and rail to Chittagong.
crazy-horse: Reports differ on Crazy Horse's birth year. Oral accounts from relatives and the biographer Kingsley Bray give 1840, while He Dog, who said they were born in the same year, is placed by census records and interviews in 1842. His father, also named Tȟašúŋke Witkó, was Oglala, and his mother, Rattling Blanket Woman, was Miniconjou. In the most widely repeated account of his vision, which comes from the interpreter William Garnett, a man rode out of a lake with an unpainted face and a single eagle feather and told him never to wear a war bonnet, to rub dust over himself before battle and never to take anything for himself.

On 21 December 1866, during Red Cloud's War, he led a decoy party that drew Captain William J. Fetterman and eighty-one soldiers out of Fort Phil Kearny into an ambush by nearly 1,000 Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors. On 2 August 1867 he led the Oglala contingent in the Wagon Box Fight near the same fort.

In the Great Sioux War of 1876-1877 he was among the leaders who struck General George Crook's column on Rosebud Creek on 17 June 1876. Crook retreated the next day, and his delay in joining George Armstrong Custer's 7th Cavalry contributed to Custer's defeat at the Little Bighorn about a week later, where Crazy Horse helped lead the combined Native forces. Contemporaries described him as reserved and shy, generous to the poor, the old and children, and he avoided being photographed.

After months of pursuit, famine and military pressure, Crazy Horse arrived at the Red Cloud Agency near Fort Robinson, Nebraska, on 6 May 1877 with about 900 Oglala warriors and laid down his arms. In September 1877 he was fatally wounded by a bayonet while being confined in the guardhouse, during what the army described as a struggle with a guard. Seventeen eyewitness accounts survive and they disagree. He left no written statements and signed no treaties, so nearly all that is known comes from interviews made decades later. He is remembered as a symbol of Lakota resistance. The Crazy Horse Memorial in the Black Hills of South Dakota was begun in 1948 and remains incomplete.
credit-suisse: Alfred Escher, called the spiritual father of the railway law of 1852 for his work against a state-run railway system in Switzerland, founded the bank with the Allgemeine Deutsche Credit-Anstalt on 5 July 1856. Its first name was the Swiss Credit Institution (Schweizerische Kreditanstalt). Its main purpose was to provide domestic funding for railway projects and so avoid French banks that wanted to exert influence over the railways.

Escher aimed to start with three million shares and instead sold 218 million in three days. The bank opened on 16 July 1856 and was modelled on the Crédit Mobilier, a French railway-financing bank founded two years earlier, though with a more conservative policy of short-to-medium-term loans. In its first year 25% of its revenues came from the Swiss Northeastern Railway, which was being built by Bruno Hildebrand and Escher's company, Nordostbahn.

The bank issued loans that helped create Switzerland's electrical grid and the European rail system. In the 1900s it began to shift towards retail banking, responding to the rise of the middle class and to competition from the Swiss banks UBS and Julius Bär. In 1978 it partnered with First Boston to form Credit Suisse First Boston in Europe and bought a 44% stake in First Boston's American operations, and in 1988 it acquired a controlling share of First Boston itself. Between 1990 and 2000 it bought institutions such as the Winterthur Group, Swiss Volksbank and Bank Leu.

Credit Suisse came through the credit crisis better than many competitors and did not have to borrow from the government. In 2007 two of its traders pleaded guilty to mismarking securities positions to overvalue them by $3 billion and so raise their year-end bonuses. 6 billion in fines and restitution.

On 15 March 2023 its share price fell nearly 25% after its largest investor, Saudi National Bank, said it could not provide more financial assistance. UBS took the bank over, and in July 2024 Credit Suisse (Schweiz) ceased to exist as a separate legal entity.

Credit Suisse Group AG was a joint-stock company registered in Zurich that operated as a holding company, with offices in the major financial centres. It offered investment banking, private banking and asset management, and it was known for strict bank-client confidentiality and banking secrecy.
cree: The word Cree comes into English from the French Cris, short for Christinaux, which came from the Ojibwe word Kinistino. The Ojibwe used it for the many communities they met north and west of Lake Superior, mostly in Manitoba. The Cree are generally divided into groups by dialect and region, among them the Plains Cree, Woodland Cree, Rocky Cree, Swampy Cree, Moose Cree and East Cree, and the Atikamekw, Innu and Naskapi are closely related.

Cree homelands cover much of eastern and central Canada, from Eeyou Istchee in what is now Quebec to northern Ontario, much of the Canadian Prairies, and into British Columbia and the Northwest Territories. The Cree number more than 350,000 in Canada, where they are one of the largest First Nations groupings. Small communities live in the United States, mostly in Montana.

In Manitoba the Cree were first contacted by Europeans in 1682, at the mouth of the Nelson and Hayes rivers, by a Hudson's Bay Company party travelling about 160 kilometres inland. In 1732 Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye, met 200 Cree warriors in what is now north-western Ontario, near present-day Fort Frances, in war paint for an attack on the Dakota and another group of Ojibwe.

A westward movement over time is strongly associated with the Cree role as traders and hunters in the fur trade. After acquiring firearms from the Hudson's Bay Company they moved onto the plains as traders and acted as middlemen with the company. The Cree and the Ojibwa were displaced from a large area north of Winnipeg by the Canadian government between 1905 and the 1930s. The Numbered Treaties cover most Cree homelands.

Historically the Cree were hunter-gatherers. The basic units were the lodge, perhaps eight to a dozen people, usually the families of two related married couples sharing a wigwam or tipi, and the band, a group of lodges that moved and hunted together. Lodges could leave bands, and bands formed and dissolved with ease. Beyond regional gatherings there was no higher formal structure, and decisions of war and peace were made by consensus. Clans each had a representative and a vote in important councils. Cree is a group of closely related Algonquian languages, a chain of dialects in which neighbours understand each other easily, and the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Canada.
crete: Crete lies about 100 kilometres south of the Peloponnese, closing the southern edge of the Aegean Sea, with the Sea of Crete to the north and the Libyan Sea to the south. It is the fifth largest island in the Mediterranean. The island is elongated, 260 kilometres from east to west, and a range of six mountain groups crosses it, among them the Idi Range, rising to 2,456 metres, and the White Mountains, cut by the Samariá Gorge. The earliest references call it Kaptara, in texts from Mari of the 18th century BCE.

Permanent settlement dates from the Neolithic, around 7,000 BCE, at sites such as Knossos. In the Bronze Age Crete was the centre of the Minoan civilisation, notable for its art, its writing systems such as Linear A and its palace complexes, with trade reaching Cyprus, Canaan and Egypt. Mycenaean Greeks took over in 1420 BCE, and the Linear B archive from Knossos holds the oldest identified writing in Greek. Rome conquered the island in 69 BCE after a three-year campaign under Quintus Caecilius Metellus, and Gortyn became capital of the province.

In the 820s Andalusian Muwallads led by Abu Hafs founded the Emirate of Crete, and Nikephoros Phokas restored Byzantine rule in 960 to 961. Venice ruled from 1212 for more than four centuries, a time of the Cretan School of painting, to which El Greco belonged. The Ottomans took the island in 1669 after the siege of Candia. After uprisings, the Great Powers decreed autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty in 1898, and Crete became part of Greece in December 1913. The Battle of Crete in May 1941 left more than 11,000 soldiers and civilians killed or wounded.

Crete is the largest and most populous island of Greece, with 624,408 people in the region in 2021, and Heraklion is its capital and largest city. Its Minoan sites include Knossos, Malia, Zakros, Petras and Phaistos. It has its own Mantinades poetry, music played on the Cretan lyra and laouto, and dances such as the Pentozali. In Greek mythology Crete is the birthplace of Zeus.
crimea: Crimea covers 27,000 square kilometres on the northern coast of the Black Sea and the western coast of the Sea of Azov. It is almost an island, joined to the mainland only by the Isthmus of Perekop, a strip about 5 to 7 kilometres wide. It was called the Tauric Peninsula, after the Tauri, until the early modern period; the name Crimea comes from the Italian la Crimea. Most of the peninsula is semiarid steppe, scattered with the burial mounds of the ancient Scythians, while the Crimean Mountains shelter a narrow southern coast with a Mediterranean climate.

The recorded history of Crimea begins around the 5th century BCE, when Greek colonies were founded on the south coast, the most important being Chersonesos near modern Sevastopol, with Scythians and Tauri in the hinterland. The south later became the Bosporan Kingdom, a client kingdom of Rome from 63 BCE to 341 CE, and stayed Greek in culture under the Byzantine Empire, the Empire of Trebizond and the Principality of Theodoro, which ended in 1475. In the 13th century the Venetians and the Genoese held some ports, while the interior fell to the Golden Horde.

In the 1440s the Crimean Khanate formed from the collapse of the Horde and soon became subject to the Ottoman Empire, which also conquered the independent coastal areas. Raids on Eastern Europe for slaves were a major source of prosperity. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 made the Tatars of Crimea politically independent, and in 1783 Catherine the Great incorporated the peninsula into the Russian Empire. From 1853 to 1856 it was the site of the principal engagements of the Crimean War, in which Russia lost to a French-led alliance.

Crimea changed hands many times in the Russian Civil War, and Wrangel's White Army made its last stand there. In 1921 it became an autonomous republic within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. Germany occupied it from 1942 to 1944, and after the Soviets regained control in 1944 they deported the Crimean Tatars and several other nationalities. It became an oblast in 1945 and was transferred to the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1954, on the 300th anniversary of the Treaty of Pereyaslav.

After Ukrainian independence in 1991 most of the peninsula became the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, and a 1997 treaty let Russia keep basing its fleet in Sevastopol, the largest city. In 2014 Russia occupied and annexed the peninsula, a step most countries do not recognise. Its population is about 2.4 million.
crimean-karaites: The Crimean Karaites are a traditionally Turkic-speaking Judaic ethnoreligious group native to Crimea. Most modern scholars regard them as descendants of Karaite Jews who settled in Crimea and adopted a Kipchak language, while others see them as descendants of Khazar or Cuman converts. Many Crimean Karaites identify as descendants of the Khazars, a theory specialists question: the Karaim language is Kipchak, Khazar Judaism was probably Rabbinic, and the Khazars disappeared in the 11th century while the first written mention of Crimean Karaites dates from the 13th. They lived alongside the Krymchaks, who practise Rabbinic Judaism, and under the Crimean Khanate had major communities at Çufut Qale, Sudak, Kefe and Bakhchysarai.

According to Karaite tradition, Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania moved a branch of the community to Trakai, although modern historians doubt the Crimean origin of the Lithuanian Karaites. Rabbinic leaders, who taxed all Jews from 1580 to 1646, regarded the Karaites as apostates, and in 1646 the Karaites obtained the expulsion of Rabbinites from Trakai. They suffered severely in the Khmelnytsky Uprising of 1648 and the wars of 1654 to 1667.

In the 19th century leaders such as Avraham Firkovich and Sima Babovich worked to change the community's status in Russian law, and Firkovich has been accused of forging documents to link the Karaites to the Khazars. The tsarist government exempted them from many restrictions on Jews, and in 1863 they gained the same rights as their Christian and Tatar neighbours, while the Krymchaks stayed under the anti-Jewish laws. Yevpatoria became their main centre.

In 1934 the Reich Agency for the Investigation of Families ruled that Karaites were not Jews under German law. Even so, German soldiers in the Soviet Union killed some of them, including 200 at Babi Yar. Ashkenazi rabbis in Crimea told the Germans that Karaites were not Jews, and many Karaites risked their lives to hide Jews. After the Soviet recapture of Crimea in 1944, 6,357 Karaites were counted. They were spared the mass deportation of Crimean Tatars, Greeks and Armenians. Assimilation and emigration have greatly reduced the community.
crimean-tatars: The Crimean Tatars are a Turkic people native to Crimea. They formed as a people there over hundreds of years and descend from various peoples who lived in Crimea, among them the Tauri, Scythians, Sarmatians, Alans, ancient Greeks, Huns, Khazars, Cumans and Italians. The connecting elements were a shared territory, the Turkic language and the Islamic religion. At the beginning of the 13th century the Cumans, the majority of the population, became part of the Golden Horde. The Crimean Tatars mostly adopted Islam in the 14th century.

In 1441 an embassy from several Crimean clans invited Hacı Giray from Lithuania to rule in Crimea. He founded the Giray dynasty, which ruled until Russia annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1783. The Khanate was among the strongest powers in Eastern Europe until the early 18th century. It officially was a vassal of the Ottoman Empire, with great autonomy after 1580. Until the 18th century it also kept up slave raids into present-day Ukraine and Russia, and Kefe was a major slave market. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774 made Crimea independent, but Russia annexed it in 1783, and many Tatars were forced to leave for the Ottoman Empire. At least 800,000 left Crimea between 1783 and the beginning of the 20th century.

More than 100,000 Crimean Tatars starved in the famine of 1921. In May 1944 the Soviet State Defense Committee ordered the deportation of all Crimean Tatars, mainly to Uzbekistan, and between 18% and 46% of the population was lost. A few were allowed to return from 1967, and in 1989 the Supreme Soviet adopted a full right of return.

The Crimean Tatar language belongs to the Kipchak group of Turkic languages and has three dialects. It was written in the Arabic script, in Latin from 1928 and in Cyrillic from 1938. The people are divided into three core groups: the Mountain Tats, the Yaliboylus of the coast and the Steppe Tatars. Large diaspora communities live in Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria.
crimean-war: The causes of the war lay in the Eastern question, the decline of the Ottoman Empire, Russia's expansion in earlier Russo-Turkish wars, and the British and French wish to preserve the Ottoman Empire to keep the balance of power. The proximate cause was Tsar Nicholas I's demand that the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox subjects be placed under his protection. After the Ottoman refusal, Russian troops occupied the Danubian Principalities in July 1853, and the Ottomans declared war in October.

Britain and France joined the Ottoman side in March 1854, after public outrage at the destruction of the Ottoman squadron at Sinop. In September 1854 the allies landed in Crimea to take the naval base of Sevastopol, won the Battle of the Alma, repulsed a Russian attack at Balaclava on 25 October, where the Charge of the Light Brigade took place, and defeated a second at Inkerman. The Siege of Sevastopol then lasted until 8 September 1855 and brought brutal conditions to both armies. Sardinia-Piedmont joined in 1855. Sevastopol fell after a French assault on the Malakoff redoubt. The British government of Lord Aberdeen fell in January 1855 after Parliament voted to investigate the war's mismanagement.

The Treaty of Paris, signed on 30 March 1856, forbade Russia to base warships in the Black Sea, made Wallachia and Moldavia largely independent, and gave Christians in the Ottoman Empire a degree of official equality. Estimates of the dead vary widely: 95,615 French, 22,182 British and between 450,000 and 630,000 Russian, most from disease. The war was one of the first to use explosive naval shells, railways and telegraphs, and was reported by William Howard Russell and photographed by Roger Fenton. Its failures led in Britain to a demand for professional nursing, associated with Florence Nightingale. For Russia, defeat drained the treasury and became a catalyst for reform, including the emancipation of the serfs in 1861.
crisis-of-the-third-century: After the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 the long period of stability ended. Septimius Severus emerged as sole emperor in 197 after the Year of the Five Emperors, and to keep the armies loyal he raised legionaries' pay and gave large donatives, a policy his successors continued. There were also no clear rules for the imperial succession, since the empire kept the facade of a republic, and any general with a large army had an incentive to seize power whenever the succession looked uncertain.

The crisis began in 235, when troops assassinated Severus Alexander, whom they judged too lenient with Germanic chieftains, and proclaimed Maximinus Thrax, the first of the barracks emperors. In 238 the Year of the Six Emperors killed all the original claimants. Generals fought each other and neglected the frontiers, where the Goths, Vandals and Alamanni raided across the Rhine and Danube while the Sasanian Empire attacked in the east. The Plague of Cyprian broke out in 251, and in 260 the Sasanians captured Emperor Valerian.

The empire then broke apart. The Gallic Empire, including Gaul, Britain and briefly Hispania, split off in 260, and the Palmyrene Empire, covering Syria, Palestine and Egypt, in 267. Claudius II Gothicus defeated a Gothic invasion at Naissus in 268 or 269, which historians see as the turning point. Aurelian, who reigned from 270 to 275, defeated the Palmyrene Empire and the Gallic Empire, so that by late 274 the empire was one again.

Many cities, especially in the west, were ruined, and towns including Rome itself, which had not needed fortifications for centuries, now built thick walls. The economy was crippled by the breakdown of trade and the debasement of the currency. Diocletian broke the cycle of usurpation by sharing rule with a colleague and then, in 293, establishing the Tetrarchy of four co-emperors. Most historians now see the crisis as marking the transition from classical antiquity to late antiquity. The empire survived until 476 in the West and until 1453 in the East.
croatia: Croatia lies on the Adriatic coast, and the sea forms its entire southwest border. It covers 56,594 square kilometres and is divided into twenty counties within four historical and cultural regions. The Dinaric Alps rise to the highest point, the Dinara peak at 1,831 metres, near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Insular Croatia consists of over a thousand islands and islets, 48 of them permanently inhabited; the largest are Cres and Krk.

In the north the hilly Hrvatsko Zagorje and the plains of Slavonia are crossed by the Danube, Drava, Kupa and Sava. Karst topography makes up about half of the country. The area around Dubrovnik is a practical exclave, separated by land from the rest by a short coastal strip belonging to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and linked to it by the Pelješac Bridge.

The area was inhabited throughout prehistory, and Neanderthal fossils from the middle Palaeolithic were found at Krapina. Illyrians and Liburnians lived there, and the first Greek colonies were established on the islands of Hvar, Korčula and Vis. In 9 CE the territory became part of the Roman Empire. Emperor Diocletian, a native of the region, built a large palace at Split and retired there after abdicating in 305 CE. In the 5th century Julius Nepos, the last de jure Western Roman Emperor, ruled a small realm from it after fleeing Italy in 475.

Avar and Croat invasions in the late 6th and first half of the 7th century destroyed almost all Roman towns. Survivors retreated to the coast, islands and mountains, and Dubrovnik was founded by survivors from Epidaurum. The origin of the Croats is debated: the predominant view is that the White Croats were a Slavic group who migrated during the Migration Period, while the Iranian theory proposes a Sarmatian-Alanic origin, drawing on names in the Tanais Tablets. The oldest stone inscription with the full ethnonym styles Duke Branimir as Dux Cruatorvm, probably between 879 and 892.

Croatia is a unitary constitutional republic with a parliamentary system. The president is directly elected for five years, and the Sabor, a unicameral parliament, holds legislative power. Its population was an estimated 3.87 million in 2024, down from a peak of 4.7 million in 1991. The 2021 census recorded 91.6% Croats and 3.2% Serbs, and about 4 million Croats live abroad. The country has ten sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The necktie derives from the cravat worn by 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in France.
croesus: Croesus was a son of the Lydian king Alyattes and one of his queens, a Carian noblewoman whose name is unknown. He had at least one full sister, Aryenis, and a half-brother, Pantaleon. As governor of Adramyttium, a city Alyattes had rebuilt as a base against the Cimmerians, nomads who had attacked Lydia in several invasions, he supplied Ionian Greek mercenaries for a campaign in Caria. A rivalry grew with Pantaleon, who may have been meant as successor, and after Alyattes died it became an open succession struggle, which Croesus won.

Croesus first marched on the Ionian city of Ephesus, whose tyrant Pindar was his own nephew. Pindar went into exile, and Croesus annexed the city and patronised the rebuilding of the Temple of Artemis. He went on to subjugate mainland Ionia, Aeolis and Doris, but made treaties of friendship with the island Greeks rather than attack them. He kept the peace with the Medes, whose king Astyages was his brother-in-law, and good relations with Egypt and Babylonia.

He offered rich gifts to Delphi, among them a gold lion weighing ten talents, and the Lydians gained precedence in consulting the oracle. He is credited with the first true gold coins of standard purity, the Croeseid, which followed his father's coins of electrum. Herodotus tells how Solon, shown his wealth, said that no man's happiness can be judged before his death; the story is regarded as a moral tale rather than history.

In 550 BCE Cyrus the Great overthrew Astyages. Croesus attacked Pteria, a vassal state, and Cyrus defeated him there, then again at Thymbra, and besieged and captured Sardis, ending the Lydian kingdom. The traditional date is doubtful, since Herodotus is unreliable on the chronology.

His fate is uncertain. Herodotus, Bacchylides and Nicolaus of Damascus say he was placed on a pyre, from which rain saved him; in most versions Cyrus kept him as an adviser, while Ctesias says he became governor of Barene. Kevin Leloux argues that he was executed. After the conquest Cyrus adopted gold coinage, and the Croeseid remained in use until Darius the Great replaced it with the daric. His name became a byword for wealth.
cross-river-state: Cross River State lies in the South-South zone of Nigeria and takes its name from the Cross River, which bisects its interior before forming much of its western border and flowing into the Cross River Estuary. It covers 20,156 square kilometres. Benue State lies to the north, Ebonyi and Abia states to the west and Akwa Ibom State to the south-west, while the eastern border is part of the national border with Cameroon.

Most of the interior is covered by the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko coastal forests, with a forest and savanna mosaic in the far north and mangroves on the southern coast. Protected areas such as Cross River National Park, the Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary and the Mbe Mountains Community Forest shelter some of Nigeria's last Cross River gorillas, drills and forest elephants. The climate is tropical, with heavy annual rainfall, and cooler on the high plateau of Obudu.

In the pre-colonial period the area was divided among its ethnic groups. Some joined the Aro Confederacy, while the Efik founded the city-state of Akwa Akpa, Old Calabar. Calabar became a British protectorate in 1884 as the capital of the Oil Rivers Protectorate, although the British did not gain formal control of the whole area until the early 1900s. The protectorate was renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate and then incorporated into the Southern Nigeria Protectorate. Much of the area became a centre of anti-colonial resistance during the Women's War.

After independence in 1960 the area was part of the Eastern Region. On 27 May 1967 General Yakubu Gowon's government created South-Eastern State from the region's eastern part. Within two months the Igbo-majority remainder of the old region attempted to secede as Biafra, and in the Nigerian Civil War Calabar and its port were hard fought over. The state was renamed Cross River State in 1976. In September 1987 its western part was separated to form Akwa Ibom State. The state had also included the Bakassi Peninsula, which was ceded to Cameroon under the Greentree Agreement.

Calabar is the capital and a major seaport on the navigable waters of the Cross River, and the state has eighteen Local Government Areas. Its peoples include the Efik, the Ekoi or Ejagham, the Yakurr, Bekwarra, Igede and many others. English is the common language, with Efik, Bekwarra and Ejagham among the principal local ones. The economy relies on farming and fishing, with crops such as cocoyam, oil palm, yam, cocoa and plantain. Visitors come to the Ikom Monoliths, a series of volcanic-stone monoliths of unknown age, to the Obudu mountain resort and to the annual Calabar Carnival held in December.
crossbow: A crossbow is a ranged weapon in which a bow-like assembly called a prod is mounted horizontally on a frame called a tiller or stock. It shoots arrow-like projectiles called bolts or quarrels. Unlike an archer, who must draw and shoot in one quick motion, the crossbow user spans the weapon and cocks it, and a trigger-released mechanism then holds the string under tension. The weapon can be carried ready to shoot, the user has unlimited time to aim, and it can be used effectively with much less training than the English longbow or the bows of steppe nomads.

The drawbacks were weight and slowness. High draw weights required gears, windlasses, pulleys or cranequins to span the weapon, which were awkward on a battlefield, and medieval crossbows had short draw lengths, so they needed very high draw weights.

The earliest known crossbows were invented in China in the first millennium BCE. Bronze crossbow locks dated to about 650 BCE have been found there, and bronze bolts from a Chu burial site date to the mid-5th century BCE. The Chinese trigger was made of three cast bronze pieces, which gave a mechanical advantage so that heavy draw weights could be released with a light pull. It shifted the role of projectiles in war, especially in the Qin unification wars. In Greece the gastraphetes, or belly-bow, appeared probably in the late 5th century BCE and was used at the Siege of Motya in 397 BCE. It was likely invented independently of the Chinese crossbow.

References to the crossbow in Europe are essentially absent from the 5th to the 10th century. It reappears in 947 as a French weapon at the siege of Senlis and in 984 at the siege of Verdun. Crossbows were used at the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and by the 12th century had become common battlefield weapons. European prods were wood until composite prods appeared in the 13th century and steel ones around the 14th, when winches and cranequins were also used. In the Islamic world the weapon was regarded as foreign, and Islamic texts do not mention it before the 14th century, though Mamluk cavalry used crossbows.
crotone: Crotone is a city and comune in Calabria. The promontory of Kroton was inhabited in the Bronze Age by indigenous peoples. The Greek foundation was led by Myscellus of Rhypes in Achaea, after the Delphic Oracle told him to cross the vast sea and found Kroton next to the river Esaro. The Achaeans were driven by lack of cultivable land and population pressure. Excavation shows that most existing settlements in the area disappeared, and that Greek settlers married indigenous women from the first generation.

Croton became one of the most flourishing cities of Magna Graecia, reaching a population between 50,000 and 80,000 around 500 BCE. From 588 BCE it produced many Olympic winners, the best known being Milo, and its physicians were the foremost among the Greeks. Pythagoras founded his school there around 530 BCE. About 510 BCE Croton destroyed Sybaris with an army under Milo. A revolt led by the oligarch Cylon then massacred many Pythagoreans.

Croton declined, was captured by Dionysius of Syracuse in 379 BCE and by Agathocles in 295 BCE, and submitted to Rome in 277 BCE. Hannibal made it his winter quarters for three years in the Second Punic War. A Roman colony followed in 194 BCE. About 870 Saracens sacked it, and the Normans later conquered it. It became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

The city was known as Cotrone from the Middle Ages until 1928, and in 1992 it became the capital of the Province of Crotone. Archaeology has recovered the ancient wall circuit, enclosing at least 617 hectares, and the layout of the Greek town. The Castle of Charles V, of the 16th century, houses the town museum, and the cathedral holds the icon of the Black Madonna of Capo Colonna. The national archaeological museum, founded in 1968, holds finds from the Sanctuary of Hera Lacinia.
crown-dependencies: The Crown Dependencies are three offshore island territories in the British Isles: the Bailiwick of Guernsey, the Bailiwick of Jersey, together known as the Channel Islands, and the Isle of Man. Their status is that of territories for which the United Kingdom is responsible, rather than sovereign states, and they are therefore not members of the Commonwealth of Nations, although all three take part in the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association and have their own teams in the Commonwealth Games. They are members of the British–Irish Council. The Kilbrandon Report of 1973 described them as like miniature states.

Each has its own legislative assembly. The Bailiwick of Guernsey has three jurisdictions, Guernsey, Alderney and Sark, with parliaments called the States of Deliberation, the States of Alderney and the Chief Pleas. The Isle of Man's Tynwald, consisting of the House of Keys and the Legislative Council, claims to be the world's oldest parliament in continuous existence, dating back to 979. Legislation ultimately requires the approval of the King in Council, though Acts of the UK Parliament do not normally extend to the islands without their consent on domestic matters.

The Crown Dependencies are distinguished from the British Overseas Territories, which are remnants of the British Empire. Their relationship with the Crown is much older and springs from their status as feudatory territories subject to the English Crown. Their political systems evolved in an ad hoc manner, so that each has particular and unique structures. Since 1290 the Channel Islands have been governed as two Bailiwicks, each headed by a Bailiff, with a Lieutenant Governor representing the Crown. In the Isle of Man the monarch is styled Lord of Mann, a title held at different times by Norse, Scottish and English kings and nobles until it was revested in the British monarchy in 1765.

The United Kingdom is solely responsible for defence and international representation, although framework agreements signed in 2007 and 2008 provide that it will not act internationally on the islands' behalf without consultation. Until a declaration agreed in 1950, the islands were considered part of British metropolitan territory for international agreements; afterwards the three were treated as distinct from the United Kingdom and from each other. The Crown Dependencies have never been member states of the European Union. They belong with the United Kingdom and Ireland to the Common Travel Area. Gavin St Pier, a former Chief Minister of Guernsey, has disputed the term itself, arguing that it was an administrative invention of Whitehall and that it wrongly implies dependence on the Crown.
crown-of-thorns: According to the New Testament, a woven crown of thorns was placed on the head of Jesus before his crucifixion, both to cause him pain and to mock his claim of authority. It is mentioned in the gospels of Matthew, Mark and John, and the gospels do not say what became of it. The oldest known mention of a crown venerated as a relic is by Paulinus of Nola, writing after 409. The Breviary of Jerusalem, dated to about 530, and Antoninus of Piacenza place it in the Basilica of Mount Zion, where it was still seen in 870. François de Mély supposed that the crown went to Constantinople not much before 1063.

The exact plant used to make the crown is not confirmed. The relic in Paris was examined in the nineteenth century and appeared to be a twisted circlet of rushes of Juncus balticus. The thorns kept in other reliquaries appeared to be Ziziphus spina-christi, the jujube tree, which grows around Jerusalem. According to de Mély, the sixty or seventy thorns that Louis IX and his successors distributed had already been separated from the band of rushes by the time it reached Paris. De Mély counted more than 700 holy thorn relics, many of them third-class relics, that is objects touched to a first-class relic.

Baldwin II, the Latin Emperor of Constantinople, anxious for support for his tottering empire, offered the crown to Louis IX of France. It was then in the hands of the Venetians as security for a loan of 13,134 gold pieces. It was redeemed and taken to Paris, where Louis IX built the Sainte-Chapelle, completed in 1248, to receive it. After the French Revolution, during which it was kept for a time in the Bibliothèque Nationale, the Concordat of 1801 restored it to the Church, and it was deposited in Notre-Dame de Paris.

Individual thorns were given by French kings to other European rulers: the Holy Thorn Reliquary in the British Museum was made in the 1390s for Jean, duc de Berry. In 1543 John Calvin, in his Treatise on Relics, listed the many places claiming parts of the crown and concluded that there must be falsehood and imposition, noting that the ancient Church never knew what had become of it. Members of the Paris Fire Brigade saved the relic from the fire at Notre-Dame on 15 April 2019, and it returned to the cathedral in December 2024.
crucifixion: Crucifixion was common in the ancient world, and Greece, Persia, Carthage and Rome are among the civilizations known to have used it widely. The earliest clear reference may be a post-mortem one in Herodotus, who says that Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos, was executed in 522 BCE by Oroetus, satrap of Lydia, and that his dead body was then crucified. In earlier pre-Roman Greek texts the verb anastauroo usually meant impale.

In Rome the Greek and Latin words covered many painful forms of execution. Crucifixion was generally meant to deter others, and victims were sometimes left on display after death. It was intended to be slow, painful, gruesome, humiliating and public, and the word excruciating comes from it. In Japan it was introduced during the Sengoku period (1467–1573) and was called haritsuke.

Crucifixion is a method of execution and torture in which the condemned is tied or nailed to a large wooden cross, beam or stake and usually left to hang until death. The gibbet took many shapes. It could be a simple upright stake, called crux simplex, or have a crossbeam at the top, in a T shape (crux commissa), or just below it (crux immissa), the form familiar in Christian symbolism. The oldest image of a Roman crucifixion, a graffito at Puteoli of the time of Trajan or Hadrian, shows a T-shaped cross.

Death could take minutes, hours or days according to the method, the victim's health and the environment. If a nail severed an artery death could follow within minutes. Josephus records that three of his acquaintances, crucified captives, were taken down at Titus's order, and that one of them recovered.

Josephus and Appian refer to thousands crucified in the Roman–Jewish wars, but archaeological remains are few. The best-known was found in a Jewish tomb of the 1st century at Givat HaMivtar in Jerusalem in 1968, in an ossuary inscribed Jehohanan, the son of Hagakol. Nicu Haas found a heel bone with a nail driven through its side, suggesting that the feet were nailed from the side.

Jesus was crucified, and the event became central to Christianity and is represented by the cross and the crucifix. Tradition holds that Saint Peter was crucified upside down and Saint Andrew on an X-shaped cross. Between 73 and 71 BCE, about 6,000 followers of Spartacus were crucified along the Appian Way between Capua and Rome.
crusader-states: The Crusader states, also called Outremer, from the French for overseas, were four Catholic polities in the Levant and south-eastern Anatolia, existing from 1098 to 1291. From north to south they were the County of Edessa (1098 to 1150), the Principality of Antioch (1098 to 1268), the County of Tripoli (1102 to 1289) and the Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099 to 1291). Their foundation followed the First Crusade, proclaimed by the Latin Church in 1095. At the Council of Piacenza that year the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked Pope Urban II for help against the Seljuks, and Urban went far beyond what the emperor probably had in mind by calling for the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont.

The settlers were called Franks or Latins, and were mainly French-speaking Roman Catholics, while the natives were mostly Arabic- or Greek-speaking Muslims, Christians of other denominations, and Jews. The name Crusader states can mislead, because from 1130 onward very few of the Franks were Crusaders.

In 1098 Baldwin of Boulogne took over Edessa in a coup and Bohemond of Taranto remained ruling prince in captured Antioch. The siege of Jerusalem in 1099 ended in a decisive victory over the Fatimid Caliphate. Edessa fell to the Zengid Turks in 1144. In 1244 Khwarazmian troops sacked Jerusalem, and at La Forbie on 18 October the Franks were defeated, with 16,000 Frankish warriors killed.

The Bahri Mamluks took power in Egypt in 1250. They captured Antioch in 1268 and Tripoli in 1289, and the fall of Acre in 1291 ended the Kingdom of Jerusalem nearly 200 years after its founding. The survivors fled to the Kingdom of Cyprus.

The states were feudal. Jerusalem's royal administration sat in the city until its loss and then in Acre, with the usual household officers of European rulers, and the courts of Antioch produced the Assizes of Antioch. Historians now regard the Franks as a minority society, largely urban and living apart from the native peoples under separate legal and religious systems. Estimates of their number range from 120,000 to 300,000, perhaps at least 15 per cent of the population. Castles blended European, Byzantine and Muslim traditions, and historians regard them as the most impressive artistic achievement of the crusaders.

The military orders emerged here. The Knights Templar, whose rule was confirmed at the Council of Troyes in 1129, grew from a brotherhood attached to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Hospitallers took up military functions in the 1130s. The states were economic centres tied by sea to Europe and by land to Mesopotamia, Syria and the Nile.
crusades: Sites linked to Jesus's ministry, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, were popular pilgrimage destinations in Roman Palestine. Jerusalem fell to Caliph Umar in 638, and by the mid-10th century three rival caliphates had emerged: the Umayyads in al-Andalus, the Shi'ite Fatimids in Egypt and the Abbasids in the Middle East. By the late 11th century, Christian just war theory, increasing aristocratic piety and the popularity of penitential journeys to the Holy Land had created a context for armed pilgrimages. In March 1095 Pope Urban II received envoys from Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who asked for military aid at the Council of Piacenza.

On 27 November 1095, at the Council of Clermont, Urban announced a military campaign against the Turkomans. According to most accounts he promised spiritual rewards, though accounts differ on whether he offered reduced penance or full remission of sin. Popular enthusiasm outran his wish to enlist only trained warriors, and Peter the Hermit attracted thousands of peasants and townsfolk. No crowned ruler joined; the leaders included Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Count of Toulouse, who led the largest force.

The campaign's successes led to four Crusader states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch and the counties of Tripoli and Edessa. When Edessa fell on 26 December 1144, most of its Frankish population was killed or enslaved, and the Second Crusade failed in 1148. Saladin destroyed the Jerusalemite field army at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187, and Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October. The Fourth Crusade, first aimed at Egypt, was diverted to the Byzantine Empire and ended in the Sack of Constantinople and the Latin Empire in 1204. Jerusalem was regained by negotiation in 1229, but the Mamluks, who had reunited Egypt and Muslim Syria by 1260, captured the Crusaders' last mainland strongholds in 1291.

The fall of the Frankish East caused dismay rather than shock in the West, and Western Christians mostly blamed the Franks' alleged immorality. Schemes to recover the Holy Land inspired treatises, and only the Alexandrian Crusade briefly revived crusading activity in the region in 1365. Over time the crusading movement expanded to campaigns against pagans, Christian dissidents and other enemies of the papacy, promoted with similar spiritual rewards and continuing into the 18th century. The Crusades created national mythologies, tales of heroism and a few place names, and modern Muslim thinkers have drawn parallels between them and later political developments.
ctesias: Ctesias came from Cnidus in Caria, a town then part of the Achaemenid Empire, and served as physician to King Artaxerxes II. He accompanied the king in 401 BCE on his expedition against his brother Cyrus the Younger and was in the king's entourage at the Battle of Cunaxa, where Cyrus fought with his Greek mercenaries, the Ten Thousand. There Ctesias treated a flesh wound of the king. He reportedly took part in negotiations with the Greeks after the battle, and he helped the Spartan general Clearchus before his execution at the royal court at Babylon.

Ctesias wrote treatises on rivers and on the Persian revenues, an account of India called the Indica, and a history of Assyria and Persia in 23 books, the Persica. The Persica was drawn from documents in the Persian Royal Archives and written in the Ionic dialect in opposition to Herodotus. Its first six books cover the history of Assyria and Babylon to the founding of the Persian empire by Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE, and the remaining seventeen cover the years to 398 BCE.

It survives in an abridgment by Photius and in fragments preserved by Athenaeus, Plutarch, Nicolaus of Damascus and especially Diodorus Siculus, whose second book derives mainly from it. According to the Encyclopædia Britannica, Ctesias mentioned that the grave of Darius I at Persepolis lay in a cliff face reached by an apparatus of ropes.

Opinion of the Persica has long been divided. Many ancient authorities valued it highly and used it to discredit Herodotus, while one modern author writes that its unreliability makes Herodotus seem a model of accuracy. His account of the Assyrian kings does not agree with the cuneiform evidence, and the satirist Lucian placed Ctesias, with Herodotus, on an island of torment for writers of false histories.

The Indica records the Persian view of India, with descriptions of artisans, philosophers and people with the qualities of deities, and of gold beyond counting. It rests on the testimony of travellers to Persia rather than on his own observation, and modern readers place it between fact and fiction. It states that the Indus varies from 40 to 200 stades in width and that India makes up half of Asia. It survives only in fragments and in the reports of later authors.
ctesiphon: Ctesiphon stood on the eastern bank of the Tigris, about 35 kilometres south-east of Baghdad, at the place now called al-Mada'in. It merged with the surrounding cities on both shores, including the Hellenistic city of Seleucia, and the whole group was known as The Cities, Mahuza in Aramaic and al-Mada'in in Arabic. The city measured about 30 square kilometres, more than twice the area of imperial Rome in the 4th century.

Ctesiphon was founded in the late 120s BCE on the site of a military camp set up opposite Seleucia by Mithridates I of Parthia. Strabo says the Parthian kings used it as a winter residence. It became the capital of the empire around 58 BCE under Orodes II. Because of its importance it was a major target for Rome: Trajan captured it in 116 and Hadrian returned it in 117, Avidius Cassius took it in 164 and abandoned it at peace, and in 197 Septimius Severus sacked it and sold thousands of its inhabitants into slavery.

By 226 the Sasanians held the city, ended the Parthian dynasty and made it their capital, enlarging it greatly. The western quarter, Veh-Ardashir, had many wealthy Jews and the seat of the church of the Nestorian patriarch. After taking Antioch in 541, Khosrow I built a new city near Ctesiphon for its captured people. The Byzantine emperor Heraclius surrounded Ctesiphon in 627 and left after the Persians accepted his terms.

After the Battle of al-Qādisiyyah in the mid-630s the Arabs occupied Ctesiphon in early 637, finding it deserted by the royal family, nobles and troops. The city then declined rapidly, especially after the Abbasid capital Baghdad was founded in the 760s, and Caliph al-Mansur took building material from its ruins.

The most conspicuous remaining structure is the Taq Kasra, sometimes called the Arch of Ctesiphon, once part of the royal palace and estimated to date between the 3rd and 6th centuries. It stands in the Iraqi town of Salman Pak. German expeditions excavated the site in 1928–29 and 1931–1932, and an Italian team from the University of Turin worked on the western side, which it identified as Veh Ardashir, in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
cuauhtemoc: The name Cuauhtémoc means one who has descended like an eagle. His date of birth is unknown, since he does not enter the historical record until he became emperor. He was the eldest legitimate son of Emperor Ahuitzotl, and according to several sources his mother, Tiyacapantzin, was a Tlatelolcan princess, though this is inferred from his rank. After education in the calmecac, the school for elite boys, and military service, he was named ruler of Tlatelolco in 1515 with the title cuauhtlatoani, eagle ruler. He married the princess later known as Isabel Moctezuma, a daughter of Moctezuma II.

In 1520 Cuauhtémoc was elected tlatoani, the most able candidate among the high nobles being chosen by their vote, to succeed his cousin Cuitláhuac, who died of smallpox shortly after succeeding Moctezuma II. He was around 25, and Tenochtitlan was besieged by the Spanish and devastated by smallpox. It was increasingly isolated, as many polities once under its control deserted and swelled the numbers of Spanish allies. He oversaw Moctezuma's funeral without the usual pomp, since he believed in armed resistance while Moctezuma had believed in negotiation.

After eighty days of warfare he called for reinforcements. Of all the Nahuas only the Tlatelolcas remained loyal, and the surviving Tenochcas took refuge in Tlatelolco. Cuauhtémoc was captured on 13 August 1521 while fleeing across Lake Texcoco with his wife, family and friends. According to Spanish sources, he asked Hernán Cortés to strike him dead with his knife, and Cortés refused. Later, when the booty fell short of the Spaniards' expectations, he was tortured by fire. Baptized as Fernando Cuauhtémotzín, he kept the title of tlatoani but was no longer sovereign and was mostly held in guarded custody.

In 1525 Cortés took Cuauhtémoc and other indigenous nobles on his expedition to Honduras, fearing an insurrection in his absence. At Itzamkanac he had Cuauhtémoc hanged for allegedly conspiring to kill him. The accounts differ. Cortés wrote that he learned of the plot on 27 February 1525 and hanged Cuauhtémoc, Tetlepanquetzal and Tlacatlec. Bernal Díaz del Castillo portrays the executions as unjust and based on no evidence, and Fernando de Alva Cortés Ixtlilxóchitl, drawing partly on Texcocan oral tradition, wrote that Cortés invented the plot. Tlacotzin was appointed his successor and died the next year.

Cuauhtémoc is the embodiment of indigenist nationalism in Mexico, being the only Aztec emperor who survived the conquest. He is honoured by a monument on the Paseo de la Reforma in Mexico City. An ossuary at Ixcateopan said to hold his remains was excavated in 1949, but the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia rejected its authenticity.
cuba: Cuba is an archipelago of 4,195 islands, cays and islets in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Gulf of Mexico meets the Atlantic Ocean. Key West, Florida, lies about 150 kilometres across the Straits of Florida to the north and northwest, Mexico 210 kilometres west across the Yucatán Channel, Haiti 78 kilometres to the east and Jamaica 148 kilometres to the south. The main island is 1,250 kilometres long and makes up most of the land area of 104,338 square kilometres. It consists mostly of flat to rolling plains apart from the Sierra Maestra in the southeast, whose highest point is Pico Turquino at 1,974 metres. The second-largest island is Isla de la Juventud.

Humans first settled Cuba around 6,000 years ago. The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno arrived from South America about 1,700 years ago and, unlike the earlier settlers, produced pottery and practised intensive agriculture. The earliest evidence of the Taíno on Cuba dates to the 9th century. Descendants of the first settlers persisted in the west of the island until European contact as the hunter-gathering Guanahatabey. Christopher Columbus first arrived on 27 October 1492, claimed the island for Spain and named it Isla Juana after John, Prince of Asturias.

The first Spanish settlement was founded by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar at Baracoa in 1511, and San Cristóbal de la Habana was founded in 1514 and moved to its present place in 1519, becoming the capital in 1607. The Taíno were forced to work under the encomienda system.

Within a century they suffered high mortality, primarily from Eurasian infectious diseases against which they had no immunity, aggravated by harsh colonial subjugation. In 1529 a measles outbreak killed two-thirds of the few who had survived smallpox. Cuba remained part of the Spanish Empire until the Spanish–American War of 1898, was then occupied by the United States, and became independent in 1902. The Cuban Revolution of January 1959 overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista and established a communist government under Fidel Castro.

Havana is the capital and largest city. Cuba is a socialist republic whose constitution names the Communist Party as the leading force of society and the state. Spanish culture, West African culture and the Guanahatabey and Taíno inheritance together shape Cuban culture. Cuba's population descends primarily from Spanish settlers, sub-Saharan Africans brought through the transatlantic slave trade, and pre-Columbian peoples, chiefly the Taíno and Ciboney. Havana, Camagüey, Cienfuegos and Trinidad, with colonial centres in Baroque and Neoclassical styles, are inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
cuban-missile-crisis: The crisis was a 13-day confrontation, from 16 to 28 October 1962, in which Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba matched American missiles deployed in the United Kingdom, Italy and Turkey, all within range of Moscow. In April 1961 a CIA-led force of Cuban expatriates had tried to invade Cuba. Khrushchev decided in May 1962 to counter the American lead in strategic missiles by placing intermediate-range missiles in Cuba. At a meeting in July 1962 he and Fidel Castro agreed to deploy them to deter a future American invasion.

On 15 October analysts identified what appeared to be medium-range ballistic missiles in U-2 photographs. President John F. Kennedy formed the Executive Committee of the National Security Council, EXCOMM, which considered doing nothing, diplomacy, a secret approach to Castro, an air strike and an invasion. On 22 October Kennedy announced a naval blockade, which he called a quarantine because a blockade is an act of war. On 26 October the Strategic Air Command was raised to DEFCON 2, the only confirmed time in American history. On 27 October, called Black Saturday, the United States Navy dropped practice depth charges on the Soviet submarine B-59, whose captain proposed to launch a nuclear torpedo; Vasily Arkhipov, aboard, did not consent.

Khrushchev agreed to dismantle the offensive weapons in Cuba, under United Nations verification, for a public American declaration not to invade Cuba. The United States secretly agreed to dismantle its missiles in Turkey. The quarantine ended on 20 November 1962. The need for quick contact led to the Moscow-Washington hotline. Khrushchev was embarrassed because the withdrawal was secret and the Soviets appeared to retreat, and his fall two years later was in part due to this. Castro saw the outcome as a Soviet betrayal. The crisis is widely considered the closest the Cold War came to full-scale nuclear war.
cuban-revolution: Batista overthrew the emerging Cuban democracy in the coup of 1952. In the 1950s Cuba ranked among the more advanced Latin American countries by averages such as life expectancy, but the averages hid sharp disparities. The economy depended on sugar and on the United States, nearly one-third of the labour force lacked full-time work, and only 15 per cent of the rural population had running water. Batista's regime kept close ties with organised crime, and was marked by police corruption, censorship and anti-communist campaigns that suppressed opposition with violence, torture and public executions.

Fidel Castro, a young lawyer, first challenged the coup in the courts. When that failed, he and his brother Raúl led the assault on the Moncada Barracks on 26 July 1953. At his trial he spoke for hours in his own defence, ending 'History will absolve me', and was sentenced to fifteen years. Under political pressure Batista freed all political prisoners on 15 May 1955, and the brothers went to Mexico.

The yacht Granma left Tuxpan on 25 November 1956 with the Castros and eighty others and landed on 2 December. Batista's army attacked three days later; no more than twenty of the eighty-two survived to reach the Sierra Maestra. In 1958 about 12,000 soldiers, around 7,000 of them untrained recruits, entered the mountains in Operation Verano, and the guerrillas defeated them. The Battle of El Jigüe in July 1958 is widely considered a turning point.

Batista left the country at the turn of the year, and on 2 January 1959 the army commander in Santiago de Cuba ordered his soldiers not to fight. Castro reached Havana on 8 January. Manuel Urrutia Lleó took office as president on 3 January with José Miró as prime minister. After the government nationalised American property in August 1960, the United States froze Cuban assets, severed relations and tightened the embargo in January 1961. The Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961, by 1,500 mostly Cuban exiles, was repulsed. The Soviet Union became Cuba's main ally, and the 26th of July Movement became the Communist Party in October 1965. Historians debate whether Castro was a communist from the start.
cudjoe: The name Cudjoe corresponds to the Akan day name Kojo or Kwadwo, given to a boy born on a Monday. The Leeward Maroons most likely emerged in 1690, when a Coromantee rebellion broke out on Sutton's estate in western Jamaica and most of the enslaved Africans there ran away into the mountainous interior. Cudjoe was probably the son of one of the leaders of that revolt. The oral history of the Accompong Town Maroons, as told by Milton McFarlane, holds that he was the freeborn son of Naquan, who led those who fled from the estate.

According to contemporary white enslavers, Cudjoe challenged a Madagascan for the leadership of the Leeward Maroons in 1720, and by defeating and killing him became their undisputed leader. His community was known as Cudjoe's Town, or Trelawny Town. For about half a century, until the treaties of 1739 and 1740, the Maroons operated outside direct British control.

During the First Maroon War of the 1730s the English colonial forces failed to win any significant victory over Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons. The agreement of 1739 recognised them as a semi-autonomous entity and freed their land from taxes. In the 1740s some Leeward Maroons who opposed the treaty rose in revolt, and Cudjoe crushed these risings.

Two descriptions of him survive from colonial writers. The physician R. C. Dallas, writing half a century after Cudjoe lived, claimed that he was short and stout, with a large lump of flesh on his back. The slaver Thomas Thistlewood, who met him in 1750, noted in his diary that he wore a feathered hat, with a sword at his side and a gun on his shoulder, barefoot and with "somewhat a Majestic look".

One source claims that Cudjoe died in 1744, but Edward Long and Thistlewood wrote of meeting him in the 1750s and 1760s. Long described him leading his Maroons in a martial performance at Montego Bay for Governor Sir William Lyttleton in 1764, and in the same year Thistlewood heard that he had been dead for some time. The treaty had named Accompong as his successor, but Governor Roger Hope Elletson had the Trelawny Town badge of authority given instead to a Maroon officer named Lewis, leaving Accompong authority over Accompong Town only. Cudjoe Day is celebrated in Jamaica on the first Monday in January.
cuenca-ecuador: Cuenca lies in the south-central inter-Andean region of Ecuador, in the Paute river basin, at about 2,538 metres above sea level, roughly 470 kilometres south of Quito and 200 kilometres south-east of Guayaquil. Four rivers cross it, the Tomebamba, Yanuncay, Tarqui and Machángara, and their confluence gives the city its Spanish name, which means a basin. The first three rise in the páramo of El Cajas National Park to the west. Its full name, Santa Ana de los Ríos de Cuenca, honours Saint Anne and the Spanish city of Cuenca, home of the viceroy who ordered its founding.

Archaeological finds trace the first inhabitants in the area to about 8060 BCE, in the Cave of Chopsi, where nomadic hunters followed the animals. Later peoples grew potatoes, quinoa and squash and kept guinea pigs, llamas and alpacas. From around 2000 BCE society became more organised, with specialised administrative and religious authorities, and later came the Cañari, who were absorbed by the Incas in the 15th century. Archaeologists believe a Cañari settlement called Guapdondelic, said to mean land as big as heaven, was founded around 500 CE.

After a bitter struggle the Incas conquered the Cañari, likely in the 1470s. They replaced the Cañari architecture with their own but did not suppress the Cañari or their achievements in astronomy and agriculture, and they renamed the city Tomebamba. The emperor Tupac Yupanqui ordered the building of a grand city called Pumapungo, said to rival Cusco, and Tomebamba became known as the second Cusco. When the Spaniards found it, they saw only ruins, and it was sparsely populated until the 1550s.

Gil Ramírez Dávalos founded the Spanish city on 12 April 1557 on the orders of the viceroy of Peru, Andrés Hurtado de Mendoza, decades after Quito (1534), Guayaquil (1538) and Loja (1548). The city achieved independence on 3 November 1820 and reached the peak of its importance in the first years of independent Ecuador, as the capital of one of the republic's three provinces, with Guayaquil and Quito.

Cuenca is the capital of Azuay province and one of the largest cities of Ecuador. Its historic centre was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. The Old Cathedral, built in 1557, is now a museum, and the New Cathedral, completed in 1975, has blue and white domes that symbolise the city. The Universidad de Cuenca, founded in 1867, is among the oldest universities in the country. Cuenca is known for its textiles and for the straw hats called Panama hats, which are made there by local artisans.
cuenca-spain: Cuenca stands on a steep spur whose slopes fall into the deep gorges of the Júcar and Huécar rivers, on the western fringes of the Iberian System mountains, at about 1,000 metres in the old town. It is also known as the Eagle's Nest. Its name may come from the Latin conca, 'river basin', or from the Arab castle Kunka. The Roman settlements of the province lay elsewhere, at Segobriga, Ercavica and Gran Valeria, and the site of Cuenca itself was uninhabited in Roman times.

Under Muslim rule Cuenca was a fortress with a wall about a kilometre long, and an economy of agriculture and textiles. In the early 11th century it fell to the taifa of Toledo. Sancho Ramírez of Aragon besieged it in 1076 without success; the first Christian troops entered in 1093, and the Almoravids took it in 1108. From 1147 Muhammad ibn Mardanis was king of Cuenca, Murcia and Valencia until 1172. In 1177 Alfonso VIII of Castile, leading a coalition, conquered the city. Cuenca received a Latin law code, the Fuero, and the diocese was established in 1183; its second bishop, St Julian, became the patron saint. Alfonso X made it a city in 1257.

Textiles and livestock brought prosperity. A Jewish community, first recorded in 1177, lasted until the expulsion of 1492, and the Inquisition prosecuted the descendants of conversos until a last trial from 1718 to 1725. In the 18th century the textile trade declined and the city lost population. It suffered great destruction in the war against Napoleon's troops.

Cuenca is the capital of the province of Cuenca in Castilla–La Mancha. The cathedral was built from 1182 to 1270 under the influence of Queen Eleanor, wife of Alfonso VIII, and is regarded as one of the first Gothic cathedrals in Spain, with Ávila's; its façade was rebuilt after the collapse of the Giraldo tower in 1902. The Bridge of Saint Paul, begun in 1533, was replaced in 1902 by an iron and wood bridge up to 40 metres high, and the old Dominican convent of Saint Paul is now a hotel. The old town was declared a World Heritage Site in 1996.
cuiaba: Cuiabá lies near the geographical centre of South America, in a transition zone between the Amazon, the Cerrado and the Pantanal, and is called the Southern gate to the Amazon. Its name is a Bororo word meaning 'arrow-fishing'. It is known across Brazil as one of the hottest cities, with temperatures often above 40 °C. An obelisk in the centre marks the middle of the continent as calculated in 1909; more accurate measurements in the 1990s placed it about 45 kilometres to the north-east, near Chapada dos Guimarães.

The first Portuguese in the region were bandeirantes, explorers, slavers and fortune hunters from São Paulo. In 1718 Pascoal Moreira Cabral of Sorocaba arrived and, after losing a battle with the Coxiponé people, found gold up the Coxipó River. The bandeirantes enslaved indigenous people to work the site. Cabral reported the discovery in a letter of 8 April 1719, and a gold rush followed. An earthquake in 1746 destroyed much of the town. In 1751 Dom Antônio Rolim de Moura Tavares became first governor of the Captaincy of Mato Grosso and founded Vila Bela as its capital.

Cuiabá replaced Vila Bela as capital of the province in 1835. The town stayed small until the Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870), which brought a brief boom as it supplied the troops, and afterwards governments used it as a place of exile for troublesome politicians.

Roads and then aviation ended the isolation from 1930, and the city grew rapidly after 1960, from 50,000 inhabitants to more than a quarter of a million by 1980, as commercial agriculture carried soybeans and rice abroad. Cuiabá is the capital and largest city of Mato Grosso and, with Várzea Grande, forms its metropolitan area. It is a trading centre for a cattle-raising and farming region and the seat of the Federal University of Mato Grosso.
cultural-revolution: Mao Zedong declared the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949. His Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 aimed to turn an agrarian society into an industrial one through people's communes, and the Great Chinese Famine of 1959 to 1961 that followed caused between 15 and 55 million deaths. After Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin in 1956 and began economic reforms, Mao and many other party members opposed the changes, fearing damage to the worldwide communist movement. In 1963 Mao launched the Socialist Education Movement, cleansing Beijing officials of questionable loyalty.

The movement has two periods: spring 1966 to summer 1968, when most key events took place, and a tailing period lasting until the autumn of 1976. On 25 May 1966 Nie Yuanzi, a philosophy lecturer at Peking University, posted a big-character poster attacking the university's leadership. Mao called on young people to Bombard the Headquarters and proclaimed that to rebel is justified. Mass upheaval began in Beijing with Red August in 1966, and young people formed Red Guard cadres across China. Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung became the object of a cult of personality.

In 1967 radicals seized power from local governments and party branches and established revolutionary committees, smashing the public security, procuratorate and judicial systems. These committees often split into factions and fought each other. After the fall of Lin Biao in 1971, the Gang of Four became influential in 1972.

The Red Guards sought to destroy the Four Olds, old ideas, culture, customs and habits, which often meant destroying historical artefacts and cultural and religious sites. Tens of millions were persecuted, including Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping and Peng Dehuai, and millions as members of the Five Black Categories. Schools and universities were closed, the National College Entrance Examinations were cancelled and over 10 million urban youths were sent to the countryside. Estimates of the death toll range from 1 to 2 million, including the Guangxi Massacre, which involved cannibalism, and massacres in Beijing, Inner Mongolia, Guangdong, Yunnan and Hunan.

The revolution continued until Mao's death in 1976, followed by the arrest of the Gang of Four. In 1978 Deng Xiaoping became paramount leader, and his reform and opening up helped dismantle the ideology of the Cultural Revolution. In 1981 the Communist Party acknowledged it as responsible for the most severe setback and the heaviest losses suffered by the people, the country and the party since 1949. In China it is often called the ten years of chaos.
cumana: Cumaná lies at the mouth of the Manzanares River on the Caribbean coast, 402 kilometres east of Caracas. It is a busy maritime port with one of the largest tuna fleets in Venezuela and the seat of the first and most important of the five campuses of the Universidad de Oriente. The municipality of Sucre, which includes the city, had a population of 358,919 at the 2011 census. Its climate is hot and semi-arid.
