Cumaná was founded in 1515 by Franciscan friars under the name Nueva Toledo, as the first Spanish settlement in Venezuela and in South America, a claim disputed by the town of Santa Fe. Successful attacks by the indigenous people, among them the Cumanagoto, forced it to be refounded several times, until Diego Hernández de Serpa's refoundation in 1569 gave it the name Cumaná. Bartolomé de las Casas, who attempted a peaceful colonisation, was preempted by Gonzalo de Ocampo's punitive raids in 1521, made in retaliation for the destruction of the Dominican convent at Chiribichi. In 1537 the Province of New Andalusia was established with Cumaná as its capital, so that it was also known as the Province of Cumaná.

The city gained independence on 15 July 1811. After the threat of Amerindian attacks faded, earthquakes destroyed it on various occasions, so that its oldest part dates from the late 17th and 18th centuries and almost none of the 16th-century architecture survived. The Castle of San Antonio de la Eminencia, begun around 1659, was built to defend the city against English, French and Dutch pirates, and José Antonio Páez was held there in 1849 until his expulsion on 24 May 1850. In the 18th century scientists including Pehr Löfling, Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland worked in Cumaná.

Cumaná is the capital of Sucre State. It was the birthplace of Antonio José de Sucre, a leading general of the independence movement who also served as president of Bolivia and of Peru, and of the poets Andrés Eloy Blanco and José Antonio Ramos Sucre. The Basilica of Saint Agnes, restored around 1853, is the oldest church in the city, and Plaza Bolívar was built in 1930 on the site of the Sucre Museum, which collapsed in the 1929 earthquake. Mochima National Park lies near the city.
cumans: The Cumans, or Kumans, formed the western branch of the Cuman–Kipchak confederation and spoke the Cuman language. They are called Polovtsy in the chronicles of the Rus', Cumans in Western sources and Kipchaks in Eastern ones. Their original homeland is unknown. The writer al-Marwazi, about 1120, says that a Turkic people called the Qun came from the northern borders of China and drove out the Śari people, and that they were Nestorian Christians. Related to the Pechenegs, the Cumans held a shifting area north of the Black Sea and along the Volga known as Cumania.

The Cumans first met the Rus' in 1055. In 1061, under the chieftain Sokal, they devastated the Pereyaslavl principality, which began a war that lasted 175 years. At the Battle of the Alta River in 1068 they defeated the armies of the three sons of Yaroslav the Wise, and afterwards they repeatedly invaded the Rus' lands, taking captives who became slaves or were sold at markets in the south. Some Cumans were also allies: David IV of Georgia married the daughter of the Cuman king Atrak and invited her relatives to settle in Georgia.

The Mongols under Jebe and Subutai defeated the Cumans in 1220. After the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus' in 1237 many Cumans sought asylum in the Kingdom of Hungary, where others had already settled. In 1239 and 1240 large groups crossed the Danube, and some were settled by John III Doukas Vatatzes of Nicaea in Thrace, Macedonia and Anatolia. Those who stayed on the steppe joined the Golden Horde and later adopted Islam.

Horses were central to Cuman life, and the main activity was animal husbandry. Robert de Clari described them as nomadic warriors who raised horses, sheep, goats, camels and cattle, moving north with their herds in summer and south in winter. They fought as light cavalry, later developing heavy cavalry, with composite bows, javelins, sabres and maces. Their religion was Tengrism, and the dead of high rank were buried under a mound with a horse and sometimes a servant or slave. The Codex Cumanicus, written between 1294 and 1356, was a manual to help Catholic missionaries communicate with them. Cuman names survive in places such as Kumanovo in North Macedonia.
cumbria: Cumbria is the most north-westerly ceremonial county of England and is mostly mountainous. It borders Scotland to the north, Northumberland and County Durham to the east, North Yorkshire and Lancashire to the south and the Irish Sea to the west. The uplands fringe the Vale of Eden, which broadens into the Solway Plain near Carlisle. The south-west holds the Lake District, with England's highest mountain, Scafell Pike, and its longest lake, Windermere. The North Pennines lie to the east.

In the Neolithic period the area held a centre of stone axe production, the Langdale axe factory, and stone circles and henges, such as Mayburgh Henge, were built across the county. The region lay on the border of Roman Britain, and Hadrian's Wall runs through the north. In the early Middle Ages parts of it belonged successively to Rheged, Northumbria and Strathclyde, and there was also a Viking presence. The names Cumbria and Cumberland both mean land of the Cumbrians, and Cumberland is first recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 945. The first king unequivocally described as king of the Cumbrians is Owain ap Dyfnwal, who ruled from about 915 to about 937.

The region became the border between England and Scotland and was unsettled until the Union of the Crowns in 1603. In the Industrial Revolution mining took place on the Cumberland coalfield and Barrow-in-Furness became a shipbuilding centre. The Lake District came to be valued for its picturesque qualities, notably by the Lake Poets.

Cumbria was created in 1974 from Cumberland, Westmorland, the Furness area of Lancashire and a small part of Yorkshire. Its largest settlement and only city is Carlisle, and it is predominantly rural. The Lake District is a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Cumberland sausage has protected geographical status, and Cumberland and Westmorland wrestling is practised at the Grasmere Sports and Show, held every year since 1852.
cumbric: Cumbric is an extinct Brythonic Celtic language or dialect spoken in the Early Middle Ages in the Hen Ogledd, the Old North, in what is now Northern England and the southern Scottish Lowlands. Place-name evidence suggests that it may also have been spoken as far south as Pendle and the Yorkshire Dales. Linguists are undecided whether to classify it as a dialect of Old Welsh or as a separate language. Koch calls it a dialect but says that some of its place names clearly reflect a developed medieval language, much like Welsh, Cornish or Breton.

The term is geographical rather than linguistic, referring to the variety of Brittonic spoken in a particular region of North Britain. Its speakers seem to have called themselves Cumbri, as the Welsh called themselves Cymry, probably from a reconstructed Brittonic word meaning fellow countrymen, and the two peoples probably felt they were one ethnic group.

No contemporary written records of the language survive, and the evidence comes almost entirely from secondary sources. Most of it is place names, found in Scotland south of the firths of Forth and Clyde and in Cumberland and neighbouring areas; Brittonic-looking names north of that line are Pictish. Examples are Bathgate, meaning boar wood, and Carlisle, recorded as Luguvalium in the Roman period, to which caer, fort, was added later. Other evidence comes from the personal names of Strathclyde Britons in Scottish, Irish and Anglo-Saxon sources and from a few words that survived as legal terms in south-west Scotland.

A distinctive naming practice joined Gos-, related to Welsh gwas, servant, to the name of a saint, as in Gospatric, Gosmungo and Goscuthbert. About 100 counting systems have been collected in northern England since the 18th century, and the scholarly consensus is that they derive from a Brittonic language closely related to Welsh. Whether they are survivals of Cumbric is disputed, though Markku Filppula, Juhani Klemola and Heli Paulasto consider it plausible.

It is impossible to give an exact date for the extinction of Cumbric. In the mid-11th century some landowners still bore what appear to be Cumbric names, among them Dunegal, lord of Nithsdale, and Eilifr, lord of Penrith. At the Battle of the Standard in 1138 the Cumbrians are noted as a separate ethnic group, perhaps still set apart by language. The prevailing view is that the language became extinct in the 12th century, around the incorporation of the Kingdom of Strathclyde into the Kingdom of Scotland. A number of words in Scots and northern English dialects have been proposed to be Brittonic in origin, such as croot, small boy, but their derivation is hard to establish.
cuneiform: Cuneiform grew out of the token system used in the Near East for accounting. Clay tokens, some with pictographic shapes of animals and associated with numbers, were in use from the 9th millennium BCE, and they were pressed onto clay envelopes and then replaced by flat tablets on which signs were recorded with a stylus. Writing is first recorded at Uruk at the end of the 4th millennium BCE, and the first unequivocal documents date from around 3300 BCE. These early tablets were purely pictographic. Tablets with syllabic elements, clearly in Sumerian, date from about 2800 BCE, when pictographs began to be used for their sound, which allowed abstract ideas and personal names to be written.

Cuneiform is a logo-syllabic system named for the wedge-shaped impressions that form its signs. In the mid-3rd millennium BCE a wedge-tipped stylus pressed into soft clay replaced the pointed stylus and made writing quicker. Writing ran from top to bottom and right to left. Most surviving tablets were left moist, not fired, and were baked by accident when fires destroyed the buildings that held them.

The Akkadian Empire adopted the script from the 24th century BCE. Akkadian is a Semitic language, quite unlike Sumerian, and its scribes wrote it phonetically with Sumerian sound signs while keeping many Sumerian signs as logograms. The script was adapted for Elamite, Hurrian, Urartian and Hittite, and it recorded letters, business documents, laws such as the Code of Hammurabi, maps and medical manuals. Old Persian cuneiform, with 36 sound signs and 8 logograms, was designed independently under the early Achaemenid rulers. From the later half of the 1st millennium BCE cuneiform fell into disuse as Aramaic replaced Akkadian.

Cuneiform was rediscovered in the early 17th century, when the trilingual Achaemenid royal inscriptions at Persepolis were published. In 1621 Pietro Della Valle gave the direction of writing, and Carsten Niebuhr copied the inscriptions in 1778 and distinguished three kinds of writing. Georg Friedrich Grotefend began the decipherment of Old Persian in 1802, and bilingual and trilingual inscriptions then allowed the older scripts to be read, back to Sumerian. The British Museum holds the largest collection of tablets, about 130,000, and most tablets in museums have not been published.
cusco: Cusco lies in southeastern Peru, near the Sacred Valley of the Andes and the Huatanay and Urubamba rivers, at an elevation of about 3,400 metres. The Quechua name is Qusqu, which derives from the phrase qusqu wanka, rock of the owl, and relates to the foundation myth of the Ayar siblings: Ayar Awqa acquired wings and flew to the site of the future city, where he was transformed into a rock to mark his lineage's possession of the land.

The Killke people occupied the region from about 900 to 1200, before the Inca arrived in the thirteenth century. Carbon-14 dating established that the Killke built the fortress of Sacsayhuamán about 1100; the Inca later expanded it. The city was the capital of the Inca Empire, and many believe it was planned as an effigy in the shape of a puma. It had two sectors, hurin and hanan, which together took in the four provinces of the empire, and a road led from each quarter to the corresponding part of the empire.

The first three Spaniards arrived in May 1533, after the Battle of Cajamarca, and Francisco Pizarro officially entered the city on 15 November 1533. Early accounts record how the beauty of its buildings and the regularity of its streets astonished the Spaniards; the troops plundered the palaces and religious buildings, among them the Coricancha, the great temple of the Sun. The city was reestablished on 23 March 1534, with most of it built over Inca monuments.

Earthquakes interrupted urban development under Spanish rule. One in 1650 destroyed almost all the colonial buildings, and the effigy of the Lord of the Earthquakes is still carried in procession every year. Another on 21 May 1950 damaged more than a third of the city's structures, while Inca architecture withstood it, and restoration at the Santo Domingo complex exposed the Inca masonry of the Coricancha. UNESCO declared Cusco a World Heritage Site in 1983.
cuttack: Cuttack stands at the apex of the Mahanadi delta, on a strip of land between the Kathajodi and Mahanadi rivers. Four distributaries of the Mahanadi run through or beside the city. The name is an anglicised form of Kataka, from a Sanskrit word meaning capital, fort or military establishment, and refers to the ancient Barabati Fort around which the city first developed. While the fort stood the city was known as Bidanasi Kataka, Bidanasi Military Base.

According to the historian Andrew Stirling, who relied on the Madala Panji, the chronicle of the Jagannatha temple at Puri, the city was founded as a military cantonment by King Nrupa Keshari of the Keshari dynasty in 989 CE. A stone embankment to protect the new capital from flooding was built in the reign of Maharaja Markata Keshari, in 1002 CE. Barabati Fort, whose moat, gate and earthen mound of a nine-storied palace survive, is attributed to him. Chudangagarh, a fort about 8 km south-west of the city, was built by Chodagandadeva of the Ganga dynasty.

The Lal Bagh Palace on the Kathajodi shows the later rulers. It was built by a Mughal governor stationed at Cuttack, and the Naib Nazims lived there until 1751 and representatives of the Bhonslas of Nagpur from 1751 to 1803, when it passed to the British. The Maratha barracks at Chauliaganj, begun in 1775 and completed in 1795, housed artillery, cavalry and infantry. Under the British the Salt House was built in 1847–48. Cuttack was the birthplace of Subhas Chandra Bose, and Mahatma Gandhi stayed at the Swaraj Ashram on his visits during the Non Cooperation Movement of the 1920s.

Cuttack is the second largest city of Odisha and the seat of the Orissa High Court, which makes it the state's judicial capital. It is known as the Millennium City and the Silver City, the second name for its silver filigree work, and it is also known for horn handicrafts and textiles. Its Durga Puja, with idols adorned in gold and silver, draws visitors from across Odisha. The population was 610,189 at the 2011 census.
cuxhaven: Cuxhaven is the seat of the Cuxhaven district and includes the northernmost point of Lower Saxony. It lies on the North Sea shore at the mouth of the Elbe and is the gateway to the nearby island of Heligoland. The town extends about 14 kilometres from east to west and 7 kilometres from north to south. Its symbol is the Kugelbake, a wooden beacon once used as a lighthouse, which marks the boundary between the river and the sea and appears on the coat of arms.

Ritzebüttel, now part of Cuxhaven, belonged to the Land of Hadeln, first an exclave of the Duchy of Saxony and after 1296 of the Duchy of Saxe-Lauenburg. In 1394 the city of Hamburg conquered the fortress of Ritzebüttel and made it its stronghold to protect the estuary of the Elbe, which links Hamburg with the open sea. A seaside resort was founded in 1816, and the Hamburg America Line built a large ocean liner terminal in 1900, joined to Hamburg by its own railway line. It was the main departure point for German and European emigrants until liner travel ceased in 1969. Cuxhaven received city status within the state of Hamburg on 15 March 1907.

In 1937 the Greater Hamburg Act made Cuxhaven an urban district of the Prussian Province of Hanover. Municipalities of the Land of Hadeln were added in 1972, and in 1977 it became the capital of the new rural district of Cuxhaven.

In the First World War the Nordholz airbase to the south was a major airship station of the Imperial German Navy, attacked by Royal Navy seaplanes on Christmas Day 1914 in the Cuxhaven Raid. In the Second World War the town hosted a base of a Wehrmacht radio network, which transmitted data on experimental weapons including rockets. The last encrypted message of the war was sent from there on 7 May 1945, reporting the arrival of British troops and ending with the words closing down for ever.

Cuxhaven has a fishing harbour and, since 1997, the deep-water Cuxport terminal, which handles vehicles, containers and wind-turbine components. Tourism matters greatly, and the quarters of Duhnen, Döse and Sahlenburg are popular North Sea resorts. It has been a state-recognised climate seaside resort since 1964. The Jacobikirche in Lüdingworth has an organ by Arp Schnitger and a lavish baroque interior. The poet Joachim Ringelnatz and the explorer Carsten Niebuhr were born in the town.
cyaxares: According to Herodotus, Cyaxares was the son of the Median king Phraortes, who led a revolt against Assyria in the middle of the 7th century BCE and was killed in battle. The Scythians, Assyria's allies, then imposed hegemony over the Medes for almost three decades. Cyaxares succeeded his father under Scythian suzerainty. In 625 BCE, as Assyria weakened, he overthrew the Scythian yoke by inviting the Scythian rulers to a banquet, getting them drunk and murdering them. He then replaced the tribal militias with a regular army modelled on the Assyrian and Urartian armies.

In November 615 BCE Cyaxares crossed the Zagros mountains and occupied Arrapha. In 614 BCE the Medes took Assur, where they massacred the inhabitants, destroyed the temples and seized the treasures. The Babylonian king Nabopolassar then met Cyaxares at the ruins and they concluded an alliance, sealed by the marriage of Nabopolassar's son Nebuchadnezzar II to Cyaxares's daughter Amytis. In 612 BCE the two armies took and sacked Nineveh after a siege of three months, and in 610 BCE they seized Harran. In 609 BCE the Medes attacked Urartu, which became a subject kingdom.

Cyaxares also conquered Hyrcania and Parthia. In 590 BCE war broke out with the Lydian king Alyattes, who refused to hand over Scythian refugees. It lasted five years, until a solar eclipse during a battle in 585 BCE, which both sides took as an omen to end the war. The marriage of Cyaxares's son Astyages to Alyattes's daughter Aryenis sealed the peace.

Cyaxares died a short time after the battle of 585 BCE and was succeeded by Astyages. After Darius I seized power in the Achaemenid Empire, rebels claimed Cyaxares's legacy: the Behistun Inscription records a Mede who said he was of the dynasty of Cyaxares, and a Sagartian who made the same claim.
cybele: No contemporary text survives to show the original character of Cybele's Phrygian cult. She may have evolved from a statue type found at Çatalhöyük, a fertile female figure accompanied by large felines, dated to the 6th millennium BCE. A Phrygian rock-cut shrine of the first half of the 6th century BCE bears the inscription Matar Kubileya, usually read as Mother of the mountain. She is ancient Phrygia's only known goddess and probably the highest deity of its state. At Pessinos she took the form of an unshaped stone of black meteoric iron.

From around the 6th century BCE Greek colonists carried her cult to mainland Greece, the Aegean islands and Magna Graecia. She was partly assimilated to Rhea and Demeter but remained a foreign goddess, Mother of the Mountains, shown with lions beside her or drawing her chariot. Her cult had a priesthood of eunuchs, the Galli, and a young consort, Attis. Athens established a Metroon, her temple, in the early 5th century BCE; it served as the state archive.

Rome adopted her cult in 204 BCE, in the 14th year of the Second Punic War, after the Sibylline oracle was found to say that a foreign enemy could be driven from Italy if the Great Mother of Pessinos were brought to Rome. Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, held to be the best man in Rome, met the goddess at Ostia. Roman writers reinvented her as a Trojan goddess and so an ancestor of the Roman people through Aeneas.

Her Roman festival, the Megalesia, began on 4 April, the anniversary of her arrival, with plays on religious themes, and on 10 April her image was carried to the Circus Maximus, where chariot races were held in her honour. Dionysius of Halicarnassus noted that Roman citizens were forbidden to take part in the procession. Lucretius describes armed dancers, perfumed Galli waving knives, and the goddess in a lion-drawn chariot wearing a mural crown. Roman sources called the Galli a third gender, and their voluntary castration was thought to give them powers of prophecy.
cyclades: The Cyclades lie in the Aegean Sea south-east of the Greek mainland, bounded on the south by the Sea of Crete. The major islands include Amorgos, Andros, Delos, Ios, Kea, Milos, Mykonos, Naxos, Paros, Sifnos, Syros, Tinos and Thira, also called Santorini, and there are many minor islands, most of them uninhabited. Naxos is the largest island and Syros the most populated, with Ermoupoli as its chief town. The islands are the peaks of a submerged mountainous terrain, except for the two volcanic islands of Milos and Santorini. The climate is dry and mild, and apart from Naxos the soil is not very fertile.

A distinctive Neolithic culture that combined Anatolian and mainland Greek elements arose in the western Aegean before 4000 BCE. It lived on emmer and barley, sheep, goats, pigs and tuna that were apparently speared from small boats. Excavated sites include Chalandriani, Phylakopi, Skarkos, Saliagos and Kephala on Kea, with signs of copper working. Each small island could support no more than a few thousand people, yet models of boats show that fifty oarsmen could be assembled from the scattered communities.

Early Cycladic culture evolved in three phases between about 3300 and 2000 BCE, by which time it was increasingly swamped by the rising influence of Minoan Crete. It is best known for schematic, flat sculptures carved from the islands' pure white marble. When the palace culture of Crete arose, the islands faded into insignificance, except for Delos, which kept its reputation as a sanctuary throughout antiquity and until the emergence of Christianity.

The first excavations in the 1880s were made by antiquaries such as Theodore Bent, at Antiparos in 1884. Christos Tsountas investigated burial sites on several islands in 1898 and 1899 and coined the term Cycladic civilisation. Interest picked up in the mid-20th century, when collectors competed for figures that resembled the sculpture of Jean Arp and Constantin Brâncuși. Burials were looted and forgeries multiplied, so the context of many figurines has been mostly destroyed and their meaning may never be fully understood.
cyclone-nargis: Towards the end of April 2008 the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone over the Indian Ocean became very active, and a tropical disturbance developed on 25 April. The India Meteorological Department classified it as a depression on 27 April, and on 28 April it was upgraded to Cyclonic Storm Nargis, about 550 km east of Chennai. It was the first named storm of the 2008 North Indian Ocean cyclone season. Nargis first moved slowly northwest, weakened briefly in dry air on 29 April, then turned east and intensified rapidly. Indian authorities are reported to have warned Myanmar of the danger 48 hours before landfall.

Nargis made landfall in the Ayeyarwady Division on 2 May 2008 at peak intensity, with winds of at least 165 km/h by Indian observations and 215 km/h by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center, which rated it a weak Category 4 cyclone. It passed near Yangon and then weakened until it dissipated near the border with Thailand. The storm surge ran 40 kilometres up the densely populated Irrawaddy delta. The United Nations estimated that 1.5 million people were severely affected, and damage was put at 13 trillion kyat (US$15.3 billion).

Confirmed dead numbered 84,537 and 53,836 were missing, with 19,359 injured, giving a total of 138,373. Labutta Township alone was reported to have 80,000 dead and Bogale about 10,000. Critics of the military government argue that the figures were under-reported, and some aid workers and organisations estimated far higher tolls. The feared second wave of deaths from disease and lack of relief did not materialise.

Relief was slowed for political reasons. On 6 May the government asked the United Nations for help but remained resistant, preferring bilateral aid, and visas were the biggest obstacle for aid workers waiting in Thailand and at Yangon airport.

On 9 May it declared that it would accept food, medicines and money but not foreign aid workers or military units. The referendum on the constitution went ahead on 10 May, with voting postponed to 24 May in Yangon and the worst hit areas. More than two weeks after the storm, relief had reached only 25 percent of the people in need. The military government finally accepted aid a few days after India's offer was taken up.
Nargis is regarded as the deadliest named cyclone ever recorded. At the time it was also the costliest tropical cyclone in the North Indian Ocean, a record broken by Amphan in 2020.
cyprian: Cyprian was born into a rich pagan Roman African family of Carthage, of Berber descent. His original name was Thascius, and he added Caecilius in memory of the priest to whom he owed his conversion. Before it he was a leading member of a legal fraternity in Carthage, an orator and a teacher of rhetoric. After what is described as a dissipated youth he was baptised at the age of thirty-five, about 245, and gave away part of his wealth to the poor. His early writings follow closely the models of Tertullian, who influenced his style and thinking.

Soon after baptism he was ordained a deacon and then a priest. Some time between July 248 and April 249 he was elected bishop of Carthage, but senior clergy disapproved of his rapid rise. In early 250 the Decian persecution began, and Cyprian went into hiding. Some clergy saw cowardice in this; he replied that he had fled so as not to leave the faithful without a shepherd.

Many Christians fell away and were called the lapsi. Cyprian demanded public penance before readmission, but in his absence some priests readmitted the lapsed with little or none, and a schism followed. After fourteen months he returned, issued De lapsis and convoked a council of North African bishops in 251. He took a middle course between the followers of Novatus of Carthage, who would welcome all back, and Novatian of Rome, who would reconcile none of the lapsed. His devotion during a great plague and famine won him further support.

In late 256 a new persecution broke out under Emperor Valerian. Cyprian refused to sacrifice before the proconsul Aspasius Paternus in 257 and was banished to Curubis, now Korba. He was imprisoned on 13 September 258 on the orders of the proconsul Galerius Maximus, examined on 14 September, and answered his sentence of death by the sword with the words Thanks be to God. He was beheaded at once near the city, before a vast multitude.

His best-known treatise, De Ecclesiae Catholicae Unitate, was written during his absence from Carthage, and about sixty of his letters survive. Churches were built over his tomb and the place of his death and were later destroyed by the Vandals. The Catholic Church keeps his feast on 16 September, with that of Pope Cornelius, and the Eastern Orthodox Church on 31 August.
cyprus: Cyprus is the third largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia. It measures 240 kilometres from end to end and 100 kilometres at its widest, and lies 75 kilometres south of Turkey. Two mountain ranges, the Troodos Mountains and the smaller Kyrenia Range, enclose the central Mesaoria plain. The highest point is Mount Olympus, at 1,952 metres, in the Troodos range. Some sources place the island in Europe and others in Western Asia, within the Levant.

Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, at about the time the island's pygmy hippopotamus and dwarf elephant became extinct. Neolithic farming communities emerged by around 8500 BCE, and the village of Khirokitia dates to approximately 6800 BCE.

From around 1650 BCE copper from the Troodos Mountains drove trade and the growth of urban settlements, and the island, identified in whole or part as Alashiya, was ruled by kings who corresponded with the pharaohs of the New Kingdom of Egypt, as the Amarna letters document. Mycenaean Greeks traded there from around 1400 BCE, and a major wave of Greek settlement is believed to have followed the collapse of Mycenaean Greece.

Later the island was contested by the Assyrians, Egyptians and Persians, and Alexander the Great seized it in 333 BCE. Ptolemaic, Roman, Arab, Lusignan and Venetian rule followed, then Ottoman dominion from 1571 to 1878. Britain administered Cyprus from 1878 under the Cyprus Convention and annexed it formally in 1914. Independence came in 1960. Intercommunal violence in 1963 and 1964 displaced more than 25,000 Turkish Cypriots into enclaves.

A coup by Greek Cypriot nationalists and elements of the Greek military junta on 15 July 1974 was followed by the Turkish invasion of 20 July, which captured the north and displaced over 150,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots. A Turkish Cypriot state declared in 1983 is recognised only by Turkey. The island is divided along a United Nations buffer zone, and two British sovereign military bases, Akrotiri and Dhekelia, remain in the south.

The Republic of Cyprus, a presidential republic, joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro on 1 January 2008. Greek and Turkish Cypriots share many customs, such as the foods souvla and halloumi, but differ in religion: Greek Cypriots are traditionally Greek Orthodox and Turkish Cypriots Sunni Muslim.
cyrenaica: Cyrenaica rests on a mass of Miocene limestone that tilts up steeply from the Mediterranean. The Jebel Akhdar extends parallel to the coast from the Gulf of Sidra to the Gulf of Bomba and reaches 882 metres, with a Mediterranean climate, and the red soils of the Marj Plain have borne wheat and barley from ancient times. To the south and east the Sahara reaches the coast in the region known in antiquity as Marmarica. The coastal region was called the Pentapolis, or Five Cities, in antiquity.

Greeks began to colonise Cyrenaica in the seventh century BCE. Its first and most important colony, Cyrene, was established about 631 BCE by settlers from the island of Thera, who had left it because of a severe famine. The five cities were Cyrene with its port of Apollonia, Arsinoe, Euesperides, Balagrae and Barce. The region produced grain, olive oil, wine and wool, and silphium, a herb that grew only there. Cyrene became a great intellectual centre, home of the Cyrenaics founded by Aristippus and of the poet Callimachus. Persian forces under Cambyses II seized the Pentapolis in 525 BCE, and Ptolemy I annexed it. Ptolemy Apion, dying without heirs in 96 BCE, bequeathed it to the Roman Republic.

The name Cyrenaica dates to the first century BCE. It became a senatorial province in 20 BCE and was split in 293 under Diocletian into Libya Pentapolis and Libya Sicca. Muslim Arabs under Amr ibn al-As conquered the region about 642, and it became known as Barqah after Barce. In the middle of the 11th century Arab tribes including the Banu Hilal ravaged it, and up to 200,000 Hilalian families migrated into it from Egypt. It later fell under Ottoman Libya.

Cyrenaica is the eastern region of Libya, between the 16th and 25th meridians east. Italy occupied it during the Italo-Turkish War in 1911 and made it a colony in 1919, and on 1 January 1934 Tripolitania, Cyrenaica and Fezzan were united as Italian Libya. In 1949 Idris al-Senussi proclaimed the Emirate of Cyrenaica, which joined the Kingdom of Libya, independent from 24 December 1951, with Idris as king. The Senussi dynasty was overthrown on 1 September 1969.
cyril-and-methodius: The brothers were born in Thessalonica, then in the Byzantine province of the same name. Cyril was born Constantine and Methodius was born Michael; Cyril took his monastic name in Rome shortly before his death, and Methodius at the Polychron Monastery on Mysian Olympus. After their father, Leo, a droungarios, died, the minister Theoktistos became their protector. Cyril taught at the University of Magnaura, and about 860 Emperor Michael III and Patriarch Photius sent him on a mission to the Khazars. Their ethnic origins are unknown, and it is disputed whether they were of Slavic or Greek origin, or both.

In 862 Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia asked Michael III and Photius to send missionaries to his Slavic subjects. His motives were probably more political than religious, since he sought independence from the Franks. The emperor sent Cyril with Methodius, and in 863 they began translating the Gospels and essential liturgical books into what is now called Old Church Slavonic. For this they devised the Glagolitic script, the first alphabet used for Slavonic manuscripts. German clerics opposed a Slavic liturgy.

Pope Nicholas I invited the brothers to Rome in 867, and in 868 Pope Adrian II received them warmly and authorised the Slavic liturgy. Cyril became a monk and died in Rome on 14 February 869. Methodius was made Archbishop of Sirmium, but East Frankish bishops deposed him and held him prisoner for two and a half years, until Pope John VIII secured his release in 873. He was acquitted of heresy in 878 and allowed to use the Slavonic liturgy again.

Methodius died on 6 April 885. Wiching, a Swabian bishop, then suppressed the Slavonic liturgy and drove the disciples into exile. Clement of Ohrid and Naum found refuge in Bulgaria, where Boris I commissioned them to teach clergy in Slavonic and found schools at Ohrid and Preslav. The Cyrillic alphabet was developed by their disciples at Preslav at the end of the 9th century and gradually replaced Glagolitic.
Both brothers are venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church as equal to the apostles. Pope John Paul II named them co-patron saints of Europe in 1980, with Benedict of Nursia.
cyrus-cylinder: The Assyro-British archaeologist Hormuzd Rassam found the cylinder in March 1879 during excavations at Babylon for the British Museum. It had been placed as a foundation deposit in the foundations of the Ésagila, the city's main temple. Rassam worked under a decree, a firman, from the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II, which allowed him to send antiquities to England. 5 cm long and 10 cm across at its widest, built in layers round a cone-shaped clay core.

It was found in several pieces, having apparently broken in antiquity, and exists today in two main fragments, A and B, reunited in 1972. Fragment B was acquired by J. B. Nies of Yale University, who published its text in 1920, and was identified as part of the cylinder in 1970. The British Museum dates the cylinder to between 539 and 530 BCE.

The surviving inscription is 45 lines of Akkadian cuneiform in a formulaic style. It opens by reviling Nabonidus, the deposed Babylonian king, charging him with desecrating the gods' temples and imposing forced labour; as a result, it says, Marduk abandoned Babylon and sought a righteous king. He called Cyrus, king of Anshan, to rule. The text gives Cyrus's titles and genealogy and says that he entered Babylon in peace.

It commends his restoration of the city, includes a prayer to Marduk for Cyrus and his son Cambyses, and records that he returned displaced people and the images of gods to their sanctuaries and repaired the city wall. In the passage on the return of the gods' images and inhabitants, the places named are Mesopotamian sanctuaries, among them Susa, Agade and Der.

Biblical scholars have traditionally read the passage as evidence for the repatriation of the Jews that the Book of Ezra attributes to Cyrus. The text does not name the Jews, Jerusalem or Judea, and the reading is disputed. The British Museum describes the cylinder as part of a long Mesopotamian tradition of kings opening their reigns with declarations of reform, and scholars call it an instrument of propaganda that used local traditions to legitimise Cyrus's rule.

In 1967 and later, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi called it the first charter of human rights, and Iran displayed it in Tehran in 1971 at the celebration of 2,500 years of the Persian Empire. Most historians have judged that reading anachronistic, pointing to its conventional Mesopotamian form. The cylinder has been in the British Museum since 1900.
cyrus-the-great: Cyrus came from Persis. The Achaemenid dynasty took its name from Achaemenes, and Darius the Great traced his ancestry to him. Achaemenes was succeeded by Teispes, who took the title King of Anshan after seizing the city of Anshan, and Teispes had a son, Cyrus I. Cyrus II was born to Cambyses I, King of Anshan, and Mandane, daughter of Astyages, King of Media, in about 600-599 BCE. Herodotus gave a mythological account of his youth: Astyages, warned by dreams that his grandson would supplant him, ordered the child killed, but a shepherd raised him instead. When Cyrus succeeded his father in 559 BCE he still had to recognise Median overlordship.

Cyrus overthrew the Median Empire in about 550 BCE. He then conquered Lydia, after King Croesus had captured the city of Pteria in Cappadocia; the Battle of Pteria ended in a stalemate and Croesus withdrew to Sardis. The exact date of the Lydian conquest is unknown, and the once common date of 547 BCE is no longer widely held. Between about 545 and 540 BCE Cyrus campaigned in the east, where an attempt on Gedrosia failed but Bactria, Sogdia, Chorasmia and other provinces were taken. The Nabonidus Chronicle shows his title changing from King of Anshan to King of Persia.

By 540 BCE he had captured Elam and its capital, Susa. Shortly before October 539 BCE he fought the Battle of Opis on the Tigris, north of Babylon, and routed the army of the Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus. On 10 October Sippar was seized without a battle. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder in Akkadian cuneiform placed in the foundations of the Esagila, the temple of Marduk at Babylon, portrays Cyrus as pleasing to Marduk and describes how he repatriated displaced peoples and restored temples. The return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity has been read as part of this policy, and the Hebrew Bible honours him for it. He divided his empire among capitals at Pasargadae, Babylon, Susa and Ecbatana, governed through satraps.

Accounts of his death differ. Herodotus says he died in battle with the Massagetae, ruled by Queen Tomyris, while Ctesias places his death in fighting with the Derbices; Xenophon says he returned to Pasargadae. He was succeeded by his son Cambyses II. A limestone tomb at Pasargadae, built around 540-530 BCE, is believed by many to be his; Plutarch gives its epitaph as an address by Cyrus, who won the Persians their empire.

Greek writers noted his tolerance of the customs and religions of conquered peoples, and Xenophon says his subjects called him their Father. Pierre Briant holds that too little is known to reconstruct his own religion. Later Persian empires often looked on the Achaemenid era as an ideal to emulate.
cyrus-the-younger: Cyrus the Younger was an Achaemenid prince and general, the son of Darius II and Parysatis. According to Xenophon he was born after his father's accession in 424 BCE. He had an elder brother, Arsicas, who became Artaxerxes II, and two younger brothers, Ostanes and Oxathres. Plutarch describes him as headstrong and vehement from his earliest youth, in contrast to the gentler Artaxerxes, while Xenophon praises his modesty, horsemanship and skill with the bow and javelin. These three authors, with Ctesias, Thucydides and an account probably by Sophaenetus of Stymphalus, are the only early sources for his life.

In 408 BCE Darius II sent Cyrus to Asia Minor as satrap of Lydia and Phrygia Major with Cappadocia, and as commander of the Persian troops. He also received the title of karanos, which made him largely autonomous. There he met the Spartan general Lysander and put his resources at Lysander's disposal in the Peloponnesian War. Plutarch says that Parysatis favoured Cyrus and hoped to see him made king when Darius fell ill, but the eldest son was proclaimed king as Artaxerxes II. Soon after, Tissaphernes denounced a plan by Cyrus to assassinate his brother. Cyrus was captured, but Parysatis secured his pardon and he returned to his satrapy.

In spring 401 BCE he gathered a large army at Sardis, including the Greek force of Xenophon's Ten Thousand, without announcing its aim, and pretended to be preparing a campaign against the Pisidians. Sparta supported him with a fleet and a detachment of 700 men. Artaxerxes was warned only at the last moment by Tissaphernes and gathered an army in haste.

The Battle of Cunaxa was fought in October 401 BCE after Cyrus had advanced into Babylonia. He had 10,400 Greek hoplites, 2,500 peltasts and about 10,000 Asiatic troops under Ariaeus. According to Xenophon, Cyrus wanted the Greek commander Clearchus to take the centre against Artaxerxes, but Clearchus feared encirclement and stayed on the flank. Cyrus charged the king in the centre and was killed. Plutarch gives a different account of his death, in which a young soldier named Mithridates struck him down, and says that Parysatis later took vengeance on those responsible.

After their commanders were taken prisoner, the Greeks fought their way to the Black Sea, an episode Xenophon told in the Anabasis. Xenophon wrote that all who knew Cyrus well thought him the most worthy of kingship of anyone born since Cyrus the Great, and praised his keeping of every agreement.
czech-republic: The Czech Republic is a hilly, landlocked country of 78,871 square kilometres, bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland and Slovakia. It is traditionally divided into three lands: Bohemia in the west, Moravia in the east and Czech Silesia in the northeast. Bohemia is a basin drained by the Elbe and the Vltava, surrounded by low mountains such as the Giant Mountains, where Sněžka, at 1,603 metres, is the highest point in the country. Moravia is hilly and drained mainly by the Morava River.

Water from the country flows to three seas: the North Sea, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea. The Czech Republic also leases the Moldauhafen, a lot in the Hamburg Docks awarded to Czechoslovakia by Article 363 of the Treaty of Versailles; the territory reverts to Germany in 2028.

The area has been inhabited since the Paleolithic, and the Venus of Dolní Věstonice, dated to approximately 29,000 to 25,000 BCE, is considered the oldest known ceramic figurine in the world. After Celtic migrations in the 3rd century BCE, Bohemia became associated with the Boii. In the 7th century the Frankish merchant Samo became ruler of Samo's Empire, the first documented Slavic state in Central Europe. Great Moravia reached its zenith in the 9th century under Svatopluk I, and was Christianized with the Byzantine mission of Cyril and Methodius, who codified Old Church Slavonic and the Glagolitic script.

The Přemyslid dynasty unified the Duchy of Bohemia in the late 9th century. In the early 13th century Přemysl Ottokar I obtained the Golden Bull of Sicily from the emperor, confirming his and his descendants' royal status, and the duchy was raised to a kingdom. German immigrants settled in the periphery in the 13th century, and the Mongols, in their invasion of Europe, were defensively defeated at Olomouc after raiding Moravia.

The Czech Republic is a pluralist parliamentary democracy with a bicameral parliament: the 200-member Chamber of Deputies and the 81-member Senate. From 1993 to 2012 the president was chosen by parliament, and since 2013 by direct election.

In the 2021 census 57.3% of inhabitants were Czechs and 3.4% Moravians. About 75% to 79% of residents declare no religion. The Jewish population of Bohemia and Moravia, 118,000 in 1930, was nearly annihilated in the Holocaust.
czech-silesia: Czech Silesia has no formal boundaries. In a narrow geographic sense it covers most or all of the territory of the Czech Republic that lies in the drainage basin of the Oder. It lies in the north-east of the country, mainly in the Moravian-Silesian Region, with a section in the north of the Olomouc Region, and borders Moravia in the south, Poland in the north and Slovakia in the south-east. Ostrava stands roughly at its centre, and after it the most important towns are Opava and Český Těšín.

About two thirds of the territory lies in the Eastern Sudetes, and the rest reaches into the Ostrava Basin, the Moravian Gate and the western Western Beskids. Its main rivers are the Oder, the Opava and the Olza, which forms part of the natural border with Poland.

In the Middle Ages Silesia belonged to Piast-ruled Poland and in the 14th century passed gradually to the Kingdom of Bohemia. At the end of the First Silesian War in 1742 the rest of Silesia was ceded to Prussia, and the part that stayed within the Bohemian Crown and the Habsburg monarchy was reorganised as the Duchy of Upper and Lower Silesia, with its capital at Opava. In 1900 it covered 5,140 square kilometres and had 670,000 inhabitants.

In 1918 it became part of the new Czechoslovakia. Cieszyn Silesia was divided between Czechoslovakia and Poland in 1920, and the Hlučín Region, formerly Prussian, joined Czechoslovakia by the Treaty of Versailles.

After the Munich Agreement of 1938 most of the area was joined to the Reichsgau Sudetenland, and Poland occupied the Trans-Olza area for a time. During the German occupation Polish activists, priests and teachers were deported to concentration camps in 1939 and 1940, and the Germans ran forced labour camps and prisoner-of-war camps in the region.

Until 1945 most of Czech Silesia, apart from the districts around Cieszyn, Ostrava and Hlučín, was settled by German speakers. After the war the ethnic Germans were expelled under the Potsdam Agreement, and the border with Poland was set again along the Olza.

Most of the population speaks Czech with altered vowels. Some of the Slavic population speak Lach, which is classed as a dialect of Czech but resembles Polish in places, and in Cieszyn Silesia a separate Cieszyn Silesian dialect is spoken, mostly by the Polish minority. Together with Bohemia and Moravia, Czech Silesia is one of the three historical Czech lands. Its notable natives include the biologist Gregor Mendel, the politician Hans Kudlich and the astronomer Johann Palisa.
czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia was founded in October 1918 as one of the successor states of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. It was championed by nationalists and by its first two presidents, Tomáš Masaryk and Edvard Beneš, and its sovereignty was affirmed in the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye. Masaryk served as first president from 14 November 1918 to 14 December 1935. The state consisted of Bohemia, Moravia, part of Silesia, Slovakia and Carpathian Ruthenia, a region of present-day Ukraine, and its territory included some of the most industrialized regions of the former empire. The Bohemian Kingdom ceased to exist in 1918 when it was incorporated into the new country.

Between the two world wars Czechoslovakia was a democratic state with a generally literate population. Beneš, as foreign minister, was the prime architect of the Little Entente, a Czechoslovak-Romanian-Yugoslav alliance directed against Hungarian attempts to reclaim lost areas, and he worked closely with France. After 1933 the German element within the country allied itself with the Nazis. On 29 September 1938 Britain and France ceded control of the Sudetenland to Adolf Hitler at the Munich Conference, and France ignored its military alliance with Czechoslovakia. On 14 March 1939 the Slovak State was proclaimed, Hungary annexed the rest of Carpathian Ruthenia and the German Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia was proclaimed. Beneš formed a government-in-exile recognised by the Allies.

The state was re-established after the war, without Carpathian Ruthenia, which was annexed by the Soviet Union. Under the Beneš decrees the government confiscated the property of ethnic Germans and expelled about 90 percent of them, over 2 million people. The Communist Party seized power in a coup in 1948, and the country joined Comecon in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955. The Prague Spring of 1968 ended when the Soviet Union, assisted by other Warsaw Pact countries, invaded. The Velvet Revolution began on 17 November 1989, and on 28 November the top Communist leaders and the party itself resigned. Growing nationalist tensions later led parliament to dissolve the state peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

Before the Second World War the economy was among the strongest in industrial Europe, producing cars, trams, aircraft, ships, turbines and arms, with firms such as Škoda, Tatra and Baťa. The Slovak lands relied more heavily on agriculture than the Czech lands. After 1948 the economy was centrally planned along Soviet lines, and the Communist Party held a political monopoly, with the media under its control. Education was free and compulsory from ages 6 to 15, and the vast majority of the population was literate. The national football team reached the World Cup final in 1934 and 1962 and won the European championship in 1976.
czestochowa: Częstochowa lies on the Warta river in the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland. Although it is now in the Silesian Voivodeship, it is historically part of Lesser Poland, and before the Partition of Poland in 1795 it belonged to the Kraków Voivodeship. Its name means Częstoch's place and comes from a personal name found in medieval documents also as Częstobor and Częstomir. A Lusatian culture cemetery of about 750-550 BCE in the district of Raków is now an archaeological reserve with a museum.

Archaeology shows the first medieval settlement was founded in the late 11th century, in Piast-ruled Poland. It first appears in a document of 1220, in which Bishop Iwo Odrowąż of Kraków listed the properties of the Mstów monastery; two villages are named, Częstochowa and Częstochówka, the latter on the hill where the Jasna Góra Monastery was later built. The town prospered in the late 15th and early 16th centuries through the efforts of Sigismund I the Old, who often passed through on his way to the Duchy of Głogów. It received the right to collect tolls on the Warta bridge in 1504 and the right to hold one fair a year in 1508, raised to three in 1564 and six in 1639.

Prussia seized the city in 1793 in the Second Partition of Poland. It joined the Duchy of Warsaw in 1807 and Russian-controlled Congress Poland in 1815. In 1809 Austrians unsuccessfully besieged the monastery, and in 1813 the Russians took Jasna Góra after a two-week siege and razed its fortifications. Under German occupation in the First World War the city lost its Russian markets, and about 20,000 people left for Upper Silesia and other German provinces. In 1919-1921 it was a centre of support for the Silesian Uprisings.

Germany occupied Częstochowa on 3 September 1939 and incorporated it into the General Government. On 4 September, called Bloody Monday, German troops killed 227 people in the city, 205 Poles and 22 Jews; some estimates put the number above 1,000. After the war the steel mill was greatly expanded, and the city became an industrial and academic centre. It was the seat of its own voivodeship from 1975.

Częstochowa has 214,342 inhabitants, making it the thirteenth-largest city in Poland, and is the largest economic and cultural hub of the northern part of the Silesian Voivodeship. Millions of pilgrims come each year to see the Black Madonna at Jasna Góra Monastery. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic archdiocese. The steelworks, first established in 1896, remain among the largest in Poland.
